In addition to his Masonic and business activities he has given freely of

his time and thought to the civic and charitable interests of Los Angeles
and of the State of California.
Brother Gist was born in 1868 in Tompkinsville, Kentucky, and removed to Woodland, California, in 1875. In 1890, at Tulare, California,
he married Luella Hatch, who was his classmate in grammar and high
school; and of this union there are two living children: Past Master
Charles Wooster Gist, who was born in 1892, and Laura Velma, who was
born in 1897. His home life has been serene and happy.
Brother Gist is a scion of the notable Gist family of Maryland and
Virginia, of which Christopher Gist, the Ohio explorer, was an exponent
and was the eminent ancestor of the Gists in America. His son, Captain'
Richard Gist ( 1684-1741) was an outstanding figure in Maryland; while
a grandson, Major General Mordecai Gist, had a distinguished military
career and served with Washington throughout the Revolutionary War.
General Gist was made a Mason prior to the Revolution and was the first
Deputy Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of South Carolina and served
that Grand Lodge as Grand Master for two years.
James Black Gist was president of the society, Sons of the Revolution, in 1919, and has been governor of the society, Sons of Colonial
Wars. He is also a member of the California Club, the Wilshire Country
Club and the Los Angeles Athletic Club.
The foregoing record briefly indicates the successful and honorable
career of our Brother. It is a career which few men as young as he can
review with equal and justifiable pride. By his modesty, sincerity, unselfishness, industry and ability he has commanded the respect and admiration of all, and has engaged the affections and won the plaudits of the
thousands who know him best.
All in all, the fraternity can always point with pride to the life and
character of Jim Gist. Truly, when Jim was born "the morning stars sang
together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy."

DEVOTIONAL SERVICE
The V. ·. R. ·. Herbert P. Shaw, Grand Chaplain, conducted a short devotional service preceded by a solo by
Henry L. Perry.
Dr. Shaw spoke in part as follows :
"My son, f~rget not my law; but let thine heart keep my commandments:
"For length of days, and long life, and peace, shall they add to thee.
"Let not mercy and truth forsake thee: bind them about thy neck;
write them upon the table of thine heart:
"So shalt thou find favour and good understanding in the sight of
God and man.
"Trust in the Lord with all thine heart; and lean not upon thine own
understanding.
"In all thy ways acknowledge Him, and He shall direct thy paths."
(Proverbs 3 :1-6.)
Who comes here this morning, my Brethren? Men wl;io have passed
through these. portals, some a long time ago, some recently. Those are
here today who, by efficiency, by application, by being worthy and well
qual.ified, have been lifted above their fellows and have become leaders,
rulers, and Masters of the craft.
And the very fact that we are here, my Brethren, must bring us face
to face with the tremendous responsibilities resting upon men and Masons
today! In this hour of uncertainty; in this hour of need ; in t?is hour
when the hearts of men are looking toward the anchorages which have

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

9

held them across the years, Masonry cannot fail Masons; Masons cannot
fail humanity and the state; Masons must not fail God.
The mayor of San Francisco, in an address yesterday morning before
a group of churchmen, Catholic, Jewish and Protestant, meeting with
labor leaders attending this great-labor convention now being held in San
Francisco, said : "We are now reaping the harvest of greed and selfishness
of the 1928 prosperity era, when we forgot spiritual things during economic prosperity."
"We forgot spiritual things," said the mayor.
Fundamental to every walk of life, fundamental to every · life, are
those great, undergirding, everlasting principles which make for the
eternities.
And today, the conditions out yonder which face us, threaten our
institutions! The government itself is questioned, and the very Name of
God, the "All Seeing Eye," is being ridiculed and scoffed.
Proverbs 3 :1: "My son, forget not my law; but let thine heart keep
my commandments. Let not mercy and truth forsake ,thee : bind them
about thy neck; write them upon the table of thine heart." So cried the
wise man in his generation. So cries the prophet today.
When a belief, when a faith issues into an action, it cannot be shaken;
but "when a belief is not allowed to prove its worth in action, it is likely
to be destroyed by the first big storm which comes along," truly said Dr.
Ernest Fremont Tittle.
"To believe in God and not to act, is to lose one's capacity for belief,
and the price is skepticism. The cost of emotion unrelated is cynicism,
and the result of cynicism.is bitterness and despair."
How can a man believe in mercy, who with tears in his eyes talks
aeout the poor and unemployed, yet closes his bowels of compassion and
writes not his check for poverty?
How can a man believe in the truth of God, who never lifts his heart
in prayer and finds the reassuring presence of the D ivine?
"Therefore, life must seem hard, and cruel, and bitter to the man
who can never lift up his eyes unto the hills and believe with all his heart
in the reality and the power of God."
The "All Seeing Eye" is fundamental to Masonry, and who knowil
but that for a time like this that Name which alone compels a Master to
doff his hat within his Lodge; who knows, I say, but that Masonry united
·together with all of like and kindred faith shall be a bulwark to stem the
tide and storm of today I We shall find a God Who can be trusted. "We
shall find that love is not weakness, but power-the greatest power we
have-and we shall achieve a life which will bear witness of itself that it
is destined to go on after death."

God grant that Masonry will produce men; men for the needs of our
civilization; men who have conviction; men who are willing to do and
dare; men who have a vision of service and are not afraid to act. Great
men, good men; men whom the spoils of office cannot buy. Men who are
willing to give themselves to worthwhile tasks for the benefit of men and
Masons.
When Lord Nelson fought his great naval battle at Trafalgar, which
victory influenced all civilization, it is said that through the smoke and
storm of battle every British tar saw written across the Admiral's flag,
"England expects every man to do his duty." Today, my Brethren, we
face the destiny of our civilization, and methinks from the battlements
of heaven God unfurls the banner with the slogan, "God expects .every
man and Mason to do his duty."

On Friday, October 13, 1933, you honored me far beyond my
deserts by electing and installing me your Grand Master, the most
exalted Masonic station, and today, in accordance with the requirements of our Constitution, I herewith respectfully submit a report of
a portion of my activities and in some measure give an account of my
stewardship.

Telegrams were received from Past Grand Masters
Boynton and Wollenberg, now in China; from Francis V.
Keesling and William A. Sherman, now in Chicago; from
Stanley S. Chapman, Grand Commander, K. T., and from
Frank K. Ebbitt, our Representative near the Grand Lodge
of Canada in Ontario.
·

I have endeavored to meet as many groups of our Brethren as
has been convenient and possible, having due regard for the necessity
of protecting my health and business. It has been my earnest desire
to promote harmony in the craft and to restore strained fellowships
wherever and whenever I found those conditions existing in the
jurisdiction. It has been my sincere purpose to administer the duties
and obligations of a Grand Master in a dignified, fir~, fair but sympathetic manner, and to acquaint the craft with the affairs of our
gra·nd jurisdiction to the utmost of my mental capabilities.

Distinguished Visitor
M.". W.". Ezra M. Wilson, Grand Master of Masons in
Oregon, was introduced and received with the honors due
to his office.

MESSAGE OF GRAND MASTER
Brethren of the Grand Lodge:

We ;i.re meeting today in our eighty-fifth Annual Communication
which takes us back in ret;ospect to a time prior to the admission of
our beloved and glorious State as an integral part of the Union. Ours
is a history of progress and achievement, of which we may justly
feel proud.
Necrology
There's a land far away, 'mid the stars, we are told,
. Where they know not the sorrows of time,
Where the pure waters wander through .valleys of gold,
And life is a treasure sublime.
'Tis the land of our God, 'tis the home of the soul,
Where the ages of splendor eternally roll;
Where the way-weary traveler reaches his goal,
On the evergreen Mountains of Life.

-J. G. Clark.
Once again as we look back over the year just passed, we are
saddened by the ravages the Grim Reaper has made in our ranks.
We are reminded of the words of Solomon embodied in the ritual:
"Man that is born of a woman is of few days and full of trouble. He
cometh forth as a flower and is cut down; he fleeth also as a shadow,
an.cl continueth not." We will never again clasp the hand or enjoy

Conference of Grand Masters
Your Grand Master, as sole representative of the grand jurisdiction of California, attended the annual conference of Grand Masters
in the city of Washington, D. C., last February 24 and 25. Forty-one
grand jurisdictions were represented out of a total of forty-nine. After
being privileged to attend the last three sessions, it is difficult to
fully estimate the great value of these conferences. In many instances
the problems of the craft in New York and Alabama, of Kansas and
Maine, are very . similar to those in California. It is of great benefit
to meet, compare notes and to learn what is being done in other
jurisdictions. We thus can profit by the successes and the mistakes
of others. We must not overlook the opportunity to work out interjurisdictional relations..Perhaps no other grand jurisdiction contacts
as many other Grand Lodges as does California, for obvious reasons.
It is an excellent thing to meet our Brethren of the other states and
talk over the many interests we hold in common. Doubtless there will
never be a general Grand Lodge. Each Grand Lodge defends its
independence, sovereignty and integrity ·with almost fierce conviction
and determination, and such attitude is in harmony with immemorial
Masonic tradition. But some measure of practical co-operation among
the Grand Lodges must be promoted, and these annual conferences
of Grand Masters and Grand Secretaries seem to provide the way.
George Washington Masonic National Memorial Association
I represented the grand jurisdiction at the annual meeting of the
George Washington Masonic National Memorial Association at the
Memorial building in the city of Alexandria, on Washington's Birthday, February 22, 1934.
The Grand Lodge of California has a very substantial financial
interest in this worthy enterprise, and we are represented on the
Board of Directors by P. G. M. Albert E. ~oynton.
Slow but steady progress is being made toward the completion
of the interior of this national monument to Masonry. As you probably are aware, there are no debts and never will be, for the reason
that the Board of Directors make no contracts until money is in the

Visitations
One of the many joys of a year's experience as Grand Master has
been the visitations to Lodges and group meetings of the Brethren
in the inspection districts. The uniform courtesy, hospitality and inn_umerable acts of kindness and respect accorded the position of
Grand Master is greatly appreciated. It has been a distinct disappointment to have been unable to cover the jurisdiction more generally ;
nevertheless it has been my great pleasure and privilege to visit 72
inspectorial districts and thereby to contact 405 Lodges.
It is more apparent each year that it is impossible for the Grand
Master to respond to more than a comparatively few of the great
number of requests for personal appearances. Permit me to again call
your attention to the .three executive divisions of this jurisdiction
established by Grand Master Robert B. Gaylord and supervised by
the Deputy Grand Master and the Senior and Junior Grand Wardens,
and the _availability of any of these line officers to represent the
Grand Master when it is impossible or inconvenient for him to r espond. You can relieve the Grand Master very materially by utilizing
the services of these Brethren.
Hawaiian Islands
Following the custom of many of my predecessors, I spent nineteen days in June visiting the eight Lodges and the Brethren on the
Islands of Oahu, Kauai, Maui and Hawaii. It was most interesting
and delightful experience. The hospitality of the Island people is traditional and justly celebrated. Mrs. Gist and I were the recipients of
many courtesies every day of our stay. I was very busy every moment
of my visit. I met a large number of our 1800 members, and also
many sojourning Brothers from all parts of the world. In one instance at Schofield Lodge, twenty-eight grand jurisdictions were represented. I was impressed with the universality of Masonry as never
before.
My experience has convinced me and confirmed my preconceived
opinion that the annual official visit of the Grand Master to the
Island Empire is very beneficial to the craft. It is practically the only
contact the m embers have with the Grand Lodge, and their appreciation is earnestly evidenced in many ways. When circumstances
have prevented a Grand Master from making the trip, their disappointment has been outspoken. I respectfully recommend the continuance
of these visits to my successors whenever it can conveniently be
arranged. It is well worth the time, effort and cost, I am sure.

Reduction of Fees
Many Lodges this year have requested permission to reduce the
fees for the degrees. I question the wisdom of this practice· and
believe the trend is in the wrong direction, but I also recognize the
fact that the individual Lodge is the final authority in the settlement
of this policy.
Reduction of Due's
I regret to note that a large number of Lodges are 'requesting
the consent of the Grand Master to reduce their dues instead of
building up a comfortable reserve. Of course, the Lodge should be the
best judge as to whether it' can afford to live on a reduced income
and at the same time maintain a safe financial condition to enable i~
to meet any possible future requirements, and particularly relief
obligations.

GRAND LODGE . OF CALIFORNIA

. 15

Delinquent Dues
Continuous, consistent and intelligent effort on the part of small
committees, I am sure, will produce satisfactory results. In the matter
of delinquent dues, it should be followed up every month in the year
in a friendly and frater'n-al but persistent campaign. It has been
·reported to me this year that in a number of instances it has been
discovered that the delinquent member was paying his dues in socalled "higher Masonic organizations" and to social clubs, but apparently felt justified in permitting his Lodge dues to go delinquent.
Such action, of course, cannot be excused. A Brother not in good
standing in his Blue Lodge should not be permitted to visit other
Masonic bodies.
Unemployment
The unemployment situation among our Brethren is still acute.
Splendid results have been accomplished by various agencies, including Lodge committees and employment bureaus. Desiring to encourage and stimulate increased effort along this line, I issued the
following bulletin, of date April 23, 1934:

To the Masters and Brethren of the Constituent Lodges
of this Jurisdiction :
It appears to be necessary and important that I again call your
attention, as has been done by the last three Grand Masters, to the
vital problem of unemployment among our Brethren, and urge your
co-operation in a united endeavor to alleviate in some measure the
present conditions, which are serious.
We must face the facts. Every Lodge should ascertain who and
how many of its members need employment. Classify them as to
occupations and organize job-finding machinery which will function
and get positive results. The opportunity is here for service. Ask
yourself this question: Am I my brother's keeper? The Masonic
answer is, "Yes, you are."
Today's challenge, then, to our fraternity is to make a practicable
application of the following principles:
The duty we owe to God,
The loyalty we owe to our country, and the
Fellowship we owe to our neighbor and our brother.
Some of the Lodges have appointed a Committee on Employment, whose duty it is to contact all members of their Lodge who
are employers and to urge them to notify the committee immediately
when any employees are needed. The Employment Committee also
makes a survey of the membership to ascertain who are unemployed,
what their qualifications are, and the nature of their experience, to
enable them to place these Brothers in positions which they are
qualified to fill. I recommend that each Lodge should have such a
committee.
The Lodges in the larger communities should also support the
collective efforts of their Brethren as represented in the Masonic
Employment Service. This agency supplements the services of the
Lodge on behalf of its members, but the primary responsibility is
that of the Lodge. Continue the support of that organization, but

also utilize the resources of your own Lodge. It is a well established
fact that a fraternal employment service is not to be confined to the
simple conduct of a labor agency. Through its fraternal resources it
must seek to meet the employment problems of the individual in a
fraternal manner. In addition to this, it must be constructive in its
aim and service. A survey of the -immediate and continued needs will
impress upon every member of the fraternity the importance of building up the value and usefulness of the Masonic Employment Service.
This is absolutely necessary if we are to meet in a real fraternal spirit
the many and increasing demands that face us now and will continue
to confront us. Through the tireless efforts of the Masonic Employment Service we secure a member of the craft a position, and in doing
this we not only assist our Brother, but we also help his Lodge.
The responsibility is yours. If your members do not obtain work,
whom do they call on for relief? It is up to you, and it is far more
desirable to get a man a job than it is to give him relief.
The question, therefore, of vital importance is not what has been
done, but what can be done to be of wider and more effective usefulness in these days. Let us all co-operate in this important task.
Fraternally yours,
JAMES B. GrsT, Gra.nd Master.

Mr. Leon 0. Whitsell,

Dear Brother Whitsell:
I have received your request that as Grand Master I authorize
the publication of the work of the History Committee of Grand
Lodge under the title of "History of Masonry in California." For
many years your committee has labored assiduously and zealously in
the collection and assembling of historical material and I deem it
appropriate that the results of your work be made available to the
Masons of California and such others as may be interested.
The history of Masonry in California is a long and honorable
one. From the early pioneer days of hardships and romance to the
present era of hundreds of Lodges and tens of thousands of members
it has reflected the accomplishment of the people of this State and
its contributions to benevolence, humanity and civilization have been
noteworthy. The volumes proposed to be published will set forth in
an orderly manner the facts of this long career, which should be made
known to our members.
I hereby sanction the proposal of the History Committee to
arrange for the publication of a History of Masonry in California.
Yours fraternally,

Life Membership Funds
Life membership funds should be carefully handled, as they
are sacred trust funds and should never under any circumstances be
commingled with any other money. The principal should not be used
for any purpose whatsoever except for income-bearing investments
legal for savings banks under the laws of California and the Territory
of Hawaii, as amended by Grand Lodge at the eighty-second annual
communication October, 1931. This is a matter of serious responsibility for each Master affected to accept and handle. I am simply
calling your attention to this v.e ry important matter at this time as
a precautionary measure.

Masonic Education
Possibly the term "Masonic Education" is unfortunate. To so
many of the Brethren the suggestion that they are to be educated
awakens a certain prejudice and at times a real hostility, yet it must
be obvious that Grand Lodge has no desire to force instruction or
information upon unwilling pupils. Perhaps some · day some wise
Brother will evolve or invent a term that will be free from unpleasant
implications, but meanwhile we m ust use fo~ want of a better designation the term "Masonic Education."
Throughout the Masonic world there is a realization that the true
Mason is the intelligent Mason, the well-informed Mason, the instructed Mason. First of all he should be well versed in the ritual,
be able to pass a creditable examination in the lectures of the degrees.
He should be able to recount in approved language the experiences
through which he passed when he received the degrees of Masonry.
This is the foundation of all Masonic education. But merely to be
able to repeat, parrot-wise, certain set phrases and answers is of
little value. The question arises, " Does he know what they mean?"
The degrees may be likened to an inexpressibly valuable and
b~autiful jewel placed in a perfect setting. That setting or framework,
or background, consists of the moral teachings of the fraternity, its
symbolism, its history, its traditions, its jurisprudence. The Mason
who truly appreciates the privilege that is his in being initiated into
the craft will not be content merely to admire the jewel in a casual
and half-hearted way; he will want to know something of this background, this tradition, or, dropping the simile, he will want to know
what Freemasonry means. The bright, alert, curious young candidate
is usualiy anxious to know, to learn, to explore. But alas, too often
we pour cold water on his enthusiasm, rebuff his questions and discourage his curiosity. This is a mistake.
There are inexhaustible depths in ·F reemasonry and an abiding
inspiration for th6se who will search out the deeper meanings. I sincerely hope ways and means may be found to make Masonic education attractive, interesting and profitable. T he older, as well as the
younger, Masons will find it well worth while.
Masonic Clubhouses
One of the most interesting, and, I believe, profitable activities
of Grand Lodge is the maintenance of the Masonic Clubhouse at

20

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Berkeley and the one at Los Angeles. These institutions are maintained for the benefit of the young people from Masonic families attending the University. Here the young folks find opportunities for
social relaxation, for study and service.
The one at Berkeley was the first of our ventures in the way
of administering to the students of Masonic affiliation. The institution
from its inception a number of years ago has occupied a very prominent place in the student life on the campus. Three presidents-Dr.
Campbell, Dr. Barrows and _Dr. Sproul-have given hearty and unsparing commendation to the strong influence of the Masonic Club
on · the students of the university. The clubhouses have given to
thousands of young men and women from our Masonic families
throughout the State something they could not otherwise have enjoyed, that social contact under the direction of wise and experienced
counselors supplied through the members of the Board of Trustees,
the hostess, the members of the faculty of Masonic affiliation, and
membership of Lodges adjacent to the clubhouses. These clu.bhouses
have now become almost as established an institution as the university itself.
An estimate recently made at Berkeley by the management, after
a comparison of estimates of those in charge of the various activities,
permits the conservative and authentic statement that an average of
125 students used the clubhouse each day during the regular sessions.
There has recently been brought about a merger of the three men's
organizations functioning at the clubhouse into one. The result has
been helpful. The Women's Masonic Club continues to be an outstanding organization on the campus, and probably its most prominent activity is the Women's Masonic Glee Club, composed of a
large number of students with excellent voices and training. On
Wednesday afternoons there is held what is called an "Informal,"
devoted to social contacts of the young people. These meetings are
usually attended by about four hundred students. Each Sunday afternoon a "Fireside" is held at which helpful addresses and discussions
are offered by members of the faculty and other prominent men and
women of the Bay area.
·
Not all of the activities of the students using the clubhouses are
devoted to sociability. The Women's Club maintains a small loan
fund which has been of great benefit to many of the club members.
During the last semester one of the y~ung men of the club was
compelled to undergo an expensive operation at the infirmary. The
club members furnished the necessary funds. Each year the students
present to the clubhouse a handsome present of useful character.
Recently the students made a sort of declaration of benefits received
from the club, which is as follows:

"The young people (using the clubhouse) feel ~hat the b~nefit
they receive from social contacts and development m leadership at
the clubhouse is comparable to the academic work on the campus."

has occupied that responsible position for a number of years, and

"I feel from years of observation t~at the Universi.ty of c;alifornia Masonic Club House fills a most important place m the hves

exemplification of Masonic charity.
Finally, bringing the students of Masonic affiliation together at
our Club Houses and providing ways and means whereby their
university life may be enriched and made more effective, is a work
certainly well worth while.
Decisions

Decision No. I: Donation of Lodge Funds to Masonic Homes Endowment Fund. Donation of Board of Relief Funds to Masonic Homes
Endowment Fuiid.
During the month of May different Lodges inquired if it is permissible for a Masonic Lodge to donate funds of the Lodge to the
Endowment Fund of the Masonic Homes. (The same question has
been asked regarding funds of Boards of Relief.)
I held that it is not permissible under Sections 88 and 89 of the
Constitution, providing for the disposition of Lodge funds. (Nor is
it permissible for a Board of Relief to dispose of any of its funds in
this manner.) The effort this month on the part of the Endowment
Committee is simply an opportunity for voluntary contribution for
this very worthy purpose on th~ part of the individual members of
the Lodge.

Decision No. 2: Donation of Lodge Funds for Expense of Conducting Public Schools Week Celebration.
Requests were made by different Lodges for a ruling on the
question of whether the funds of a Lodge can be used to defray expenses in sponsoring Public Schools Week programs.

I here report my ruling:
It is my opinion that Section 88 of the Constitution does not
warrant such expenditure. I am further of the opinion that such. expenditures from the refreshment fund are fully authorized and justified, inasmuch as ·it is an activity directed by Grand Lodge itself, and
while it may be said to be a departure from th.e general plan of
Masonry, neverthe.less as long as Grand Lodge encourages it the
Lodges should be permitted to use a portion of their entertainment
funds for necessary expenditures in connection therewith.
Under Section 89 of the Constitution the refreshment fund can
be used for the "promotion of fraternal intercourse." In the language
of Grand Master Bledsoe, "the promotion of fraternal intercourse is
a very comprehensive expression, and as long as a subordinate Lodge
in good faith uses the social fund to such end as the general interest
and increased activity of the work of the .order is promoted, it is my
belief that the ·s upervisory powers of the Grand Lodge should be held
in restraint."
It appears to me that the same line of reasoning would apply to
the present question as to the circumstances under consideration
when the above opinion was uttered. It is therefore my ruling that
it is permissible for a constituent Lodge to use a portion of its entertainment fund for the purposes above referred to.
Decision No .. 3: Expense of Presenting Trowels to Candidates.
I held that the expense of procuring trowels to be presented to
candidates in the ceremony of conferring the degrees was proper, but
must be defrayed out of the refreshment fund.

Decision No. 5: How Often Can Charity Be Dispensed to Same Recipient in a month?
I was asked how many times during the month between stated
meetings charity may be dispensed to ~he same recipient in excess
of the sum stipulated in the by-laws; and if the Charity Committee
does have the authority to dispense to the same recipient as frequently as it chooses, whether it then becomes necessary for the
Lodge to approve such action.
This involves the interpretation of Article X, Section 1 of the
Uniform Code of By-laws wherein the Charity Committee is given
power to draw upon the Treasurer for any sum "not exceeding" the
sum specified-in this case twenty dollars "at any one time."
It seems to me that it is clearly the intent of this by-law to
restrict the payment of twenty dollars to one individual to one payment per month. How.e ver, if under certain circumstances it appeared necessary to make more than one payment I presume the
Lodge would approve; but in any event, all payments of charity
should be reported at the next stated meeting of the Lodge for its
action, as to approval or disapproval. Splitting a sum greater than
twenty dollars into installments in an attempt to appear to comply
with the wording of the by-law is clearly a subterfuge and a flagrant
violation of Masonic law.
Decision No. 6: Divorced Wife Asking for Relief.
A Master of one of our Lodges asked a ruling in the following
case:
The divorced wife of · one of our members, at present in good
standing, has been left destitute with three minor children, aged sixteen, eight and three. The oldest boy is earning ten dollars a week,
which is the sole support of the family. Until recently the father has
contributed to their support, but he has now left the State and since
then has contributed nothing.
The wife appealed to the Master for assistance and a small
amount was given, pending the action of the Lodge at its next stated
meeting.
My ruling was, as follows:
"Our Constitution (Sec. 163) limits those who · have a right to
ask for and receive relief from the Lodge of which a Master Mason
is a member. During the life-time of such Master Mason he is the
only,.one wh.o has a right to ask f?r or receive relief from his Lodge.
Facts, ~f any there are, showing such Master Mason to be guilty
of unmasomc conduct, should be brought to the attention of the
J_unior .Warden of h_is Lodge. (See Const., Sec. 189, and Digest sections cited thereunder.) Whether or not he is entitled to remain in

24

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

good standing, and whether or not he is in distress, are facts that
your Lodge should determine promptly. Even though unworthy, until
suspended or expelled, he remains technically in good standing. So
long as he so remains technically in good standing he has a right to
ask for and receive relief from his Lodge during such periods as he
may be in distress. If in distress, and in good standing, this assistance
may be rendered by the Lodge through relief extended to a dependent
relative. The divorced wife is no longer a dependent relative.
"The determination of the question: whether such relief should
be rendered, may be through investigation by the Lodge without the
request of the brother. The action of the Charity Committee of your
Lodge (Art. X, Sec. 1, Uniform Code), or your action on your own
initiative, in granting relief to his dependents, prior to investigation
by the Lodge, should not be subject to legitimate criticism. Full investigation should proceed, however. If it be found that he is in distress and unable to aid his minor children, the Lodge should assist
them during his period of distress. If he is unworthy, the period oi
this assistance should be reduced by his trial and suspension or expulsion."

Decision No. 7: Incumbent Treasurer Must Be Installed.
I held that under Section 135 of the Constitution an incumbent
Treasurer must be installed as soon as practicable after his re-election.
Decision No. 8: Objection Made Before Initiation.
The Master of a Lodge asked a ruling on the following problem:
A petition for the degrees was presented to .a Lodge. Before it
was received formally a member called on the Master and registered
an objection, volunteering in detail his objection, and agreed with the
Master that investigation should be made by both the objector and
the Master. Each investigated the story leading to the objection, and
each agreed that the objection was not good, the objector withdrawing his objection. The committee on investigation made a full and
favorable report in due time, and the petitioner was elected. Before
the Lodge closed, the objector again interposed an objection, giving
the same reasons as theretofore. Query: Does Section 111 apply
here; that is, can the same objection be made a second time? The
objector was present at the meeting at which petitioner was elected.
I replied that Section 111 applies only when an objection is made
after initiation. One who has been made a Mason occupies an entirely
different position from one not yet initiated. He is entitled to certain
rights and privileges, including the right to be advanced in the absence of sufficient cause to the contrary.
Section 108 of the Constitution applies when the objection is
before initiation. Whether or not there is cause for such objection
is immaterial so far as its effect under Section 108 is concerned. As
interpreted by the Jurisprudence Committee (Proceedings 1879,
p. 168; D_igest 353) : "It is sufficient if the Master is advised by the
brother objecting that he does object."

Decision No. 9: Physical Insufficiency.
Some Lodges have apparently wilfully ignored our law as to
physical qualifications of candidates and have received petitions from
applicants for the degrees that the officers must have known were
physically insufficient.
Magnolia Lodge No. 242 received the petition for degrees of a
candidate who had been rejected by that Lodge in 1931 because the
loss of a foot made it impossible for him to conform to what the
several degrees required of him. The Master, stating the above facts
and also that he was familiar with our Constitution and Decisions
relative to physica.1 qualifications of candidates, persisted by asking
a ruling from the Grand Master on facts that he admitted made the
candidate ineligible.
Antioch Lodge No. 175 admitted such a candidate. I wrote the
Master the following letter:
"My attention has been called to the fact that there has been
raised in your Lodge a brother who was physically insufficient, in
that his right hand was off.
"I call your attention to Section 94 of the Constitution and a
decision in the Digest No. 247, on p. 251. This decision was made
by Past Grand Master Ross and supported by the Jurisprudence
Committee and adopted by the Grand Lodge. I call your attention
particularly to the language: 'It is, however, the question of fact of
the physical insufficiency of the candidate that is to be determined
and not the question as to whether or not the Lodge is willing to
admit him in spite of the fact that he is physically insufficient. The
latter misconception of the law is found among many of the Lodges
and has led to admission of applicants physically insufficient. I have
'held that the fact for the Lodge to determine is whether or not the
applicant is physically able to conform substantially to what the
several degrees require of him without the aid of an artificial hand
or leg.'
"In cases of this kind the important matter is whether the candidate can conform or not conform to the requirements. In this particular case he undoubtedly could not conform. Therefore, it is my
opinion that your Lodge has committed a flagrant violation of the
law and you are warned at this time that should another violation
occur your Lodge will be disciplined. I would be inclined to take
measures to punish your Lodge at this time were it not for the
possibility of misunderstanding which seems to be somewhat prevalent throughout the jurisdiction. Therefore I am giving you the
benefit of the doubt as to your good faith in admitting this candidate."
This matter is so important, so fundamental, that it must be
admitted that a Lodge which wilfully admits a man in spite of the
fact that he is physically insufficient is incompetent to hold its
charter; and that a Master who permits it is unworthy to continue
in his office. I therefore recommend that it is the sense of this Grand
Lodge that if such a case occurs again, both the Lodge and the
Master should be disciplined.

Decision No. IO: Withdrawal of Petition.
I have advised that in cases of ineligibility for want of proper
qualification the withdrawal of the application as provided for in
Section 104 of the Constitution is more courteous and . friendly than
to reject the candidate by a · negative ballot. I have held that when
a Master is aware that a candidate is ineligible for want of proper
physical qualifications it is not necessary to ballot upon the application. It is the duty of the Master to direct the withdrawal of
the application and return the fee to the candidate without further
action.
Decision No. I I: Liquor.
Many questions were asked relative to liquor. My decisions were all
in accord with the following bulletin:
"San Francisco, November 28, 1933.

"I am in almost daily receipt of letters from Masters of Lodges,
making inquiry in the event that the 18th Amendment to the Constitution of the United States shall be declared repealed-and in all

'Sec. 129A. No Lodge shall receive an application for the

including membership in any Lodge.'

unnecessary, in view of the fact that under .the law of the land there

of conducting a bona fide hotel or restaurant.

Decision No. 12: Lodge Funds Can Be Used to Purchase Masonic
History of California.
I was asked: Is it a proper expenditure of Lodge Funds for the
Lodge to subscribe for a set of the History of Masonry in California,
the same to be for the use and benefit of the members of the Lodge?
My answer was: After reading Section 88 of the Constitution
and Decision 431 and 431A in the Digest, made by Grand Masters
Bledsoe, Ross and Wollenberg, my decision is that, in my opinion,
there is no question but that a Lodge can spend its funds for the
purchase of books and maintenance of a library for the benefit of its
members.

Decision No. 13: Relief for Family of Deceased Brother Not Member For Three-Year Period.
Application had been made to the Masonic Homes of California
by one of our Lodges for relief of the chil!ren of one of its deceased
members who had not been a Master Mason for three years prior to
his decease. Under the rules of the Masonic Homes, as approved by
this Grand Lodge, children of a deceased member who had not been
a Master Mason for a period of three years prior to his decease, are
not eligible to admission. Relief having been necessarily denied by
the Trustees of the Masonic Homes, application for financial assistance was then made direct to the Grand Master on the ground that
the resources of the Lodge were insufficient for the relief of these
children.
I held that under our system of relief in California, assistance is
rendered directly by the Lodge (Const., Sec. 90) and " Must be determined by the resources of the Lodge and need for assistance by
other members of the Lodge." (Digest, 437a.) Inasmuch as Grand
Lodge has no system for furnishing funds to supplement the resources of the Lodge for the relief of its dependents, I refused to
authorize the expenditure of Grand Lodge funds for such purpose.
Decision No. 14: Suspension of Indigent Member for Non-Paymmt
of Dues.
It appears that on August 3, 1934, a Brother was on the roll of a
Lodge as a member in good standing; that said Brother was then delinquent in his dues since January 1, 1933; that at your stated meeting on
August 3; 1934, the Secretary duly notified said Brother "that unless at
the next stated meeting" (September 7, 1934) "either your dues be paid,
or sickness or inability to pay be shown as the canse of such refusal or
neglect, you will be suspended from all the rights and privileges of Masonry."
Replying to this notice in a letter addressed to the Master, dated
August 18, 1934, the Brother stated:

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

29

"I can only repeat what you already know, my inability to find
work wherewith to pay my dues, and again request Covenant Lodge
for extension of time to December 31, 1934. I have· been promised a
SERA work order for my services in our unemployed co-operative
unit No. 29. ... If I am fortunate enough to receive a work order
I can then pay in full."
To this letter the Master replied on August 27, 1934, as follows:
"Since receiving your letter of August. 18 requesting an extension
until December 31, 1934, for payment of your arrear dues, I wish to
state that _after considering your case from every angle, I still see no
. reason why the request should be granted. Therefore, please be advised that unless your dues are brought to date by the September
stated meeting there will be no alternative from suspension on that
date."
The Master carried out this ultimatum at the stated meeting on September 7, 1934, and declared him to be suspended for non-payment of
delinquent dues from July 1, 1933, to June 30, 1934.

It is my decision that declaration of the Master is void and of no
effect, and that the Brother is in good standing in the Lodge. The Brother
had shown that inability to pay was the cause of his neglect to pay his
dues, and until the Master had reported this showing to the Lodge and it
had refused to remit the Brother's dues or grant him further time for
their payment, the Master had no jurisdiction to declare him suspended.
Regulation 442 of the Digest is particularly applicable to this case.

If true, as stated by the Brother, that he was unable to pay dues for
the year from July 1, 1933, to June 30, 1934, due to the fact that during
that period he was simply receiving provisions and food from the co-operative unit and that all his savings had been used up, it would ·be the duty of
the Lodge to issue him a receipt for dues to date, charging the same to the
Lodge. This should be done whether he requests it or not; otherwise, his
dues will accumulate and be still more impossible for him to pay.

· Public Schools Week in April
No other institution in our country surpasses in importance the
public school system, nor is any more intimately associated with our.
daily lives and our future well-being. It is the mold and the fashioner of the lives and character of our children. Its establishment
and maintenance has long been distinctly and outstandingly an American institution, in harmony with the principles upon which our
nation was founded, and it is pre-eminently in accord with the principles of Freemasonry. Masonry in America has ever been alert to
its needs and active in its support. None .may gainsay the marvelous
achievements of our public schools under a constantly progressing
development. They are the priceless heritage, the strong bulwark of
a free people, established by the state and maintained by public funds.
Their financial structure and practical operation are subject to the
control of legally constituted representatives. The funds are supplied
by the P.e ople, the instruction and guidance of our youth are committed to the teachers and administrators. Even though these
agencies discharge their functions fully, is this enough? Will not
much be lost unless there be complete cooperation between the home
and the school? Will not also much be lost unless there be enlightened interest on the part of all others in our communities, those who
are actively in charge of the schools, our legislators, and the parents
of our school children?
The demands of the present day are such that it is difficult in an
individual, solitary way to keep ourselves informed about many things
that vitally concern us. It was for the purpose of keeping the general
public informed and-interested in the work, the problems and achievements of the schools, that Public Schools Week was first conceived
by P. G. M. Chas: Albert Adams and is now observed annually each
April in California. During this period attention is focused · upon the
schools in every community in the State. It has become entirely a
civic event, welcomed by the people generally and by the school
people especially. Through prosperous and adverse conditions it has
served as a means of bringing into closer relationship all connected
with or inte.rested in the training of our youth. During the last few
years of unparalleled distress, it is well there has been kept before
our people the necessity of preserving from destruction or serious impairment our great system of public education, and no means is more
potent than the exhibition of their work and the friendly interchange
of ideas brought about by this public observance.

PROCLAMATION
FIFTEENTH ANNUAL OBSERVANCE PUBLIC
SCHOOLS WEEK

To the Masters, Wardens and Brethren of the Several Lodges of This
Jurisdiction:
The week beginning with the fourth Monday in April of each
year is Public Schools Week in California. MONDAY, APRIL 23,
1934, marks the opening of the Fifteenth Annual Observance.
The crisis in public education to which attention was called by
my predecessor in his proclamation last year still confronts us.
United States Commissioner of Education, George F. Zook, has expressed the belief that this year more than at any time in our recent
history the quality, and even the existence, of the schools in many
communities is at stake; and that we are in the grip of a social difficulty from which we shall extricate ourselves only with great effort
and pain.
·
Everywhere throughout the country generally not only in the
rural areas, but as well 1n the cities, where schools have not been
closed the terms have been shortened, classes have been increased in
size and some of the most valuable educational opportunities have
been materially restricted.
The situation prevailing in some of the rural districts is tragic.
For lack of funds almost 2000 rural schools failed to open last fall.
There are approximately 18,000 which will remain open for not more
than six months; and of these there are 700 in which the school term
will not exceed three months. As a result of this situation there are
over a million children in the rural communities who this year are
either being entirely denied educational opportunities or are grievously
handicapped by reason of the greatly shortened school term.
In California, while some educational opportunities have been
discontinued or materially curtailed, we have thus far escaped the
disastrous situation elsewhere prevailing. There can be no question
that this is due to the widespread interest of our people resulting from
the knowledge they have of the aims, purposes and achievements of
their public schools; and there is no movement better calculated to
maintain ·that interest than the annual observance of Public Schools
Week, when parents and the public are afforded an opportunity of
obtaining first hand information with respect to their local schools.
It is therefore my request and direction :
1. That Public Schools Week, commencing this year on Monday, the 23rd day of April, 1934, be observed by all our Lodges
according to custom:
2. That no "work" be done in any Lodge on the night on which
there is any gathering for the observance of Public Schools Week in

A Downtown School
A notable observance last year included what was called "A
Downtown School.''. Arrangements were made for the use, rent free,
of a large building which happened to be vacant; and ten classes
ranging from grades one to six were held here-each for a half day.
Two classrooms were set up in the front of the building next to the
windows facing the sidewalk-one for upper, and one for lower,
grades. These classes were taught alternately; one class meeting in
the morning and the other in the afternoon.

will acquaint themselves with this particular work and visit the two

Masonic Home Survey by Outside Agency
At the last communication of Grand Lodge a recommendation of
the Finance Committee was adopted, authorizing the Grand Master
to employ some .recognized qualified agency to make a survey of the
Homes. On investigation it became apparent that both Homes could

36

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

not be properly surveyed by one agency, owing to the dissimilarity
of their types of work. It appeared that the organization best quaiified to survey the Covina Home was the Child Welfare League of
America of New York City, and I accordingly employed them for
that purpose.
They sent as their representative Mr. H. W. Hopkirk, who has
visited and studied more than 250 children's institutions in this country, and consequently has a wide knowledge in that field. He spent a
week at the Covina Home. His report, covering forty-seven typewritten pages, touches every phase of the Home's set-up and operation. He summarizes his findings in the following words:
"It has been shown in this report that for the most part the work
of the Masonic Children's Home is on a high level. It is not luxurious, but it is good enough to meet the principal needs of most of the
children. There is need for continuation and in some cases extension
of some services. The additional workers needed for these purposes
will add a little to the budget, but will add much more to the improvement of services which the children need.
"The principal items in the budget have 'b een scrutinized to ascertain where reductions might be made. There is. evidence of economie.s
already practiced. Any further substantial reduction of the budget
would mean an unfortunate impairment of the standards of good
service."
I am aware that the primary thought in the minds of those who
suggested this survey was the hope of discovering means by which
a. material reduction of expenses could be effected. From that standpoint the survey was not productive of the result hoped, for.. I am of
the opinion, however, that it was well worth while. It brought forth
convincing evidence that your Trustees throughout the years have
used careful thought and good judgment in their management, and
have already gone as far in effecting economies as can b.e done
without materially reducing the service we are rendering to our dependent wards. The report contains a number of constructive suggestions for improvement in carrying on the Home. It mus.t b.e said
that most of these are things which the Trustees have already had
in mind, but which they have not felt justified in adopting on account
of the added expense which would be entailed. It states that the two
principal items of expense, food and salaries, are about what may be
'e xpected in a well-managed institution. It points out that the hours
of duty per week exacted from those immediately in charge of children are more than they should be. The Trustees have long known
that to be true, but have not felt justified under present conditions in
adding to the number of employees.
A majority of the recommendations made would, if adopted, lead
to increase rather than reduction of expense. All of the recommendations are referred to the Trustees for their careful consideration, with ·
full confidence that they will give due weight to all conditions before
increasing the cost of operation.

37

In view of the outcome of the survey of the Covina Home I felt
there was doubt of the advisability of going ahead and incurring the
expense of a similar survey of the Decoto Home. It has been under
the management of the same Trustees as the Covina Home and it
seemed fair to assume that its management has not been less efficient.
If Grand Lodge still desires such a survey made the same can be
indicated at the present communication.

Boards of Relief
The fifteen Boards of Relief are working harmoniously with one
anoth.e r and with the Board of Control and performing a wonderful,
humanitarian service to sojourning brothers in their respective localities. I want to pay a tribute to the brothers who direct the various
boards and handle their affairs. Their duties have been particularly
arduous and difficult during these unhappy days of stress and strain:
They have been called upon to grapple with an increased and increasing volume of distress calls, with a diminished and diminishing
source of supply. They have met the obligations with devotion, selfsacrifice and efficiency and are to be warmly commended not only for
their practical effectiveness, but for the tact and sympathy with which
they have done their work. After all, the dispensing of charity, or, as
we are pleased to call it, relief, the getting of employment and the
rendering of material aid, supremely important though they be, are
only part, and possibly the least important part of their work. Kindly
advice, hearty encouragement and the imparting of moral and spiritual strength when hope has flown and the morale is broken down,
are more necessary than dollars and cents. This significant service is
being rendered to discouraged brethren every day in the Boards of
Relief. There is where you see Masonry in action.
Inspectors
The Grand Master is fortunate indeed in having the generous
support and assistance of the splendid group of devoted, self-sacrificing and qualified inspectors. We appreciate more than ever that
the easy and efficient functioning of the craft in all its activities depends upon the Inspectors. It is impossible for the Grand Master to
maintain his supervision over the individual Lodges, and this responsibility devolves upon the Inspectors. As I have traveled over the
State I have been gratified by the beautiful, fraternal spirit prevailing
in the relations between the various Inspectors and the Lodges in
their care. Usually a real affection exists between the Inspectors and
the Masters. The Inspector is indeed the Big Brother, maintaining a
watchful, yet kindly eye, over the Lodges, quick to detect shortcoming in the ritual or procedure, earnest in holding high standards of
performance, but generous and sympathetic in spirit, always ready
to commend good work and earnest service, and constantly available
for counsel and assistance. Too frequently the Inspector is neglected
and unappreciated and very often made a target of criticism and complaint, but the high position held by the fraternity and the harmony
and good feeling prevailing throughout the jurisdiction are due in no
small measure to the special work of our Inspectors. T hey are of invaluable assistance to tlie Grand Master and deserve the cooperation
of all the brethren.

District Officers Association

"You will recall Grand Master Gaylord divided the State into
three Executive Districts, thereby removing the responsibility of supervising ceremonies, visitafrons, etc., from one man to four : the Grand
Master, Deput:,• Gmnd Master and the Senior and Junior Grand Wardens.
"In line with this policy, and in the interest of economy and
efficiency, it has been decided to appoint a Grand Lecturer, without
salary, and a Deputy in each of the three Executive Districts above
referred to, who will also serve without pay, to teach the ritual to
Inspectors only, and they, in turn, to the officers . of the Lodges of
their respective districts. Thus the Inspector will be the final" authority on ritual in his i;listrict.
"The Chairman of the Ritual Committee, Past Grand Master
Dana R. Weller, himself a Past Inspector and a very efficient ritualist, will have direct charge of this work and methods of operation
through the Grand Lecturer and the three Deputies. He will be the
final authority on all misunderstood or disputed questions relating to
the ritual. I have accordingly appointed Grand Lecturer, Brother
Foster G. Dyer, Inspector of the 4Sth District, in San Francisco. He
will have supervision over thirty Inspection Districts, twenty-eight in
the vicinity of San Francisco, and two in the Hawaiian Islands, the
latter to be contacted during Grand Lodge week annually: Inspection
District Numbers 29 to 48, Sl to S4a, 102, 103 and 113 to llS.
In Executive District No. 1, twenty-seven fqspection Districts.
Brother Leslie E. Wood, Inspector of the 22nd District in Sacramento: Numbers 1 to 26 and SO.
In Executive District No. 2, eighteen Inspection Districts.
Brother Past Inspector Chest-el' H. Warlow in Fresno: Numbers
27, 28, 49 and SS to 69.
In Executive District No. 3, forty-three Inspection Districts:
Brother Sidney K. Lehman, Inspector of the 72nd District in Los
Angeles: Numbers 70 to 101, 104 to 112 and 116 and 117.
"We confidently expect the whole-hearted coop era ti on of the
Grand Lecturer and Deputies and the Inspectors and Lodge Officers,
and if we have this we cannot fail. Should the experiment prove
satisfactory, proper legislation will be presented at the next communication of Grand Lodge to make the plan permanent.
Fraternal!_y yours,
JAMES B. GrsT, Grand Master."

A particularly valuable phase of our Grand Lodge activity is our
District Officers Meetings held monthly in the Iospection Districts
un<ler the direction of the Inspector. This is a practical educational
s-yS'tem for .the preparation of officers for the positions ahead of _them.
The efficiency of this plan has been demonstrated over a per10d of
years, and I u.nqualifiedly recommend its continuance, and request
the cooperation of all members concerned.
Thes.e associations are no longer an experiment. As a result of
the success that has attended this activity in recent years, it has
definitely taken its place as a vital and integral part of our institution.
This monthly meeting of officers of the district has a positive educational value and is i~ a real sense the school of instruction, so that
when the Master is installed he is fairly well versed in Masonk law
and procedure. It also provides an opportunity for the officers to
talk over their common problems and benefit by one another's experiences. Not the least advantage is the feeling developed ·by such
association of the oneness of the fraternity. Any association that
brings the officers of the Lodges together as such and creates this
spirit of comradeship .and mutual service is well worth w·hi!e.
New Ritual Plan
The sudden death of Brother Thomas J. Baker, our Grand Lecture;, December 27 last, presented a problem for solution as to
whether we should continue as heretofore or change our system of
ritual instruction. After a great deal of consultation and careful consideration, and in the interest of economy and .efficiency, it was decided t-0 try a new plan, viz., a Grand Lecturer and three assistants
or deptlt·ies. T'his new method £.or teaching the r itual has now been
in opemtiGn five months and the results will be fully reported by both
the chairman of the Ritual Committee and the Grand Lecturer. Following is a copy of the Grand Master's circular letter on this new
plan effective May l, 1934:
"NEW METHOD FOR TEACHING THE RITUAL. EFFECTIVE MAY 1, 1934

Baker, the subject of how best to perpetuate t_he te~ching of .the ritual
has occupied the serious and d,eliberate cons1derat10fl of your Grand
Lodge Officers and associate Masonic leaders.
"We have agreed u,pon .a plan which is sim_Ple ai:id worthy of a
fair and impar.tial trial by all concerned and .which will save at least
$6000 annually to Grand Lodge, an impo~t~nt item we cannot afford
to ignore, particularly under present cond1t1ons.

Appreciation
I am very happy to avail myself of this opportunity to express
my sincere appreciation for the uniform kindly cooperation of the
brethren all over the jurisdiction, and particularly the Past Grand
Masters and line officers, the Deputy Grand Master and the Senior
and Junior Grand Wardens. The Grand Secretary has been a tower
of strength in many ways. He has been a wise counsellor, philosopher and guide, and has relieved the Grand Master of many exacting
details. The Grand Lecturei:, and the three Dep.uties, together with
the Inspectors, have been of invaluable assistance to the Grand
Master in relieving him of a portion of the responsibilities of his
position.

. 42

Conclusion
In bringing my message to a close I must express regret at my
inability to have made a more beneficial impression upon the craft
for the good of Masonry in general.
This year has been a marvelous exp.e rience in renewing old
friendships among the brethren and making many new ones all over
this wonderful jurisdiction.
I have been a member of this Grand Lodge for twenty-nine
years. It has honored me many. times and I acknowledge my grateful
appreciation. It has a very warm place in my heart and I wish for it
and my successors in office the fullest measure of usefulness and successful achievement.
Finally I bid you farewell as Grand Master.
"May the blessing of Heaven rest upon us and all regular Masons!
May brotherly love prevail, and every moral and social virtue cement
us!"
Most cordially and fraternally,
JAMES B. GrsT, Gralld Master.

October 9, 1934.

REPORT OF GRAND SECRETARY
To the M: ·

w: · Grand Lodge of California:

In presenting this, my twenty-seventh annual report for the
fiscal year ended July 31, 1934, a falling off of membership is again
shown by unusually large numbers of suspensions and loss of revenue
also by remissions of dues. · The suspensions would indicate that the
Lodges are stronger in fact by the lopping off of members who were
not at any time imbued with th.e true spirit of Masonry, and that we
are now getting to a point where we represent a unity of purpose and
a keen desire to exemplify "a sincere wish to be serviceable" to our
fellows and to the community at large. The many members whose
dues were remitted also indicates clearly that the spirit of helpfulness
is much alive, and that the paying members are cheerfully carrying
on the rolls all worthy brethren who .are in distress.

Unpaid Grand Lodge Dues
Last year twenty Lodges were unable to pay their dues to Grand
Lodge, and fifteen Lodges made partial payments, the total sum of
unpaid dues amounting to $13,843.55. On the recommendation of the

44

Finance Committee, the dues of five Lodges were remitted, and the
thirty other delinquent Lodges were requested to execute notes payable in six months, to cover the amounts due. Twenty-five of these
notes, aggregating $12,835.17, have been paid.
This year nineteen Lodges have failed in whole or in part to
pay Grand Lodge dues, the total arrearages being less than $3,000.00.

Fifty-Year Tokens

By order of the Grand Master, a duplicate of the charter of
Mount Diablo Lodge No. 448 was issued, the original having been lost.

T·here appear to be more veteran Masons in our Lodges than in
any other jurisdiction, indicating clearly-what we all know-that
California climate is indeed an aid to long life. In the year past, 101
fifty-year buttons have been issued, making a total of 992 since 1929.
The oldest veteran reported this last year was Benjamin Allen Price,
who was made a Master Mason in Eel River Lodge No. 147, May
12, 1876, and affiliated with Hartley Lodge No. 199 :in 1908, of which

In accordance with your authorization, we have completed an
audit of the books of account of the Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of
California for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1934. We submit herewith the following financial statements :

Exhibit B: Grand Secretary's Report of Cash Received for the
Account" of Masonic Homes.
Exhibit C: Grand Treasurer's Report of Cash Receipts and Disbursements-General Fund.

31, 1934.
The scope of our examination included a verification of total
cash funds received during the fiscal year ended July 31, 1934, from
annual returns for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1933. Funds received
and on hand at the date of our audit, from annual returns for the
fiscal year 1934, were not included in our examination. Total receipts
due from subordinate Lodges as per individual annual returns on

AFTERNOON SESSION
Tuesday, October 9, 1934.
Grand Lodge was called on at 2 o'clock, the Grand Master presiding.
REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:

Obedient to the requirements of our Constitution, I herewith submit
my report as Grand Lecturer, with certain observations for your consideration.
In my report to the Grand Lodge, it might not be inappropriate to
say that I appreciate the high honor which has come to me by appointment
to serve as Grand Lecturer for the unexpired term of our beloved Brother,
Thomas John Baker. Brother Baker served this Grand Lodge with all
that he had for more than a quarter of a century. He had more friends
than any other in the jurisdiction. He loved those friends and they loved
him. Those of us who knew him best loved him most. He was so much a
part of the Grand Lodge that it is difficult to realize that he is gonegone Home, where the Keeper of the Pearly Gates will find a seat for
him on the Golden Throne. Not dead to us who loved him ; not lost, but
gone before. He lives with us in memory and will forevermore.
During the past five months, beginning May 1st, I have acted as
Grand Lecturer with direct supervision over the Inspectors of the San
Francisco Executive District and the Deputies in the Los Angeles, Fresno,
and Sacramento Executive Districts.
At the suggestion of the Grand Master, the chairman of the Ritual
Committee, Past Grand Master Dana Weller, the Deputy Grand Lecturers
Sidney K. Lehman, Chester Warlow and Leslie R. Wood, ·and the Grand
Lecturer met in the Grand Lodge office on April 28 and 29, for the purpose of agreeing upon the wording and interpretation of the ritual, and
the methods of application of the new ritual plan. We were together two
full days and had many interesting discussions on the ritual and the new
plan as given us by the ·Grand Master. A number of corrections and interpretations of the ritual were agreed upon and have been given to the
Inspectors, and through them to the Lodges. These suggestions as to corrections and interpretation have all been well received by Inspectors and
officers· of the Lodges. The Deputy Grand Lecturers have contacted all
of the Inspectors in their districts, and report that they have had excellent

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

59

co-operation on the part of the Inspectors in the promotion of the new
ritual plan.
The report on the present plan of teaching the ritual with relation to
the Grand Lecturer will be presented to Grand Lodge by the chairman of
the Ritual Committee. Because of my position as Grand Lecturer, I refrain
from any comment here.
I have counseled and advised with the Inspectors of the San Francisco Executive District singly and in groups, and held lodges of instruction for the Inspectors.
. At the invitation of Inspectors, I have attended district meetings in
an advisory capacity.
The Forty-fifth Inspection District, over which I have presided for
many years, has held officers' meetings monthly. I have attended these
meetings and carried on the duties of Inspector as heretofore.
At the invitation of various Lodges and officer groups, it has been
a pleasure to address them on Masonic subjects. When on missions such
as this, while in districts other than the one over which I preside as Inspector, I have carefully avoided discussing ritual. Under the new plan,
this is the province of the Inspector, the Grand Lecturer contacting Inspectors only on matters pertaining to that subject.
In the interest of economy, I have refrained from any unnecessary
traveling, this as agreed upon with the Grand Master. Many invitations to
meet with and address the Brethren have been declined, with economy in
view.

Officers' Associations
The officers' associations have been very successful in a great majority of the districts.
In sections where these meetings have been held regularly, the officers
and Inspectors have shown a sincere interest in Masonry, and real progress is being made in the development and the training of the Brethren in
the administrative as well as the ritualistic work of the Lodges. The
Inspectors are to be highly commended for their efforts in behalf of these
group meetings, the object of which is the development of more proficient
officers and better Lodges. It seems almost unnecessary to sound a note of
warning. The discussion of controversial subjects should not be permitted
in these meetings for the same reasons that they are not permitted in the
Lodges.
In remote sections of the State, the Inspectors report that the district
meetings of officers are not practical because of the great distance between
Lodges and the condition of the roads in the mountain districts. There
are thirteen of these districts, nearly all of which are situated in the
northern part of the State.
There is so much to be gained by the interchange of visits between
the officers of the Lodges and discussion of their problems that I offer the
suggestion that the Inspectors in the remote districts endeavor to bring

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

60

61

PROCEEDI NGS OF THE

the officers into joint meetings at least two or three times a year. The
result to be obtained will be worth the effort.
Too many Masters of Lodges are elevated to that important position
with little or no knowledge of their executive duties or the fundamentals
of procedure which are so necessary for the proper government of their
Lodges. This condition is gradually being improved by the free discussion
of the everyday Lodge problems in the officers' associations, and it is
well to urge the junior officers to enter into these discussions in order
that they may be prepared for advancement. The form of the examinations
for Masters and Wardens should and no doubt will be revised to include
hypothetical questions setting forth the various Lodge problems with which
the Master may be confronted from time to time. And when the Master
has answered these practical problems, he will be better prepared to
administer the affairs of his Lodge.
Ritual
I should like to emphasize the statement that the ritual is a very
important part of Masonry, and those thousands of officers and more than
a hundred Inspectors throughout the jurisdiction of California who are
teaching and endeavoring to perfect themselves in the rendition of the
esoteric work are to he commended highly for their intense interest and
attachment to this activity.
Too many members treat the efforts of these Brethren lightly. Take
the ritual away from Masonry and you have but an empty shell. The
ritual is not the last goal in Masonry, but it is a very important fairway
along which Masons may travel in search of perfection.
Condition of Lodges
The reports of the Inspectors i:ndicate that the Lodges throughout
the jurisdiction are functioning .in a wholesome manner.
The ·great majority of these have had very few or no petitions, and
with the absence of degree work, the officers and members have had more
time for fellowship. Many of the Lodges have made a real effort to supply
iriteresting entertainment and social gatherings on meeting nights when
there are no degrees.
Others have improved their meetings by discussion of educational
subjects, not only Masonic, but also social and economic questions being
presented by competent and informed civic workers, who are generally
members of the craft.
To quote in part from one of the reports: "We are suffering frcm
not drawing the practical application of our Masonic principles into the
affairs of our communities, our states and our nation. Where ultraconservative organizations are siding in the solution of vital social and
economic problems, Masonry, wh1ch has a liberal background in principle
and profession, remains dormant and inactive, and ~s consequently losing
its influence in m;my communities. The discussion of social and econcmic

problems does not, of course, involve taking a position on economic questions, nor committing Masonry to any particular position, nor introducing
controversial subjects, but it may have a pure and effective educational
influem:e upon the members of the craft which would bring them back
into the Lodges for enlightenment."
One of the greatest problems facing the Lodges is the collection of
dues. In most cases, the Inspectors report that committees are doing yeoman service in this most important work. The efforts of these Brethren
will be reflected in the financial report as made to Grand Lodge.
It is gfatifying to n~te in many of the reports the splendid work of ·
the Lodges in caring for their needy and distressed members, and looking
after employment. Too much praise cannot be given to those Brethren
who have given so liberally of their time, effort and influence in this most
important work.
Summing up the information contained in the reports of the Inspectors in a general way, the interest of the officers in their Lodges, and
their attention to duty is commendable. The general condition of the
Lodges reflects improvement throughout the jurisdiction.
Inspectori>
Through the evolution of circumstances and requirements, the importance of the office of Inspector has been greatly enhanced in recent
years. We cannot overestimate the services performed by an efficient and
attentive Inspector.
The Constitution says that an Inspector is an important officer of ·
Grand Lodge.
The question is often asked : What is the Inspector supposed to do
other than teach the ritual to the officers? What are his powers? It is not
so in;iportant to know what his powers are as it is to know what his duties
are. The Inspector is the local representative of the Grand Lodge, in
charge of the Lodges in his district. He is the representative of the Grand
Master, the Grand Lecturer, and the Grand Secretary, and in their absence
he should counsel and advise with the officers of the Lodges in his district coocerning the administration of the law as laid down in the Con~
stitution, and its application to the operation of the Lodges. He should
· also instruct, qualify, and supervise the officers in the per_formance of
their Lodge duties and in the rendition of the ritual.
In order that the Inspector may be more effective in his district, I
suggest that consideration be given to a i>!an whereby requests for decisions or rulings by the Grand Master be made through the Inspector of
the district, and the decisions or rulings be given to the Lodges through
the Inspectors. Under this plan, all important communications between
Grand Lodge and the constit1:1ent Lodges would be carried on through
the Inspector, and in cases where this is not practical, the Inspector should
be furnished with copies of the correspondence.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The Inspector is an important officer of Grand Lodge, and business
of · importance should be transmitted through him to and from the Lodges.
The foregoing will prevent such embarrassment as occurred several
years ago, when a Master was removed from office by the Grand Master
for cause, and several weeks later the Inspector learned of the incident
through one of the junior officers of the Lodge.
In another case, an executive officer resigned, an election was authorized, and installation date arranged, without consulting or advising the
Inspector until he was requested to qualify the advancing officers.
The Inspector should be informed concerning all matters of business
which are transacted in the district over which he has jurisdiction.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MESSAGE OF
GRAND MASTER

62

To the Ins~ectors I extend my sincere thanks for their wholehearted
co-operation and assistance which has been so freely given to the Grand
Lecturer in his efforts to carry on the duties of his office.
The Deputy Grand Lecturers Leslie R. Wood of Sacramento, Chester
Warlow of Fresno, and Sidney K. Lehman of Los Angeles have given
freely of their time and talents in the discharge of their duties as assistants to the Grand Lecturer. Their co-operation and support is sincerely
appreciated.
To the chairman of the · Ritual Committee,' Past Grand Master
Dana R. Weller, I offer acknowledgments for his counsel and advice. He
is to be commended for his active interest in the affairs of Grand Lodge.
To the Most Worshipful James Black Gist, Grand Master, I offer
· special acknowledgment for the confidence which he expressed in selecting
· me as a member of his official family. His graciousness and tact in directing the affairs of Grand Lodge have endeared him to all of us. I shall
cherish his friendship for all time.
In conclusion, may I say that Masonry is an instrumentality for good
in every community where it exists, and there is more reason for its
existence today than ever before in its history.
"More potent today than at any period of the world's history are the
instrumentalities for good. Let each Craftsman realize his responsibility,
his high privilege, in these earnest days, of bearing some humble part in
working out the great designs that look to the purification, the uplifting
of mankind. With such aids, such · inspiration, the· world wiJI, with the
rolling years, grow better ... the sum of human happiness will be increased. Truly, the future is resplendent with hope. Out of the shadow of
night, the world moves into light; it is daybreak everywhere."
Respectfully submitted,
FosTER G. DYER, Grand Lecturer.

Referred to the following committee: Oakley K. Morton,
Arthur E. Overton, Wesley W. Kergan.

To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
The committee to which the message of the Grand Master was referred begs leave to make its report.
The message of the M.". W.'. Grand Master, delivered to us this
morning, recounts his activities during the past year and gives a detailed
report of his stewardship, hut, necessarily, we must look between the lines
to see the hours and days of strenuous labor for the good of our beloved
fraternity. It cannot but inspire us to strive the harder that the tenets of
Freemasonry may become a part of our everyday life and conduct.
For more than thirty years our Grand Master has been a member of
this Grand Lodge and has taken an active part in its deliberations and
has assisted in directing its activities and shaping its policies. For more
than fifteen years our Grand Master has rendered invaluable service to
the fraternity as a member of the Board of Trustees of our Masonic
Homes. With this background and this experience, it is little wonder that
his year as Grand Master has been filled with hwnan interest and true
Masonic understanding.
His monthly messages have been a source of inspiration and encouragement, and have made us realize more than ever in these days of depression, when communism, atheism, and other kindred forces are striving to
tear down and destroy, that the principles of Masonry are not dead, but
must be relied upon more than ever to maintain the true spirit of brotherhood and to maintain and protect our national government.
