To the M.". W.". Grand Lodge of California:
The committee to which was referred the report of the Very W orshipful Grand Secretary, begs leave to make its report.
The Grand Secretary has presented his twenty-seventh annual report
to this Grand Lodge. We congratulate him upon passing another milestone
in Masonic service. In passing the milestone he has made many new
friends both in and out of this jurisdiction. The Grand Lodge is very
fortunate in having our efficient Grand Secretary on the job at a time
like the present, when it becomes necessary to cut expenses at every
corner.
He again reports a loss in membership. We are very sure that the
Lodges have not suspended any worthy member; and, therefore, we
agree with the Grand Secretary when he states :
"The suspensions would indicate that the Lodges are stronger,
in fact, by the lopping off of members who were not at any time
imbued with the true spirit of Masonry."
We believe that the greater the number of delinquents, the more
necessary it is that we have strong committees on delinquents. Dues are
payable quarterly in advance ; and if this is impressed upon the membership and upon the Committee on Delinquents, and the delinquent members
referred to the committee promptly, we believe that the Lodges will have
fewer suspensions and will be able to collect their accounts receivable in
a much more satisfactory manner.

ANNUAL ORATION
Most Worshipful Grand Master,
Officers and Members of the Grand Lodge:
The beginnings of Freemasonry are lost in the dim vistas of
antiquity. An ancient tradition links our venerable institution with
the Dionysian Artificers, that marvelous fraternity of architects and
artisans that flourished in the centuries preceding the Christian era
and left the enduring memorials of their splendid achievements in
the massive temples and magnificent stadiums of Asia Minor, (1)
and with the Roman Collegia, that heroic order of builders who in the
glamorous period of Rome's sky-ranging grandeur constructed cities,
raised monuments and erected public works whose proportions and
symmetry awaken our admiration and astonishment even today
when we can view them only in ruins. (2) But for our purposes we
need not go so far afield.
The earliest Masonic records extant are made up of soaring
spires and flying buttresses, of ornamented rose windows and delica~ely carved pillars. I allude, of course, to those supreme creations
of human genius, the glorious cathedrals of Europe. "These grand
cathedrals rose, one by one, out of the fervent heart of the time and
by the well-taught head and hand. So when they touched a stone,
it blossomed into beauty, and where they laid it, there it stayed.
They never made a false line and never carved an ugly thing, except
by" pure intention." (3) Goethe called these cathedrals "frozen
music."
Through the centuries we trace the history of Masonry. In one
age it builds miraculous cathedrals. In another age it lays aside the
apron and the trowel and assumes the sword in valiant warfare for
liberty of thought and freedom of conscience. In still another it
formulates a priceless ritual through which it instructs the neophyte
in the age-old truths of philosophy and morals. Again it battles for
free education.
. As Masons we are proud of our history. And justly so. Nor do
we forget that the past was the matrix of the present, even as tomorrow lies expectant in the womb of today. We may appropriate and
apply the senfentious words of Dean Inge: "Believe me, the only
promise of a better future for our country is to be looked for fro.m
those to whom her past is dear." ( 4) So with the light of the past
shining upon us we gaze into the future.
Disconcerting Statistics.
The future of Masonry! Ah, that thought gives us pause! Has
Freemasonry a future? There are those, critics speaking exultantly,
and devoted adherents speaking sorrowfully, who point out that the

68

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

craft is suffering a serious decline in membership. In 1931 the total
membership of the fraternity in the United States was 3,287,153. In
1934 the membership totals 2,910,273. A loss in three years of 376,980;
nearly 12 per cent. -(5) What greater proof do you need, ask our
enemies, that Freemasonry has reached its apogee and is now in
process of rapid disintegration? That the imperial page~nt passe~ and
moves to a drab, inglorious end? And the figures are d1sconcertmguntil we remember that the pessimism rests on an error, the obvious
fallacy being the belief that membership statistics are a true test of
the vitality of the Masonic institution.
I do not wish to speak unkindly or disparagingly of those who in
the stressful years just past have left us, nor do I w ish to underestimate any significance there may be in their going, but I do assert
that when men -d rop their m embership in a Masonic Lodge because
they are unwilling to make the sacrifice necessary to pay their dues
the craft is stronger for every such man who leaves it. We have constitutional ways of taking care of the unfortunate Brother who, -h aving
fallen upon evil days, must ask the indulgence of his Brethren in the
matter of dues ; butrhen a man is not willing to give up a package
of cigarettes a week lo keep himself in good standing in his Lodge, it
is proof apparent that he never really belonged.
Let us face our own responsibility frankly. Let us place the blame
where it belongs. A sardonic wit has said that the present t1me is
notable for three passings-the passing of the buffalo, the passing of
the Indian, an d the passing of the buck. Let us not maK:e that error.
The fact is, during the days of h ectic prospedty we were so "hypnotized with the fascination of our rapidly mounting membership figures
that we fai led in the first and last and most important care of a Lodge
of Masons when convened-to see the Lodge duly tiled-and vast
numbers slipped through the carelessly g uarded doors who never
should have been given admitta nce. Now they are teaving us, a11d we
wish them Godspeed. They never were -duly and "trttly prepa:red, t'hey
never learned the true password. It .is -a purging that our fraternity
sorely needed.
Hear me I The strength of Freemasonry is not found in the number of its members, in its wealth, nor in its prestige. Our ritual alludes
to the pestilence that fell_ upon Israel because David numbered the
people. ( 6) Go back with me to the second degree and rehea rse once
more the significant story of Gideon. (7) We Americans are especially prone to fall into the error of thinking in terms of numbers,
statistics; tables.
[t is a perversion of values to measure the Masonic fraternity by
membership tables. Mere quantity _is a dangerous yardstick. There
are more bacilli in a putrefying ca rcass than there are men in a great
city. A billion m ay be less than one if you are comparing beetles
with the brain of a n Einstein. The re is only one thing in life worth

GRAN D LODGE OF CALI FO RNIA

69

measuring, and that is quality ; and quality can be appraised, but it
cannot be measured. You can weigh beef and count .g arbage cans, but
mother love and patriotism and human genius and religion defy your
measuring rods and your chemical retorts, because they are spiritual
qualities.
·Strength of Masonry
The strength of Freemasonry lies in its spiritual possessions: its
teachings, its symbolism, its venerable history, its ancient tradition,
and above all, in the character of its members.
This is o ne reason why you cannot reduce Freemasonry to a
formula or confine its free spirit within the limits of a definition. In
m y libra ry I have a folder with many definitions of Freemasonry :
some are eloquent, some are bizarre, some are unique, so me are
ingenious, some are challenging, but I have yet to fi nd a definition
that is adequate. The best, the most comprehensive, leaves something
unsaid. Masonry being in essence spiritual, it cannot be defined, it can
only be characterized. You search the Scriptures in vain for a definition of Deity, but the writer of the letter that bears the name of
St. John gives us a perfect characterization : God is love (8)-and we
feel that is adequate and in it we have received a revelation of the
F ather.
So grasping the great universal symbols we are enabled to characterize Freemasonry and obtain an understanding of its genius, its
inner power, its essential nature; determine whether or not its vitality
is spent; and from that vantage point glimpse somethi ng of the part
it is to play in the world of the fu ture.
Masonry Defined
What is F reemasonry? Freemasonry is the sky. Who shall encompa,ss it? Like the resplendent canopy of heaven, it o'erarches human
life ; at times a translucent radiance, at times an alluring m ystery, a
velvet darkness tremulous with stars. The scientist can calculate the
flight of a sunbeam and stretch his measures over t he vast spaces, bu t
can he capture the elusive beauty that quivers in the twilight or imprison the su btle influences that rain from those s hining orbs? Its
vastrfess, as limitless as eternity, declares Infinity.
Freemasonry is the sea. Who can plumb its depths? Moved by
cosmic impulses, it elibs and flows responsive to compelling forces
behind the dis tant suns. T ouching all shores, it is circumscribed by
none. Receiving into itself all ri"vers, it loses not its identity; being
enriched by all tributaries, it absorbs yet is not changed. Unfathomable, it forever reflects with undimmed purity the ever-changing beauties of the changeless sky.
Freemasonry is the light. What shall withstand it ? As silently as
the dawn it comes. Before its irresistible advance t he noxious things

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of shadowy night flee in terror. The sun of righteousness with healing
in his wings arises, and at his smile the earth is flooded with glory.
The mission of Masonry was formulated on that first day when the
Creator scattered the prevailing darkness with the potent word: Let
there be light! Light, all-pervading, life-giving, world-conquering
light!
Freemasonry is the wind, blowing where it listeth, bearing on
its wings a fragrance of acacia broken but blooming hard by a mound
of fresh-laid clods, bringing an odor of myrtle and cypress, suggesting
the perfume of blood-red roses blossoming on a crown of thorns;
bringing, too, an echo of old-time chants in sacred groves to longforgotten gods, a murmur of immemor.ial prayers richly intoned by
deep-voiced priests, reminiscent of all the beautiful dreams and aspirations of humanity-a dynamic wind, a breath, a spirit, causing the
prophet to cry, "0 wind, breathe upon these slain that they may live!"

"It is by the real that we exist; it is by the ideal that we live. Would
you realize the difference? Animals exist, man lives." (9)
Our trouble is that our understanding of Masonry is too narrow,
too circumscribed. We . have been content to think of the institution
merely as one more fraternity whose main business is the conferring
of ritualistic degrees, the cultivation of social contacts, and the practice of. a petty philanthropy. Now, of course I do not depreciate degree
work, good-fellowship, and benevolence. These are all good in their
place: but they should be simply means to an end. When the end is
forgotten in an overzealous cultivation of the means, they become
trivial and unworthy. With good old Walt Whitman I cry:
"Long enough have you dreame\i contemptible dreams;
Now I wash the gum from your eyes;
You must habit yourself to the dazzle of the light,
And of every moment of your life." (10)
We are like those jungle people to whom was given a sundial, and
they wishing to honor it, builded over it a windowless hut and there
in the darkness they rendered it homage. At last a wise man came
along who tore down the hut, and for the first time the glory and the
purpose of the sundial were revealed: From the fathers, we, the
Masons of today, have received a priceless possession. In our overanxious efforts to honor it and them we have hidden it under ritualistic
precisianism and Lodge routine minutae and have missed the transcendent meaning and purpose of our Masonic inheritance. The time
has come for a reassertion of values.
My good friend, H . L. Haywood, whose book, "Symbolical Masonry," is one of the finest interpretations of Masonic teaching, tells
us that one evening he missed his little son, four years old. Going out
into the yard, under the cloudless splendor of a desert sky, he found
the little lad, pail in hand, clambering up a stepladder. "What are
you doing?" asked the father. And the little fellow replied: "Why,
daddy, I'm going to get a bucketful of stars." So today, frankly, I am
trying to hand you "a bucketful of stars." You may toss them aside.
You may admire them and wear them as jewels on your heart. You
may use them to light you along the pathway of life. Or you may let
them guide you, as a certain lustrous star led the wise men of old, to
a sacred shrine where you will bend the knees of your soul in worship
and offer a loving sacrifice of gold, frankincense and myrrh.
Lest you think I am alone in this exalted conception of Freemasonry, may I quote that great commentator on Masonic symbolism,
to whom I have already alluded, Brother H. L. Haywood, who asks:
"What is a Mason, if not an architect of the mystical
order? In so far as he is true to his Royal Art he is one
engaged in building up within himself a real, but viewless
Temple; its foundations laid deep in character, its walls

70

Freemasonry is the ancient sphinx dreaming by the crowded ways
of men. Who shall read her riddle? Her voiceless lips propound the
tragic challenge upon which hang the issues of life and death. Deliberately she misleads her children and bewilders them with .explanations
of her symbols that confuse and distract. Ruthless, she casts aside the
wretched mortal whose · darkened mind brings no solution, but
wreathes with immortal bays the brow of him who answers well her
questioning. And it is well. He only is worthy of the high revelation
who gives his soul to obtain it and will not be satisfied with trivialities.
Tinsel may be bought for a farthing, but gold must be digged from
the depths.
Freemasonry is one with that transcendent mystery that broods
o'er every cradle, smiles o'er every marriage bower and watches with
an infinite tenderness by every bier. It is the wonder of the child, the
ecstasy of the lover, the question of the scientist, and the vision of the
seer. The shekinah shedding its mystic light over the mercy seat, the
lambent flame illumining the holy altar, the radiance shining from
the luminous pages of every Scripture, the ineffable splendor of the
Sacred Name-Freemasonry is that! We do not know what it is,
but it gives meaning to life. We cannot touch it, but it is more real
than the sun that glows at noontime. In its presence we are dumb,
yet it makes the soul articulate. Possess it and find immortal life.
Thus I characterize Freemasonry.
Star-gazing and High Values
You say I rhapsodize. I admit it. I do not apologize for lifting
this discussion of Freemasonry out of the drab and commonplace into
the realm of ideals. By our more literally-minded Brethren I expect
to be scorned as a star-gazer and a dreamer of dreams. So be it. But
I remember the words of that great French Mason, Victor Hugo:

World Needs Masonry
In describing Freemasonry as a spiritual force I would not have
you think that Masonry consists of beautiful but impractical ideals;
a kind of fairy fantasy woven of rainbows and gossamer, poetry and
high-flown sentiment; as alluring as the lovely Antares, yon red star
clinging to the neck of the Scorpion, glorious but unattainable.
. My contention is that the distinctive doctrines of Freemasonry
are eminently practical; that until mankind frankly, sincerely and
wholeheartedly adopts them as its social and political objectives it will
wander lost and bewildered in the wilderness of confusion and distraction; that when the principles upon which Freemasonry is based
are accepted as the foundation stones of civilization and the teachings
of our gentle craft are taken as the working program of statesmanship
and social progress, the golden age of which man has dreamed and· of
which poets have sung, will be close to realization.
THEREFORE THE WORLD NEEDS FREEMASONRY ,
AND BECAUSE OF THAT NEED THE FUTURE OF FREEMASONRY IS ASSURED.
May I ther~fore, in the remainder of the time that is allotted to
me, direct your thought to Freemasonry as a social force in this
modern world, in the years of the immediate future, in this period of
unparalleled importance and significance.
Marvelous Modern World
We are living in the most marvelous and pregnant age in the
woFld's history. I have no sympathy with those fearsome, defeatist
Brethren who read the future in the terms of cataclysm and disaster.
It is true that at the present time society is in a state of ferment.
Institutions that have endured for centuries are crumbling into ruins.
The ancien·t authorities are flouted and the immemoria l traditions are
discredited. But these disturbances are not signs of decadence, they
are the bir.th-pangs of a new era. Civilization is being reborn. Stupendous forces are at work remolding the social order. High-power machinery, mass production and scientific management are giving us a
new ir1dustrial ocganization. Radio, the telegraph, rapid transportation
have shrunk the globe into a very small ball. Tomorrow morning the
happenings of toda-y in London, Calcutta, Buenos Aires, Cape Town,
will march across our breakfast tables.

The first and most fundamental of these teachings t o whf h I

Religion Without Superstition
I pass quickly to the third great ideal: PURE RELIGION THE
BASIS OF A HUMANE CIVILIZATION. "No civilization has yet
survived after the downfall of its gods," declares Sir Philip Gibbs. "Its
doom is declared when the faith and idealism which formed the basis
of its laws, the inspiration of its art, and the meaning of its life are
challenged by skepticism, and then abandoned in disbelief." To this
statement Masonry would give full acceptance.
Freemasonry is not a religion, it is religion. ( 16) Its creed may be
simply and quickly stated. It believes in the fatherhood of God, the
brotherhood of man, the infinite value of the human soul, the inescapable obligation of the moral law, the Golden Rule, and immortality.
A Mason may believe more; he cannot believe less. Upon these indispensable beliefs the whole structure of our English-speaking civilization rests.
There are those who tell us that religion is outgrown and that
man has no further need of it. Certain nations are trying to get along
without it. But alas, where religion is suppressed the emotions and
urges of the human soul find expression in the wildest excesses of
superstition and perversion. A writer in the London "Sphere" tells of
an experience in a Russian village. A commotion on a village street
awakened him at midnight and he went out to find the entire populac
tion engaged in the weirdest ceremonies of witchcraft, in which men
were beating naked wo1nen with knotted thongs. This is said to be
a common occurrence in the Russian hinterland.
Deprive the masses of the moral incentives of religion and they
rapidly descend to the level of the beasts. Take away from your intellectuals the stabilizing, sanative influence of religion and their mental
brilliance withers and dies under the blight of a shallow cynicism or
a despairing pessimism. A nation, even though it be rich and prosperous, that neglects the cultivation of the spiritual life of the people,
slips quickly down the primrose ways to decadence and death. May
I quote you a provocative word of our own great Californian, Dr.

76

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Robert A. Millikan, who says: "Personally, I believe that essential
religion is one of the world's supremest needs. And I believe that one
of the greatest contributions the United States ever can, or ever will,
make to world progress-greater by far than any contribution which
we ever have made or ever can make to the science of governmentwill consist in furnishing an example to the world of how the religious
life of a nation can evolve intelligently, wholesomely, inspiringly,
reverently, completely divorced from all unreason, all superstition,
and all unwholesome emotionalism." ( 17) Every Mason conversant
with Masonic history would give unqualified endorsement to this vivid
statement of the present need.
Now this concept of RELIGION APPLIED TO AFFAIRS OF
STATE GIVES US DEMOCRACY, and for three centuries Masonry has struggled to establish in human relations the principles
of liberty, justice, equality, toleration, sympathy, altruism-all synonymous with and included in democracy-and to inculcate the spirit of
fraternity in the hearts of men. Time does not permit an extended
discussion of these dynamic ideals of free society, but may I dwell,
just for a moment, . upon two-liberty and toleration. These two
principles are inextricably interwoven. You cannot have one without
the other, and no form of human society is worthy of this glorious
modern age that does not elevate as of greatest worth-liberty and
toleration.
To understand the truth of this assertion scan with me the pages
of history.
Five centuries before Christ, Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, teacher
of Pericles and Euripedes, was banished from Athens for asserting
that the stars were red hot balls of fire and that the sun was thousands
of times bigger than the whole of Greece.
The Stoic, Cleanthes, two centuries later, denounced Aristarchus
of Samos, as impious because he attempted to prove that the earth
moved around the sun.
Hypatia of Alexandria, bright star of paganism, renowned teacher
of philosophy and science, was brutally killed in the fifth century of
our era by a mob of infuriated monks. In their frenzy they dragged
the exquisite maiden, naked, through the streets and scraped the very
flesh from her bones with oyster shells.
In the sixteenth century Giordano Bruno swept the midnight
skies with a crude telescope, then shouted across Europe that the
stars wert flaming worlds. He paid for his audacity with his life and
died at the stake on February 17, 1600.
Servetus, the discoverer of the lesser circulation of the blood,
was burned by Calvin at Geneva in 1553, a victim of fanaticism and
cruelty.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

77

Thomas Woolston, a Fellow of Sidney Sussex College, Cambridge, in the eighteentli century subjected the miracle stories to a
searching criticism and for his temerity he was deprived of his fellowship, was prosecuted for libel, and sentenced to a fine of £100 and
a year's imprisonment. Unable to pay, he died in prison. (18)
These instances could be multiplied a thousand times. Pitiful,
indeed, are the stories of cruelty and heartbreak that clutter up the
pages of history.
;roday _there are in the world powerful movements, social, political, mdustnal, that depend for their success upon the suppression of
free speech, free activity and individual initiative. Men imbued with
the spirit and traditions of Freemasonry cannot look with complacency
upon their advance to places of dominance.
Freemasonry, acting through its inspired votaries, has combated
fanaticism and intolerance in all its forms, and on a thousand bitter
battlefields has lifted its white standard of liberty and toleration.
Perhaps even in this radiant age of scientific progress and economic
development it may again be necessary to unfurl the snowy banner
of freedom in challenge to those forces that would lay the human
spirit under the thrall of despotic authority and control and if that
hour arrives Freemasons will not be found wanting.

. In a. challenging speech recently delivered, Dr. E. C. Moore,
v1ce-pres1dent and provost of the University of California at Los Angeles, declared that fascism and communism in contrast with democracy were "iron ways of governing flesh and minds. They are
molochs created by the human imagination and worshipped with
human sacrifices." "The future of democracy," he continued, "is more
democ~acy-?emocracy r~cher and fuller-for under no other plan can
each smgle life come to its full flowering, " a state of social relationship, where "the poorest he may live his life as the richest he." To
such a social relationship liberty and tolerance are indispensable.
We must never let our children forget that this is the meaning of

Education and World Concord
The three remaining principles that must prevail in the new social
order now corning into being-principles that grow out of Masonic
teachings as naturally and as inevitably as the Giant Sequoias rise out
of the soil of our majestic Sierras-I can do no more than mention.
EDUCATION THE RIGHT OF EVERY CHILD, WITHOUT DISTINCTION OF CASTE, CONDITION OR RACE! This
right must be emphasized and reiterated now when under the stress
of economic stringency there are those who advocate drastic curtailment of popular education. Such a policy in a democracy is suicidal.
Again I quote Victor Hugo: "Compulsory education is a recruitment
of souls for the light. Henceforth all human advancement will be accomplished by swelling the legions of those who read. The diameter of
the moral and ideal good corresponds always to the caliber of men's
minds.· In proportion to the worth of the brain is the worth of the
heart .... What humanity requires, is to be fed with light." ( 19) Feeding human souls with light! What a challenging conception of education! And it is one to which Masonry can give full approval.
WORLD-WIDE AMITY AND CO-OPERATION, AS
AGAINST WAR AND NARROW NATIONALISM! The Masonic
order is the world's greatest peace society. It ramifies through all
nations, all castes, all religions, all races. Men of divergent creeds
whose religious taboos will not permit them to break bread together
nevertheless meet as brothers around the Masonic altar and unitedly
lift hands of prayer to the common Father. International compacts,
diplomatic treaties, and trade agreements serve a noble purpose, but
at the last the only sure defense against war is a sense of world-wide
brotherhood, transcending all our petty suspicions and sordid hates,
and fusing all our differences in a globe-girdling affection. Said Emerson: "This great, overgrown, dead Christendom of ours still keeps
alive at least the name of a lover of mankind. But one day all men

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

79

will be lovers; and every calamity will be dissolved in the universal
sunshine." (20) This is part of the radiant hope of Masonry.
Onward Forever
The last dynamic truth I would bring before you as being distinctively Masonic is THE BELIEF IN HUMAN PROGRESS; and
I remind you that Masonry is a progressive science.
Einstein interrupts his contemplation of the infinite vastness to
observe that there is no hitching post in the universe. The foremost
scientist of the age tells us that exploration of the cosmos does not
reveal any tethering stake. What is true of the universe at large is
true of humanity. Forever the marching orders are given: "Get thee
out of thy country ... into a land that I will show thee." (21) The
Spirit of Life forever commands: "Speak unto the children of Israel,
that they go forward." (22) The Kingdom of Heaven is kinetic, not
static.
In our own ritualistic ceremonies, just when we think we have
attained and the precious jewel glitters on our breast and we sit down
to rest, we are summoned to the East, the Master bids us travel, and
we set off anew upon our journey.
Science interprets the rhythm of the universe in the terms of
evolution, and history is understood as a colorful pageant showing
humanity on the march; sometimes swinging along like a victorious
army with all flags flying and bands playing. At other times the dust
of horrid conflict and ruthless warfare obscures the line of advance.
But still mankind moves on, lured by an unquenchable hope, impelled
by an irresistible interior power.
This emphasis upon evolution discourages red revolution and
cataclysmic social upheavals. Freemasonry is a stabilizing influence
in human affairs. It is opposed to violent and revolutionary programs.
Human society is not a machine to be knocked down and put together
again according to some blue-print of academic reform. It is a living
thing, like a tree, like an animal; it grows, it develops according to
fixed laws and logical progress. The power that reforms, redeems,
recreates man is not an imposition from without. It lies at his heart,
it resides in his soul. Men are gods in the chrysalis, and as the cocoons
of selfishness, hatred, and meanness break, the spirit is released and
takes the higher forms.
In the palace builded by the enchantment of Merlin were fom
zones of sculpture:
"And in the lowest, beasts were slaying men,
And in the second, men are slaying beasts,
And in the third are warriors, perfect men,
And in the fourth are men with growing wings."

Masonry Militant
But that you may get the full significance of the mission of Freemasonry in the troublous but potent years of the immediate future,
may I call to your remembrance the spectacle of the workers who rebuilded the ancient city of ] erusalem after the Captivity, how "they
that builded on the wall, and they that bore burdens, with those that
laded, every one with 0 ne of his hands wrought in the work, and with
the other hand held a weapon. For the builders, every one had his
sword girded by his side, and so builded." (25) So I am not unduly
confusing the similes by calling upon the Masons of today to be
builders and crusaders at the same time. In one hand a trowel with
which to build, in the other a sword with which to fight.
The warfare of Freemasonry is not against men or institutions,
not against governll'ents or churches, but against the tyranny that
would reduce men to mere automatons, standardized, repressed, regimented; against the superstition that would befog m en's minds with
lies and corroding fear; against the spiritual thralldom that would
shrink a band of iron around the brow of man and forbid the thought
of man to expand, to develop, to grow; against the despotism that
would prevent the freest expression of the human spirit; against
slavery of every kind, whether it be to an autocrat, to an industrial
overlordship, to a soulless bureaucracy, to false doctrines, or to
craven, self-created terror; against ignorance, prejudice, hatred, materialism, Phariseeism, and all the black brood of shams and pretensions that have weighed like an unutterable anguish upon the soul of
man.
It is a glorious war. A war for human rights, for the cause of
righteousness, for little children yet unborn. It is the warfare of
Socrates, of Martin Luther, of Wilberforce, of Washington, and, I say
it re~erently, of that Divine man who gave his life upon the cruel cross
that men might be free.
·
There is a legend in the Frankish Alps that .C harlemagne did not
die but that angels carried him to a mountain cavern where they
laid him, cap-a-pie, with his falchion by his side, and there he sleeps,
waiting un til humanity, bowed beneath its woes, migh t call him to
the rescue.
Freemasonry is that ·legendary Charlemagne, and humanity, embattled and distraught, calls upon the craft to make good its an cient
tradition and draw sword in defense of those eternal principles to
which it is dedicated. The hosts of light are gathering under the white
banners of freedom and brotherhood. The trumpet sounds the advance.
Already the advanced forces are ·clashing with the enemy. This is no
time for cowards and self-seekers. Only men with stout hearts and
clear minds and consecrated souls are equal to the demands of this
great day.

"New occasions teach new duties;
Time makes ancient good uncouth ;
They must upward still, and onward,
Who would keep abreast of truth." (23)
And Freemasonry assumes the resolve that Plato puts at the end
of his Republic: "We will ever cleave to the upward road."
Temple of Humanity
So, to use a simile familiar to every Mason, the craft in this latter
day adds its contribution to the building of a spiritual temple. High
engraved over the portal of the beautiful Scottish Rite House of the·
Temple in Washington the declaration is made: "Freemasonry builds
its· temples among the nations and in the hearts of men." And it is so.
This modern order of craftsmen is engaged in e~ecting an invisible
but vitally real tem"ple in the souls of men, builded of hopes and
dreams, of prayers and noble resolves, of kindly sentiments and
loving deeds-the temple of a redeemed humanity. We may adopt the
description of the spiritual temple that Charles Rann Kennedy, brilliant dramatist and earnest Mason, puts in the mouth of Manson:
"You must understand, this is no ·dead pile of stones and unmeaning timber. It is a living thing. . . .
·
"When you enter it you hear a sound-a sound as of some mighty
poem chanted. Listen Jong enough, and you will learn that it is made
up of the beating of human hearts, of the nameless music of men's
souls-that is, if you have ears. If you have eyes, you will presently
see the church itself-a looming mystery of many shapes and shadows,
leaping sheer from fl.oar to dome. The work of no ordinary builder! ...
"The pillars of it go up like the brawny trunks of heroes; the
sweet human flesh of men and women is molded about its. bulwarks,
strong, impregnable; . the faces of little children laugh out from every
cornerstone; the terrible spans and arches of it are the' joined hands
of comrades; and up in the heights and spaces there are inscribed the
numberless musings of all the dreamers of the wotk!. It is yet building- building and built upon. Sometimes the work goes forward in
deep darkness; sometimes in blinding light; now beneath the burden
of unutterable anguish; now to the tune of a great laughter and heroic
shoutings like the cry of thunder. Sometimes, in the silence of the
night-time, one may hear the tiny hammerings of the comrades at
work up in the dome-the comrades that have ~limbed ahead." (24)

that the method set out in the Message of the Grand Master
be adopted. After full discussion the further consideration
of the subject was postponed until Wednesday. On W ednesday afternoon the -chairman of the committee amended his
original motion by recommending that a Grand Lecturer
be elected and paid a salary to be fixed by Grand Lodge,
and that said elected Grand Lecturer shall have power to
appoint,_ subject to the approval of the Grand M aster, four
assistant Grand Lecturers; the duties of the Grand Lecturer
and his assistants to be as outlined in the circular letter
and Message of the Grand Master, and the present plan of
ritualistic instruction be continued for the ensuing year.
Grand Lodge concurred in the report.

To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
We have the honor to submit herewith the forty-third annual
report of the property, condition and operation of the Masonic Homes
for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1934.
As required by the Constitution, the board organized immediately
following the close of Grand Lodge, October 13, 1933, as follows:
President, Charles M. Wollenberg, term expires 1934.
Vice-President, John Stewart Ross (1935).
Samuel E. Burke (1936).
Chas. Albert Adams (1937).
Randolph V. Whiting, Deputy Grand Master.
Earl Warren, Senior Grand Warden.
Rollie W. Miller, Junior Grand Warden.
Treasurer, William P. Filmer.
Secretary, John Whicher.
Last year we looked forward with hope for better times, but our
hopes ended in disappointment. We take heart, however, in knowing
that the men of our fraternity still have faith in those cardinal tenets
of Freemasonry, brotherly love and relief; and also iQ knowing that
notwithstanding hard times, the members of our great fraternity have
pleasure in contributing to the relief of those in physical and mental
distress, and cheerfully assist in the maintenance of our Homes. At
the Home for adults at Decoto our Lodges provide a shelter and a
shield against the adversities and infirmities which are too often the
heritage of old age; and at the Home for children at Covina provision
is made for the care and education of little ones who have been bereft
of father or mother, and who otherwise might become social outlaws.
The labors of the fraternity are a part of the splendid work of exemplifying Masonic charity, and no Mason will deny to our poor the shelter
and care provided by the Homes.
The reports of the superintendents of the Homes, submitted herewith and made a part of this report, disclose the internal conditions
at the Homes. Brother Hartman at Decoto and Brother Downen at
Covina are doing splendid work as superintendents, and we take pleasure in commending them, particularly for the whole-hearted, enthusiastic spirit manifested in all their labors. The report of the Secretary
and the auditors employed by the Committee on Finance are also
appended, references to which will appear later in our report.

Placing Children Who Leave the Home
In our annual report last year we referred to the responsibility
of Lodges to children who are honorably dismissed from the Home
by reason of age or graduation from high school.
We stated that "these children are dismissed at an age when they
seriously need a warm and welcome friendship on the part of the
Brethren; they need employment; they need the fostering assistance
of friends who can be trusted to divert them into paths of good conduct; they need to be directed in their new environment to keep good
company. They stand in truth 'where the brook and river meet'."
During the fiscal year 39 children were dismissed. The Secretary of the Homes wrote to each Lodge interested, soliciting aid in
the way of employment or further schooling for them, and sad to
relate, only one Lodge, le Progres de l'Oceanie, responded in a
material way.
However, the seed sown in our appeal last year was not wholly
thrown on stony ground. The Southern California Past Masters'
Association at its annual meeting in January, 1934, appointed a committee to assist the young people who graduate from the Covina
Home each year. The_ committee is composed of Rollie W. Miller,
William B. Ogden, Wilbert J. Stewart, William L. Hovis, Hubert W.
Walker and Frank G. Falloon. Fifteen of the children dismissed in
June were expected. to remain at or near Los Angeles. We are informed that this committee has not been idle, but has taken a real
fatherly interest in the youngsters, and either personally or through
the interested Lodges is carrying out .the full spirit of our request.
Reappointment of Children
In 1931 your Board of Trustees adopted a resolution providing
that the continuance of any child in the Home beyond the age of
16 must be authorized by special action of the board. The superintendent notified each child coming within the rule to make written
application for reappointment, which applications are considered by
the board at the May meeting. This year 22 boys and 19 girls had
reached the age limit, and proper showing having been made they
were continued" at the Home for another year.

mobile, fully equipped with all modern gadgets, including radio, to
the Covina Home, for which we tender_ our thanks.

In c.onnec.tion with our reference to the indebtedness to the Endowment Fund, mention may be properly here made of the fact that
that indebtedness was incurred only because the Trustees did not
have sufficient money to pay for the buildings authorized by Grand
Lodge to be erected at Decoto and Covina; and that the money so
borrowed was used only for that purpose. This was the procedure
suggested by Grand Master Keesling during the course of the construction of the buildings at Covina. The building funds were exhausted and it became necessary to arrange for the money needed
for the completion of the buildings. He recommended "as the best
plan to be pursued, borrowing the necessary funds from the Endowment Fund upon note of the Trustees," and pointed out that "to
the reimbursement of the Endowment Fund the Grand Lodge is as
much obligated as it would be to pay any indebtedness."
Your Trustees have heard the statement made that the fund
raised by the fifty cent building tax has been used for maintenance
purposes. Now, the exact converse is the fact. Instead of using any
part of the building fund for llll!intenance purposes, we have paid a
large part of the cost of the buildings out of the maintenance fund.
The building fund was created in 1912, and the total amount collected since that date is $1 ,092,439.55. During the same time there
was expended for building $2,244,961.29. In other words, the cost of
the buildings was $1,152,521.74 in excess of the amount received from
the fifty cent building tax. Of this amount there is still due the Endowment Fund $200,000, and the remainder, to-wit, $952,521.74, has
been paid out of our other funds.
In considering the expenses of the Homes it should be remembered that we have a problem that is not comparable to those met
with in a going business where merchandise of one sort or another
is bought and sold. There is no question that in such a business, cut
after cut can be made in rents, wages, overhead and other items, and
the merchandise on the shelves will not suffer; but in our Masonic
Homes we are dealing with human beings who cannot be treated as
merchandise, i.e., handled for profit.
We believe that with the reductions we have already made, our
schedule of salaries and wages is as low as ca n be justified for the
services rendered. If any further curtailment in our expenditures is
to be made it must be in food, clothing or medical attention. It is
our belief that Grand Lodge would not favor any retrenchment which
must be so effected.
·

88

Care of Bodily Afflicted

In 1920, Grand Lodge gave careful consideration to the subject
of outside relief. To quote from the report:
"Our regulations provide that an applicant suffering from any
disease or ailment necessitating hospital treatment will not be received. As pointed out elsewhere, our hospital is overcrowded with
those who became ill after their admission to the Home. The Grand
Lodge should give this regulation most careful consideration. Are
we fair to the brother Mason in good standing for many years, who
becomes incapacitated through paralysis or other ailment, spends his
savings in attempted cure, and after years of Masonic fraternalism,
when he needs help and wishes to end his days among his brethren,
is refused admission to the Home?"
The Grand ~odge authorized your Trustees to give aid to such
cases.
In 1921 there was spent $570.00. For the ·year just closed the
expense was $46,721.50.
There is some question as to whether this amount should be
charged to the Homes expense, as the cases involved are not eligible
to the Home in most instances, according to the regulations of Grand
Lodge.
We would suggest that your Trustees be authorized to carry this
account as a separate activity of Grand Lodge, .separating it entirely
from Hom_e affairs. It will not result in any additional expense, but
will result in giving a true picture of the Home expenditures.
Finances
Your Trustees have devoted a not inconsiderable amount of time
to the study of ways and means whereby the expenses of the Homes
might be reduced; and we are pleased to be able to report that substantial economies have been effected and our financial condition has
been materially improved. And this notwithstanding the continuance
of the economic condition which has resulted in not only a material
decrease in our revenue, but as well in an increase of those in need
who must be cared for by our Homes.
We entered this year (August 1, 1933) with a deficit of $13,020.
This deficit was due to the fact that in addition to meeting the
current expenses of the Homes we had made a payment of $25,000
on our indebtedness to the Endowment Fund.
This year, instead of a deficit of $13,020, we had a surplus of
$25,759.52-a net gain over expenditures of $38,779.52 for the year.
We therefore, on September 1, 1934, made another payment of
$25,000 to the Endowment Fund, thus reducing the original indebtedness of $325,000 to $200,000.

Report of Auditors
To the Board of Trustees, Masonic Homes of California:
In accordance with the authorization of the Finance Committee,
we have made a general audit and examination of the books of account of the Masonic Homes of California, giving particular attention to the verification of the balance sheet as at July 31, 1934.
Sufficient examination and testing of detailed revenue and expense
accounts was made as to satisfy ourselves as to the correctness of
the accounting. We present herewith the following financial statements:

COMMENTS

Sernrities, Notes Receivable and R eal Estate, Etc.:
All of the general securities listed under Schedule B-3 have been
donated with the exception of 10 shares of the Glendora Water Company stated on the books at cost. The stated, or book value, in the
case of donated securities represen ts the value placed upon the
securities at the time of donation. Where such value has been difficult to determine, because of its being an unlisted or closely held
security, or of uncertain value, then the par, face, or a nominal value
is entered on the books by the office solely as a matter of record.
Notes receivable vali.Jes represent the unpaid portion of notes receivable on hand. All but two notes are secured by real estate as
noted in Schedule B-3 by the letter "S." Insurance policies, received
mainly from residents of the Homes have been listed on the books

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

by the office at the face or value recoverable upon the death of the
insured, as a matter of record. (In 1933 the cash surrender value of
these particular kind of policies was $1,630.00).
The securities contained within the Students' Loan Fund,
Schedule B-2, are stated on the books at cost, with the exception of
the 100 shares of Masonic Temple Association received by donation
and valued on the books at par.
Real estate donations have increased through bequest and donation from a relatively few parcels to as many as forty parcels during
the last few years, some of which are of considerable value. As noted
in former reports, it has been the practice, in the absence of appraised
values, to record such values, only as and when sold and a value thus
ascertained, and then set up in the books as a note rece.i vable as per
Schedule B-3. Beginning August 1, 1934, these properties are being
recorded in the books at the assessed value for record purposes. A
list of the forty items of r eal estate is being furnished the Finance
Committee separately rather than increase the size of our report.

The total book value of cash and securities of the Endowment Fund
($772,614.59) is set out in Exhibit B-Page 6 of the separate Endowment Fund report.

General:
The change made in the system of accounting at Covina has
resulted in the necessity of adjusting the general books to take up
the July, 1933, sundry Covina revenue ($1,242.28) which under prior
procedure was entered in the books a month later, for each month
throughout the year, as and when received at San Francisco in cash.
While there appears to be a decided improvement in classification of
accounts and detailed information furnished, the necessity of now
submitting separate statements materially lengthens the report.
The building fund tax, which is Constitutional, has been carried
on the books along with other maintenance revenue accounts, and
not considered as a separate fund. However, it is interesting to note
that an analysis made by the office of the Grand Secretary of the
annual Proceedings back to 1912 shows $1,092,439.55 collected under
the building fund tax, and $2,244,961.29 expended for buildings and
improvements, etc.

To the Endowment Fund Committee, Masonic Homes of California:
In accordance with your authorization, we have audited the accounts of the Permanent Endowment Fund of the Masonic Homes
of California for the fiscal year enaed July 31, 1934. We present herewith the following statements:
Exhibit A: Statement of Cash Receipts and Disbursements.
Exhibit B: Statement of Composition of Fund (six pages).
In the case of securities purchased the stated value referred to
above represents cost. However, many of the securities included
within the Endowment Fund have been donated. In the case of such
donated securities the stated value represents the vilue placed upon

108

PROCEEDINGS OF T'HE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the securities at the time of donation. Where such value has been
difficult to determine, because of its being an· unlisted or closely held
security, or of uncertain value, then it has been the practice of the
office to .enter the par, face, or a nominal value solely as a matter
of record.
We have re-arranged the securities alphabetically, and have
marked with a "D" those bonds received by donation or bequest. All
stocks have been acquired by donation or bequest. Additions during
the fiscal year 1933-34 have been set forth at the close of Exhibit B-:page 6 for ready reference.
We ce.rtify that the attached statements, in our opinion, set forth
the condition of the Permanent Endowment Fund as at July 31, 1933,
with exception as to the stated value of the securities on hand, and
that a proper accounting has been made of all receipts and disbursements.
Respectfully submitted,
RucKSTELL & LAND, Certified Public Accountaiits.
By FLOYD T. WEBB.

Report of Superlntendent-Decoto Home
To the Board of Trustees:
I hereby present for your consideration my twenty-fifth annual
report as Superintendent of the Masonic Home at Decoto, California,
for the year 'e nding August 31, 1934.
There has been but little change in the policies governing the
management of the Home during the past year.
For many years past, it has been the purpose of our endeavor to
assist the members of our large family in developing a home-like
atmosphere. This in a large measure, has been realized and it is this
family spirit that has created an esprit de corps that practically dominates and controls the daily life of the Home.
The facilities now afforded by the fraternity enable the management to render a higher standard of service. To care for the
members of a Home where each one has his or her own individuality,
their own self-expression, calls for a consecrated spirit of service on
the part of those whose duty it is to minister to their physical, moral
and spiritual welfare.
While every reasonable effort is made to promote harmony and
contentment, yet it is a truism that each one brings to the Home his
or her own personality, the sum total of which leaves its impress on
the social life of the Home.
In connection with the above, I am pleased to state that, as a
whole, there has been a marked improvement in the general conditions. The family, generally speaking, are conscious of and deeply
appreciate the provisions made for their comfort and well-being.
It has always been our aim to operate the Home as economically
and efficiently as possible, to have the buildings and grounds present
a neat and attractive appearance, and provide every comfort possible
for the residents of the Home.
Residents.--At the beginning of the fiscal year, there were 359
residents·. There were admitted during the year, 68 residents, making
a total of 427. 58 have passed away. T here are now at the Home, 369
r esidents. 197 men and 171 women; of this number there are 33 married couples.

' '

Health-The general health of the Home has been normal with
the exception of those who are infirm and 'feeble owing to advancing
years.
Hospital-There are now 50 of qur members being cared for in
our hospital department. Equipped with every sanitary device, the
facilities afforded enable our physician and nurses to give to those
who are ill every care and attention for their comfort. Day and night

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALil''OR.NIA

nurses are in attendance. The number requiring hospital care is constantly increasing.
In the near future when necessity requires it, additional room can
be provided by the completion of the interior of the second floor of
the two wings of the hospital building, which are at t.he present time .
unoccupied.
Industrial-All the members, in keeping with their strengtll, are
encouraged to interest themselves and assist in the dally routine work.
During the past year, a large number of the men residents have contributed to the welfare of tile Home by their services in the hospital,
engine room, laundry, eal'penter, paint and barber shop!!, care of
garage, mail, passenger, e'Kpress and freight au.to service, kitchen,
pantry, dining· rooms, vegetab~ room, store rooms, office work,
library, club and reception rooms, janitor work, teleph()!le switch
board, information desk, floral decorations, care of elclvatol'S, flower
beds, and lawns, watering trees, plants and shrubs, vegetable and
berry gardt:ns, operation Gf stage, stereopticon and moving picture
machines, poultry yards and many other light duties in a genera.I way.

The aerating building which receives the sewerage water after
passing through the two septic tanks, has been repaired and painted,
and water can now be used for irrigation in the orchards and fields.
The banks of the creek, south of the main buildings, have been
cleared of all brush, the trees have been pruned; all this has resulted
in a great improvement in the appearance of the grounds. Many trees,
shrubs, fruit and ornamental, have been planted in the orchards and
about the grounds. Many more will be set out the latter part of the
year. All the garages and farm buildings, with the exception of the
barn, have been repaired and painted.
The roads about the grounds have been graded and prepared to
receive gravel, when needed.
Library and Club Rooma--There are now 6500 be>oks on the
shelves of our main library and branches located in the several•departments of the Home. The Masonic Hill branch of the Alameda
County Free Library continues to enable our family to obtain many
of the latest books, and on application, to secure special ones. In addition, we are the recipients, through friends and members of the
fraternity, of books, daily papers, magazines and periodicals which
are placed on the tables in the hospital, library and club rooms, and
the ladies' social halls.
Social Life-Th~ social life has been greatly enriched by literary
and musical entertainments given by generous volunteers from Oakland, San Francisco and nearby towns. Our assembly hall, with our
modern stage and moving picture equipment has made possible the
presentation of dramatic plays, operettas, etc., given by visiting
Lodges, Eastern Star Chapters and friends, all of which has contributed to the pleasure of the members of our family. The evening
programs often close with dancing.
All holidays have been observed with appropriate exercises. The
specials are those held on New Year's Eve, New Year's Day, Lincoln's Birthday, Washington's Birthday, Easter, Memorial Day,
Fourth of July, Halloween, Thanksgiving Day and Christmas. All
these programs are prepared and presented by the members of the
Home.
A Happy Hour Club has been organized by the members of the
Home, and they hold their meeting every Monday evening in the
Assembly Hall. All are privileged to attend and take part as dancers
or onlookers. The old-time quadrilles, Virginia .Reels, waltzes and
two-steps are the favorite dances. The members furnish their own
music and appoint their own floor manager. Card parties are held
in the library and reception rooms every Tuesday evening, chorus
practice on Friday evenings. Every Sunday afternoon fi nds the residents of the Home in the Assembly Hall for Sunday services, after
which, a selected musical program is given by the Home orchestra,
or by visiting friends.

116

The women residents attend' to the making, mending and marking of all linen, sheets and pillow-slips, table-cloths and napkin&, etc.,
aloo assist in the preparing of fruit and vegetables in the kitchen and
dining rooms, wiping of silver, changing tal:>le•linen, diet kitchen,
clerical work, attending telephone calls, showing visitol's about the
Home, care of music and reception rooms, care of their rooms and
general light household duties, etc.
During. the year, all the 65 rooms, halls, floors and woodwork in
the men's Dormitory· building have been painted, the beds enameled
and the furniture varnished, repairs of furniture, windows, doors, lock
and keys, radios, etu. All this work has been done by the brethren
of the Home.
Farm-As heretofore, the greater part of the hill ranch has been
leased or on cash rental. The farm has supplied plenty of frtiit, figs,
berri~ and nuts for table use. The return from the hay 1;rop has
been light this year on account of the scarcitr. of rain fall. The garden has supplied a variety of vei;:etables, etc, The chicken ranch
has supplied all the eggs for table use, the surplus ·being sold or
preserved.
Water-Our deep well pump continues to furnish. a plentiful
supply of water for household, garden and irrigating purposes, also,
for fire protection. Our reservoirs, with a storage capacity of 600,000
gallons are full at all times.
During the year, our two large reservoirs were emptied, one at a
time; the walls were repaired and cleaned, and are now in good serviceable condition.

,

118

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Radios have been installed in the Club and Reception Rooms,
where at all times, the members of the Home can enjoy them. In
addition, many of the residents have radio sets in their rooms. This
privilege is particularly appreciated by those who are blind and those
who are confined to their beds in the hospital department.
A reading class for the blind and those with failing eyesight,
meets daily in the small reception room, at which time the daily
papers, etc., are read to the·m.
Arrangements are made, whereby, the members of the family, a
few at a time, may enjoy an outing to nearby places of interest; also
an occasional visit to nearby Lodges and Eastern Star Chapters.
During the year, many trips have been made to Oakland, San Francisco, and towns in the vicinity of the Home.
Grand Master James B. Gist and officers of the Grand Lodge,
have made a number of visits to the Home during the year; also, a
large number of brethren from various Lodges, etc. The number of
visits this year show an increasing interest in the welfare of the
Home.
From time to time, Masonic Degrees are conferred in our Temple
by the officers of visiting Lodges for the benefit of the brethren of
the Home.
In conclusion, I wish to extend my appreciation of the services
rendered by the officers and employes, throughout the year, in their
respective departments, and to express to the members of the Board
of Trustees my sincere gratitude for the counsel and advice given
when meeting the various problems connected with the management
of the Home.
FRANK B. HARTMAN, Superintendent.

Report of the Superintendent-Covina

140

Monthly Total August, 1934.................................,..........................$2,469.05

141

To the Trustees of lhe Masonic Homes:

As in previous years, details of the operation of the Covina Home
have been made known- to you in monthly reports. In summarizing
the work of the past yea~ there is little to recount in the way of innovations. This is not a t~e for innovations; we should be satisfied
if we can hold the gains previously made.
Health-The health of the children during the year was on the
whole excellent. An average of 3.2 per cent of the children was under
care in our hospital. Surgical work done included the following:
Tonsillectomy ................:............................... 13
Appendectomy .............................................. 6
Hernia repair ................................................ 1
Coccyx removed ..........................................
Circumcision ...........................................•...... 1
Abdominal abscess ...................................... 1
Epidemic diseases included five cases of scarlet fever, one case
of chicken pox, and one case of infantile paralysis. The epidemic of
poliomyelitis (infantile paralysis) in southern California during the
summer of 1934 caused us to restrict the movements of children and
the visitations of Lodges. On medical advice we also kept the children at Covina during the summer instead of sending them as usual
to the camp at Balboa. One case of ihis dreaded disease made its
appearance in the Home, a little boy eight years old. Fortunately he
made a good recovery without any ·impairment of function.
Dietary Study-We were fortunate in securing a careful study
of the diet of the Home, made without charge by the Home Economics Department of the University of California. This study was
based upon the total consumption of all foodstuffs for the month of
October, 1933. Not only were the menus taken into consideration
but an analysis was made of the total consumption of the variou~
classes of ~oodstu~s. The report states: "The meals are well planned,
and there 1s a variety of healthful foods each day, which is essential
to the normal growth of children. . . . The diet furnishes sufficient
calories, proteins, calcium, phosphorus and iron ... . There are sufficient vitamins present." The cost of the dietary was found to be
10.8 cents per meal.
Admissions and Discharges-The admissions during the year have
numbered 26, of whom 10 were boys and 16 were girls. During the
same period we have discharged 39, the largest outgoing number in
any one year of the Home's history. The causes of discharge were
as follows:

Of those discharged, 22 were boys and 17 were girls. The average age of those discharged was 15 years. The average length of
their residence in the Home was 5 years, 7 months.
Placement of Graduates-The placemertt of those who leave the
Home by reason of graduation or age limit continues to be an important problem, rendered more acute by the general unemployment
situation. Appeals have been made to Lodges that they assume responsibility for their wards upon discharge from the Home, and in
some cases a most excellent response has been made. This work has
further been aided by the Southern California Past Masters' Association, which has created a Covina Home Placement Committee. Acknowledgment is also made of the interest and effective work of
Brother W. P. Jeffries in finding places for several of our boys.
These youngsters passing out from the portals of the Home, fill ed ·
with hope but bound for an uncertain destination, appeal strongly to
those who have been concerned in bringing them thus far along the
road of life.
'
How They Turn Out-The ultimate· test of the work done in
caring for children in the Covina Home must be their ability to take
their place in life as members of society. They were taken into care
by the fraternity because of circumstances which would have deprived
them of the normal •advantages of childhood, and the lack of which
threatened to prevent them from growing up as normal human beings.
How well, then, have these boys and girls succeeded in developing
as normal people?
The class of 1930, now away from us four years, included four
boys and ten girls. Nine of the fourteen secured further vocational
training after leaving the Home. Three of them have graduated from
College. One has had the same job in a legal office ever since he left
here. One boy, with a talent for drawing, spent several years working on shipboard, has saved his money, and is now attending an art
school in New York. Of the ten girls, six are married and are
making a success of their domestic life, refuting the charge sometimes
made that being brought up in an institution disqualifies an individual
for normal family life. Not one of the fourteen is a failure or living
on charity.

Worthy\f remark is the success of Grayson Merrill of the class
of 1929, who i'l\June was graduated from the U. S. Naval Academy
at Annapolis, rahl<ing 41st among the 465 members of his class.
The Home an~he Community-It used to be thought that if a
child could be with rawn from the outside world and placed safely
within an institution, e could be ideally prepared for life in that protected atn:ospher~. In N;_cent years it has come to be recognized that
the best kmd of hfe for a\?roup of children in an institution is one in
which they have the samt contacts with the community in which
they live as are enjoyed by children who live in private homes. We
now believe that what the child needs is not segregation from the
world in the sterilized atmosphere of an institution, but rather a
chance to live normally in the world under favorable conditions, and
thus gain experience and knowledge of real living.
It is fortunate that the Covina Home has from the beginning
been committed to the policy of providing such contacts for its
children. They attend the public schools, where they mingle with
~he _children of the community; they take their part in school organ1zat10ns. and clubs; they attend entertainments and make small purchases m , the local stores; they exchange visits with other children
of the community. All of this has its effect in building up their selfrespect and in keeping them free from that peculiar stigma which
many an orphanage-raised child has carried through life.
The Children's Money System-An important factor in our children's learning the art of living is their experience with money. The
pract.ical concerns of the everyday lives of all of us have to do at
every turn with money; the man or woman who is unskilled in its
use is not apt to succeed in life.
We carry an individual money account with every child. After
they reach the age of thirteen or fourteen, we begin to pay them for
work which they do in the Home, not in actual cash but in credits
on their accounts. At the same time we begin to charge them for
most of the things which they receive, except board and room and
~ealth _care. From the standpoint of our operating expense, it makes
httle difference whether we pay a boy for his work and charge him
for his shoes, or require him to work for nothing and give him his
shoes. However, it makes a tremendous difference to the boy in his
attitude toward work and in the way he takes care of the shoes.
Money for spending by the children is disbursed only upon checks
signed by them and countersigned by their housemother. Their expend_itures are carefully supervised. Much pains is taken day by day
to give them useful practical experience in the handling of money.
While the operation of this system costs something there can be
no doubt of its great value as training for life.

There is little "discipline" in the Home,
of rigid
control. Where two hundred people live together, as e do, a certain
degree of routine and regularity is essential, but e have as little
mass movement, as few bells, signals, and drilt;ss possible. Obedience is required and secured, as well as a decen
respectful attitude
by children toward staff members in authority ver them.
Visitors are almost invariably impressJ by the atmosphere of
freedom. We think it better to allow the «j{ildren too much freedom
than too little. Sometimes there is an older boy who does not seem
to get along welt in this atmosphere, and whose behavior suggests
that a term in the navy or in a military school would do him good.
Since we cannot make the Home or any part of it into a military
establishment, occasionally it is necessary in the interest of harmony
and good order to remove such a one. Three discharges of this kind
were made in the past year; in two of these cases those discharged
were placed in outside care under our supervision.
It is fortunate that by the time a child gets old enough to be
troublesome in his conduct, he is usually able to realize his advantages
as a member of the Home and to know that he cannot expect to continue enjoying those advantages unless he does a reasonable pa~t as a
member of our Home community. The rule adopted a few years ago,
making the continuance of membership of each child beyond the age
of sixteen dependent upon annual reappointment ·by the Trustees, has
had a marked effect in causing the older boys and girls, leaders of
thought in the group, to value their privilege of membership, and to
strive to deserve it.
Interest of the Fraternity-On many occasions during the past
year the children have been made to realize that they are the objects
of love and interest of Masons throughout the jurisdiction. The
visitations of Lodges and other Masonic bodies, listed separately herewith, have brought to them a desirable contact with the great outside
world, and have given them that sense of being secure and of being
cherished wh~ch is one of the rights of childhood.
A fine thing was done for the Home by the Masonic Digest of
Los Angeles, in the presentation of ten free scholarships in the Mackay
Business College. These scholarships have been eagerly sought by
our graduates, placing at their disposal vocational training which is
greatly needed.
The cash donations made by many Lodges and other Masonic
bodies at Christmas are listed herewith. These generous contributions
have been used, not only for toys and gifts at Christmas time, but
also· to meet recreational needs throughout the year.
Miscellaneous donations are also listed herewith. One of these
deserves special mention, the gift of a complete Western Electric
Talking Picture equipment, from Mount Olive Lodge No. 506. This

145

Lodge, compo ed largely of men in the motion picture industry, has
long been spec1 Hy interested in the children of the Home. It is a
signal achieveme for one Lodge to have made so splendid a gift,
one that will long c~tinue to bring happiness to many children.
