REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE
To the M. '. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
The decision of the Grand Lodge at its last annual communication,
and as matter of economy, to omit the Report on Correspondence from
the proceedings, has p·recluded its preparation. The committee has, however, ventured to write briefly, with hope of bringing within the compass
of a few pages something of the more important trends within the
American craft. There are in the fraternity movements discernible and
influences at work that should be known and estimated by the Brothers
generally, if they are to think and act intelligently in their Lodges.
As might be expected, the continuing period of depression and uncertainty assumes first place in the thought of all. This holds true for the
deliberations of Grand Lodges and the discussions in the constituent
bodies. The whole craft has been injuriously affeeted by the disturbed
conditions, as have all institutions. Revenues have progressively decreased,
as result of unemployment and financial losses reaching to the membership. Economies have been forced, and many activities have suffered. The
problems facing those in places of authority and responsibility are serious
beyond precedent.
There has come, as a consequence of the economic pinches, a great
falling away of membership. Many, timid or uninformed, have expressed
fears not justified by the facts. A survey conducted by the Grand Lodge
of the District of Columbia has discovered that, contrary to the generally

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA '

accepted belief, the suspensions for non-payment of dues do not represent
the largest loss in membership. In other words, the voluntary action of
those who have left the Lodges is responsible for the greatest losses. This
would indicate an inferior class of material gathered during the years of
easy money and consequent carelessness. Therefore, instead of regretting
that such men have left the fraternity, there is cause for congratulation
in that they have voluntarily severed a relationship of no worth to themselves, and the continuance of which would constitute a dead weight to
the Lodges of their membership.
In attempting to cope with the decreasing revenues, many Lodges have
advocated a lowering of dues and fees. In several Grand Lodges this has
been a subject for earnest discussion. But the weight of informed opinion
has been against any effort to place Masonry upon the "bargain counter."
The effect of such cheapening would be, as has been pointed out, to bring
in a new crop of candidates, financially and mentally unfit, thus repeating
the same mistakes that have contributed to the present troubled condition.
The need for strictest economy is apparent in all jurisdictions, and
this phase of the situation is commanding the attention of Brothers best
fitted to deal with such subject. It is realized that there is nothing to be
gained by impulsive or disruptive effort. A clear knowledge of conditions,
as to causes and effects, must precede any beneficial action. Impatience,
natural to those who suffer, must be held in curb, until such time as plans
can be formulated and put into operation.
In the meantime, the old "hit and miss" style of dealing with finances
of the Lodges must be ended, if the Brothers are to have peace of mind
and the sense of solvency in their fraternal relations. It was possible a
few years ago to meet any deficit from the fees. Thus carelessness was
engendered ; dues were allowed to remain unpaid and to accumulate in
amount. The Lodges operating in such manner were unable to meet the
strain to which they were unexpettedly subjecte>d. The demand is ·no'Oll,
however belatedly made, that the dues or other certain income of a Lodge
must be wholly relied upon to cover expenditures, and plans to gain such
desirable end are being worked out in many of the juri§dktions.
The financial troubles of the Lodges have neeessarily affected the
Grand Lodges, and here again economies have been forced because of a
diminution of revenues. To such an extent has such decrease gone that
at least in one jurisdiction (Indiana) the annual communicaticn could not
be held. In several others the annual sessions have been shortooed to the
bare minimum of time required for a hurried transaction of essential
business. In all the governing bodies important services have been threatened, have been cut down or suspended. The great organized charities of
the craft have suffered severely. Faced by ever-increasing demands, and
with diminished revenues, the outlook has in some cases assumed a-perilous
aspect. The particulars in several instances would supply important information, but are beyond scope of this brief writing. A proposal, farreaching and to many minds revolutionary, was put forward by the Grand

Master of Oregon. He would have the Grand Lodge take over the care
and management of all funds of the constituent Lodges. Such proposal
is now presumably before the Brethren for consideration. But it is not
likely to gain acceptance.
These are the darker shades of a picture, that must be brushed in
to accurately portray the situation. There are, however, brighter colors
to be used in a truthful limning of the view. American Masonic Lodges
have not lost heart, nor are the Brothers ceasing intelligent efforts to deal
with troubled conditions. Indeed, it may be said that optimism grows,
based upon well-founded hope of coming betterments. As an example of
the spirit of the craft we quote from the annual address of the Grand
Master of North Dakota-a state in which unprecedented drouth and
crop failures were added to the general difficulties. He could still strike
a hopeful, even a triumphant note, as thus: "We owe much to Masonry,
and should recognize the fact that we cannot uphold the reputation of the
great order by encouraging increase of membership by any lowering of
fees and dues. It appears that we should not become panicky when confronted with financial difficulties, or to the making of concessions to be
regretted later."
·Everywhere clear-.sighted Brothers are finding cause for encouragement, placing reliance upon the solidity of the Masonic character and
having faith in the manhood of America to conquer all difficulties of the
time, and to find out the right even in the confusion of present-day conditions. The losses of membership, startling at first sight of the figures,
can be regarded as a blessing in disguise, in removing from the rosters
the names of many who were not fitted of mind and heart to be of value
to the craft · who could not appreciate the value of the Masonic relationship. The r;nks of true Masons are closing up, with a new determination,
an increased hope and a larger faith in themselves, their fellows and the
future.
Connected with this general subject of financial conditions, is the
matter of life membership, which has assumed importance and been generally discussed. In many of the·older Lodges such permanent exemptions
from dues-paying have been dealt out with lavish hand, for services .real
or imagined, or on account of length of connection, until now such Brothers represent a considerable proportion of the memberships, and the situation has become serious. Again, where the life memberships have been
purchased, too o.ften the amounts thus paid have not been kept separate,
with only the interest used, as was the intention in all cases. As a result
such payments have been spent, and the number of those exempted have
been increased, ·without the countervailing advantage. In the latter cases
the Brothers affected have not been to blame; they have acted in good
faith. The Lodges themselves are derelict; they must suffer for the carelessness of their officers and the culpable negligence of the entire membership. This situation has resulted in new legislation on the part of several
Grand Lodges, designed to correct abuses in the future. Some have

164

165

166

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

proposed to do away with all life memberships, except those actually
purchased at a rate which at current interest would bring in the actual
amount of dues.
A matter that has occasioned considerable debate has to do with the
consolidation of Lodges. One may say that the general expression of
authority is on the side of consolidations, where the bodies are too weak
to stand alone 'in a manner creditable to the fraternity and of worth to
the membershi~s. In the cities it has been found that Lodges were multiplied beyond need. Many of these are living precariously, and some in
sheer desperation have openly solicited candidates against all Masonic
rule, bringing themselves into disrepute and working injury to the good
name of the era ft.
The present ease of travel and the abundant means of transportation,
even in the rural districts, have been almost fatal influences upon the
small and isolated Lodges. Many of these exist only on sufferance of the
authorities, no longer having force or influence in their communities. It
would be to advantage of all concerned if such bodies can be induced to
consolidate at some central and accessi·ble point, with a membership sufficient for real self-support and able to make Masonry respected and
beneficial to the communities they represent.
It must be acknowledged, however, that there is a very real argument
presented by some of these small bodies, in that they have a long and
honorable history, in some cases extending from the earliest pioneer
period. The few members cling to the old name and number, which the
fathers made meaningful. This· natural pride must be taken into account
in any general plan for consolidation. But, as already proven in many
places, a happy adjustment of conflicting claims is possible if the particular
situation is approached with knowledge and sympathy.
One who could come to a survey of Masonry of the day, as nationally
manifested, not being aware of changes in sentiment and practice during
the past decade, would be amazed at the freedom of expression now
allowed on many subjects formerly held as entirely beyond the province
of craft consideration. In Lodges and even in Grand Lodges matters are
brought to the fore that are of the common life and only incidentally
related to Mason.ry. The Brothers refuse to·longer abide in a sterile land,
while the great world of which they and their institution are a part is
concerned with the fate of the nation, the safety of their homes and the
welfare of their children.
But the old conservatism dies hard. California showed the wise and
safe way of progress to many who were eager but doubtful when it openly
espoused the cause of the public schools, .and made its position manifest
by annual observance of Public Schools Week. The voices of those who at
the first were clamorous in protest against such action have strangely
quieted since. More and more vocal are those of other jurisdictions who
believe our course has been amply justified by experience. One other Grand
Lodge (Montana) has copied the California plan, while several others are

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

167

considering a similar course of action. The prophecies of inevitable discord
so confidently uttered a few years ago are no longer heard, and erstwhile
opponents are becoming convinced or have ceased their criticisms.
Such enlarged freedom of expression among Masons has found strong
exponents among the Grand Maste~s. Especially notable is the plain speaking as to the danger from subversive elements tha_t are disturbing the
placidity of those who had believed American institutions were safe
against all assaults. It has been proven that dangerous doctdnes, entirely
alien in form and intention, can make headway among the polyglot masses
of our population, and become a very real peril. There are many Masons
who might formerly have remained silent for fear of breaking the anci~nt
taboo supposed to embrace all practical matters, yet who now recognize
the growing peril, and are warning their Brothers in no uncertain term~.
This is certainly not "politics," within meaning of the time-honored prohibition of the craft; it is the expression of a patriotism that has never been
tacking in the fraternity; it represents the prompting of the instinct of
self-preservation, inherent to every true American, and called forth when
democratic principles are endangered.
In all that is thus said no attempt is made or anticipated that Masons
shall be pledged to any specific course of action, or be urged to join with
this, that or the other group or party to combat real or imagined foes. The
true function of Masonry is and will remain educative, in this as in other
matters. It is certainly within the province of Masonic authorities, competent for the task, to inform their Brethren of dangers threatening t~e
nation, setting forth clearly and dispassionately J:he nature of the pent;
the purposes of those who would subvert or destroy our democracy, and
pointing the duty that should actuate every true American. The Mason
worthy of the name will need no more ; being shown the right he will require no further prompting to do his utmost as 'a man and a patriot. The
fear that apparently lingers in conservative minds, that the craft will be
led from the path of fraternal rectitude into the morasses of partisan
politics, is entirely without foundati on in fact. Not even the most advanced
of Masonic Modernists has any such thought in mind. The same line of
argument holds for other themes that are of engrossing ·interest and even
vital to our institutions. Sooner or tater, in its own defense, Masonry must
come to consideration of matters that concern civic righteousness, moral
betterments and the exaltation of justice among the people.
A most ususual proposal, in this connection, comes from the Grand
Master of Oregon. In an edict recently issued he calls upon the Lodges of
his jurisdiction to purge themselves of any who hold to the tenets of
communism. These, according to the terms of the edict, are to be tried,
and if found guilty, expelled. We doubt the necessity or the wisdom of this
action. To conceive of a Mason who could honestly hold to the doctrines
of communism requires a considerable mental effort; the two things are
diametrically opposed ; wherever communism in any form is dominant,
Freemasonry is actively persecuted and proscribed. Then again, it is doubt-

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

ful whether the average member of a Lodge is ·prepared by knowledge of
the various cults and isms to decide upon the communist character or profession. Radicalism runs through a long range of opinion, from the harmless to the most virulent. It embraces profoundly philosophical theories,
Utopian day drealils, and so through easy gradations to purposes that are
most violently destructive.
At the risk of being accounted tedious in this unusual though altogether inadequate attempt to fill in the gap occasioned by absence of a real
Report on Correspondence, one subject more may be touched upon. Our
Brothers have heard vaguely, mostly from disconnected news dispatches or
interested statements, that Freemasonry is under attack in various countries. Such attacks come from the right of reactionism and the left of
radicalism. While these forces are opposed to each other, and do not in any
casi: act as allies, they find a common object of hatred where Masonry is
concerned. The regrettable conditions in Italy and Germany, where Masonry is proscribed and the Lodges dormant, has seemingly given fresh
impulse to those in other countries who would destroy whatever stands for
freedom of conscience. It is just now doubtful if the comparatively new
but vigorous Masonry of Austria can long survive, as a hostile ecclesiasticism sustaining a weak dictature is dominant in that hard-pressed land.
There is a greater surprise in finding the Grand Lodge "Alpina" of Switzerland preparing to fight for its life. There the referendum has been invoked, in effort to declare the fraternity inimical to the life of the nation
and therefore to be banned. Those having acquaintance with European
Masonry will agree that. the craft of the Swiss republic is high-minded
beyond the common, being foremost in good works, and standing as a model
for strict adherence to the tried principles of the institution.
Nor is the list as yet exhausted. In Greece the Orthodox Church has
lately violently attacked Masonry, using the ancient and long-exploded
argument that in the Lodges a religion is secretly practiced, not according
to the plan of salvation, as interpreted by the ecclesiastics. In Holland, also,
where the Grand Lodge of the Netherlands has long occupied a position of
recognized probity and gained respect of the people, the Synod of the
Evangelical Church launched attack. To this the Brethren wisely opposed
a campaign of education, designed to give information as to the history,
the methods and the purposes of the craft. Books dealing with the fraternity
were placed in the public libraries and the aid of the press invoked. For the
time being, at least, the enemies of Masonry seem to have failed.
In Spain, where the long period of Masonic persecution came to an
end with establishment of the republic, there has been of late a recrudeseence of monarchial and ecclesiastical strength and influence. Again
there are threats of a renewal of espionage and attacks upon the freedom
. of members of the Spanish Lodges, who have certainly not abused their
new-found literty. Similar threats are heard in Portugal.
It is evident that wherever the extreme of radicalism or that other of
fascism has force and reaches to authority, there Freemasonry is doomed.

The re is in this a warning that might be taken to heart even by Masons of
the English-speaking countries, where true freedom still exists, for in these
favored lands there are elements working for the downfall of democratic
government and destruction of all institutions that are for freedom of
thought and liberty under the law.
This brief writing may serve, should it see the light, to give the
Brethren some idea of the subjects of vital importance that are within the
range of Masonic discussion. In another and more prosperous time it is
to be hoped that the Grand Lodge of California will again provide for the
annual reports of this committee, which in years past have contributed to
its high standing among the jurisdictions of the continent.
Jos. E . MoRCOMBE, Chairman.

RESOLUTION
BOARD OF CONTROL
Whereas, at the last annual communication of Grand Lodge, upon
recommendation of the Grand Master, funds were appropriated for the
purpose of defraying the expenses of the chairman of the Board of Control to the biennial convention of the Masonic Relief ·Association of the
United States and Canada, and:
Whereas, in the opinion of the Board of Control, the presence of the
chairman of the board at this convention, not oilly promoted a better understanding by the other jurisdictions of· the United States and Canada, of the
relief problems of our grand jurisdiction, but also has resulted in saving
and conserving the funds of this Grand Lodge; now, therefore, be it
Resolved, that the Board of Control recommend to Grand Lodge that
the Finance Committee, in preparing their 1934-35 budget for Grand Lodge,
include therein $200.00 in the allowance for the Board of Control for the
purpose of defraying the expenses of the chairman of the board to the
1935 convention of the Masonic Relief Association of the United States
and Canada at Fort Worth, Texas.
FRANK M . WrsE,
ROBERT F. CALLENDER,

JAS. R. ERSKINE,
EUGENE ELKUS,

The board held a meeting in San Francisco on January 27, 1934, the
following members being present: W. P. Jeffries, Reynold E. Blight,
Arthur S. Crites, Louis C. Drapeau, Eugene S. Elkus, James T. Fraser,
Robert B. Gaylord, Judge John F. Pullen, David W. Schick, Harry F.
·
White, Leon C. Whitsell.
The main topic for discussion was whether the board should ask the
Brethren throughout this jurisdiction; through the Lodges, for a voluntary contribution to the endowment fund. This was discussed by all of
the members of the board very freely, and the following resolution was
unanimously adopted :

"Resolved, that it is the conviction of the Masonic Homes Endowment Board that the wants of our needy aged Brethren and of
our children, in the Masonic Homes of California, are of sufficient
importance that a solicitation of the craft be made for some contribution toward the endpwment fund during the year 1934; all the
proceeds thereof to be devoted exclusively · to the permanent endowmen~ fund, and.
"Resoh•ed further, that this solicitation be made throughout the
jurisdiction of California during the month of May, 1934, and that
request be made of the Grand Master accordingly, and
"Resolved further, that it be impressed upon the· craft that any
contribution, however small, will be welcome; but that there should
be secured this year for this most worthy object, an average of a
minimum of $2.00 per member."

Sixteen Thousand Contributors
The Secretary of each subordinate Lodge in the jurisdiction was furnished with a duplicate report sheet, one copy of which he was requested
to send to your board with names and addresses of contributors, so that
copy of this report could be mailed to each donor. We are pleased to say
that the great majority of the Lodges have sent in the reports as requested,
and the records show that more than 16,000 Brethren made voluntary
contributions to the endowment fund during the year 1934.
Brother W. C. Hutchison, Master of Temescal Lodge No. 314,
F. & A. M., recently wrote your board as follows: "Our Brother, William
Seymour Davis, passed away August 31, 1934, and in the place of the
usual flowers at the funeral we are sending you a check as a memorial.
This may seem an unusual bequest, but it seems to us that it might be a
fine thing if more of the Lodges would do this in the place of sending
flowers to wilt and be forgotten."
Your board has had many letters, from officers of Lodges as well as
from individual contributors, who feel that the efforts to increase the
endowment fund should not be allowed to lay dormant, and that there
should ·be at least an opportunity given annually, to the Brethren, to
make such contributions. Your board, therefore, offers the following resolution, and recommends its adoption:

"Resolved, that the Masonic Homes Endowment Board be authorized to issue an appeal for voluntary contributions from the membership in this jurisdiction during the month of March, 1935, and
"Be it further resolved, that the officers of the subordinate Lodges
be fraternally requested to mail to all of their members the literature
placed in their hands by the Endowment Board, and to co-operate in
every manner possible to increase the permanent endowment fund of
the Masonic Homes."

Bequests
During the year, your board requested the Secretaries to send n a
list of all attorneys, trust officers and others who customarily entrtain
intimate relations with those preparing wills and other documents r the
distribution of their estates. Practically every Lodge in the State sent in
such a list, which, when compiled, was found to represent apprqkimately
3,000 persons. A letter having been prepared by Brother Gaylorq; member
of your board, setting out the needs for an endowmeht, and a history of
the fund, it was mailed to all persons whose names were submitted.
A number of Brethren, members of the bar, have writtert in, stating
they had put bequests in wills, and in a number of cases, Masonic attorneys
had agreed to draw wills free of charge if a bequest was left to the
Masonic Homes Endowment Fund.
Brother .G. · F. · Conant; a member of Southern California Lodge
No. 278, recently wrote your board in part as follows: "It gives me quite
a little pleasure .to be able to inform you that in the making of the will
of Mrs. Mary Bowman in 1927, I prevailed upon her to leave $5,000.00
to the Masonic Homes, although she was not at all interested in Masonry.
Mrs. Bowman died July 7, 1934, and it will probably take a year to settle
the estate."
Your board desires to impress upoh the Brethren the splendid work
which can be accomplished if they will always keep in mind that the endowment fund can be greatly augmented by bequests in wills, and many times,
even a person who has no Masonic affiliations will leave a bequest where
they know it is going to such a worthy charity as the care of the aged
and the education of orphans.
Many bequests in wills often read "For Masonic Homes" or "For
Covina Home" or "For Decoto Home," without specifying that it go into
the endowment fund. So that Grand Lodge shall definitely establish a policy
of putting into the endowment fund all such bequests, we offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:

"Resolved, that all bequests and donations to the Masonic Homes
of California, or to either the Home at Decoto or the Home at Covina, other than for a specific purpose, shall be trans fer red to the
endowment fund."

Give While You Live
In our recent appeal to the Brethren for voluntary contributions to
the endowment fund, we had a number of inquiries as to whether the
Masonic Homes issued annuity contracts. We found that some of the
Brethren regard annuity gifts as a form of deferred legacy. Many persons
desiring to give wbile they are yet alive, a fund which they wish to make
available at the time of their death, often choose the annuity method. Such
gifts, so long as the donor lives, fr ans fers from the donor to the donee, all
risks and liabilities connected with the safekeeping and investing of the
funds given, and in addition, requires the donee to make stated annual or
quarterly payments to the donor.
Annuity Contracts
More than one hundred non-profit educational, religious and charitable
institutions in the United States are issuing a~nuity contracts.
Several kinds of annuity contracts are in use by insurance companies,
but only two kinds are in common use by organizations writing annuities
for benevolent incomes. These are the Single Life Contract, and the Survivorship Life Contract with annuity payments during the natural life of
the per sov. or persons named in the contract.
Singlf Life Contract-This is the most common form of contract,
and the annuity is only payable to one person during his or her lifetime.
The <1nnuity begins at once and is payable to the annuitant at stated intervals as agreed upon when the contract is issued. The amount of annuity,
the time and place of payment of the annuity and who the annuity is payable to, are clearly designated in the contract.
Survivorship Life Contract-On this form of contract two or more
persons are mentioned as annuitants, and the same rate and time of payment of the annuity is payable by the organization as long as either person
mentioned in the contract shall live. Where there are two people whose
ages are nearly the same, and each one desires to protect. the other with
the annuity payments, this is a popular form of contract. It is usually not
advantageous to have more than two people mentioned in any contract.

Need of an Endowment Fund
One thing quite noticeable this year throughout the Masonic world
has been the difficulty experienced in financing Masonic Homes. The loss
in revenue to Grand Lodges which has occurred because of a falling off
in membership and a lack of new applicants has seriously curtailed the
income for the upkeep of our Homes.
The Masonic Homes of California collected per capita tax from the
subordinate Lodges for the four years ending July 31, as follows:
1931...................................................
on 140,606 Members

A liberal estimate of the number of members on which the tax for
the Homes will be collected for the year ending July 31, 1935, would be
120,000, or a loss of 20,000 members in the last four years, which, at
$1.25, being the amount of the Homes tax, would represent a loss of
income for the sup1>0rt of the Homes of $25,000 annually from that
source alone.

liberal estimate for 1935 would be $50,000. Hence, you. can readily

$130,000 per annum.
The\ only method which your board can suggest is the one for which ·
it was created. That is, to create an. endowment fund to insure the perpetuity of our Masonic Homes: If our endowment fund amounted to
$5,000,000, our membership could decline to one-half the present number
and new applications cease altogether, but our Masonic Homes would still
be assured of almost an everlasting existence.

Appropriation
It will be noted from this report, that your Endowment Board expended, during the year ending July 31, 1934, the sum of $8,194.31. However, more than $2,500.00 of this amount had been contracted for and was
really expended prior to the opening of our campaign for voluntary contributions, so that the actual expenditures during the year, on the campaign,
were approximately $6,000.00. A considerable portion of this amount was
spent on educational work from which it is hoi>ed that many future bequests
will be· secured. The total cash addition to the endowment fund this year
was $60,891.05, so that if no future benefits accrued to the endowment
fund, the cost of raising the money secured this year was approximately
10 per cent.
The Constitution of Grand Lodge, under which your Board was
created, prohibits the use, for expenses, of any of the moneys which are
·contributed to the endowment fund. Therefore, if this work of materially
increasing the endowment fund is to go forward, a substantial appropriation should be made by Grand Lodge at this session.
We offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption :
"Resolved, that the sum of $6,000.00 be and is hereby appropriated.
from the funds of this Grand Lodge, to be paid to the Masonic Homes
Endowment Board for their expenses for the year ending July 31,
1933."

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON NECROLOGY
Organ solo, "Asa's Death," from Peer Gynt Suite, Grand Organist.
"I wiil lift up mine eyes uri.to the hills, from whence cometh my
help.
My help cometh from the Lord, which made heaven and earth.
The Lord is thy keeper : the Lord is thy shade upon thy right
hand.
The sun shall not smite thee. by day, nor the moon by night.
The Lord shall preserve thee from all evil : he shall preserve
thy soul.
The Lord shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from
this time forth, and even for evermore."

195

Once again we pause in our deliberations to pay tri'bute to the memory
of those members of the Grand Lodge who have completed their duties
on earth and have .experienced the great adventure.
One hundred sixty-three members of Grand Lodge answered the call
of the Supreme Ruler since the last report of your committee and are
now numbered with that ever increasing majority in the supreme Grand
Lodge which no time can close.
Many of these departed Brethren were leaders in Masonry and in the
communities in which they lived. Time will not ·permit even a brief statement of the manifold services performed• by many of them to California ·
Masonry and to the public at large.
Our sympathies and words of encouragement go out to the members
of Pomona Lodge No. 246 and to Garvanza Lodge No. 492, these Lodges
having suffered the loss of their respective Masters.. We know of no
greater hardship a Lodge can endure than to have its program disrupted
by the loss of its Master.
Your committee would feel that it had not performed its duty, however, if some mention were not made of a few of the departed who have
performed long and faithful services for the Grand Lodge.
Two of our Past Grand Masters have been taken from our midst,
George F. Rodden and Gustav A. Hutaff, and also our greatly beloved
Grand Lecturer, Thomas J. Baker. The Grand Master has appointed lifelong friends of these Brethren to give us a detailed report of their
services, which will be heard later on this program.
Grand Lodge and the Hawaiian Islands experienced a great loss in
the passing of John T. Moir, Past Master of Kilauea ·Lodge No. 330.
His life history is one of fraternal and community service. We regret
that we are unable to give it in full. We will, however, give a sketch of
his Masonic career. He was raised to the sublime degree of Master
Mason in Montrose Kilwining Lodge No. 15 of 6cotland in June, 1880,
demitting to St. Johns Lodge No. 15' of Stonehaven, Scotland, shortly
thereafter. In 1896, after residing in the Hawaiian Islands for eight
years, he again demitted and became a charter member of Kilauea Lodge
No. 330, being installed Master of his Lodge December 23, 1901, and
served Grand Lodge as Grand Sword Bearer in 1931. In addition to his
symbolic Masonry he received all of the Scottish Rite degrees, both
honorary and otherwise, and was Almoner at the time he passed to his
reward.
Corona Lodge No. 324 reports the passing of Brother Lemuel L.
Test. Brother Test was Master of his Lodge in 1907, and later served
Grand Lodge as Inspector for eighteen years, resigning in 1926. His
place will be hard to fill in Pasadena Masonry.
The list of our departed Brethren is as follows:

It is eminently proper and appropriate that we pause and pay our
respects to those Brethren who have laid down the working tools of the
craft and answered the final summons. They have finished the work that
was given them to do. No 1>9wer of friendship or fraternal affection can
bring them back.
.
It is difficult to comfort ourselves when we realize that we will not
again take these Brethren by the hand or listen to their friendly words of
greeting; But the memory of our association with them remains-this, at
least, can not be taken from us. ·And so, in the same spirit in which we
delighted to recognize their virtues while they were with us, let us honor
them in death, and
Weep not that their toils are over;
Weep not that their race is run;
God grant that we may rest as calmly
When our work, like theirs, is done.

WM. H. PARCELS,

J. KARL LoBDELL,

In Memoriam George Frederick Rodden
Grand Master 1920:21
By Kent J . C. Sey1I1-0ur, Inspector, Fifty-first D istrict
A dearly beloved member of ·o ur order passed to eternal rest March 8,
1934. His cheery smile, toss of head so characteristic, friendly handclasp
and hearty greeting are missed 'sadly today.
·
Brother Rodden, our fifty-fourth Grand Master, was a native of California, born at Montezuma, Tuolumne county, December 24, 1867. His
father, George Rodden, a native of Vermont, came to California during
the gold rush of 1851 and in 1864 married Caroline Thornton of Cincinnati, Ohio. Four children were born of this union, of whom George Frederick was the second.
Acquiring the rudiments of his education in his native town, Brother
Rodden later attended high school in the city of San Francisco. Entering
the University of California, from which institution he had the distinction
of being the youngest graduate in its history, he finished his course of
studies · in the year 1887, too young to receive his degree,. that of Doctor
of Dental Surgery, which degree was conferred after he had attained his
majority. He entered upon the practice of his chosen profes~ion in San
Francisco, in 1888, which remained continuous there until rhis death. His
home was in the city of San Rafael.
He was married in 1910 to Amy Elizabeth Jackson of Chicago. They
were blessed with two children, Amy Carolyn and George Frederick, Junior.
Thus was engendered a home of love, culture and refinement.
To the family so sadly stricken by the passing of the husband and
father, we extend our tender love and sympathy. A natural leader, Brother
Rodden gave much of his time and energy to the civic, social and cultural
life of his community. lri 1915 he was elected to the City Council of San
Rafael, and in 1919 he was chosen mayor of the municipality, serving
always with dignity and with full realization of the responsibility of public
trust. A lover and student of music, he had for years an important part
in the musical development of the community. He was one of the leaders
in establishing the Marin Junior College at Kentfield. Elected a member
of the first Board of Trustees, he served continuously as vice-president
until his death. Serving with steadfast purpose, he lived to see this institution develop into what is recognized as an important unit of our State
public schools system
It seems natural that Freemasonry should attract him and have his
earnest and enthusiastic support.
He was initiated in Marin Lodge No. 191 on the 8th day of October,
1898, passed to the degree of Fellowcraft on the 12th day of October, 1898,
and raised to the sublime degree of Master Mason on the 19th day of
October, 1898, a period of eleven days.

•

204

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

He was elected Master of his Lodge in 1902, making his first appearance in Grand Lodge in 1903, at which time Grand Master Nutting appointed him to serve as Gr-and Marshal. He was again appointed in 1904.
In 1904 he was appointed Inspector of the district comprising Marin
county and the southern half of Sonoma county, which position he held
until his election as Junior Grand Warden in 1917. His service as Inspector was one of his important contributions to our beloved institution.
His interpretation of our esoteric work was of such nature as to express
its beauty in graceful, impressive and intelligent manner. During his incumbency as Inspector he originated the scheme of a general participation
of all the Brethren of the jurisdiction in the effort to raise a million dollars
for the endowment fund of our Masonic Homes, which will eventually be
accomplished.
His first committee assignment in Grand Lodge was in 1905 as a
member of the Committee on Returns. In 1914 he was appointed chairman
of the very important Committee on Finance, which position he ably filled
until 1917. He was a member of the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes from 1917 to 1934.
He was a member and the first High Priest of Marin Chapter No. 102,
R. A. M., and a member of California Commandery No. 1, Knights
Templar. He was an active participant in the forming of the Marin Mutual
Benefit Association of Masons, serving as president from its inception until
his death.
A kindly, gracious Grand Master, withal a forceful one, his achievements are written deeply in the hearts of the thousands of loyal Masons
of the jurisdiction of California, that came first to know him and then
to love him.
One quite unusual association resulted from his visit as Grand Master
to Washington Lodge No. 20, on which occasion he acted as Master during
the rendering of the third degree by the Past Masters of that Lodge.
Thereafter each year up to and including the year 1933, the custom was
maintained, the event being termed Rodden Night.
His address to Grand Lodge in 1921, of graceful and expressive diction, was comprehensive; so much so that it will remain an important contribution to Grand Lodge annals.
Though serving loyally in the ranks for some thirteen years thereafter, his year as Grand Master was the culmination of that love for, as
well as devotion to our beloved institution, that had been evidenced from
the time of his first step in Masonry. Masonry is the richer by reason of
his service. The writer would feel remiss, indeed, were he not to express
the obligations he owes to this friend, by reason of almost daily contact
with him for more than thirty years, during which time they were closely
associated in civic and fraternal affairs.
As Masons we profess a profound belief in an all-wise, just and
living God. May we not, therefore, look upon that which we term Death

\

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

205

as the ~thway to Immortal Life, and thus, with full confidence, feel that
this dev('1:ed son, loving husband and father, just and loyal friend and
Brother, has safely traversed it and is at home in his Father's House.

In Memoriam Gustav Albert Hutaff
October 5, 1879-0ctober 17, 1933
By Will H. Fischer, Past Grand Master
The Most Worshipful Gustav Albert Hutaff, Past Grand Master of
Masons in California, passed from this life on October 17, 1933, four days
after the close of our last annual communication. As had been his custom
for many years, Brother Hutaff attended Grand Lodge. He was evidently
a very sick man. At parting, we spoke words of encouragement to him
and bade him be of good cheer ; but even as we did so our hearts were
heavy, for we knew we were saying farewell.
When he surrendered the gavel of o.ffice to his successor in October,
1929, Grand Master Hutaff appeared to be in excellent health and destined
for a long life. In the following year, however, his wife, to whom he had
given his adoration from early youth, passed to the Great Beyond, and
his grief came to him with a shock from which he seemed unable to rally.
In course illness came to him in the form of an internal malady requiring
extensive surgical procedure. Thereafter, although he went his way among
men and attended to his various duties with the scrupulous care so characteristic of him, excruciating pain harassed him constantly. Gradually his
fine physique yielded to the inevitable forces of physical decline. The end
came as a desired and welcome release.
Gustav Albert Hutaff was born at Santa Rosa, California, on October 5, 1879, the son of Henry Hutaff, a native of Alsace-Lorraine, and
Maria Rebecca Atover Hutaff, a native of Hanover, Germany. Henry
Hutaff first came to California in 1860. Subsequently he went to Germany,
married, and with his bride returned to make his home here permanently.
To this pioneer couple four children were given, two daughters and two
sons. John Harry Hutaff, now residing in Alameda, is the sole survivor.
When Gustav Albert, or "Gus" as we always knew him, was a lad of
about six summers, the family moved from Santa Rosa to San Francisco.
The growing boy attended Horace Mann and John Everett grammar
schools. One of his classmates, as he passed through the grades, was Alberta Moller, daughter of another German family which had come, before
her birth, from Hamburg to make their home in San Francisco. An
imperishable love budded in these two youthful hearts, as sweet, as trusting, and as pure as ever existed between lad and maid. The romance continued, and years later, in 1904, the young couple exchanged the vows of
holy matrimony. The issue of the union was a daughter, Helen, whom

/

206

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

they worshipped and in whom were united the fine attributes
both
parents. Helen now resides in Berkeley.
By the' time Gus Hutaff was ready to enter high school th of his
parents had died, leaving him as his heritage his character, his industry
and his ambition. Determining to complete his education he found employment in a drug store conducted by D. H. Wulzen. He lived with the
Wulzen family, attended high school by night and worked in the store by
day. Still working his way, he entered the College of Pharmacy, University of California. Shortly before completing the course, the SpanishAmerican War having broken out, he decided that he owed his services to
his country. On May 21, 1898, he enlisted as a hospital steward in the
Eighth Army Corps and went to the Philippine Islands. He was honorably discharged June 21, 1899, after having been decorated three times
for meritorious action. He returned from the Islands, resumed his studies
and was graduated with honors, the youngest member of his class, receiving the degree of Ph. G. in 1900.
After graduation he procured a position in. a dr.ug store at Dunsmuir.
He worked hard, practiced thrift and subsequently purchased the store,
which he sold in 1919, He also engaged in the jewelr:ir business for several
years. Meanwhile, in 1910 he had been elected a director of the State .
Bank of Dunsmuir. In 1913 he was advanced to a vice-presidency and in
1916 was elected president, in which position he remained until 1927, when
the bank was sold to the United Security Bank and Trust Company, which
later became a branch of the Bank of America. Remaining with the institution, Brother Hutaff was chairman of the local board of directors, and
vice-president, until he resigned in 1931.
Brother Hutaff was initiated an Entered Apprentice Mason on September 26, 1901 ; passed to the degree of Fellowcraft October 17, 1901,
and raised to the sublime degree October 24, 1901, in Dunsmuir Lodge
No. 297. He served his Lodge as Marshal, Deacon, Secretary, Treasurer,
Warden and Master. For sixteen years he was an Inspector, serving the
Siskiyou mountain Lodges. Among them his memory will live as a tradition. He was a constant attendant upon Grand Lodge, serving as chairman
of the Pay of Members Committee. He was later a member of the Finance
Committee.
He was elected Junior Grand Warden in October, 1925; Senior Grand
Warden in 1926, Deputy Grand Master in 1927 and Grand Master in 1928.
To each of these offices, and especially to that of Grand Master he gave
to the limit of his ample abilities.
·
In addition to ,these Masonic affiliations and ·distinctions Brother
Hutaff was a member of Cyrus Chapter No. 15, R. A. M. ; Mount Shasta
Commandery No. 32, Knights Templar; Sacramento Consistory, Scottish
Rite, 32°, K. C. C.H.; Ben Ali Temple, A. A. 0. N. M. S., Sacramento.
He was also a Past Patron of the Eastern Star and a member of the
Sciots.

\

ln '{msiness Brother Hutaff was energetic, courteous, painstaking and
honest. ~ his family life he was a husband and father who gave always
a loyal an'IJ abundant love. In Masonry he was the unfailing friend, counselor and ~rvant of the craft. No distance was too gre~t to be traversed,
no storm coUJd dismay, no excuse could stay him when the call to service
came from his Brethren of the little Lodges of the Siskiyous. As a Grand
Master he upheld the high traditions of his exalted office. He walked
humbly in the way of honor, with duty as his guide.
Apart frcm these concerns his greatest joy was in the out-of-doors:
. He rejoiced to commune with nature and found delight in all her elements
and moods. His spirit responded to the challenge of the sea and sky. He
was moved by the miracle of the return of seasons. He found pleasure in
the sight of growing crops, or herds browsing in a meadow. He knew the
wild creatures of the hills and was their friend. He knew where trout
lurked in the sparkling streams. And always he turned for inspiration to
the beautiful mountains of the Northland. We who loved him well believe
they imparted to his spirit a measure of their might and majesty.

In Memoriam Thomas J. Baker
By Dana R. Weller, Past Grand Master
Thomas John Baker, for more than a quarter of a century our efficient
and beloved Grand Lecturer, laid aside his earthly working tools on the
27th day of December, 1933, and has taken his seat among the immortals
in the Celestial Lodge above. While we bow in humble submission to the
w~!l of the Supreme Grand Master, we pause for a time to pay loving
tribute to the memory of this good man and Mason, whose life was
devoted to the service of the fraternity and whose work has indelibly
stamped its imprint upon the pages of the history of this Grand Lodge,
as well as upon the tablets of our memory.
Brother Tom was the best-known and best-loved Mason in the State
of .California. In every city and town in the State where a Lodge existed
he was at home among friends. To his schools flocked the Masons of th~
jurisdiction to receive from him those necessary instructions in order to
pass them on to others, and thus to preserve and perpetuate the landmarks
of our institution. While he labored diligently in his chosen field the work
was his greatest pleasu;e. No distance was too great or any ~ommunity
too small to command his attendance and.kindly advi_ce and assistance.
Due to his wide acquaintance and his intimate knowledge of the many
local problems arising from time to time, he was an invaluable aid to the
several Grand Masters with whom he served. By them his courtesy and
unfailing loyalty will not be forgotten.

I
208

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

/

His untiring zeal and devotion merited and received the aprobation
of his Brethren, and our faith justifies us in the belief that he }fas found
favor at the hands of the Almighty Father, the aflluence of 'fhose love
/
embraces all of His children.
Thomas John Baker was born on the 10th day of O)"°ber, 1864, in
Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. He was married to Jessie Florence Schepp on
October 10, 1904, at Sacramento, California.
He was initiated in Union Lodge No. 58, at Sacramento, on January 13, 1897, passed January 27, 1897, and raised April 14, 1897; served
as Senior Deacon of his Lodge in 1898; elected Junior Warden December 5, 1898, and Master December 4, 1899. He served as Inspector of the
Eighteenth District in 1902 and 1903. He was Secretary of his Lodge from
1902 to 1907.
In Grand Lodge he served as Junior Grand Steward in 1901, and as
Senior Grand Deacon in 1905 and 1906. He was elected Grand Lecturer
October 11, 1907, and retained the office until his death.
This brief resume of dates and offices represents but a brief sketch
of a life filled with action and accomplishment, and devotion. The complete story of these is safely recorded in every Mason's heart, and the
lapse of time will not erase them from our memories.
Tom, we shall miss you as the years pass by: May our Heavenly
Father grant that when our time shall come to enter that sanctuary, it
shall be our privilege to meet and greet you as in the days of yore I

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON GRAND
LECTURER'S REPORT
To the 111:.

w:.

Grand Lodge of California :
Your Committee on .the Report of the Grand Lecturer submits the
following:
We fully approve the commendation set forth therein of Past Grand
Lecturer Thomas J. Baker. It is true he enjoyed a great circle of friends
among our membership, and we all keenly miss him. His memory we will
fondly cherish.
Since May 1, 1934, the ritual has been taught under what is known
as the new plan of the Grand Master. We heartily commend Grand Lecturer Foster G. Dyer and his Deputies, Sidney K. Lehman, Chester H.
Warlow and Leslie E. Wood, and Past Grand Master Dana R. Weller for
their careful and detailed review and rechecking of our ritual. Beneficial
results are bound to come from the combined effort of such conscientious
endeavor. We congratulate the Grand Lecturer on the co-operation he has
secured from the Inspectors in administering the new plan. Progress and
development can only come through trial and experimentation. We feel
the present arrangement is entitled to a fair trial.
We join in the strong indorsement of District Officers' Associations
made by the Grand Lecturer. As he stated, "In sections where these meetings have been held regularly, the officers and Inspectors have shown a
sincere interest in Masonry, and real progress is being made in the development and the training of the Brethren in the administrative as well as the
ritualistic work of the Lodges. The Inspectors are to be highly commended
for their efforts in behalf of these group meetings, the object of which is

210

I

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

the development of more proficient officers and better Lodges.'.'
strongly indorse the thought of setting forth practical Lodge oblems,
as well as those concerning Masonic law, in th,e examination q stions of
the officers.
There is no question but what the ritual is the keystonf to the Masonic structure; therein is set forth the very principles of our fraternity.
Its perfection must be maintained. We concur in the thought of all questions of ritual and Masonic law being handled through the Inspectors.
As to the condition of Lodges, and their more active participation in
present-day social and economic questions, may we urge a more active
contact between the Grand Lodge officers and their executive districts for
the proper guidance in these activities. Their experiences and wider contacts will be of real benefit to the Brethren of constituent Lodges. They,
too, are in a position to keep the Brethren informed of Grand Lodge activities, its problems and of all subjects vital to the craft.
Under the present administration a considerable saving in money has
been effected, and all are to be commended for this accomplishment.
In the hands of this cabinet of the Ritual Committee, the Grand Lecturer and the Deputy Grand Lecturers, we feel our ritual can be safely
entrusted during the coming year.
ARTHUR E. OVERTON,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON EDUCATION
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
During the past year the subject of Masonic education has again
been under review. The resolution of Grand Lodge at its last communication, adopted pursuant to the report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes, directed a consideration of "the means and methods of
supplementing the ritualistic instruction now given the candidate," considering "only such methods as may be adopted voluntarily by the Lodge and
the candidate, attempting to arrive at some standard practi,ce which can
be used by all Lodges desiring to adopt the plan.''
Inasmuch as the formulation of such a plan as above referred to is a
difficult undertaking, it is felt that .before such work is initiated, that
Grand Lodge should definitely determine whether or not a plan for Masonic
education should be adopted. That if the decision on such question be in
the affirmative, it would then be in order for steps to be taken toward the
presentaticn of a plan.
In order that such questions may properly come before this communication, it is recommended :

\

\

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

211

1. Tpat Gr.and Lodge adopt a plan for Masonic education, which plan
shall con111rise the means and methOcls of supplementing the ritualistic
instruction ~ow given the candidate and attempt to arrive at some standard
practice whkh can be used by all Lodges voluntarily desiring to adopt
such plan.
2. That if recommendation No. 1 above set forth .be adopted by this
communication of Grand Lodge, that the Grand Master be authorized and
directed to appoint a committee for the purpose of formulating such plan,
said committee to report to the next annual communication and present
such plan for consideration at such time.
3. That the sum of $500.00 be appropriated for the use of such committee under the direction of the Grand Master.
Respectfully submitted,
IRVING MAGNES, Chairman.

"t will state that the contract for the building has been let for
$44,566.50, and is approximately two-thirds completed at the present
time. We have in cash and pledges by the members of the Visalia
Masonic Lodges approximately $40,000.00. The stock is to be all owned
by the different Masonic bodies which meet in Visalia, except one
share each which is held by the directors and endorsed so that it will
go to their successors, and when completed the building will be owned
entirely by the Masonic bodies and not by any individual, and no
repayment of any moneys paid by members for the construction of
the building is to be made, but is given entirely as a donation. We hope
to have the building entirely paid for when completed, but in my
opinion we will not owe more than $5,000.00 under any circumstances."
Mt. Shasta Lodge No. 281, F. & A. M., situated at Anderson: This
Lodge was given permission to borrow $2,000.00 for a period of ten years,
same to be paid off at the rate of $200.00 per year, for the purpose of .
remodeling their building.
Alta Loma Lodge No. 643, F. & A. M., situated at Signal Hill: On
March 6, 1934, this Lodge was given permission to enter into a lease with
the Brayton Brothers for a period of five years, at a monthly rental of
$75.00, or a total of $4,500.00, for the entire upper floor, and a room on
the street floor to be used fc.r social purposes, of a building to be erected
by them in Signal Hill.
Brother Goldman, member of your committee, inspected the building
and the lease, which we considered satisfactory.
Fillmore Lodge No. 3i9, F. & A. M., situated at Fillmore: On
June 1, 1934, this Lodge was given permission to purchase $2,000.00 of
stock in the Fillmore Masonic Temple Association, with the understanding
that after the purchase they have on hand sufficient funds to pay Grand
Lodge dues.
Laurel Lodge No. 245, F. & A. M., situated at Willows : On July 23,
1934, this Lodge was given permission to purchase ten shares of stock, of
a par value of $100.00, in the Willows Masonic Temple Association.
Their statement showed that they had on hand $1,705.00, and that the
dividend on the stock. already owned would bring their balance. up to

$2,000.00 as of August 10; also, that their Grand Lodge dues would not be
more than $300.00. The temple association had outstanding 50 shares of
common stock and 300 shares of preferred stock, of which Laurel Lodge
No. 245 owned all of the outstanding common stock and 158 shares of
preferred stock.

212

213

Anah1im. Lodge No. 207, F. & A. M., situated at Anaheim: On
March 26, 1934, th is Lodge was given permission to purchase two shares
of stock of the Anaheim Masonic Temple Association, a t $100.00 per
share, which is par, from a member of the Lodge.
It was reported that the stock had paid 6% dividend during the past
eight years, that the total number of shares issued was 470, and that the
Lodge was the owner of 284 shares.
Masonic Temple Association of Fruitvale, situated at Fruitvale: On
October 27, 1933, this association was given permission to increase the
authorized capital of the association from $25,000.00, represented by 5000
shares of common stock at $5.00 per share, to $100,000.00, represented by
15,000 shares of class "A" common stock at $5.00 per share; thereafter,
to exchange present common stock of the association for new class "B"
common stock, share for share, and to sell the class "A" stock to net the
association $5.00 per share, with the provision that the proceeds would be
used only to reduce the mortgage debt, or to retire benefit certificates.
Your committee felt that, by following this method, they would transfer from a fixed, interest-bearing debt on their notes and an obligation to
pay certificates on the death of the holder, to stock which would pay dividends only if, as and when earned. .
Montebello Lodge No. 451, F. & A . M., situated at Montebello: On
February 27, 1934, permission was given to this. Lodge to purchase all of
the furniture, furnishings and equipment owned by the Montebello Masonic
Temple Association and to pay for the same by assuming the notes held
by members and others, in the total sum of $3,925.00.
Correspondence was also had with the following Lodges: Searchlight
Lodge No. 567, F. & A. M., situated at Long Beach; Lancaster Lodge
No. 437, F. & A. M., situated at Lancaster; Azure Lodge No. 533,
F. & A. M., situated at Fullerton; Bellflower Lodge No. 523, F . & A. M.,
situated at Bellflower; Bakersfield Masonic Temple Association, situated
at Bakersfield. However, no permission was granted for the expenditure
of any funds
Your committee has received full co-operation from all the officers of
the Lodges, in their effort to comply with both the spirit and letter of
the Constitution governiiig the investment of funds and building of Masonic temples.
WILLIAM P. JEFFRIES, Chairman;
W ILLIAM P. FILMER,
HERBERT C. GOLDMAN,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON RETURNS'
The depression is still with us, as evidenced by the net loss of membership for the year of 4363, which is 421 more than last year. But we
do not think the loss of Masons has been as great as the loss of membership. These trying times have given the Lodges a chance to weed out many
who have been members only. The total of membership is 132,331, which
shows a loss for the year of 4363. Yet there are some elements of consolation, as the following figures will show:

1933

1934

Initiations ................................1810
2098-A gain of 288
Passed ...................................... 1897
1991-A gain of 94
Raised ......................- .............. 1997
1898-A loss of 99
Restored .................................. 302
477-A gain of 175
The number of withdrawals has been fewer. ·There have been more
suspended for non-payment of dues, but against that we have the necessity
of remitting the dues of 536 Jess than last year. But the number of members who have had their dues remitted has reached the large total of 7368.
It is to be hoped that the Lodges will be very careful in their selection
of material for membership, neither their eagerness for work nor. their
need of funds influencing them · in selecting anything but the best.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

REPORT OF TRUSTEES, U. C. BERKELEY
CLUB HOUSE
To the M.". W.". Grand Lodge of California:
The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Club of the University of
California, Inc. submits herewith the audit of the books o{ the organizatkm
for the past Masonic year, together with the proposed budget for the
year 1934-35.
Little of importance out of the ordinary has occurred during the past
year of sufficient interest to take up the time of this Grand Lodge. The
club has continued to function in harmony and with efficiency. The financial condition of many of the young people has improved, but for many
others the year at the University would have been distressful and discouraging had it not been for the advantages of fellowship and association
offered by the club.
Mrs. J. H. Quinn, the hostess at the institution, has been a steadying
and helpful influence to the large number of our young people who use
the facilities of the club. The officers of the university continue to speak
in the highest terms of commendation of the work of the institution.
The Board of Trustees offer one suggestion to our Masonic Brethren
throughout the State, and that is this: It would be most helpful if advance
information, so far as possible, <:ould be given to the Masonic Club prior
to the date of registration in August for the new term at the university.
Although every effort is made by the student committees having in charge·
the matter of seeking out students of Masonic affiliation, numbers of them
are not contacted. Some of the students appear diffident about making
themselves known, although every facility is offered for that purpose. Consequently, if our Masonic Brethren could inform the club in advance of
the arrival of members of their families, it would be of much assistarn:e
in making every possible contact, particularly with the new students.
The proposed budget for the ensuing year, substantially the same as
the past year, has been submitted to the Finance Committee for its approval.
WILLIAM H. WASTE, President.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON HISTORY
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California :
Your Committee on Masonic History begs leave to submit the following report:
During the past year your committee 11as continued its research work
and has obtained much additi onal data and information necessary and
essential to a complete History of Masonry in California.
We have visited numerous constituent Lodges, checking and verifying
facts contained in Lodge committee reports, and have discovered and

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

229

preserved much interesting source material not heretofore contained· in
our files. We have investigated 'the personal and Masonic activities of many
pioneer Masons whose history had escaped the scrutiny of local committees
and of our investigators, and we feel that the immense amount of illuminating material obtained has fully justified the efforts and time expended
in this branch of our work.
We have recently obtained from the Grand Lodge of Iowa a comprehensive history of one Masonic Brother who played a most conspicuous
part in Masonry, not only in California but also 1n the state of Oregon.
We refer to Brother Berryman Jennings. The additional history of this
distinguished Brother thus obtained will enable your committee to more
correctly ·i nterpret his personal and Masonic activities, some of which
have heret,o fore placed him in a rather unfavorable light.
We have also obtained much long-sought-for information with respect
to Brother John Bidwell which we think will fully clear up some doubtful
points and shed much light upon this colorful Masonic character. We have
fully co11;1pleted our studies of the activities of the eight distinguished
Brothers who played so important a part in the formation of the California
Constitution in 1849. We are at present pursuing our research into the lives
of all Brethren of the craft who were members of the Constitutional Convention of 1879. These studies when finally completed should enable us to
tell the full story of the part Masons played in the establishment of constitutional government in this State.
The members of your committee have, during the past year, visited
numerous Lodges, assisting local History Committees in completing their
reports and directing them in additional investigations.
Your committee has, during the past year, interviewed a number of
fifty-year Masons and obtained from them many interesting details of
their Masonic experiences and numerous historical incidents connected
with their eventful lives. There still remains a large number of fifty-year
Masons whose life's story has not been prepared, and we earnestly request
the officers of constituent Lodges to undertake the task of immediately
interviewing all of their older members and to send to the committee their
stories and experiences.
We also desire to respedfully urge all Lodge History Committees
which have not forwarded to us their reports, to redouble their efforts and
send in the information at once. This is imperative if they desire the. data
included in the forthcoming historical publication.
At the 1931 annual communication, Grand Lodge ii1structed your committee to gather the historical facts and prepare a Masonic play having
for its purpose the portrayal of the lives and activities of Masons who
played a leading part in the pioneer history and development of northern
California. The committee accordingly collected the necessary data and
information and procured the services of Brother Jesse M. Whited, who
wrote the play. It was the intent of the committee to present this play at

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the following session of Grand Lodge. Just prior to the meeting of Grand
Lodge in 1932, the distinguished Brother of the craft who°had undertaken
the presentation of the play was suddenly stricken ill and died. In the very
limited time left, it was not deemed advisable to present the play at that
communication. This play has since been revamped, greatly improved and
will be presented to the members of Grand Lodge and their ladies at the
Scottish Rite Temple on Wednesday evening, October 10, 1934. The play
bears the .title, "The Never-Sweats of Rooptown." You will see and hear
Brothers in the cast representing Peter Lassen, Isaac Roop, Rough Elliott
and Captain Hill, all Masons, and that friend of the white man, Chief
Winnemucca. It is a ·purely historical presentation of the actual events in
which these pioneer Masons took part. It is a true interpretation of the
interesting phases of the lives of these characters in what is now known
as Susanville. These men lived their Masonry. It was a very important
factor in the stirring events of the Honey Lake valley. These Masons
were preeminent in the civilization of that interesting part of our State.
Your committee feels that there is much work yet to be done in piecing
together the full story of Masonry in California and that a continuation of
the committee during the coming year is fully justified and advisable.
We therefore recommend that the History Committee be continued
during the ensuing Masonic year.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
WEEK ON FIFTEENTH ANNUAL OBSERVANCE
To the M:. w:. Gra11d Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The story of the Fifteenth Annual' Observance of Public Schools
·Week ca1)not be told in a report of this character. Only the reports
from the Lodges and the newspaper clippings would convey anything
l'ike an adequate idea of the extent and scope of our latest observance,
and of what was accomplished.
In referring to the local observance in a city in which Public
Schools Week has been for several years an outstanding success, one
of the newspapers characterized it as "reaching a new ·peak" and
"transcending all previous observances in the number and elaborateness of the programs." And this was true of the observance generally
throughout the state.
This year's unprecedented success is easily accounted for. In the
first place, the reports from the Lodges indicate that this year there
was a more general compliance than ever before by the local committees in charge of the arrangements with the suggestions emanating
from our committee, and which are of course based on past experience; and particularly with respect to the advisability of making
evident in every way possible the fact that the observance of Public
Schools Week is not a Masonic event, but a community affair. And
there were innumerable instances in which it would appear that every
civic organization in the community had joined in the observance.
This, however, was only one of the reasons for the success
achieved. And perhaps more than any other was the nation-wide
situation with respect to public education and the publicity which has
been given it.
Our schools have been receiving during the last few years more
attention than was ever before given them by the public at large.
This awakened interest began with the problem of increased taxes and
declining values; and there was .developed what seemed to be a
hostile attitude in certain quarters toward a continuance of the opportunities being offered by the modern school. Under the plea of the ne'\
cessity for a retrenchment in public expenditures, an effort was made
to so materially reduce the appropriation for the support of the schools
as would seriously cripple them. And there was implanted in the minds
of even friends of public education a doubt as to whether or. not the
criticism· which was being directed against the schools was justified.
The people wanted information with respect to their schools; and the
observance of Public Schools Week furnished a good opportunity to
obtain it. .The situation was admirably expressed in an editorial in a
newspaper which has always given enthusiastic support to our observance, and from which we quote the following:

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

235

"The depression with its accompanying realization that the
tax burden has grown too rapidly and that it has reached dangerous proportions has caused the people to believe that public
education has now reached a 'stock taking time'- a time when
the tendency toward expansion, experiment and innovation that
has been evident in recent years will be discontinued while our
educational system is carefully examined to determine what of the
new is valuable and what is non-essential. ...
"Public Schools Week can well serve to acquaint the public
with what their schools are doing so that they can then more
properly judge how much value they receive-from the tax dollars
they invest."
With a knowledge of the existing condition, the school people
were especially active this year in providing the opportunity Public
Schools Week is expected to furnish; and there were teachers who
never before had taken the interest in the observance which it would
be assumed they should, but who were this year indefatigable in
their efforts to bring home to the people a knowledg~ of what was
being actually done in the schools.
In this connection we quote from a report received from a County
Superintendent of Schools who has from the first sensed the value of
our observance, and has materially contributed to its success:
"Probably never in the history of our schools until this
Spring did the teachers sense so deep a need for and give
expression to so real an interest in the program of that week.
The educational crisis of 1933 at Sacramento awakened the classroom teacher to a more direct responsibility toward bringing the
home and the school into a closer relationship. From all reports
the next session in 1935 will mark an intense fight for the maintenance of school needs, so the teachers are endeavoring to
inform the public of conditions as they exist today and to point
otit the needs for tomorrow. I credit that state of ' teacher mind'
as being one of the reasons for the interest taken in Public
Schools Week in our county. Then, too, the parents have been
aroused by speakers and the press to seek to know their schools
better, and last but not least the observance year after year has
grown to such proportions that the thought originally behind the
program is now being realized. . . .
"In summing up our program, I might say that we emphasized more than ever t he personal contact between parent and
teacher to the end that the child might be better understood by
both the home and the school. In certain districts, every teacher
made a 'home call,' during that week. We took our boys and girls
to many of the service clubs during the luncheon hour to enter-

236

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

tain and at the same time instruct the members. Of course we had
Open House, exhibits, and afternoon and evening programs. One
new idea was the Science Fair ....
"No doubt in every county in California teachers, children
and parents were brought together under similar conditions so
our week was in many respects like all others. However, it is ~ith
a deep feeling in my own heart of appreciation that I recall . all
that was accomplished in the cities and in the rural schools and I
look forward to next year when we shall be able to do even more
than we have in the past.... "
Not only was there this year a greater public interest than ever
before in the local programs, but the observance itself attracted
more attention not only here in California, but elsewhere. Numerous
inquiries were received by our committee from people who apparently
had theretofore had no knowledge of the movement and whose
curiosity had been probably awakened by what they had read in the
~ewspapers and had heard over the radio; and from other jurisdict10ns came q:quests for details with respect to the manner in which
our observance is handled and for whatever literature was available.
In connection with the foregoing it is exceedingly gratifying to be
able to report that because of what has been accomplished here in
Calif~rnia a Public Schools Week was this year observed by the
Masons of Montana. M." · w:. Ernest L. Marvin, Grand Master, issued a proclamation along the lines of that with which our Public
Schools Week was originated; and in a letter received from him he
said that he intended recommending that it be made a permanent
activity of his Grand Lodge. His proclamation was not only enthusiastically received by his Lodges, but attracted favorable newspaper
comment. In an editorial on "School Problems" one of the newspapers
said:
·
"'.Fhe problems of the public schools come close to the lives
and homes of the American rank and file for the schools are the
common property of all. The Masons of Montana are calling
attention to that fact this week by observing 'Public Schools
Week in the Masonic Lodges.' ... The movement will impart to
the younger generation a more vital interest in the public schools
and will help parents to direct more intelligently the welfare of
their children. After all the home is the bulwark of the public;
and fireside discussions of today determine the nation's thought
of tomorrow. Education now needs all its friends. Montana
Masons are to be congratulated upon their efforts to gain for
themselves, their wives and children, a clearer and broader conception of today's school problems."
As evidence of the widespread interest this year, it is to be noted
that it appears from the reports and from our newspaper clippings

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

237

that in many communities, particularly in the larger cities, there were
events held in observance of the week which had not been scheduled
by the committee in charge of the local observance. In some instances
it was on the initiative of the school people and in the schools; but
there were also luncheon meetings and other gatherings arranged by
organizations which have no direct connection with the schools, and
at which there were addresses delivered by outstanding educators and
well informed laymen interested in public education. Notable among
these were the luncheon meeting of the Commonwealth Club of
California and that held during the annual Convocation of the Royal
Arch Masons of California.
In connection with our reference to the public interest aroused by
the radio talks, it may be here stated that this year for the first time
our committee was able to arrange for a definite comprehensive
state-wide radio program in addition to our newspaper publicity.
Local committees everywhere have always received the hearty
cooperation of the broadcasting stations in their vicinity, which have
been exceedingly generous in their allotment of time. This year, in
addition to that service, there was a coordinated program of broadcasts with subjects suggested by our committee. This was made
possible through the splendid cooperation received from Mr. Arthur
S. Garbett, Director of Education of the National Broadcasting Company, and from the various organizations which have allotments of
time over that system for educational broadcasts. The program was
started on the Saturday preceding the beginning of our observance
and was continued throughout the week with from two to fo\lr broadcasts each day. Every address made included a reference to Public
Schools Week and dealt with some phase of public education with
respect to which it was believed the public desired information.
The newspaper publicity has been especially valuable this year
because of the increased amount carrying information not only with
respect to the crisis confronting public education, but also concerning ·
specific questions now being asked by parents and taxpayers. And it
would seem as though there were not a single newspaper in the state
which had not urged upon its readers the advisability, if not the
necessity, of availing themselves of the opportunity offered by Public
Schools Week to obtain first hand and authoritative information as to
what the schools were actually doing and whether the criticism to
which they were being subjected was, or was not, warranted.
The newspapers, radio talks and the addresses at the public
meetings were not the only media through which facts with respect
to the schools and educational policies were presented to the public.
There was this year an increased number of instances in which
printed or multigraphed matter was distributed to those in attendance
at meetings or visiting schools. Some of these were in the form of
question and answer and were especially valuable where there were

be remembered, are located for the week in the business and shopping
districts with the pupils working in classes just as they wou.I.d be in
their regular schools. As was pointed out last year, this is not only
