which cannot be otherwise obtained.
In the community which originated this feature of the observance,
the idea was this year further developed. To emphasize the progress
of public education there was in one corner of the building in which
the downtown school was held a representation of "A School of 1834."
Not only were the teacher and the children in the costumes of the
period, but there was a faithful reproduction of the furniture and
"furnishings,'' including the· "dunce stool" and the pail of water with
the dipper out of which all the children drank with apparently no fear
of microbes and bacilli. The routine of the school of that day, with
the syllabic spelling of Con-stan-ti-no-ple and Miss-iss-ipp-i, was a
reminder of days gone by, and was particularly enjoyed by those who
even at a much later date had attended a school not altogether
unlike it.

arranged with. the idea of providing for the public information with
respect to the schools rather than mere. entertainment. One of the

from the County Superintendent, from which we · have quoted. This

combination of fruit, poultry and flower shows, with exhibits by the
pupils of the public schools and a display from the agriculture, biology
and .g eneral science classes of the high school.
Critics of the schools who believe that the "fundamentals" are
being neglected, and particularly those who insist that the children
are not being taught to spell correctly, would have found especial
interest iµ one of the programs presented during Public Schools.
Week. A feature of that program was a spelling match between
pupils of the junior high school and a team of six "champion spellers"
from the Lions Club. The result is set forth in the following excerpt
from a newspaper account of the event: "That not only are local
schools carrying their educational program into advanced fields of
political and exact sciences, as was demonstrated by the surprising
performances of the junior college debaters and engineers, but that
they are also holding their place with respect to grounding and fundamentals, was shown last night when a team of junior high school
spellers put to rout' the best spellers of the ... Lions Club .... The
score was two errors for the children and fourteen for the Lions.
Five of the six youngsters on the school team went through the match
without an error." In that community there will be less ·heard of the
good old days when children were t'aught to spell. And, by the way, a
"spelling bee" was a feature of many programs reported.
We are always loath to refer to any special observance because
there are so many worthy of mention. There was one, however, this
year, unusual in the fact that the week's program included_ a community meeting held in the afternoon, as well as one in the 'evening;
and especially significant was 't he fact that while the afternoon meeting was being held all the stores were closed.

In a school in which most of the pupils are of foreign parentage,
the entire program, including the menu of the dinner served in the
school cafeteria, was in Spanish, as was also a fine address delivered
by a prominent' citizen. After dinner, and before assembling in the

241

There has been a rather curious development in connection with
the observance of Public Schools Week of what might be termed a
"by-product," to which reference has been made in more than one
report received by our committee during recent years. Adjacent communities in the rural districts among which there is not that general
cooperation which would result to their mutual advantage, are always
ready '.to join in the observance of Public Schools Week. And this
comment is prompted by what' appears in a newspaper clipping
attached to one of the reports this year, and from which we quote the
following (omitting, of course, all names, in accordance with our
practice): "Focusing proper attention on the school work of the
various communities is not, however, the only ·benefit that ... has
derived from Public Schools Week. Each year it has been the basis
for bringing together all communities of the valley in one effort. Each
year ... and ... (and four other named communities) join together in
one single effort and each year with marked success." There would
seem to be little doubt that such cooperation in the observance of
Public Schools Week might well pave the way for a coordinated
effort for other purposes.
A few words should be said with respect to the reports received
from our Lodges. Although our committee maintains ~ontact with
City and County School .Superintendents, and with the parent bodies
of those organizations which cooperate in the observance of Public
Schools Week, it is through these reports from the Lodges that our
knowledge is obtained of the details of the local observances and of
the results thereof; and it is with the knowledge thus acquired that
our committee is enabled to make suggestions for future observances.
While probably the majority of these reports are confined to filling
in the blanks in the questionnaire sent out by our committee immediately prior to the close of the observance, there are many which are
supplemented with reports in narrative form, giving not only details
of the observance, but as well of the way in which it was handled;
and the number of these is continually increasing. And we are availing
ourselves of this opportunity to express our appreciation of the care
and detail with which such reports are prepared. Incidentally, it may
be mentioned that every Lodge has its own file in which its reports are
preserved; and not infrequently through reference to that file we are
enabled to be of assistance in some situation which has developed.
Earlier in this report we referred to the leaflets and circulars
distributed at public meetings and which set' forth facts with respect
to our schools. We conclude this report by quoting the last paragraph
of one of these which contains an admonition every friend of the
public school should ever have in mind:

"We urge that every citizen interested in the future of our
children and in the destiny of our nation assume personal responsibility to keep in constant contact with the educational situation

schools open and effective. In this crisis we must depend upon
an aroused public opinion · to insure to the children of the country
educational advantages as adequate as those made available in
past years to present-day adults. We must not for a moment
forget that education is the bulwark of our democratic society
and our surest guarantee !or the future."

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON LIBRARY
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California :
Having been honored with appointn:ent en the Library Committee of
the Grand Lodge, it is meet and proper that my committee make some brief
report for presentation to the Grand Lodge, to indicate, at least, that the
honor was accepted with the intention of rendering service if circumstances seriously' required attention to library matters.
The chairman of the library committee felt, however, that its functions
need not necessarily be active unless warranted by occasional circumstances
arising, whereby ·it might have ·been called upon in an advisory capacity.
· Shortly' after receiving his appoin~ ment this writer consulted with the
Gran·d Secretary, and under Brother Whicher's guidance made a survey
of ·the library quarters, .its stock of bo~ k3, etc., and decided that under the
p~esent stringency of funds we were not justified in adv:ising any new
purchases. At-the same time. it was felt that if urgent need or desirability
for any particular work had arisen, the Grand Secretary's office would
promptly have· notified your committee.

243

It is believed, therefore, that service was rendered in this particular
and trying period by our inactivity, and it is hoped this view will be taken
in passing upon this report.
]OHN R . RucKSTELL, Chairman.

The following extract from an editorial contained in the club house
publication at the opening of this semester is proof of this fact:
"The Masonic Club and the organizations within the club keep up
a round of social activities and provide the social life which college
students of today have deemed necessary to college life. And in the
midst of our pleasure, we have not forgotten those individuals less fortunate than we. Philanthropic work is carried on with the activities
of Areme, a women's philanthropic organization.
"Surely no other campus organization offers the diversity of interests which the Masonic Club offers, and no other group of students is
more fortunate than Masonic affiliates in having the opportunity to
enjoy its privileges. We who know the joys of the Masonic Club can
best voice our thanks by perpetuating Masonic ideals and living our
thanks to those farsighted and generous men who have made the
Masonic Affiliate Club possible."

Los Angeles, namely, Hiram No. 45, Caballeros de Oriente, and Minerva
Lodges, were withdrawn in 1932 after an unsuccessful attempt to attain
recognition from our Grand Lodge. We find, however, that in July, 1933,
a new Lodge was chartered under the name of Nirvana No. 8 by the
Grand Lodge Benito Juarez of the State of Coahuila, Torreon, Mexico,
under the mastership of one Victor Behar. In December, 1933, one Emilio
Espinosa was elected Master and one Estanislao Llera elected Secretary.
Espinosa had formerly been the Deputy Grand Master in Southern California. This Lodge met at Korbell Hall on East First Street in the city
of Los Angeles.
We are informed that the Grand Lodge Benito Juarez again withdrew
the charter of this Nirvana Lodge in the spring of 1934, and it is not now
operating. The Grand Lodge Benito Juarez still entertains the hope that
it will attain recognition from the Grand Lodge of California and that
that group of men who were allegedly made Masons in the three or four
Lodges that existed in southern California will some day be accepted in
the subordinate Lodges of our grand jurisdiction.
As to Negro Masonry: The Most Worshipful Sovereign Grand Lodge
of Ancient Free and Accepted Masons, also known as the Prince Hall
Masons, is still very active with some forty-two subordinate bodies working. It has held an annual communication last year.
The other group of Negro Masons known as the Most Worshipful
Hiram of Tyre Grand Lodge of Ancient Free and Accepted Masons has
declined markedly in both numbers and activity. There are probably about
nine subordinate Lodges in this rite, and they are not active to any extent.
A recent factional quarrel within their bodies as to where the last annual
communication was to be held, came to the attention of the courts of Los
Angeles county. One faction claimed that the annual communication was
to be held in Oakland, and the other claimed it should be held in Los Angeles. The Oakland group won. The Grand Master is William H. Robinson, residing at 1522 West 36th Street, Los Angeles, and the office of
Grand Lodge is at a place called Masonic Hall, 4414Y, Central Avenue,
Los Angeles.
The co-Masonic bodies have also suffered severely. The pseudo Hollywood Lodge, which formerly met in a regular hall at Hollywood Boulevard and Serrano Streets, city of Los Angeles, has moved to a small
room in the premises of an independent Catholic church in Hollywood.
The other co-Masonic Lodge is called "Helios" and meets irregularly in
an Odd Fellows Temple at Washington and Oak Streets. There is another
Lodge meeting in Ojai at the Theosophical Camp there. None of these
Lodges are very active or prosperous.
We do not wish to be understood as stating that clandestine Masonry
is dead in California. There is still considerable life left in it, and with the
return of normal economic conditions, we may expect a revival of some
of it.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON CLANDESTINE
MASONRY
To th~ M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Clandestine Masonry begs leave to report as
follows:
While the e.conomic and financial depression has been a dire tragedy in
many activities of life, it has not been an unmixed evil in all relations. In
the matter of clandestine Masonic Lodges, it has undoubtedly resulted in
the subsidance of much activity. The various members of our committee
have found that the irregular Lodges have to a considerable extent become
dormant, while a few have continued their existence for mere social purposes.
We have previously reported that in the main there were five separate
irregular Masonic groups of Lodges. Of these, the Rito Nacional Mexicano
is for the most part dormant. A few of the Lodges, one in San Bernardino,
sev~ral in Los Angeles, and one in San Diego, are continuing some social
activities but little or no alleged Masonic work. It may be said that this
rite is practically a thing of the past and will probably not be revived to
any formidable extent in the near future.

to functio~. a complete change in the officers for the year then ensuing
must be made. A meeting of the members of the Lodge was then had,
which was largely attended, and they were informed of the plan of the
committee, viz., to recommend to the Grand Master that the · charter be
restored upon the understanding that at the annual election to be held in
December, the officers elected should be members of the Lodge satisfactory
to the Grand Master, and the officers appointed by the Master-elect should
be likewise satisfactory, and that no member then holding office either by
virtue of election or appointment be included among the officers to be
elected and appointed. There was no dissent ex{>ressed t-0 this plan, either
by the officers or other members present, and receiving the recommendations of the committee, the Grand Master did on November 15, 1933, order
the charter restored on the condition, in addition to that as to the election
and appointment of officers, that there be no recurrence of the condition
reported by Grand Master Mixter as the reason for the arrest by him of
the charter, under penalty of the further arrest of the charter "which is
hereby only conditionally and provisionally rest-0red."

The Lodge then renewed its activities, and at the meeting in December,
new officers were elected who were satisfactory both to the committee
and the Grand Master, as were those appointed. In a most commendable
manner, the old officers stepped aside, surrendering their own ambitions
without hesitancy or evident dissent. Their successors took up the performances of their duties with enthusiasm, looking not backward but
forward only, striving earnestly to restore the peace and harmony which
should prevail in a Lodge of Masons, and it began to look as though their
efforts were not in vain.

that peace and harmony have been restored to the Lodge, they justify us,
we believe, in recommending that the charter of Fairmount Lodge be continued as only conditionally and provisionally restored and upon the understanding that if there is a recurrence of the conditions which warranted

As a part of its duties it has included the passing upon and recommendation to Grand Lodge Finance Committee of reimbursement to Lodges
and Boards of Relief for moneys expended for relief during the year.
It has devolved upon the Board of Control to render assistance to the
Lodges and Boards in securing these reimbursements from the Lodges in
other jurisdictions for whose members these bodies have rendered relief.
And thus, after the foremost work of standardizing and making uniform
their procedure had been accomplished, it has developed that one of the
principal duties of the Board of Control has been to secure these reimbursements and thus to conserve the funds of Grand Lodge.
Comparisons may not always be advisable and yet we .believe that the
successful work of the Board in this matter of reimbursement cannot be
too often repeated to Grand Lodge, as a means of justification of this
Board.

REPORT OF BOARD OF CONTROL
To the M.". W.". Grand Lodge of California:
Your Board of Control now comes to Grand Lodge with a resume and
report of its activities during the Masonic year;" a resume and report which
we believe will be most satisfactory and'pleasing to Grand Lodge; a resume
and report which in our opinion reflects the co-operation and s~pport; the
uniformity and harmony and intelligent action of the respective Boards of
Relief, and which justifies the procedure of the Board of Control during
the seven years of its existence.
The men whose observations of the procedure and conduct of Boards
of Relief and the general procedure of Grand Lodge in matters of charity
and relief prompted them to propose the organization of the Board of
Control bui)ded better than they knew.
•
Their proposals that the work of the Boards of Relief and Employment Service should be supervised; that it should be standardized, and made
uniform; that there should be more efficiency in operation with less overhead expense; that there should be a better understanding and co-ordination
between the respective Boards of Relief, between the Boards and Grand
Lodge, have all been realized.

During the year just closed the Board of Control has been enabled
to reduce the amount of reimbursements by our Grand Lodge to the lowest
figure in the history of Grand Lodge, namely, $1,796.01. This great reduction has been brought about just by the splendid co-operation and intelligent
acti on of the Secretaries of Boards of Relief; and secondly, by reason of
the fine contacts and understandings established between our own jurisdiction and other jurisdictions of this country, by the representative o~ the
Board of Control delegated by Grand Master Mixter in 1933 to attend
the convention of the Masonic Relief Association of the United States
and Canada.
As a result of those contacts and the friendships and better relationships, as well · as the better understandings of the conditions that exist in
California, the Board of Control has been enabled this year to clean up
and settle all claims against the jurisdictions of New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Nebraska, Michigan and others, and it has received prompt and

and many others, totaling over $2,000.00.
Because of the splendid work of the respective boards during the year
the work of the Board of Control has been reduced in an amazing degree.
Whereas there were 131 cases of relief and reimbursement involving
volumes of correspondence and negotiations before the board last year,
there has been a total of but 14 cases before the board this year. Excepting a number of cases involving considerable sums left over from last year,
the cases and claims presented thi°s year have been very small, indeed. To
their credit it must be said that the Secretaries of Boards of Relief havr
secured authorization and therefore reimbursement this year.
Meetings
Your Board of Control has held four meetings during the year. These
meetings h<We been called by the chairman to dispose of accumulated business, and were necessary: There was one less meeting than last year, and
with the simplifying of our procedure and with the lessening of the amount
of work, there will probably be few er meetings during the coming year.
The year's ll)eetings have been held at Ventura in February, at Long
Beach in June, in San Francisco in August and in San Francisco during
this session of Grand Lodge.

Refusal to Sign Compacts
Section 37 of our Constitution provides that the Board of Control
shall with the consent and by the direction of the Grand Master, have
pow~r to compel any Lodge within this grand jurisdiction_ to becom~ a
member of the Board of Relief nearest its place of meetmg. N otwithstanding this provision and regardless of the fact that at least two Grand
Masters have ruled that Lodges must sign compacts and become membe rs
of Boards of Relief, the Board of Control continues each year to have
trouble with Lodges which fail to correctly interpret this or the orders
of the Grand Master.

Sacramento Board of Relief: Three requests for reimbursement-

$5.00 each on account of Walter Albert Anderson, Parkway Lodge
No. 1008, Chicago; Elmo Kerr, Twin Falls Lodge No. 45, Idaho ; -Loran
Rodgers, Hendricks Lodge No. 404, Oklahoma.
In each of these cases the secretary of the Board of Relief did not
write to and/or make any effort to collect from the Brother's home Lodge.
We believe that the Board of Relief, even in emergency cases, should make
some effort to secure authorization and should communicate with the
Brother's Lodge after relief is granted. An attempt should be made to
secure reimbursement from the Lodge before reimbursement is asked by
our Grand Lodge.
Furthermore, we believe that the Board of Relief will secure reimbursement if the secretary will take the trouble to write to the respective
Lodges.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON BY-LAWS
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on By-Laws has had before it resolutions of the
various Lodges providing · for changes in their By-Laws. These changes
are substantially as follows:
Nmnber of Resolutions
Decreasing initiation fees to $30.00.................. 1
to $50.00.................. 28
37
above $50.00.................. 8
Excepting holidays from stated meetings.................... 15
Changing time of stated meetings.................................... 14
Changing place of meetings..........................:................... 7
Decreasing dues .................................................................. 7
Eliminating affiliation fees.................................................. 6
Reducing affiliation fees ........................................ :............. 5
Increasing dues .................................................................... 2
Increasing affiliation fees.................................................... 1
Total resolutions ------------------------····---------·-·······-------------94
All of the resolutions have been found in order and heretofore approved by the Grand Master, and we therefore recommend their approval
by Grand Lodge.
Since 1932 each successive Grand Master has viewed with alarm the
reduction of fees for the degrees upon the ground that the reduction of
fees tends to cheapen our fraternity. Notwithstanding the admonitions of
Grand Masters, the Lodges acting under the discretion vested in them,
have seen fit to decrease their dues and initiation fees. We are pleased to
note, however, that during the past year less than one-third of the number
of Lodges have reduced fees in comparison with the reductions of previous years. We repeat the hope expressed by us last year that no ill
effects will be felt by reason of the decreases, and that we will maintain
the high standard of membership which has been ours through the years.
ARTHUR JOEL,

JULIUS GABRIEL,

w ARREN E. LIBBY,
IRA D. WHEELER,

Committee

Adopted.
PAY OF MEMBERS
To the M.'. W.'. GraiuJ Lodge of California:
Your committee cha rged with the duty of ascertaining cost of transportation for one person from the location of each Lodge in the jurisdiction to the place of meeting of Grand Lodge and return, and of reporting

in attendance from each Lodge, as well as grand officers, Past Grand
Mast~r~, chairfii__en and mei:ibers of standing committees, and Inspectors,
for their necessary expenditures to and from Grand Lodge, report that
they have carefult~ discharged this duty. It may be noted that the allowance for transporta\ion is somewha.t less than in previous years. This is
due to the lowered railroad and pullman rates which went into effect subsequent to the last Annual Communication. Transportation allowance is
fixed by the Constitution at twice the single first-class one-way fare, plus
sleeper charges where necessary.
Notwithstanding that it is a legal holiday, it has been arranged to
have the necessary cash and tellers available to cash transportation checks
on Friday immediately following the election of the Junior Grand Warden.
This committee desires to express its appreciation for this exceptional
courtesy on the part of the Anglo-California Bank, extended through
Brother Louis Sutter, Past Master of Brooklyn Lodge No. 225, in making
this arrangement possible.
We herewith submit the following statement:

REPORT OF ACTIVITIES COMMITTEE
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grand Lodge Week Activities respectfully report
that we .Provided the following entertainments for members of Grand
Lodge and their ladies this week :
Monday, October 8, with the co-operation of the East Bay Masters
and Wardens Association, a trip to the Masonic Home at Decoto.
October 9, in the Palm court of the Palace hotel, the annual gettogether dinner, attended by nearly one thousand representatives of Lodges.
October 10, automobile tour of the city, attended by 193 ladies. Tea
was served at the Palace hotel.

ILLNESS OF PAST GRAND MASTER MURPHEY
Word having reached Grand Lodge that Past Grand
Master John D. Murphey was seriously ill in a hospital at
Oakland, the Grand Secretary was directed to telegraph to
him the ·regrets of his Brethren and their sincere hopes for
his speedy recovery. He replied as follows:
"Thank you, John, and the Grand Lodge for yo~r thoughtful consideration. I know how you all feel, but it is nice to have you say it. This
is my first absence in thirty years. It is my hope to serve you further."

REPORTS OF COMMITTEE ON GRIEVANCES
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
In the matter of the petition for restoration of J. H . S., expelled
March 19, 1923, by Fremont Lodge No. 497, we recommend that the petition be granted and that he be restored to all the rights and privileges of
Masonry.

Adopted.
In the matter of trial record No. 821, from Los Banos Lodge No. 312,
wherein the accused .was found guilty and sentenced to expulsion, we
recommend that the judgment of the trial Lodge be reversed and the case
remanded for a new trial.

The report was adopted; subsequently Grand Lodge reconsidered its action, disapproving the report of the committee, and ordering that the judgment of the Lodge in
expelling the accused be affirmed.
Your committee, to which had been referred the petition of S. N. 0.,
who at the time of his expulsion on October 6, 1925, was an Entered
Apprentice of Loyalty Lodge No. 529, recommend that the pl!tition for
restoration to the rights of an Entered Apprentice Mason be granted.

Adopted.
Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred trial record
No. 809, reports as follows: Charges were preferred against accu.sed,
who was then the Master of John D. Spreckels Lodge No. 657, by five
Master Masons. The Grand Master appointed three disinterested Past

In the matter of the petition for restoration of G. J. B., formerly a
member of Alexander Hamilton Lodge No. 535, who was expelled July 1,
1929, your Committee on Grievances recommends that the petition be
granted and that he be, and is, restored to all the rights and privileges of
Masonry.

Adopted.
Your Committee on Grievances has carefully considered trial record
No. 837, a member of Yorba Linda Lodge No. 469, who was suspended
August 2, 1934, and is of the opinion that the judgment of the trial commission in finding the accused guilty of unmasonic conduct be approved,
but that the penalty be raised from suspension to expulsion.

Adopted.
Your Committee on Grievances has carefully considered the petition
for restoration of H . A. S. (trial record No. 257), a former member of
Hawaiian Lodge No. 21, tried and expelled by Mission Lodge No. 169 in
1919, and recommend that the petition be granted' and that H. A. S. be,
and is, restored to the rights and privileges of Masonry.

· Adopted.
Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred trial record
No. 818, ·from Madera Lodge No. 280, report as follows: The accused
was charged with the offense of murder. He was convicted, but the entire
evidence concerning his guilt consists of the testimony taken at the coroner's inquest. His conviction was then made to depend on hearsay testimony, not within the purview of Section 202 of the Constitution. We,
therefore, offer the following resolution: Resolved, that the finding of
guilty of the accused, in the above trial record, and the fixing of the
penalty of expulsion be, and the same is hereby, reversed, and the trial
commission instructed to subpoena the witnesses, hear their evidence and
pass thereon.

Adopted.
In the case of trial record No. 808, from East Bay Lodge No. 489,
who was acquitted by the trial commission, and from which judgment of
acquittal the accuser appealed, we are of the opinion that this is a case
which should have been brought, if at all, in the civil courts and not ·before
a Masonic tribunal. We therefore recommend that the finding of the trial
commission, in acquitting the accused, be affirmed.

Adopted.

Your Committee on Grievances has carefully considered tp(al record
No. 804, relating· tu a member of Sola.no Lodge No. 229, who ~as expelled
Se~tember 11: 1933; by proceedings pursua~t of .section=9 ~f the Constitution. In this case the accused was convicted m the S enor Court for
the commission of a felony but was not imprisoned pur uant to such conviction, Instead; the court suspended sentence for a .z\eriod of years and
admitted the accused to probation. Under the very ,Pfain terms of Section
192, automatic expulsion can only be had in cases of conviction of a crime
classified as a felony when the accused had beer¥ imprisoned pursuant to
such. conviction, There being no imprisonment in this case we recommend·
that the expulsion of H. L. S. be set aside and that Solano Lodge No. 229
be instructed· to cause proper charges. to be preferred against the accused
and that the trial thereof be had in the manner prescribed by our Masonic

Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred trial record
No. 810, begs leave to report- as follows:
The accused was charged with unmasonic conduct as alleged in two
specifications, the first of which sets forth a violation of the narcotic act.
The second specification sets up that accused was convicted of the offense
in the Federal Court. As we have observed on many occasions, a specification merely charging a court conviction does not state a Masonic offense.
The evidence introduced before the trial commission on behalf of the
accuser consisted of the record of the Federal Court showing that the
accused had been found guilty of two counts of an indictment charging.
accused with violation of the Harrison Narcotic Act and with conspiracy
to violate the act. He was sentenced to three years in the penitentiary and
fined $5,000. The prison term was later set aside by a modified judgment
.rhd the fine has been paid.
The evidence on behalf of the accused consisted of his testimony
alone in explanation of the offense. From his lips we learn.that he owned
and operated a drug store ; that he was assisted therein by his co-defendant
in the Federal case,. who also was a Mason, and who has been expelled by
Grand Lodge £.or his part in this offense. This assistant was approached
by a woman who desired to purchase an ounce of cocaine. The assistant
told accused he was considering making the sale and in reply the accused
states that he told his assistant that making such a sale was a dangerous
thing to do. Thereafter the sale was made and the assistant took the
ninety dollars he received therefor and handed it to accused who took and
retained the money. One 0£ the trial commission asked accused this question: "Why did you take this money from him?" To which accused
replied: "I can't explain it. It is impossible."
In addition the accused virtually admits that he committed perjury
before the Federal Court but attempts to justify his conduct in this respect
as being inspired by a desire to shield and protect his assistant.

Emergency Relief
Brother Wesley W. Kergan, Inspector of District No. 35, proposes
that Section 90 of the Constiution be amended by adding the following
sentence to the end of said section :
"Where reimbursement is expected, no relief should be extended beyond the amount authorized by the Lodge or the jurisdiction to which the applicant belongs, except where an emergency
exists, and in emergency cases complete and immediate notice of
the emergency, together with an estimate of the amount necessary
to relieve, should be sent such Lodge or jurisdiction for its information or approval."
. . The consideration of your committee has been given to this proposal,
which has, for its purpose, the limitation of the broad terms of Section 90
in such manner that a Lodge would be protected in the expenditure of
relief funds for the assistance of a Brother belonging to another Lodge or
in another grand jurisd'iction. Your committee is in sympathy with the
purpose of the proposal, but instead of approving the same at this time
desires that the matter be postponed for action until the next communication of this Grand Lodge. The reason for seeking such a postponement
is that the obligations of relief and the conditions of its administration
are scattered through portions of the ritual, sections of the Constitution
regulations, decisions, approved reports of committees and rules, and con~

277

stitute a patchwork in which there are overlappings, contradictions and
uncertainties. Your committee believes that there should be a statement
or restatement of the obligations of Masons, Lodges, the Grand Lodge
and its instrumentalities on the important subject of relief and relief
administration. During the interval between this and the next annual
communication, your committee will endeavor to formulate for submission
to Grand Lodge such a restatement, and in formulating the same due
consideration will be given to the proposal of Brother Kergan.
Your committee, therefore, recommends that further consideration of
the proposed amendment by Grand Lodge be postponed until the next
annual communication.

Adopted.
M asters and Wardens on Committees
Your committee has considered the proposal that Section 27 of the
Constitution be amended by providing that all standing committees of
Grand Lodge shall be increased by two members and shall include at least
one Master and one Warden of a constituent Lodge. This amendment, if
adopted, would require the Grand .Master to appoint at least one Junior
Warden and one Senior Warden on each standing committee, for the
reason that the appointments are made in October of each year, and in
the ordinary course a brother holding the position of Master would become
a Past Master within ninety days. In no event could the Grand Master be
assured that a W arden would be re-elected or would advance to higher
station.
The proposal would be objectionable for the further reason that the
Grand Master is the executive head of Grand Lodge and, as such, should
be entitled to use his best judgment and discretion in the appointment of
the members of the standing committees which are a part of the administration of the affairs of the craft during his incumbency of his high
office. If a Grand Master cannot be trusted to make proper appointments
of committeemen and others, then he has not the confidence of Grand
Lodge and should not be elected Grand Master.
The provision for the appointment of two additional members of each
of the standing committees in our judgment would serve no useful purpose. Under present provisions of our law an adequate personnel is
required on each of the committees.
While the foregoing reasons are sufficient to constrain us to reject the
proposal, yet we are in sympathy with the underlying reasons for its
presentation. We believe that the Grand Master in his wise discretion
should, from time to time, seek to call into the service of Grand Lodge in
its committee work, Masons of attainments and zeal to the end that the
committee would always be in close touch with active work of the Lodges,
and that experience may be gained by those who, as the years go on,
Grand Lodge will turn more and more to rely upon for guidance and
direction. We believe that an inspection of the personnel of committee

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

278

279

-PROCEED1NGS OF THE

membership not only at the present time, but over a period of many years,
will demonstrate that Grand Masters have been actuated by an inclination
and desire to call into Grand Lodge committees the type of men · who the
proposer of said amendment has in his thought.
· We therefore recommend that the proposed amendments to the Constitution be not adopted.

Recognition of the Grand Lodge of Amazon and Acre
Your Committee ~n Policy and General Purposes has before it the
request of the Grand Lodge of the Amazon and Acre, which has exclusive
jurisdiction in the states of Amazonas and the Acre Territory in the Republic of the United States of Brazil.
It appears that this Grand Lodge conforms to the standard for recognition adopted by the Grand Lodge of California, that it requires a belief

in God, is secret, follows the symbolism of craft Masonry, confers the
three symbolic degrees, bases its ritual on the temple legend, prohibits
political and religious controversies, exhibits the three great lights of
Masonry, having the open Book of the Law on its altars, and that it has
twenty-two subordinate Lodges of its obedience, some of which are more
than fifty years old.
This Grand Lodge at one time recognized the Grand Orient of Brazil,
but in 1931 withdrew such recognitiori in order to make it consistent for
this Grand Lodge to recognize the Grand Lodges of the states of the
Republic of Brazil, which Grand Lodges had been set up in conformity
to the standards set by the English and American Grand Lodges. The
Grand Lodges of six of such states have heretofore been recognized by
this Grand Lodge, and the application now before us for recognition was
postponed until this annual communication because of lack of sufficient
information upon which to base our final action.
This committee is now satisfied that the Grand Lodge of the Amazon
and Acre should be recognized, and it is so recommended.

Adopted.

We are of the opinion that the adoption of this resolution would not

T ransfer of A ffiliation With Continuous Membership
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had under consideration the resolution offered by Brother Don D. Donahue, Past Master
and Secretary of Hackett Lodge No. 574 of San Diego, at the request of
the Officers' Association of San Diego County, proposing an amendment
to section 161 of our Constitution for the stated purpose of clarifying the
same.
Section 161 provides the method by which a transfer of affiliation with
continuous membership may be accomplished. Reasons for the proposed
amendments as stated in a copy of a letter to the Grand Master, under
date of July 28, 1934, are that a "strict compliance of the provision.s of
section 161 has a tendency to discourage affiliation, to subject the applicant
to the payment of duplicate dues, and that the proposed resolu~ion wo~ld
take away the incentive for an evasion of the law in order to avotd working
a hardship on the candidate by either disregarding the law entirely or by
the fictitious date of his membership after election."
· Your committee, after careful consideration of the subject matter, is
of the opinion that no useful purpose could be accomplished by ~he .ado~
tion of the proposed amendment, which has been in our Conshtut10n m
its present form for seven years. It was quite -0bviol!sly. the thought .of
Grand Lodge when this section was adopted that the applicant for a~ha­
tion could complete his transfer within three months, and your committee
feels that this would be done, except in very rare instances, if the Masters
and Secretaries used reasonable diligence in handling the details connected
with the transfer.
Your committee agrees that in some cases a small duplication of payment of dues might result under the present plan, but it does not feel
that the proposed change or, in fact, any other similar proposal, would
remedy this situation and at the same time secure for the Brother the
protection for the continuity of membership as now afforded under the
section in its present form.
We therefore recommend that the resolution be not adopted.

Report adopted.

Reaffirming Allegiance to Our Government
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes presents the following resolution and moves its adoption:
Resolved, that the Grand Lodge of California, acting for itself,
its constituent Lodges and all Masons of its obedience, hereby reaffirms the allegiance of Masonry within this grand jurisdiction to the
Constitution of the United States of America and the fundamental
principles symbolized by .the flag of our country. We hold that under
the inspiration of our Constitution the citizens of our beloved Republic
have enjoyed and do now enjoy rights, privileges, opportunities and
benefits unmatched under any other system of government thus far
devised by mankind. We oppose all men and movements proposing to
subvert the foundations of our government and the institutions of
progress it has nurtured. We call upon every Mason within our jurisdiction to labor unceasingly for the defense and preservation of the
priceless heritage of liberty and progress created for us through the
blood and sacrifice of our fathers: to honor his government; to abide

Adopted by unanimous vote.
Exemplification of Degrees by Lodges of Other Jurisdictions
Brother Paul Nathan has proposed that section 121 of the Constitution, relative to the authorized ritual, be amended, permitting a Lodge of
this jurisdiction to invite a Lodge of a foreign grand jurisdiction to confer
a degree of Masonry upon its own candidate in accordance with the ritual
of its grand jurisdiction in a Lodge of this grand jurisdiction. The ~vident
intent of such a change in our law is to facilitate fraternal courtesies between Lodges located on opposite sides of the boundary line of the state.
In order to promote fraternal courtesies and visitations, it is proposed that
the long settled policies of this Grand Lodge be modified to permit the
exemplification of ritualistic work different from that authorized by this
Grand Lodge in a Lodge of this jurisdiction by the officers of a foreign
Lodge. While the purposes to ·be accomplished by such change are laudatory, the means proposed therefor do not meet with the approval of this
committee. We have established by law the policy and procedure for the
conferring by courtesy of the degrees of Masonry upon a California candidate in a foreign jurisdiction, in accordance with the ritual of such
jurisdiction," and for the conferring by courtesy of the degree of a can?idate of a foreign jurisdiction in a California Lodge, in accordance with
the California ritual. As a matter of policy, we do not think it advisable
to proceed further by providing for the conferring of a degree by the
officers of a subordinate Lodge of a foreign Grand Lodge, in accordance
with the ritual of such foreign Grand Lodge, upon a candidate of such
subordinate Lodge in a California Lodge, nor, conversely, that the California Lodge may depart from this grand jurisdiction with its candidate
to confer a degree in the Lodge of a sister grand jurisdiction.
For the foregoing reasons, your committee recommends that said proposal to amend the Constitution be not approved.

The report was referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, with instructions to rewrite the proposed amendment. That committee reported back recommending that
section 121 be amended by adding the following:
"Provided, further, that a Lodge in this jurisdiction, conferring a
degree .upon a candidate elected to receive such degree in another jurisdiction, may for such purpose, with the consent of the Grand Master of
this jurisdiction, use the ritual of such other jurisdiction."

Grand Lodge concurred, and section 121 was thereupon
amended by unanimous vote.

Annuity Contracts by Masonic Homes
That part of the report of the Masonic Homes Endowment Board
recommending that this Grand · Lodge, under certain specified conditions,
approve the issuance of annuity contracts by the Masonic Homes of California, has been considered by your committee.
This subject is new to Grand Lodge and is of such importance that
a thorough investigation of its merits and practicability should be made.
Such a study will require considerable time and effort. For this reason
we respectfully recommend that the said recommendation of the Endowment Board, with respect to the adoption of an annuity plan, be postponed
for consideration to the next annual communication. As the matter now
appears to your committee, it is a practicable plan for adoption and will
result in appreciable additions to the endowment fund at small, if any, risk
of loss. We are convinced that such plan will afford a means of giving by
benevolently disposed persons who cannot at this time forego all income
from a fund which eventually will become a part of the endowment fund
of the Homes.

Report adopted.

the committee be continued and requested to submit at the next annual
communication some definite plan of Masonic education.

Adopted.
WILIAM RHODES HERVEY,
WILL H . FISCHER,
WILLIAM H. WASTE,

Life Memberships
Your Committee on Jurisprudence has examined the resolutions for
life membership adopted by various Lodges and· approved by the Grand
Master during the past year and finds the same to be in accordance with
law .
. In connection with the resolution adopted by Speranza I taliana Lodge
No. 219, however, we call attention to the fact that the resolution purports
to authorize investment in securities not permitted by section 129 of the
Constitution. Restrictions upon investment stipulated in section 129 are
not a subject for action by the Lodge, with the exception of the authority
of the Lodge to still further restrict the securities in which life membership
funds may be invested.
We recommend that the action of the Grand Master be approved.

Adopted.

Masonic Homes
22. The report of the Trustees of the Masonic Homes has had the
careful consideration of your committee. The report is complete in every
detail and fully sets forth not only the income and expenses, but, in rather
minute detail, every activity of the Homes. We wish to commend the
trustees for the thoroughness of the report.
Due to the fact that this activity is making the greatest call upon the
funds of Grand Lodge, a most thorough study of the report has been
made, and particularly every item of expense has been scanned. It is pleasing to note that there has been a reduction in the cost of the maintenance
of the Homes. While it is not great, it is in the right direction. While the
Trustees probably do not need to be reminded of the necessity of the
strictest economy in the operaticn of our Homes, yet this committee cannot
refrain from again making mention of this necessity.
It is also to be noted that the receipts for the Homes have not only been
sufficient to meet their needs, but also to effect a $25,000.00 reduction in
their debt. This is also a move in the right direction and equally gratifying.
There is one item in the report which has given this committee the
most concern, and that is the item of outside relief, which is still mounting,
this year approximating $48,000.00, or an increase of $3,000.00 over the
previous year. It is also to be noted that the outside relief expended by
the Grand Master has mounted .this past year and is not included in that
administered by the Trustees. In digesting this expense, your committee
notes that the amount paid per person in the northern part of the State
is considerably greater than the amount paid per person for the southern
part. It is also to be noted that in the southern portion the Trustees have an
outside worker who checks up, not only on the H ome admissions, but also
on this expenditure. Your committee is sure that the employment of someone to do work of this kind is money well expended. This committee, therefore, suggests to the Trustees that the outside relief in the northern part
of the State be given the same scrutiny as that administered in the south.
It is also to be noted that neither of the Homes are operated to the
"full capacity. It would seem to your committee that the Homes could be
operated to full capacity with practically no increase of operating expenses
over that of actual food and clothing required. It would therefore seem
that no outside relief should be administered either to the old folks or
to children where recipient could be admitted to the Home, until after
the Homes are filled to capacity. We commend this thought to the
Trustees.
The report further discloses that the Homes are holding many items
of real estate scattered throughout the entire jurisdiction. It is the opinion
of this committee that a continued effort should be made to dispose of this
real estate. Most of it is unproductive of income and, of course, all subject
to taxes. We would therefore suggest that some program be adopted by
the Trustees towards placing sale prices on all of this real estate and then

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

296

efforts made to dispose of the same. It might be done by furnishing the
Inspectors and Lodges with list and prices of such real estate as may be
within their respective jurisdictions, or by listing it with real estate
agents. While this may not be considered a fortuitous time for sales, yet
~he possibilities for improvement are so uncertain that your committee
feels certain that some plan should be adopted and a sustained effort be
made for the disposal of this real estate.
While Grand Lodge has established a quota for the admission of
residents to the Home for Adults at Decato, no such quota has ever been
established for admission to the Covina Home. We can see no good reason
why a quota should not be established for the latter; Such quota would
result in a more equitable distribution of the benefits to the several Lodges.
We commend this thought, also, to the Trustees.
For the guidance of future .committees, a statement of estimated income of the Homes for the coming year is included. It is as follows :
Maintenance ........ ,...................................................$ 90,000.00
Building fund .......................................................... 60,000.00
$25.00 tax ................................................................ 54,000.00
Rule 16 ...................................................................;.. 15,000.00
Interest, endowment fund...................................... 25,000.00
State aid .................................................................. 4,000.00
$248,000.00
It would seem to your committee that this should be sufficient income
for the maintenance of the Homes. No attempt is made to budget expenses,
due to exigencies which cannot be foreseen.
In addition to the 50 cents provided for in the Constitution for the
funds of the Homes, it will be necessary to provide for a special tax. It
had been the hope of this committee that less tax than last year for this
purpose could be recommended. After assembling all figures, however, it
does not seem possible to reduce the amount. Therefore, under resolution
providing for the total levy on Grand Lodge, a resolution is being presented
providing for the same amount as last year, that is, 75 cents per member
in addition to the 50 cents provided by the Constitution.

Adopted.
WM. P. JEFFRIES,

Friday, October 12, 1934.
Grand Lodge was called on at 10 o'clock, the Grand Master presiding.
The minutes of Thursday's sessions were read and approved.

ANNUAL ELECTION OF OFFICERS
The annual- election of officers being now in order, the
Grand Master appointed tellers, and the election was held,
the result being as follows:
The R. ·. W. ·. Randolph V. Whiting of King Solomon's
Lodge No. 260 was elected Grand Master.
The R.'. W.'. Earl Warren of Sequoia Lodge No. 349
was elected Deputy Grand Master.
The R.'. W.'. Rollie W. Miller of Sunset Lodge No. 352
was elected Senior Grand Warden.
The W.'. James T. Fraser of Humboldt Lodge No. 79
was elected Junior Grand Warden.
The V .'. W .'. William P. Filmer of King Solomon's
Lodge No. 260 was reelected Grand Treasurer.
The V.'. W.'. John Whicher of King David's Lodge
No. 209 was reelected Grand Secretary.
The V .'. W .'. Leslie E. Wood of Provident Lodge
. No. 6C:S was elected Grand Lecturer.
The Grand Master-elect caused to be read the names of
the appointive officers, as follows:
Grand Chaplain, Rev. Herbert P. Shaw of Ingleside
Lodge No. 630.
Grand Orator, Ira F. Thompson of Liberal Arts Lodge
No. 677.
Assistant Grand Secretary, Frank G. Hobbs of Alexandria Lodge _No. 531.
Grand Marshal, Henry G. Mathewson of Argonne Lodge
No. 514.

Grand Standard Bearer, Nathan F. Coombs of Yount
Lodge No. 12.
Grand Sword Bearer, Marquis F. Calmes of Maui Lodge
No. 472.
· Grand Bible Bearer, Harry Horne of Redlands Lodge
No. 300.
Senior Grand Deacon, Albert Wollenberg of Starr King

No. 374.
Grand Tiler, Frank G. Watson of Presidio Lodge No. 354.
The M.'. W.". Dana R. Weller, Past Grand Master, was
appointed Master of Ceremonies, and the officers-elect and
appointed, excepting the Grand Standard Bearer, Grand
Sword Bearer, Senior Grand Steward, and Junior Grand
Steward, were installed by the retiring Grand Master in
due and ancient form.
The Grand Master then invested his predecessor with a
diamond-studded lapel pin and the apron of a Past Master;
the Adams lapel pin was transferred from the retiring to the
present Grand Master; the other chair officers interchanged
their lapel pins; and Alexander D. Potts, Master of Lodge
le Progres de l'Oceanie No. 371, in behalf of the Brethren
of the Hawaiian Islands, invested the Grand Master with
~ beautiful lei, speaking_in part as follows:
"Every country has its language
And its word in greeting you,
But Hawaii has the sweetest
Of all I ever knew-

334

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

That beloved word 'Aloha'lt means so much to us.
It's a greeting when you're happy,
It's a comfort when you're blue,
For Aloha means we love you,
And seals friendship staunch and true."

Brother Henry S. Cohen, in behalf of the oldest Lodge
in Los Angeles-Los Angeles Lodge No. 42-pres~nted an
engrossed set of resolutions, done on parchment and bound
in vellum, to Past Grand Master Gist.
Jam es T. Fraser, in the name of the Grand Lodge, then
presented to Brother Gist a fine wr.i st watch and a set of
silver.
The Grand Master then announced the appointment of
Charles M. Wollenberg to be Trustee of the Masonic Homes,
vice self, term expired, and at 2 :30 o'clock, all business being
completed, Grand Lodge was closed in Ample Form.
RANDOLPH V. WHITING,
Grand Master.
JOHN WHICHER,
Grand Secretary.

Randolph Virginius Whiting
Grand Master 1934-1935

On October 11, 1935, Randolph Virginius Whiting completed his labors as
the sixty-eighth Grand Master of Masons in California. By exemplifying the
sincerity of his intentions in the business in which he was engaged, and by giving
a sympathetic ear to all those who came to him for counsel and advice, he has
retained the confidence, respect and admiration of his brethren.
He was born in Quincy, Plumas county, California, and was the fourth son
of a family of eight children of Fenton Berkeley Whiting and Martha Jane
(Mastin) Whiting. His father, who came to California from Virginia shortly
before its admission into the Union, was the owner and operator of the express
line between Quincy, Oroville and Marysville in the days of the gold rush. His
uncle, George C. Whiting, who was Acting Secretary of the Interior upon several occasions, was Grand Master of Masons in the District of Columbia at the
time of his death in 1867, after having served in that capacity for a period of
almost eight years ; and George C. Whiting Lodge No. 22, F. A. A. M., at
Washington, is named for him.
Brother Whiting received his early education in the public schools at Quincy,
and, after taking certain preparatory work at Bowen's Academy in Berkeley,
entered the University of California with the class of 1893 and subsequently
graduated from Hastings College of the Law in 1895. He immediately entered
the practice of law in San Francisco and has continued in that profession to this
date. On May 29, 1900, he married Mary Rosslet Bowen, the charming daughter
of the founder of the academy at which he took his preparatory work and in
which he later taught.
Public duty first called him in 1900, when he became assistant district attorney in San Francisco under District Attorney Lewis F. Byington, and he
remained in this position until 1906 and took part in the investigation which led
to the subsequent graft prosecutions in that city. He has been editor of the
California Decisions and California Appellate Decisions since 1897, and was
appointed assistant reporter of decisions for the Supreme Court and District
Courts of Appeal in 1915. He was advanced to the office of reporter in 191$
and now holds that position. During the period of the participation of the
United States in the World War, he gave his entire time to service on Draft
Board No. 12 in San Francisco. He was president of the San Francisco Bar
Association in 1930-1932, and the present home of that association is a monument to his efforts during his term of office.

RANDOLPH V. WHITING

Grand Master 193•
~lnl!lllU/1111111111!11~

On April 21, 1902, he was made a Master Mason in King Solomon's Lodge
No. 260, in San Francisco, and soon became active in the affairs of the Lodge,
serving as its Master in 1909. He received the Royal Arch degree in April, 1903,
in California Chapter No. 5, and was knighted in California Commandery No. 1
on January 29, 1904. He is also a member ( 32') of San Francisco Bodies No. 1,
A. & A. S. R., and of Islam Temple of the Shrine. He served as a member of
the Committee on Appeals and Grievances of Grand Lodge from 1912 to 1917

and from 1924 to 1928. In 1929 he was appointed chairman of the Committee
on By-Laws and served in that capacity until his election as Junior Grand Warden
in October, 1932. He was elected Deputy Grand Master in 1933, and Grand Master on October 12, 1934. From October, 1932, to October, 1934, he served as a
member of the Board of Trustees for the Masonic Homes. In February, 1935,
he was elected and served as chairman of the Conference of Grand Masters of
Masons in the United States, held in Washington, D. C.
The foregoing brief summary of the life of Randolph Virginius Whiting is
indicative of his unselfish desire to be of service to his fellow-man, and shows
that he has merited the esteem of his brethren and the confidence reposed in him.

Devotional Service
Rev. Herbert P. Shaw, Grand Chaplain, spoke as follows:
Were I to take a text this morning, a text which I would feel appropriate to
the occasion of the times and the conditions facing us, it would be the clear
clarion call of one of the greatest prophets of Israel in his great urge to his
people-Isaiah 54 :2, "Enlarge the place of thy tent, a~d let them stretch forth
the curtains of thine habitations ; spare not, lengthen thy cords, and strengthen
thy stakes."
As in the day of Isaiah, so in our day today, in our great nation, in our own
beloved State, the time has come when God must have a chance, when every man
and every Mason must "enlarge the place of his spiritual tent," when he must
"stretch forth the curtains of his spiritual habitation," when he must "spare not"
to lengthen his spiritual cords and strengthen his spiritual stakes.
The prophet is saying a simple thing in strong language. He gives enunciation to a great principle in sirriple statement, that God cannot be pushed out of
the life of a nation, nor the life of a state, nor the life of an individual; and the
nation, the state, or the individual live. To push God out, says the prophet, is to
"make a covenant with death." And the prophet says such a covenant is like a
"bed shorter than that a man can stretch himself on it; and the covering narrower
than that he can wrap himself in it."
Have you ever slept with someone who wrapped himself in the covers, leaving you just a corner? And you slept cold all night? The prophet says that "For
the bed is shorter than that a man can stretch himself on it ; and the covering
narrower than that he can wrap himself in it" is like trying to establish a civilization by leaving God out.
There never was an age with such tremendous mechanical miracles as today:
Miracles on land, miracles in the air, miracles on sea, miracles under the sea.

393

One of the greatest of such miracles is in . our own neighborhood: the
great bridge between Oakland and San Francisco. Down at the Ferry Building
is a slice of the great cable used on the Oakland-San Francisco bridge. If my
figures are correct the great cable is composed of three-eighths inch solid
wire, 474 such wires being spun into each strand. There are 37 strands in the
cable, or 17,538 wires. This total creates a huge solid mass twenty-eight and
three-quarters inches in diameter, the equivalent of two and one-third feet.
There are seventy thousand miles of wire in the cable, which mileage is
nearly three times around the world at the equator. And the weight! The wire,
p\us clamps, plus wrappings, is 2000 pounds, or one ton, per square foot. The
total weight of the cable is 18,700 tons.
But, brethren! All the cables, all the tremendous power, plus the power of
the towers, the power : hydraulic, electrical, and steam, plus the engineering
skill and engineering genius; this, plus all the ability necessary to create such a
marvelous miracle, could not of .itself pull one single man out of the gutter and
put him on his feet. Such mechanical miracle needs something else; it needs
spiritual power, it needs spiritual strength, it needs God. It needs the kind of
spiritual truths taught in Masonry: Brotherly Love, Relief, Truth.
Oh my brethren ! What an hour of need is there today for temperance, fortitude, prudence, justice. For regard for the sacred book as the Great Light. For
a reliving of important duties to God, to our neighbors, and to ourselves : To
God, with reverence, to neighbor, upon the square; to ourselves, by enlarging
the place of our spiritual tent, by stretching forth curtains of our spiritual
habitations.
It was my privilege this past summer to visit the Republic of Panama.
Panama, which contains another one of the modern miracles of engineering
skill and genius. Panama, which has within it the constant picture of man's
creation. Yet, in the back country and outlying districts of Panama there is much
need for enlightenment, for education, and fo r spiritual power.
Upon one of our excursions we "followed a trail into the jungle. We went
down a steep bank, across a flowing stream, over a fallen log, up the steep
bank on the other side, and into a trail which led ahead through a mass and a
maze of tangled tropical jungle.
·
On either side of the trail was the tangle of poison vines, massive trees,
and dense growth of every tropical variety. It was a temptation and an enticement for one to leave the trail and follow the songs of singing birds, the flaming
blossoms of the wild banana, and the very breath and allurement of the jungle
itself. However, to leave the trail meant to be swallowed up and lost in the
maze and tangle, and the unknown darkness of overhanging danger.
To keep the trail meant to come out on the other side where were native
huts, built on stilts, with thatched roofs, grass in the yards, chickens and little
pigs. Homes where was the laughter of little children and the joyous harmony
of husband and wife.
In the experience, my brethren, I realized that in the jungle of our modern
life and living in the maze of uncertainty of our every day experiences, there
is but one course, one trail, that leads through and beyond into the everlasting
home, the home of God. That trail is the spiritual trail, the lengthening of the
spiritual cords and the strengthening of the spiritual stakes.

MESSAGE OF RANDOLPH V. WHITING, GRAND MASTER

Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
As I am about to pass the gavel of Grand Lodge to my successor, I take
this opportunity of expressing to you and to the craft my deep appreciation ~f
the great honor bestowed upon me in my selection as. Gra~d. M~st~r of .this
grand body. It is an honor of which any man, whatever his position m hfe, might
well be proud.
I accepted the position with a keen sense of responsibility, for I felt .the
duties of the office would tax the ability and energy of one far more capable
than myself. I relinquish the office with some sense of disappointment, as I
realize how little can be accomplished in the brief period of a yea~-.
I have endeavored to visit as many Lodges and con.tact as many Brethren as
possible but I found it humanly impossible to cover the whole jurisdiction
thoroughly, and all that I can say to those whom I was unable to reach . is that
it was only the shortness of time, and the multiplicity of my duties, that prevented me from doing so, and that I am keenly disappointed in not having had
the opportunity of meeting them. The contacts that I was able to make ~ere
most agreeable and pleasant; indeed, the pleasure that the Grand Master enioys
in this regard is ample compensation for the labors he performs in the discharge
of his duties.
Assistance of Officers
I desire to express my sincere gratitude to the officers of Grand Lodge for
the generous support and assistance given me throughout the year. The R. W .
Deputy Grand Master, Brother Earl Warren, and the R. W . Senior and Junior
Grand Wardens Brother Rollie W. Miller and Brother Thomas Fraser, have
on all occasion~ genen;msly contributed their time and energies to assist in
relieving my burdens.
Throughout the year I have had the valuable counsel and sympathetic
encouragement of our distinguished Past Grand Master and Gran? Treasurer,
Brother William P. Filmer, as indeed I have had for the past thirty years or
more. His friendship has been one of the most genuine that I have had the good ·
fortune to enjoy at any time. I am confident that the generous heart of Grand
Lodge beats in loving sympathy for him in this, his greatest hour of grief and
bereavement, in the irreparable loss that he has recently suffered.
It gives me a special pleasure to acknowledge my indebtedness to our Grand
Secretary, Brother John Whicher, for his untiring kindness and gene;ous support of my efforts, without which my labors woul? h~v~ b_een greatly 1~crease?.
His long efficient and loyal service to this grand iunsd1ct1on has contributed m
a very l~rge measure to placing it in the enviable position it enjoys among the
grand jurisdictions of the country. He has richly earned and, I feel sure, enjoys
the affectionate gratitude of every Brother within our jurisdiction. I congratulate
him on having attained his eightieth birthday, and wish for him many years of
health and happiness, which we are glad to say he now enjoys; and for ourselves
we hope we may have a long continuance of the benefit of his efficient services.
The Departed ·
In addition to the usual loss by death, Grand Lodge has suffered a particular
loss in the passing of Brothers Past Grand Master David J. Reese, Inspector
Roderick G. Guyett and William P . Jeffries, all of whom were mos.t devoted
and efficient in their long service to Grand Lodge. These dear Brethren, as well

but we confidently believe they have passed to a life eternal to enjoy the rewards

395

Visitations
It is regrettable that time does not permit the Grand Master to visit all
Lodges in the jurisdiction. His visits are made occasions for large gatherings of
the membership, and, I believe, have a very stimulating effect. The Lodges are
most generous and hospitable in their entertainments and seem to deeply appreciate the presence of the Grand Master. I was particularly struck with the
universal respect paid by the craft. to the office of Grand Master, representing,
as he does, the great fraternity to which we are all proud to owe allegiance.
Unfortunately, in these practical days, too little respect is paid to positions,
either public or private, political or fraternal, and I believe that the critical
state of the public mind in this regard is most destructive. Ideals have their
value and a wholesome public opinion is necessary to support constituted authority
and our social structure. While criticism, if constructive, is necessary for progress, criticism without suggested improvement is of but little value, and in my
addresses to Lodges I have constantly urged the creation of a wholesome and
constructive attitude toward public offices, and those upon whom we must depend
for the conduct of our government.
State of the Fraternity
I have . been greatly gratified to find on my visitations to Lodges that the
fraternity seems to be strong and healthy, notwithstanding the distressing times
we are passing through. The "spirit of Masonry" seems virile and active in all
the Lodges visited. I was particularly pleased with the personnel of the Lodges,
and, generally speaking with the officers, all of whom seemed keenly interested
in their work and active in seeking to carry out our purposes.
Conference of Grand Masters
I had the unusual pleasure of attending the conference of Grand Masters,
held annually in Washington, D. C., and, as a tribute to the Grand Lodge of
California, I was elected chairman of the conference and presided during its
sessions. I found it most interesting and instructive, and I believe well worth
while. In the absence of a grand jurisdiction of the United States, this is the
only opportunity for a ready interchange of ideas and discussions among the
grand jurisdictions of our country on subjects that are of common interest. A
number of outstanding and able papers were read on subjects of general public
importance and many addresses delivered on particular Masonic topics, general
discussion ensuing with a beneficial exchange of ideas. The agenda were as
follows:
1. Lodge Attendance. How may it be improved? What methods to secure
increased attendance are most effective? (a) Masonic lectures and addresses;
(b) programs of general entertainment. Give outline of plans which have
been successful.
2. Lodge Dues. What methods of collection have been found most effective?
In what manner may· Grand Lodges assist? Are specific regulations by Grand
Lodge on the subject, such as prescribing uniform time for action on delinquents and mandatory compliance with regulations desirable?
3. Dimits. Consideration of survey of laws of the several jurisdictions and their
operation as made by a committee of the Conference of Grand Secretaries.
Is greater uniformity in practices of various Grand Lodges desirable and
how may it be obtained?
4. Masonic Burial Service. How may present tendency to decline such service,

observed· in some jurisdictions, be counteracted? Is service too long or its
·
content objectionable in any way?
5. The Eighteenth Amendmmt. How may conditions growing out of repeal be
met? (a) With reference to petitioners connected with the liquor business?
(b) With reference to members engaging in the business after initiation?
6. New World Conditions. To what extent and in what sense should Masonry
endeavor to adapt itself to meet changed conditions in the outside world?
Can these changes be made without conflict with the basic principles and

George Washington Memorial
Upon the adjournment of the Conference of Grand Masters, the members
of this body who comprise the George Washington Memorial Association held
a meeting of the Association in the Memorial Auditorium at Alexandria.
According to the report of the President and the Board of Directors $3 963 352.24 have been expended on the memorial, to which California Mas~ns 'ha;e
contributed over $170,000. The building is still uncompleted and the project will
require about $500,000 more. Urgent requests were made for further contributions, as it was considered a reflection upon the fraternity to allow the work to
remain unfinished, the ground floor presenting an unattractive appearance to the
visiting public and creating the unfavorable impression that Masonry is either
apathetic or negligent in this great patriotic enterprise. I believe we should make
further contributions, as others are doing, when our financial condition will
permit.
Hawaiian Islands
My visit to the Hawaiian Islands was particularly pleasant and interesting,
not only on account of the proverbial hospitality of the local members, but also
because of the unusual conditions which prevail there. In my travels around the
four islands, on which there. are eight Lodges in all, I found sterling groups of
Masons, many of them occupying leading positions in industry. By reason of
the great foreign population, much of which is not assimilable in Masonry the
Masonic field is restricted, but it is apparent that Masonry has a pow~rful
influence in the industrial and social life there, and that it plays an important
role in shaping the destiny of this vital Pacific outpost of our continent.
Special Communications
We have held a number of special communications during the year and
several cornerstones of public buildings and temples have been laid by Grand
Lodge, with impressive ceremonies, supported by local bodies. Generally speaking, on these occasions preparations had been carefully made and the ceremonies
well conducted, but local bodies should be careful to see that members who fill
the stations in these ceremonies are qualified to do their work creditably, as
these are among the few occasions open to the public, which receives a favorable
or unfavorable impression according to the way the ceremony is conducted.
