Fairmount Lodge No. 435
I am happy to say that the differences of Fairmount Lodge seem to be
ended and the Lodge restored to a state of harmony. Too much credit cannot be
given to the committee of the Grand Lodge consisting of Past Grand Master
Adams, Past Grand Master Wollenberg and Past Grand Master Jones, for their
wise and considerate direction under which this Lodge operated for a. time; nor
can too much praise be given to Worshipful Past Master Daniel Bosschart and
Worshipful Master Max Cowan for their able administration and energetic efforts to restore harmony. The members of this Lodge are also entitled to great
credit for ultimately suppressing their individual feelings and, in a spirit of true
Masonry, uniting in their efforts to remove factionalism and to restore peace.
I congratulate them all and commend their generous spirit and great interest
in their Lodge.
Decisions .
Decision No. I: Demit.
I was asked by a member of Crocker Lodge No. 454, who was a Past
Master of that Lodge of long standing, for a ruling on his status in the Lodge
under the following circumstances :
The undisputed facts were that on January 2, 1934, at a stated meeting of
the Lodge, the Brother requested a demit (without recommendation) ; no action
was taken by the Lodge at that time, but a committee was appointed by the
Master to ask the Brother to reconsider. The committee waited upon him upon
one or more occasions to discuss the matter, and on June 2, 1934, he wrote the
Master refusing the demit. The Brother had paid his dues for the last quarter
of 1933, but had not paid for the first quarter of 1934.
I ruled that the Brother was not entitled to a demit at the time he applied
for it, for the reason that his dues for the quarter beginning January 1, 1934,
were not paid and that such dues had become due and payable on the 1st of
January, 1934. Under the provisions of article XI of "The Uniform Code of
By-Laws of Lodges," and under section 150 of the Constitution, he was not
entitled to receive a demit, and the demit thereafter issued was void.

Decision No. 2: Information as to .Standing of Member.
I was asked to determine whether a Secretary or Master of a Lodge has
the right to issue a letter of standing of a member in the Lodge without the
consent or request of that member. The information was sought by a sister of a
member for the purpose of joining the Eastern Star.
I ruled that neither the Secretary nor the Master had any right, without the
consent or request of the member, to furnish such information.
Decision No. 3: Physical Qualification of Officer.
An inspector requested a ruling as to whether a Brother who had been
elected Senior Warden, and had an injury on his left knee, preventing him from
kneeling on it, was disqualified from election or serving in that capacity.
I ruled that this did not disqualify him.

398

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Decision No. 4: Objection to initiation. Sale of Beer by Petitioner.
A Lodge asked for a ruling on an objection to the initiation of a petitioner ·
who had been elected to the Lodge, the objection being that the petitioner ran a
pool room and sold beer over the counter as draught beer, the beer being
so-called 3.4 beer, rated by the United States Government as non-intoxicating.
I ruled that, under section 108 of the Constitution, objection might be made
by any member of the Lodge any time before initiation, and that the petitioner
could not receive the degree unless such objection was withdrawn within sixty
days, and that unless it were withdrawn it had the effect of rejection by ballot.
Decision No. 5: Master Elect. Loss of H a1id.
An inspector asked for a ruling as to whether the fact that a Master Elect
had lost a hand disqualified him from serving as Master.
·
I ruled that it did not, provided he was able to perform the duties of that
·
office.
Decision No. 6: Objection to Petitioner After Initiation by Non-Member
of Lodge.
The Master of. a Lodge requested a decision on an objection made after
initiation of a petitioner by one not a member of the Lodge. After the objection
was made the Lodge unanimously voted to overrule it.
I held, first, that the objector had no standing, not being a member of the
Lodge, to make the objection, and, secondly, as the Lodge unanimously overruled the objection it was in order to proceed to confer the degrees.
Decision No. 7: Duplicate Pictures of Past Masters. Payment for.
A Lodge requested a ruling as .to whether the expense for i>ictun:s of Past
Masters, to be placed in a fire-proof safe to be used in the event the originals
were lost, could be taken from the general fund of the Lodge.
I held that this was not a proper or necessary expense of the Lodge and that
the cost should be supplied, if at all, by individual contributions, basing my
decision upon the ruling of Grand Master Preston, noted at section 176 of the
Digest.
Decision No. 8: Investment of Lodge Funds.
A Master of a Lodge requested a ruling as to the legality of investing
Lodge funds in the securities of a building and loan association.
I ruled that under section 87 of the Constitution, the investment of funds by
a Lodge was only permitted in securities prescribed as legal by the laws of
California or the Territory of Hawaii for investment by savings banks; that
under the law of California there was no authority for the investing of such .
funds in building and loan company securities. My decision was based upon the
law as it existed at the time of the decision.
Decision No. 9: Remission of Dues of Forty-Year Members.
A decision .was requested as to the legality of a proposed amendment to the
by-laws of a Lodge, providing for the remission of dues in favor of members of
forty years' standing, or m·ore.
I ruled that the policy of Grand Lodge had been to require all members who
are so circumstanced that they can pay their dues to continue to contribute to
the support of the Lodge, regardless of the length of time that they have
belonged to a California Lodge, and that the amendment should be remodeled to
conform to the opinion of Grand Lodge.
Decision No. ro: Objection to a Petitio11. Erroneous Overruling of O/:Jjection. Status of Petitioner.
A Master asked for a ruling as to the legal effect of overruling an objectioi'i,
made before initiation by a member of the Lodge, to a petition for degrees, and

also as to the status of petitioner after an erroneous overruling of the objection.
I ruled that under section 108 of the 'Constitution, neither the Master nor

As to the status of the petitioner, I ruled that it was that of a Fellowcraft

Decision No. II: Dispensation to Re-ballot on Candidate.
I had a number of requests for permission to re-ballot upon the petitions
of rejected candidates, some of which I granted and some I denied.
I ruled that under the Constitution and decisions of Grand Lodge, a dispensation to re-ballot on the petition of a rejected candidate should not be granted,
unless there ·was good reason to believe that a mistake had been made, or other
extraordinary circumstances existed, and that a showing should be made to the
Grand Master of reasons for granting the dispensation.

Deci~ion No. u: Exemption of Past Masters From Payment of Dues.
. A Lodge requested an opinion as to the legality of exempting Past Masters
from the payment of dues.
I ruled that under section 128 of the Constitution a Lodge has no power
"by amendment to its by-laws, resolution or otherwi'se" to remit the dues of its
members, or any of them, for any stated period, or in advance, except as to one
who has been a member in good standing in a Lodge for a period of forty years
or more, but it may annually remit the accrued dues of those of its members who
have rendered special service for the Lodge, or who are unable to pay them.
I further held that under sectiori 88 of the Constitution, a Lodge may in its
discretion appropriate from its funds any amount for the i>urchase of a testimonial for its "retiring Master," and that under this provision the Lodge would
have the right to purchase a life membership for, and present it to, its "retiring
Master."

Decision No. IJ: Jurisdiction.
Objection was made to the raising to the sublime degree of Master Mason
of a petitioner who had . been previously rejected in three Lodges, in one of
which he was rejected four times. The circumstances briefly were that the
petitioner had for a number of years owned a home and resided in San Pedro,
with his family, where he conducted a business, and after his last rejection by
the Lodge in this district he changed his registration for voting purposes, as he
states, upon the advice of a Master of one of the Lodges, to Pine Knot, where
he had a summer home. Some time after this he presented a petition to Big Bear
· Lodge and was elected, initiated and passed, after which objection was made to
his being raised, and I was called upon for ruling on the case.
I appointed a conunittee to investigate the case and was present at a hearing
of the committee in Riverside, at which the committee and myself listened to
statements of officers of Big Bear Lodge with reference to the case. I thereafter
· propounded certain questions to the petitioner with reference to his residence,
which, with other evidence surrounding the case, satisfied me that the petitioner
had never in fact abandoned his residence in San Pedro. I held that a person
under Masonic law, as well as under civil law, can have but one place of residence at a time, and that I was satisfied under the evidence that the petitioner
had never abandoned his residence in San Pedro and, therefore, that Big Bear
Lodge had irregularly received his petition. I ordered the latter Lodge to return
to the petitioner the fees he had paid it for the degree of Master Mason, and to
turn over to the Lodge of proper jurisdiction the fees he had paid for the
Entered Apprentice and Fellowcraft degrees. I further decided that the petitioner
had the status of a Fellowcraft Mason, but could not be raised to the sublime
degree of Master Mason except upon proper proceedings therefor in the Looge
having jurisdiction.

Decisio11 No. I8: Sale of Intoxicating Liquor. Restaura11t and Hotels.
I was requested by the Master of a Lodge for a ruling as to the propriety
of a Lodge receiving a petition for degrees by one who owns and operates a
cafe and holds a retail license for the sale of wine and beer, and who on occasions himself served his customers, for consumption on the premises, but ordinarily the service being performed by his employees.
I ruled that under section 129A of the Constitution, a petition for degrees by
one who is legally selling intoxicating liquors in connection with the operation of
a bona fide hotel or restaurant may be received and acted upon; and the fact that
the peti tfoner occasionally serves customers does not alter the case, provided he
· is the owner and operates the hotel or restaurant business in good faith.

I am sorry to say that in a few isolated cases I believe Lodges have
been too inconsiderate in their treatment of distressed brethren, and in some
cases they have not only not shown the proper Masonic spirit, but have
failed to carry out the spirit of the Constitution. Under Sections 117 and
118 of the Constitution it is obvious that a member should not be suspended for nonpayment of dues where it is shown nonpayment is the result
of sickness or inability to pay. The committees of Lodges should make
careful investigation of the circumstances of a brother before suspension,
where it is possible to do so; and relief should be granted him, if a meritorious case, even though pride may prevent him from asking for it.

. Entertainments in Lodges
I am advised that entertainments are permitted in social activities of Lodges
of an indecent character, and that frequently risque and eY'!n vulgar stories are
told on such occasions. This, of course, is absolutely unmasonic and should not
be tolerated under any circumstances. The Master of a Lodge should strictly
forbid any such occurrences and scrupulously insist upon a proper adherence to
this rule. Considering the high moral purposes of our fraternity, it is unthinkable
that such things are permitted or countenanced in a Masonic Lodge. The Master
should be held to a strict accountability in these matters.
My attention has also been called to the fact that even athletic activities
outside the Lodge precincts are patronized and in some cases paid for out of
Lodge funds. Such practice, in my opinion, is not within the domain of Masonic
activity and might involve financial 1liabilities resulting from injuries, which
would fall upon the Lodge; nor should Lodge funds be devoted to any such
purpose.

404

Financial Obligations of Lodges
During the depression, Masonry has naturally suffered with all other institutions, and, unfortunately, many building enterprises were started during
good times for which large obligations were assumed by Masonic groups and
which, with the coming of the financial crash, they were unable to meet. My
attention has been called to one or two instances where the attitude of such
groups toward their obligations has been criticized as not reflecting any credit
upon Masonry. In this connection I desire to say that I have no sympathy with
any Masonic group which does not meet such a situation squarely and perform
its obligation to the full extent of its ability. Any other course by a group or
individual Masons reflects no credit upon the craft.
Advertising Through Masonry
My attention has been called repeatedly through the year to the practice
O·f advertising through Masonry. This is done for business purposes, political
purposes, and even for meetings of churches. Various means and devices are
resorted to and the practice has become so prevalent as to be decidedly objectionable and should be stopped. I believe our present laws are sufficient to cover
the matter and should be enforced, but if not, further penalities should be provided against individual members who resort to this misuse of the fraternity.
Masonic Activities
As to the limit of proper activities of Lodges there seems to be some
difference of opinion, but I have considered and acted upon the theory that
matters of fundamental, general public concern are well within the purview of
our purposes, and that the presentation in the proper way, for the information of
the brethren, of data on such matters is entirely proper. It is, of course, obvious
that no subject should be presented that may result in dissension or inharmony,
and, naturally, no religious, political or personal questions should be considered, as
the discussion of such questions in all probability would ultimately result in
discord. However, as Masonry enjoins the obligation of patriotism and good
citizenship on its members, I believe discussions of such subjects are quite
within the range of our activities, as, of course, are subjects of Masonic history, ritual and the moral principles upon which the Institution rests. In fact,
there are almost innumerable subjects within these general classes that could be
presented for the information, benefit and entertainment of the membership, and
I believe that such activities should be encouraged in Lodges in order to stimnlate
interest. I find that this is being done in some Lodges, but it would be very
desirable, in my opinion, to have it more universally practiced. Masonry can
be made a powerful inst.rument for public good if, in addition to promulgating
its spiritual and moral precepts, it seeks to create through its membership a
wholesome public opinion and activity in matters of vital and general importance.
I am not, however, in favor of Lodges or other groups passing resolutions on
such subjects. It must be left to Grand Lodge to declare policies and the minds of
. members should be kept open until such matters are presented and considered in
the annual Communication.

405

Objectionable Activities
Complaints have been made during the year about activities of groups in
organizations which prescribe membership in the Blue Lodge as a prerequisite
to membership in those organizations, which activities, it is claimed, tend to bring
Masonry into disrepute. These activities, in a general way, may be described
as resorting to games of chance to raise funds for the particular organization,
improper use of intoxicating liquors, and the staging of indecent performances.
The groups particularly complained of are Shriners and Sciots. It would serve
no useful purpose at this time to go into the details of these activities, for I
believe that the fraternity is quite familiar with them as a matter of common
knowledge.
t
In another jurisdiction the Grand Master saw fit to put on trial individual
members who had been charged with promotion of a game of chance, and, I am
informed, some of these members were convicted and ordered expelled. After
mature consideration, I have come to the conclusion that this is not the effective
way to check such activities. When it is remembered that the promotion of a
lottery or other game of chance by a few members of an organization is done
with the knowledge and approval of that organization, which organization
accepts the benefit, if any, of the enterprise, in my opinion, the organization itself
should be held responsible and proper means taken to discipline it as far as
Grand Lodge has that jurisdiction. I, therefore, recommend for consideration
by the Policy and Purposes Committee the question of the advisability oi putting
under a ban any such organization which is found to be indulging in, or permitting its members to indulge in, any activity that is found by Grand Lodge
to be injurious to the reputation .of Masonry in general; and while the organization is .under such ban all Master Masons be forbidden to join or remain members
of it. If such policy should be adopted, legislation should be provided for carrying it into effect, and specific penalities should be prescribed also for individual
Master Masons who indulge in such forbidden activities. I can easily understand
that members of such <>rganizations, in their zeal for their organization and
ambitious to raise funds for its purposes, may be carrjed away with their enthusiasm, but the organization itself should see to it that its activities and the
activities of its individual members are not such as may be detrimental to
Masonry. Grand Lodge has · jurisdiction over every Master Mason and has
power to insist upon such course. It might be ;;idvisable to provide for a standing
committee to receive complaints and investigate such alleged objectionable
actions.

Masonic Homes
Under the able direction of our diligent Board of Trustees, and the capable
administration of our superintendents, our two Masonic Homes are functioning
with the usual fine results. Too high praise cannot be given to the brethren of
the Board of Trustees who have served for many years with all the fidelity ·and
ability that could be displayed in any private enterprise. The fraternity as a
whole ·has little knowledge of the time and attention devoted by these brethren
to this important work. Their devotion to the cause entitles them to our everlasting gratitude. We are also particularly fortunate in having such capable and
well qualified superintendents as Brothers Downen and Hartman in charge of
the Homes. Their long experience and loyalty to the institution fit them for
the positions as few men in the country are fitted. While the Homes are performing a wonderful service, the Lodges which place children or old people in
them, I am sorry to say, are not doing their part in one regard. There is too
little interest shown by many Lodges in the welfare of the children on leaving
the Covina Home, and in the old people while at their Home at Decato. The
Lodges should realize that, in a sense, they are the guardians of those whom
they place in the Homes and should contribute to their happiness and welfare
by some attention while there. It is especially important that Lodges should
interest themselves in placing children leaving the Home in positions and suitable surroundings. Frequent complaints have been made of lack of interest in
this regard. It should also be remembered that those in the Homes are without
means to make small purchases which will contribute to their comfort and entertainment, and if their Lodges would constantly bear this in mind and make
regularly, or at least frequently, gifts to them of small amounts of money, or
suitable articles, this would add much to their happiness., We must not forget
that we aim not only to provide for their material necessities, but to make them
as happy as their circumstances will permit.

Masonic Club Houses
My observation convinces me that the Masonic Club Houses are performing

Masonic contact and Masonic influence. This influence cannot start too early,
and its importance cannot be o.verestimated.
New Ritual Plan
The new plan for instruction in ritual has, I feel, been a?ly put into practi~e

As to the relative merit of this system over the old system, I am not as able
to judge as those who have had more intimate connection with it, and I there.fore
refrain from making any recommendation, preferring that it shall be submitted
to Grand Lodge for determination, after the subject has been presented by those
who have had more detailed experience with it than I have had.
I am deeply appreciative of the uniform courtesy and assistance which I
received at the hands of the Grand Lecturer and his assistants throughout the
year. They have been more than generous in their kindness and willingness to
assist in relieving my burdens.
Inspectors
In my visitations to Lodges I have been deeply im~ressed by the charac.ter
of our Inspectors. I have found them, generally speaking, men of outstanding
ability ·and position, devoted to and keenly interested in their work, as ~ell as
our other activities. Many have served for years with the greatest fidelity and
zeal. · They have been of great assistance to me in making necessary i_nvestigations
and other services and I sincerely appreciate their hearty cooperation.
Masters and Other Officers of Lodges
While I have found, as a general thing, that the Masters and other office~s
of Lodges have been apparently competent and well qualified to perform their .
duties I am sorry to say that a number of cases have come to my knowledge
wher~ Masters were mentally unqualified and temperamentally unfit to serve
as Masters and the inevitable result has been inharmony and dissension in their
Lodges. 1n' this connection I make the suggestion that those memb.ers who con- .
tinue their interest and activity throughout the years should use their best efforts
to see that brethren with the proper mental equipment are put in line for offi~e.
It is necessary in any orga_nization that there should be :3' g~oup or g_roups wh1c?
maintain a steady interest in the welfare of the orgamzahon, and m Lodges it
might well be expected of Past Masters, office~s and ~t~ers of e~perience . to
maintain such interest and activity, and to exercise a gu1dmg hand m the maintenance of a high standard of proficiency in the work. I b~liev_e, ~!so, th.at Inspectors who come in clos~ contact wi~h the Lod~es of their d1st~1cts, without,
of course, endeavoring to improperly interfere with the free choice of officers
by the membership, should keep an eye on the personnel of the offi~ers ~nd constantly promote the policy of maintaining the proper standard. I belteve 1t would
be a good practice for Lodges to try out officers up ~o a~d t.hrough t~e. office. of
Senior Deacon, and, if such officer does not by t?a~ time md1cate qua!1t1e~ fittmg
him for the position of Master, he s.hould be eliminated and others m- !me who
are qualified should be advanced.
Masters and Wardens Associations
I have had the pleasure of attending a number of Masters and Wardens
Association meetings and found them interesting and instructive. I believe that
these associations can be very useful in discussing matters of Masonic procedure
and policy, as well as questions of fundamental publi~ importa~ce._Th.ey furnish a
means for imparting information to the membership of their districts and can

promote programs which will stimulate and incite interest in their various
Lodges.
I feel it my duty, however, to caution them, as I have cautioned Lodges
repeatedly, to be careful not to take up or allow discussion of controversial .
matters or of a religious, political or personal character that will tend to produce
inharmony. I am sure · the good sense of the leaders and members of these
associations will restrain any such tendency. It is obvious that it would be disastrous to Masonry to engage in controversies which would result in bitterness
and inharmony, and, of course, they should be avoided.
Officers·Associations
I have had several outstanding cases brought to my attention showing the
lamentable ignorance or disregard of our rules and regulations by Masters of
Lodges. It happened that the particular matters were such that there was no
excuse for the action of the Masters in reference to them, and they exemplified
in a pronounced degree the importance of the Master's functions.
Officers Associations can be, and should be, very useful bodies in instructing
officers with reference to the laws, regulations and procedure, and the Inspectors
should be particular to see that the officers are thoroughly schooled in this
regard. I have no doubt that much is being done in this line in the associations,
but my experience as Grand Master has taught me that there are too many
Masters who are either unqualified to perform their duties, or are negligent or
weak in their discharge. A Master's position is not only one of dig!)ity, but of
extreme importance. A Lodge's harmony and usefulness can be utterly destroyed by an incompetent or negligent Master.
Subversive Activities
In my addresses to Lodges during the year I have taken as my main theme
subjects allied to patriotism and government, and in this connection I have presented data on subversive organizations that are opposed to, and violently attacking, principles which -are fundamental in Masonry. I refer particularly to
the Communist Party of America, which is an organization dominated by the
Third Internationale of Russia.
In 1931 a committee of the House of Representatives made what appears
to have been a thorough investigation of this organization in all places in the
United States where its activities were evident. Its report states that hearings
were held in practically every section of the United States where Communist
activities were reported and that witnesses were examined representing all walks
of life; many of the prominent witnesses being named. Testimony verbatim of
some of the leaders of this party was also set out in the report. Among other
things the committee found as follows:
"The principles and aims of communists in Moscow and communists in
Berlin, Paris, London, New York, Los Angeles, Tokyo, and Pekin are the
same; they stand on the same platform and advocate the same principles,
and all take their orders from the Communist Internationale, with headquarters in Moscow, and obey them implicitly.
"It is not difficult to find out exactly what these principles are, and
to define communism so that he who runs can read, as communists do not
attempt to hide their fundamental purposes and admit and are apparently
proud of taking their orders from Moscow and giving allegiance to the
red flag and the Soviet Union.
"The following is a definition of communism, a world-wide political
organization advocating: ( 1) Hatred of God and all forms of religion; (2)
destruction of private property, and inheritance; (3) absolute social and
racial equality; promotion of class hatred; ( 4) revolutionary propaganda
through the Communist Internationale, stirring up communist activities in

foreign countries in order to cause strikes, riots, sa?otage, bloodsh~d, and
civil war; ( 5) destruction of all forms of representative or democratic governments · including civil liberties, such as freedom of speech, of the press,
of assembly, and trial by jury ; (6) the ultimate. and final objective is by
means of world revolution to establish the dictatorship of the so-called
proletariat into one world union of soviet socialist republic with the capital
at Moscow.
" Communism has also been defined as an organized effort to overthrow
organized governments which operate contrary to the communis~ plan now
in effect in Russia. It aims at the socialization of government, private property, industry, labor, the home, education, and religion. Its objectives are the
abolition of other governments, private ownership of property, inheritance,
religion, and family relations."
The report also shows the nature of the activities of this organization and
the means and methods of propogating its subversive and revolutionary ideas
among our people, especially among the youth of the country; and also
activity among labor organizations in stirring up strife, riots, and gen.era! ~1s­
order, all with the aim of weakening the morale of the country and 1mposmg
its atheistic, despotic and anarchistic principles upon our people.
This organization, as shown by the report, has many affiliates and adopts
many devious means and organizations to carry out its purposes. Am.ong those
organizations used to reach the youth of the country are the Young Pioneers of
America and the Young Communist League. The report shows that• Many
Young Pioneer Summer Camps, conducted by th~ Workers' I?ternationale Reli.ef,
have sprung up in various sections of the Umted States smce 1925, at which
time there were two camps. In 1929 the number had increased to twenty, located
in eight different states. New York state predominates, with five such ca~ps,
all teaching hatred of God, of our form of government, and of the A~encan
flag. In New York state alone over fifteen thousand young commum.sts are
turned out each year, according to the report, from these camps, tramed to
promote class hatred and to urge the destruction of all American ideals and
traditions. The report further states that a very large percentage of these
Young Pioneers are either aliens or foreign-born, probably eighty per cent, ancl
most of the remainder are children of foreign born parents, with perhaps not
more than five percent of native born Americans.
This report is so full of astounding information that it should be in the
hands of every citizen of our country. It is too long even to epitomize. Emanating as it does from our federal government, and showing .the care with whic.h
the material contained in it was gathered, I have deemed 1t the most authentic
information to be obtained on this subject. In addition to it, however, there .~re
·many other evidences of the activities of this nefarious organization in our
midst among them a report by William Green, President' of the American
Fede;ation of Labor, made to the President of the United States in July, 1934,
which is filled with similar alarming information. There is reliable evidence
that this organization has increased to a great extent in the past four years
and has a very large membership in the State of California, where its work
has been openly manifested.
There is reason to believe this organization has insidiously infiltrated our
higher educational institutions, public schools, civic organizations, public offices,
and even · to some extent churches, the Army and Navy and other government
departments.
.
.
Many patriotic organizations have vigorously taken up the fight to drive this
alien, atheistic, despotic and anarchistic organization out of our country, among
them various Masonic bodies, the American Legion, the American Federation
of -Labor, the Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks, and others.
The objects and purposes of this organization are so fundamentally anti-

Masonic and so contrary to the spirit and genius of our government and our
religious' and social institutions, that I have deemed it not only a proper subject
for presentation in Lodges, but as imposing an absolute obligation on every
Mason in this jurisdiction to advise himself as fully as possible with reference
to it, and to use every legitimate and lawful means to prevent the spread of its
influence and teaching. It is regrettable, but none the less true, that by the most
insidious methods, the promulgators of these poisonous and destructive theories
have enlisted the sympathy of many of our high-minded and well-intentioned
people who have been misled by lack of proper information and misrepresentation
and w'ho have stood upon the principles of the right of political liberty and
freedom of speech to justify their position, but these rights certainly give no
alien and not even a citizen of the country, the right to advocate the overthrow
of o~r government by force and violence, nor can any Mason tolerate a doctrine
that teaches hatred of God and all forms of religion.
The committee which rendered the above report stated it was convinced that
the surest and most effective way of combating communism in the United States
was to give the fullest possible publicity to the fundamental principles and aims
of the communists, which are the same throughout the world, as they are not
likely to prove acceptable to any considerable number of American citizens, unless
camouflaged by extraneous issues, such as unemployment insurance.
Bigotry and Intolerance
I .have observed with chagrin in the . past few months some evidence of
bigotry and intolerance in some members of the craft. This spirit is foreign
to the teachings and precepts of Masonry, which has no creed and opposes no
creed. Masonry stands upon the broad fundamental principle of a belief in, and
reverence for God and support of religion in general as a human institution
for the education ;f mankind in moral principles and as an elevating influence
in matters spiritual. It must be remembered that one of the fundamental ideas
upon which our country was founded was that of religious liberty and the right
of every individual to worship God in such manner as his conscience shall dictate.
Masonry has always stood for human liberty and liberty of conscience, and nothing could be more detrimental to it than a spirit of intolerance and bigotry, which
would inevitably breed inharmony and discord in our ranks. I, therefore, urge
the craft to discourage at all times any tendency in this regard.
Law and Order
In the last year we have had some striklng and tragic instances of lawlessness resulting in lynching, tar and feather proceedings and other illegal activities.
It is' not difficult to understand that under the stress and strain of great emotion
caused by dastardly .outrages, even ordinarily law-abiding citizens may take the
law in their own hands, but in sober moments they must realize the futility of such
proceedings and the detriment that is caused to the administration of justice. by
such acts. Masonry stands for law and order and for orderly procedure in the administration of justice between man and man, and cannot acquiesce in individual
action outside the law and judicial procedure. If such actions were countenanced,
society would inevitably disintegrate and chaos result. The due administration of
justice requires the sober, calm and deliberate action of minds that are unbiased
by excitement, passion, prejudice or self-interest, and "mob law,'' so-called, is
never administered under such conditions. Injustice is too likely to be done under
the stress of strong feeling and passion. We must, therefore, stand firmly for
the regular and due administration of justice through the channel of our courts
and under the procedure defined by our laws.
·
It is unfortunately true that too often there is a failure of justice in the
administration of our laws, but it is far better that we should devote our thoughts
and energies to reform our legal procedure than to countenance "mob law" with
its demoralizing tendencies. Much of our trouble comes from the lack of a whole-

some and strong public opinion in the matter of the administration of justice, as
well as in other things. We should seek to create a strong and healthy sentiment
in our communities for a rigid and strict enforcement· of our laws and the due
administration of justice. Each Mason can do his part in this regard in his immediate community, if he will interest himself.
Our Naturalized Brethren
I have found that in one or two cases serious inharmony in a Lodge; has
resulted, at least in part, from bitter controversies arising over the affairs of
foreign countries, and I am therefore prompted to suggest to our naturalized
Brethren that in acquiring citizenship in this great country they also assumed
obligations to it. If they prize their citizenship they should recognize that their
first duty is to our government and the .welfare of our country, rather than to the
country of their birth. It is easy to understand that one may have a lingering
interest in, and affection for, the land of his birth, but we cannot afford to have
matters of foreign controversy injected into our local affairs, especially where
they tend to breed inharmony in our ranks. We are concerned with the governments of other countries and their domestic affairs only to the extent that they
may interfere with and involve our own country and, therefore, we should _
scrupulously avoid injecting into our Lodges any disturbing questions with reference to foreign. theories of government or domestic regulations.
W arid Conditions
Pessimism and cynicism have no place in Masonry. We are taught to look
onward and upward and unceasingly to strive for the betterment of the human
family. But in the disturbed and distressed condition of the world today all
Masons are called upon to give thoughtful consideration to the threatening situation, lest democracy perish and despotism reign supreme.
A survey of the circumstances of the Old World presents a serious and sad
picture. We observe many of the leading nations under the domination of despotic
or militaristic governments which seem to have no regard for individual liberty,
and under which freedom of religion, freedom of the press and freedom of
speech and action have been almost completely suppressed. In these same countries
Masonry has been put under the ban for the obvious reason that its spirit of
democracy is directly and unalterably opposed to the rule and aims of such governments. Freemasonry has always been the implacab!;) enemy of tyranny and
oppression, and the champion of fundamental human rights.
History seems to repeat itself in this regard, for looking back over the ages
we observe despots and tyrants ruling for a time, and almost without exception
they have plunged the world into the catastrophe of war, with all its horrors and
legacies of hate, disaster and costs to humanity.
It is almost incomprehensible that, in these days of advanced education,
spiritual development and marvelous accomplishments of science, man's reason can
be so completely dethroned by the hysteria of war psychology as to cause him tu
turn all his accomplishments and powers to the destruction of his fellow-man and
the benefits of civilization. Unfortunately, the intense spidt of nationalism :rnd
the inordinate personal ambition of militarists, prompted by the lust for power
and material gain, seem stronger, at times, than the spiritual teachings of the
Master, and "man's inhumanity to man" seems to reach its extreme point of
brutality and to reap a full harvest of hate and misery.
Let us hope that a time shall come when man's moral and spiritual development shall prompt the nations of the earth to settle their controversies by reason
rather than by brute force.
Our Government
In the light of the tragic circumstances which face us today, it would seem
that we should be more appreciative than ever of our own form of government,

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

under which we have lived in happiness, prosperity and contentment for one ·
hundred and forty-eight years. We should remember that our forefathers fled
from the intolerance and despotism of rulers of the Old World and established
on this continent a civilization and government which have been the admiration
of peoples of all countries.
The spirit and genius of America, which were developed by our revolutionary
fathers, insuring religious liberty, free speech, free press and freedom of individual action as far as is consistent with the rights of others, have been embodied in our Constitution, and we should cherish and jealously guard it. It has ·
survived the stress and strain of civil and foreign wars, internal disturbances and
the attacks of foes within and without our gates.
The statesmen of the world have proclaimed our instrument of governmen.t
to be the greatest that the mind of man has yet conceived, and that those who
conceived and framed it were the greatest group of statesmen that ever gathered
together at one time. These founders of our Government had endured the hardships of war, the trials and tribulations of domestic strife, and had the task of
harmonizing the contentions of the people of a new and struggling country impoverished by war and harassed by the difficulties attending a vast, undeveloped
country, and out of their wide experience and mature wisdom there was developed
a theory of government which seems to have met the requirements of our civilization, and no condition seems to have arisen which requires any substantial modification of its fundamental principles.
Masons played an important role in laying the corner stones of our Government, and it was founded upon the fundamental, Masonic principle of democracy,
guaranteeing equal rights to all.
In the first Constitutional Congress of 1774 fifteen members were Masons;
of the total fifty-six signers of the Declaration of Independence twenty-nine, a
. majority, were Masons, and of the ultimate number of forty-two delegates to
the Constitutional Convention of 1787, which adopted our Federal Constitution,
twenty-eight, a majority, were Masons.
As Masonry had such an influential part in giving to us our great Govern.ment, so should it stand guard to see that this rich gift shall not be impaired by
the subversive influence of enemies, within or without the borders of our country.
The framers of our . Constitution, zealously guarding the spirit of democracy,
wisely placed certain checks on the powers that were therein conferred; among
them being a division of authority in three co-ordinating and independent departments of government: the legislative, with power to formulate and promulgate laws for our government; the judicial, to interpret and pass upon the validity
and constitutionality of such laws ; and the executive, as the head of the administration department.
Time has proven the wisdom-of this division of powers and responsibilities,
and its preservation is essential to the perpetuation of our democratic ideals and
truly Masonic spirit of equal rights for all. Any encroachment of one of these
departments upon the other would inevitably lead to the destruction of our
fundamental theory and tend toward despotism.
In the light of the tragedies which are ·now being enacted in other parts of
the world through the policies of despotic rulers, this result should be carefully
avoided. Until our Constitution shall be amended by the calm and deliberate
action of the people we must look to that great tribunal, the Supreme Court of
the United States, in passing upon legislati0n, to preserve the spirit and intent
of our organic law. Fortu.nately, that court, from its beginning, has retained
the respect and confidence of the nation.
Our Constitution provides a method for orderly and deliberate change when
circumstances require it, but I believe that no substantial change in it should be
made in time of great distress, when the public mind is warped and impassioned
by temporary conditions.

We are too prone to believe that every new emergency or complaint should
be met by new law, but we must remember that our Constitution safeguards our
fundamental principles and secures to us the spirit and substance of democracy.
Let us rededicate our lives to the service of God and country, and reaffirm
our faith in our Government and our institutions.
With the dark clouds of war gathering over the nations of the Old World
and even threatening to envelope our own great country, I know of no more
appropriate Masonic sentiment than that from the Great Boo'k of Light, which
is the rule and guide of our faith:
"Glory to God in the highest,
And on earth peace, good will toward men."
In bidding you farewell as your Grand Master, I invoke the blessings of
heaven upon you and all mankind.

Presentation To Our Museum
Robert E. Allan, for many years chairman of our Committee on
Returns, Past Master of Mission Lodge No. 169, presented the Past
Master's jewel of his father. It bears the following inscription: "Presented
by the brethren of Tyne Lodge No. 991 to Brother George A. Allan, P. M.,
as a mark of esteem. January 1, 1877." Bob received his Masonic degrees
in Tyne Lodge.
Brother Allan also presented two boxes of jewels formerly owned by
the late Brother Frederick Hemsley Shanks; one box containing a set of
Royal Arch jewels formerly belonging to Grandfather Shanks. The other
box of jewels contained a card reading as follows: "Worshipful Brother
Joseph George Shanks, Major in the Royal Marine Light Infantry, F. R.
G; S., Knight of the Imperial Order of the Medjedie, was in 1897-98 Master
of Cothele Lodge No. 2166 (Calstock, Cornwall, England) and on retiring
from office he presented a set of jewels to the Lodge, who by resolution gave
him these jewels, which were then sent to me to be used .at the dedication
of Lodge Thiele Lautoka, Fiji Islands."

418

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

. Brother Shanks was an enthusiastic Mason, receiving his craft degrees
at Suva, Fiji Islands, in 1898, and was a member of San Francisco No. 1,
Scottish Rite bodies. At the time of his death on October 19, 1931, he
was a member of Hawaiian Lodge No. 21.
Shorter Roll Call
Many members appear to want some method adopted whereby less
time would be consumed in the calling of the roll at the annual election
and at other times when a roll call may be required. There is only one
way for the accomplishment of this desire, and that is to provide that each
Lodge represented shall be entitled to a fixed number of votes. And for
the purpose only of an expression of opinion by Grand Lodge, I offer the
following resolution:

4
•

That section 22 of the Constitution be amended to read as follows:
Sec. 22. Each Lodge represented by a Master, Warden, Past Master,
0r Representative duly elected, shall be entitled to one vote.
That sections 21, 23, 24 and 25 be repealed.

Report of Auditors
To the Finance Committee,
Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California.

Pursuant to your instructions, we have completed an audit of the
books of account of the Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California for the
fiscal year ended July 31, 1935. The following statements are submitted
herewith:
Exhibit A: Grand Secretary's report of cash receipts and . disbursements-General Funci.
Exhibit B: Grand Secretary's report of cash received for the account
of Masonic Homes of California.
Exhibit C: Grand Treasurer's report of cash receipts and disbursements-General Fund.
Exhibit D: Grand Treasurer's report of assets on hand July 31, 1935.
The scope of our examination included a verification of total cash
funds received during the fiscal year ended July 31, 1935, from the annual returns covering the fiscal year 1933-34. Funds received and on hand
held in suspense based upon the annual returns for 1934-35 are not included in our examination. Total receipts due from subordinate lodges
as per individual annual returns were found to be in proof by total number of membership, classification of source of revenue, and total amount
of gross revenue received, as evidenced by the recapitulation record of all
subordinate Lodges. Total of ali receipts were found accounted for and
cash received therefrom deposited in bank accounts. Bank accounts were
reconciled and verified, and sufficient examination of detailed vouchers
was made as to satisfy ourselves as. to the correctness of the accounting.
The following amounts due Grand.Lodge previously carried in memorandum, have been entered in the general ledger as at July 31, 1935, in
permanent form.
(a) Unpaid dues from annual returns, July 31, 1935:
Fiscal year 1931-32......................................................$ 300.00
Fiscal year 1932-33...................................................... 322.95
Fiscal year 1933-34................................•..................... 849.50
Total ·................................................................................$1,472.45
(b) Unpaid cash loans:
(due from Lodges Nos. 174, 485, 616) ....................$ 1,440.00
Total ................................................................,......:......$ 2,912.45
All _of the above are covered by notes, which were examined in detail.
Market values of securities have b'e en determined and set out in tota l,
Exhibit D.
Subject to the foregoing, we certify that, in our opinion, the attached
statements, with exception as to the stated or book value · of securities
on hand, reflect the fi nancial condition of the Grand L odge, F. & A. M.
of California, as at Ju ly 31, 1935, and that a proper accounting has been
made of all receipts and disbursements.
Respectfully submitted,
RUCKSTELL & LAND,
Certified Public Accountants.
By FLOYD G. WEBB.

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Twelve months ha'l:e passed since this Grand Lodge elected me to the
office of Grand Lecturer and charged me with the duty of trying out the new
ritual plan for another year. After a thorough and impartial trial on the
part of the Assistant Grand Lecturers and myself, I am pleased to make a
report of our activities.
At a meeting with the Grand Master, early in the year, four Assistant
Grand Lecturers were appointed : Oscar L. Harris for the northern district,
Lloyd E. Wilson for the San Francisco Bay area, Chester H. Warlow for
the central section of the jurisdiction and Sidney K. Lehman for the southern
district.
The Assistant Grand Lecturers have covered every Inspectorial District
in the jurisdiction (with the exception of the Hawaiian Island group) at least
twice; and in some districts as many as four and five meetings have been
held. Particular attention has been given to Inspectors in outlying districts
and I feel sure that greater uniformity of ritual and a more proficient group
of Inspectors has resulted from these Schools of Instruction.
In the month of May, a questionnaire was sent to the Inspectors and
among other questions asked was the following: "What is the comment in
your district, regarding the present plan of teaching the ritual?" The answers
showed that ninety-three per cent were in favor of the new plan. Seven per
·
cent were either indifferent or opposed to the present set-up.
To show the reaction of the Inspectors to this plan, I take the liberty of
making a few quotations from their reports. One says : "I believe from
observation that the present system is far superior to the former method, as
it leaves the responsibility of teaching the ritual- 'in the hands of the Inspector
and thereby avoids considerable discussion such as we have previously had to
contend with. As an example of this, we had one Master last year who
attended the School of Instruction at Grand Lodge in 1933 and on h_is return
was instructing the officers that the statfon of the Senior Deacon was in front
of and to the right of the Worshipful Master in the East. He' was so con. vincing in his arguments that he had the Inspector believing there had been a
change. Such action as this has a tendency to lessen the confidence of the
officers in the Inspector and at the same time discourage him in his efforts to
have the work uniform."
Another writes: "The present plan of teaching .the ritual to the officers
by the Inspector only seems to be perfectly sat is factory to this district. I
have had very hearty cooperation from all concerned. "The Assistant Grand
Lecturer has proven himself not only proficient in the work, but willing to
give me all the help required. I strongly favor .the present. plan."
Another: "I have heard much favorable comment concerning the new plan
and would say that it is being well received. Am getting splendid assistance
from the Assistant Grand · Lecturer."
Another reports as follows: "All of the officers in this district are in
favor of the present plan. The criticism was, that the old system did not fill
the need. One visit a year did not give the results hoped for. The present
plan gives the Inspector the proper standing among the officers. The only
objection I hear comes from self-appointed Inspectors among the Past
Masters."
And still another: "The present system is very satisfactory, both to the
officers and myself. We have more Schools of Instruction and the officers
seem to take more .interest in their work, under the present method."
I could go on for some time quoting from these reports, but feel that
the few quotations I have made will give a general idea of how the plan has
been received in the various districts.
During the past year, I had the pleasure of visiting several of. the Lodges
with the Grand Master. i installed the officers of sixteen of our Lodges and

assisted the Grand Master at the installation of several others. It has been
my pleasure, during the past year to attend many interesting meetings, some
of which were very unusual. At a meeting held in Hartley Lodge of Lakeport, on June 15th, the third degree was conferred on four brothers. This
meeting was made the more unique by 1he fact that the father of the boys
is a member of the Lodge and the Master is their brother-in-law. It was my
pleasure to present pins · to these brothers at the request of the father, who
for sentimental reasons was not equal to the occasion. I have also presented
fifty year buttons to several of our veteran brothers, at the request of the
Grand Master. This is always a very pleasant duty and . one which is much
appreciated by the recipient. I have met with many Officers' Associations to
address them on Masonic subjects and have spoken before a number of the
Lodges on the subject of Masonic Homes Endowment. I wish to express my
appreciation for the many courtesies shown me by the officers and members
at these meetings. Their kindness has done much to make the past year one
of pleasant memories.

Condition of Lodges
From the reports of the Inspectors it is evident that the condition of the
Lodges generally is much improved over the past few years of depression
and economic strife. Many of the Lodges report they are receiving more
petitions fo~ .. the degrees, which has caused greater interest in Lodge work.
Perhaps the most encouraging report is that dues are coming in more readily;
thereby enabling many of the smaller Lodges, who for the past fe}V years
have been hard pressed to meet their financial obligations, to carry on in a
more normal manner.
Many of the Lodges are finding time for fellowship and education. On
meeting nights, when the Lodge room would otherwise be dark, speakers are
provided to address the brethren on subjects of general interest ; not only
Masonic, but also of a social or economic nature. The command "Let there
be light" is being answered in a practical way. The Master is informed at
his installation that it is his duty to spread and communicate light and in.
struction to the brethren of his Lodge. Masters are learning more and more
that a Lodge is not only a place where degrees are conferred or the business
of the Lodge dispatched as quickly as possible, but rather is, or should be a
ce11;ter. Qf learning. They are trying to carry out this instruction by means
of educational meetings. The practice is commendable and worthy of imitation.
Great care must necessarily be taken to prevent these meetings from becoming
political or controversial on any subject foreign to the policies of our institution. I believe the Masters can be relied upon in this regard. Summing up the .
reports, I would say the Lodges in this jurisdiction are in a healthy condition,
with the future promising to be even more bright.
Officers' Associations
The Officers' Associations are functioning throughout the jurisdiction in
a smooth and efficient manner and are accomplishing the results for which
they were formed; namely, the development of officers who will be more ·
proficient in matters pertaining to the government of a Lodge. I would suggest that these meetings be devoted more to matters of constitutional law and
procedure than to ritual; for while the ritual. is one of the most important
parts of Masonry and exemplifies those teachings upon which our Institution
is founded, it does not teach officers how to deal with the many perplexing
problems which confront every Lodge sooner or later. Schools of Instruction
are held for the sole purpose of perfecting officers in the ritual and for that
reason I believe the time should not be taken from the meetings of the
Officers' Associations.
For many years past, it has been the custom to prepare a different set
of questions for the Masters and Wardens. The Junior Warden has been
required to ·answer about fifteen questions, the Senior Warden twenty-five or

Assistant Grand Lecturers
The Ritual Committee has held four meetings this year for the purpose
of reviewing the ritual and perfecting themselves therein. These meetings
have all been two day sessions, making in all eight days that have been
devoted entirely to the study of the ritual. I feel safe in saying, that these
meetings, with their intensive application to the matter of ritual have developed men who are imminently well qualified to teach the work throughout
the jurisdiction, with a uniformity nearing perfection.
It is impossible to estimate the value of the assistance given this committee by Past Grand Master Dana R. Weller, who has been in attendance
at all of these meetings. His long service on the Ritual Committee and his
thorough understanding of the work, has made the progress of this committee
more rapid and enjoyable. We owe him a debt of gratitude and I here
acknowledge our appreciation.
My association with the Assistant Grand Lecturers during the past year
has .been most pleasant. Their loyalty and splendid cooperation has made it
possible to give the new plan a thorough trial. If my year as Grand Lecturer
has been, in any degree successful, it is due in no small measure to their
efforts.
Funerals
Masonic funerals have no doubt been mentioned more in reports to this
Grand Lodge . than any other one Lodge activity; but when we realize the
importance of · a good appearance before the public, we should endeavor to
act with the greatest dignity and decorum. Because of some peculiar quirk
of human nature, the world is slow to praise but quick to criticize; and we
should be more than careful in the performance of this sacred duty. Unfavorable . comm.ent is· not directed at the particular officer at fault, but is an
aspersion against the fraternity at large for allowing it to happen.
One case in particular which comes to mind, was that of a ·Past Master
who .had been requested to conduct the funeral of a deceased ·brother and
while thus engaged, spat tobacco juice near the head of the open grave. Had
I not been a witness to this disgraceful exhibition, I doubt if I would have
believed that any member of our craft c;ould have so little respect or reverence for the dead or could be so utterly without regard for the honor and
reputation of our fraternity. It is needless to say that this Past Master has
acted in that capacity for the last time.
Where the Master of a Lodge feels he is not qualified to conduct funerals,
I suggest that he delegate the duty to some member of the Lodge who is
better fitted to perform this function with credit to the fraternity. Through
lack of confidence, fear or plain nervousness, many men are not able to conduct funerals in a creditable manner. When one is so afflicted, it is far
better to admit the limitation and ask another to perform for him. Conferring a degree is one thing; to conduct a funeral is something entirely
different.
I know of one district in which one Past Master conducts practically all
the funerals. Because of his peculiar fitness for this work, his easy carriage
and his splendid delivery, the Masters are content to relinquish their rights,
knowing that in so doing the last sad tribute to the departed brother will be
paid with proper solemnity and dignity.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

It might not be inappropriate at this time to mention the sad lack of
attendance at the funeral services of sojourning brothers. In many cases these
services are handled through the B-0ards of Relief, at the request of the deceased brother's Lodge. A brother dies while away from his home and is
buried by a L-Odge, not his own. Because the brother is little known and is
without relatives in the locality, he is usually accorded a Masonic service with
barely enough members present to act as officers. This condition could be
remedied if the Master of the Lodge would appoint a committee whose duty
it would be to attend the funeral services of all sojourning brothers, whom the
Lodge has been requested to bury. · This committee should be composed of
brethren who can leave their business worries behind, when the call comes.
We have such members in all of our Lodges who would be perfectly willing
to act on such an important committee if the need were explained to them.
It is not so much neglect on the part of the members as it is thoughtlessness.
I do not make these remarks in a spirit of criticism, but with the hope that
Masters will give serious thought to the subject and will attempt to overcome
a sad condition.

To make personal mention of all who have so generously and wholeheartedly cooperated with me this year would take reams of paper an~ would
require hours ·of reading. Therefore let me say that I deeply appreciate the
honor conferred and hope I have, in some small measure, proven worthy of
vour confidence.
Respectfully submitted,
LESLIE E. ·Wooo,
Grand Lecturer.

Cost of Administering the New Plan
The best way to bring out the value of anything is through comparison.
For that reason alone, I make the following statement of facts. The Assistant
Grand Lecturers and I have covered more than seventeen thousand miles
throughout the length and breadth of this grand jurisdiction in the performance of our duties. Our expense accounts have totaled less than eighteen
hundred dollars. Under the former plan of a full time Grand Lecturer the
expense to Grand Lodge was approximately seven thousand two hundred
dollars; fifty-four hundred dollars salary and a traveling expense averaging
eighteen hundred dollars. This shows a saving of approximately five thousand
four hundred dollars over the former system.
Conclusion
May I say in closing that I have endeavored to make a comprehensive
report of my activities as Grand Lecturer during the past year without taking
too much of the valuable time of this Grand Lodge. The duty assigned to me,
I have performed to the best of my ability, always having in mind the wishes
of this Grand oody.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Master I wish to express my appreciation
for his kindness and hope that his year has been as pleasant and profitable to
him as my year has been to me.
To the Very Worshipful Grand Secretary, Brother John Whicher, and
the members of his office, I am indebted for their many courtesies and kind
assistance. They have shown a willingness to help me on all occasiOns.
To the officers and members of the Lodges of the jurisdiction, I offer my
sincere thanks for their reception of me as Grand Lecturer and for the many
kindnesses they have displayed.
The Inspectors are deserving of the highest commendation and praise for
the work they are doing. Without them the efforts of any officer of Grand
Lodge would ·be in vain. They have given me every assistance and cooperation and have proven beyond doubt that without their services, Masonry in
this jurisdiction would be greatly handicapped. Under the present plan, the
Inspector must teach the ritual to .the officers of his district, as well as maintain a general supervision over the affairs of the Lodges. They have shown
their willingness and ability to do this and to them I acknowledge my
gratitude.
My association with the Assistant Grand Lecturers has been one of the
most pleasant experiences of the year. Aside from their ability as ritualists,
they possess in abundance that spirit of good fellowship and brotherly love
which makes their friendship something to be cherished through the years.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON GRAND SECRETARY'S
REPORT
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your committee on the report of the Grand Secretary, submits the following report for your consideration:
It is refreshing to note in the first paragraph that California Masonry has
again resumed its forward march. Two new Lodges enter the ranks well
located. Candidates receiving the Master Mason Degree during the past year
show an increase of 395 over 1934. Affiliations from other jurisdictions increased by 57 over the preceding year. Not only did we secure considerable
new material, but restorations also show an increase of 103. T his shows consideration by the officers for those within the fraternity, who, for one reason
or another, have had difficulty. In a reorganization for an active program of
work, the way must be cleared, and those not interested, have withdrawn.
However, suspensions have decreased almost 1,000, as compared to 1934, which
just about equals the decrease in net loss. Remember, brethren, that Masonry
does not suspend a brother who has a bona fide desire to retain his membership.
The amendments dealing with the increase and decrease of dues and fees,
show that this question.is one to be dealt with only after careful consideration.
We recommend that the Grand Secretary's Report be segregated and
portions thereof be referred to the following committees :
Unpaid Grand Lodge Dues: To Committee on Finance.
Budget: To Committee on Finance.
Shorter R oll Call : To Committee on Policy and General Purposes.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

New Lodges: To Committee on Charters.
Trial Records: To Committee on Grievances.
Life Memberships: To Committee on Jurisprudence.
Amendments to By-Laws: To Committee on By-Laws.
Unfinished Business: To Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
At the end of this report, we find a familiar name the owner of which
is loved and admired by Masons throughout our jurisdlction and beyond the
boundary lines of our Golden State. It is his able guiding hand and mind that
has helped to bring about these betterments we have just noted and his rich
experience that furnish the sound advice when needed.
'
This twenty-eighth annual report closes another year of his loyal service
to our debloved fraternity.

By Ira F. Thompson

Most Worshipful Grand Master, Officers and Members of the Grand Lodge:
There can be no doubt that it would be interesting for us to review more
or less in detail the history of our well loved craft, and to elaborate upon the
part it has played in advancing the cause of civilization and the establishment
of liberty. But I entertain the notion, either correctly or err,oneously, that we
are confronted wit1- a problem of tremendous magnitude, not only deserving
but also commanding our most earnest and consecrated consideration. And while
I approach the task assigned to me in the spirit of humility, yet I am impressed
with the firm conviction that in these troubled times we should lay aside all
desire to speak in oratorical style, embellished with rhetorical flourishes and
ornamented with figures of speech, and should attempt within the limits of our
powers, in plain, blunt fashion, to declare those principles which niay help in
the solution of the problem mentioned.
The world seems all awry. Our fraternity stands condemned upon groundless accusations by those in charge of governmental affairs in two of the great
nations of the world. In another it is suppressed, if not quite extinguished.
It seems at times as though many men in whom we ought to repose confidence
have lost the capacity for straight, clear thinking and that, in the prophetic
words of Scripture, our "old men . . . dream dreams" while "our young men
. . . see visions." In fact, confusion of thought and an amazing response to
every appeal to the passions and prejudices characterize the years. What we
have been told constituted the "wisdom of the ages" is questioned and we are
almost torn loose from our moorings. There is a school of propaganda (I
decline to call it thought) which embraces every opportunity to stir up envy
and hatred. It preaches a doctrine abhorrent to Masons, of distinctions between
men, setting up class against class. Denying the existence of the Great Architect
of the Universe, they constitute materiality and material things their God, and
upon this basis deny the importance of the individual except as an adjunct or
chattel of the State. Under the guise of what would otherwise be laudable
peace movements or movements for youth or class betterment, they insinuate
their Godless doctrine and hate messages among the very elect of the people.
And the credulity of man stands appallingly revealed. Out of the darkness of
envy, hatred, suffering, false promises and Godlessness we seem to hear the cry:
Is there no truth? Is there no such thing as the great power of goodi charity,
brotherly love and tolerance? Is the doctrine that it is man's birthright to be
free, and adoring his great Creator, to so develop and mold his character that
he shall be ready to take his place in that spiritual building not made with
hands, to be overthrown?
The answer of Masonry to the first two questions is an emphatic "yes"
and to the last a calm and vigorous dissent. Coming down to us from the dawn
of civilization, gathering in its tireless quest for truth from the experiences and
meditations of men, it exhorts its devotees to stand still and contemplate the
miracle of miracles, the creation of the universe and all that is therein contained. The infinity of its extent, its order and grandeur, the tinted beauty of
the flower, the patient stateliness of great trees, the majesty of granite peaks,
the "still small voice" in man, and the loveliness of compassioned love, all bid
us have no doubt, that we are not the children of chance and caprice, but
creatures of an all-wise, omnipotent Father. An unknown poet has framed it in
·
this fashion :

l_; .

Our God has opened wide my eyes
To see the beauty of the skies.
The trees, the flowers that once seemed wondrous fair,
Have .now an added glory, and the rare

We agree, as did Aristotle, Plato and Newton, that we cannot understand
the universe without God, who, according to Holy Writ: "Stretcheth out the
north over the empty place, and hangeth the earth upon nothing." (Job 26 :7.)
In truth, the conclusion ·is so inescapable that Masonry,• as its sole dogma;
requires its acceptance. With its acceptance, however, we establish the existence
of Truth, the principle of all created things.
We turn to inquire concerning the creature--man. Here we find no dogma,
unless we can say that because. we seek to impress through the medium of a
universal language the thought that man is largely the architect and master
workman of his own character, we dogmatically insist that man shall be free
to become, through the evolution of his own internal life and with the aid of
an almighty Parent, the master of his own destiny. Not dogmatically, but with
overpowering persuasiveness, we assert that men were not born-some to rulaand others to slave-but as children of a loving God, bound together by ties of
brotherly love and affection. In our ceremonies we require no man to kneel to
another as his superior. We assert only that he should kneel to his God for
guidance in the affairs of life-in the spirit voiced by that eminent member of
ou_r Order-philosopher and sage, Benjamin Franklin-when on an historic
occasion he addressed his fellow members of the Constitutional convention, in
these words: "I have lived, Sir, a long time, and the : longer I live, the more
convincing proofs I see of this truth: That God governs in the affairs of men.
And if a sparrow ·cannot fall to the ground without His notice, is it probable
that an empire can rise without His aid?. We have been assured, Sir, in the
Sacred Writings, that 'except the Lord build the House they labour in vain
that. b~ild it.' I firmly believe this; and I also believe that .without His concurring aid we shall succeed. in this political building no better than the builders
of Babel. We shall be divided by our little partial, local interests; our projects
will be confounded, and we ourselves shall become a reproach and a.byword down
to fu-~ure a,g,es, And what is worse, mankind may hereafter from this unfortunate
instance despair of establishing governments by human wisdom and leave. it to. ·
chance, war and. conquest." The power. of a great people is grounded in rever"
ence, good, charity, brotherly love and affection. Consider the divine something
in. the great friendships of fable and history, Hercules and Hy las, David · and
Jonathan, Pylades and Orestes,. Castor and Pollux, and D<i.mon and Pythias.
Contemplate the power of a few immortal · sentences vibrating with the compassionate wve of mankind to break the chains of despotism, free from slavery,
or establish justice. Masonry believes that the greatest good it can render is to
nourish and maintain this spiritual quality in our national life. It is our special
function, not only within ourselves, but within our young, to erect a strong
bulwark against the forces of hatred, materialism and bigotry. This is what
we are and should be engaged in doing. How?

The quotation does not suggest that we should supinely relinquish principle.
The greatness of Masonry lies in the fact that it is founded in Truth and maintains its principles. It is evidenced by the fact that though natio~s rise and ~all,
and the greatest works of man crumble into dust, Masonry survives to contl?ue
its quest and inspire man with ideals of equality and liberty and hope of 1?1mortality. Its adherents have become illustrious because in times of necessity
they have undergone every "pain, peril" and "danger" to establish and protect
the opportunity of every man to serve the purpose of his earthly existence.
This is one of its principles-that man shall be privileged in his own way and
not in another's to serve his God, and to work forward toward that state of
perfection which will the better fit him to take his place in the life her~after.
If you please to put it in more prosaic words, that m_an sh~ll have the right. to
make of his life not a mere drab picture of material existence, but a thmg
beautiful, crowded with constructive achievement, full of compassion and kindness, a picture to be remembered with joy by friend and kin. To be still mo:e
practical, it is interesting to .observe from a survey of those who lead 1.n
enterprise in this country of ours what a great percentage embarked on their
prosent vocation as a matter of necessity and in their bar_e feet, .so to speak.
In this connection, let me make use of one further illustration. Several
years ago I was sitting, meditating on the beauty of a grove of trees sp;ead
out before my eyes. For some reason, I observed that each tree was entirely
different from every other. And my mind went back to boyhood days, when
I would cut a limb suitable to be shaped into a sled runner, and then search for
days, weeks and even months for another sufficien~~y similar to _be fashioned
to match the first. I could not resist the thought: How much hke man they.
are. Each has a different shape, different limbs, different form, yet each is a
delight to the eye as is the composite whole. How impossible and foolish it
would be to attempt to compress each majestic tree into a set mold and form."
Still more impossible it · is to seek to restrict man to a given pattern.
A corollary to the foregoing principle is the fact that one man cannot
wear the character vesture of another. He cannot have what he does not merit,
by his own labor and experience. He who would share with us the wages of
nourishment, inspiration and joy must become a laborer in the house. He cannot
take spiritual verities by force, nor attempt it without bringing down upon
himself catastrophic consequences. What he cannot do by force he cannot
accomplish by fraud or deceit. There is just one avenue--that by earnest
application and endeavor to divest himself of the vices and superfluities of life
and to invest himself with the charitable and true.
Man however was not created to live unto himself, but as a member of
society. 'The prin~iple applicable to the growth and development of his life
and character must be allowed to prevail with equal force with every other
member. We discover through Masonry the true basis of fellowship. We
learn that men "the high and the low, the rich and the poor,'' are all created
by the same almighty parent. We determine that one of. the. greatest. se;vic~s
one can render to his Maker was voiced by the same Beniamm Franklm m his
daily prayer, in these words: "0 ! Powerful Goodness! Bountiful Father I
