Merciful Guide! Increase in me that wisdom which discovers my truest interest! Strengthen my resolutions to perform what that wisdom dictates!
Accept my kind offices to Thy other children as the only return in my power
for Thy continual favors to me!" Society so organized and governed rests
upon the cement of tolerance and justice. It extends to the individual the right
to be the master-workman of his own character, restrained only by the rule that
every other member shall have a similar privilege. Resting on such a foundation
classes and distinctions have no place, and bigotry and hatred are outlawed.
Trouble comes when men insist that the principle be applied for their benefit,
but refuse to apply it to themselves for the benefit of others.
As Masons, we are grateful and have a right to point with pride to the
part played by our brethren of former years, in the sanguinary struggle to
establish a government, the declared purpose of which was to protect these
inalienable rights with which man is endowed by his Creator. To effect such
a noble purpose, however, was not the work of a few years, but the culmination
of the labors of liberty-loving men over hundreds - yes, thousands of years.
We have enjoyed its blessings-perhaps at times unconscious of the toil," the
sacrifice, and the bloodshed it entailed. Is it possible that, because we have
not been denied its bounties and the beneficence of freedom, we have become
blind to its worth? Such a state of affairs is possible.
From these observations, it follows that the individual is not static. As a
Mason, he has been instructed in the progressive art. He must progress or go
. backward. As it is with the individual, so it is with society. For centuries
man has craved to be supplied with power in order to be relieved of drudgery.
Power has been given to him in abundance. It seemed as though his energies
were to be loosed for greater achievement in the mental field, the sciences,
philosophy, literature and the arts. But like the children of Israel, when being
delivered by Moses from the bondage of Egypt, we hear the plaint: "Would
to God we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt when we
sat by the flesh pots, and when we did eat bread to the full." The Israelites
went forward to safety and their destiny. Whether we go forward or back. ward will depend upon our devotion to the ideals which have brought us thus
far in our journey. It stands to reason that the genius which was about to
deliver man from the bonds of drudgery will also carry him forward to his
destiny, if we but have the fortitude to abide by those principles, which are as
eternal as the Deity himself.
We dare not, however, prophesy the future. We know not whether another
overturning must be endured before He comes whose right it is to reign. We
· have no way of forecasting whether ground won will be lost, to be retraced
at a future time with great tribulation and bleeding footsteps, or whether we shall
with faces toward the Light continue to go forward. Only this much do we
know-that some day, either now or later, the Spirit of Masonry-the Truthfinding expression in the lives and character of our Brethren will rise triumphant
to carry him forward to the place where justice and brotherly love prevail, and
know no envy, no hatred, no tyranny.

HOME }' QR AGED--RULES GOVERNING ADMISSION

To be eligible for admission to the Masonic Home for Aged the applicant must be:
(a) A Master Mason who for at least five years preceding the. dat~ of
application has been continuously a member m good standing m a
Lodge in this jurisdiction, or
(b) The wife of such a Master Mason, or
(c) The widow of one who was such a Master Mason at the time of
his decease.
Applicants must be in destitute circumstances, unable to earn a li".elihood because of age or permanent physical disability, and without relatives
who can be compelled by law to support them. It is not the purpose. of the
Home to relieve children of their moral and !~gal duty to care for t?e1r aged
parents. If there be children who cannot entirely support an. applicant and
he or she is 011 that account admitted to the Home, they will be expected
to aid. financially in maintaining the applicant in the Home to the full extent
of their ability.

OUTSIDE RELIEF

Applicants must be of good character, of sound mind, of temperate
habits, and not addicted to the use of narcotics. They must be free from
contagious or communicable disease. They must be in sufficiently good
health not to require nursing or other personal attention.
Before entering the Home, and as a condition precedent to admission,
every applicant must transfer and convey to the Masonic Homes of California all property by him owned, or to which he may be or become
entitled. The transfer and conveyance shall be in such form as the Trustees
may require.
The Lodge must see that every applicant admitted to the Home is
furnished with suitable wearing apparel on admission and must agree to
keep such applicant decently and properly . clothed while a resident ·therein,
and to pay the necessary funeral expenses in case of death while a resident.
Each Lodge in the jurisdiction may have maintained at the Home for
Aged two residents without charge, and one additional resident for each
three hundred members or fraction thereof in excess of three hundred, on
the roll of the Lodge. For each resident in excess of the quota allowed a
charge will be made in an amount fixed from time to time by the Board of
Trustees.
HOME FOR CHILDREN-RULES GOVERNING ADMISSION

A child to be eligible for admission to the Masonic Home for Children
must be the child of a Master Mason of a Lodge in this jurisdiction:
. (a) Who has been a member in good standing continuously for not
less than five years next prior to application, or
(b) Who is in good standing at the date of application and who is
totally incapacitated, either mentally or physically, or
(c) Who is dead and was in good standing at the time of his decease.
The child must furthermore be in circumstances of need and dependency, so that the relief sought is necessary to procure for it those benefits
which are commonly recognized as the necessities of childhood. If there be
a surviving parent, he or she will be required to aid financially in maintaining the child in the Home to the full extent of his or her ability.
The child must be normal, or approximately normal. The Trustees will
exclude children who are mentally defective or who have shown tendencies
toward delinquency or whose physical condition in their judgment renders
them unfit for membership. The child must be old enough to attend the
public schools in the first grade. As a general thing, children over fourteen
will not be admitted, but the Trustees may receive children of older age in
exceptional cases if they think the circumstances justify . .
BOTH HOMES-RULES GOVERNING ADMISSION

Applications for admission to the Homes must come through and from
the Lodge.
The Trustees shall have the right to reject any application, even though
it seems to fall within the letter of the rules, if in their opinion the granting
of the same would result in advantage being taken of the fraternity. Evidence of membership having been taken with design to benefit from the
charity or under circumstances which rendered it probable that charitable
aid would be required shall be reason for rejecting an application.
Under such conditions, and subject to such rules and regulations as
may from time to time be made by the Trustees, any applicant who is a
member of a Lodge in this jurisdiction, or who is the wife, widow, mother;
child, or grandchild of any such member, or of any deceased member who
at the tirhe of his death is eligible for admission, and for whom no provision is hereinabove made, when in the sound judgment of the Trustees the
circumstances presented justify such action, may be admitted to the Homes
or receive outside relief.

Instead of admission to the Homes, outside relief may be granted in
cases where, in the opinion of the Trustees, applicants can be better or
more economically cared for outside the Homes.
Outside relief may be granted only to:
(a) Those eligible for admission to the Homes, or
(b) Those who are otherwise qualified but who are inadmissible by
reason of disease or physical or mental infirmity, or
. .
(c) Children who are otherwise qualified but who are under the m1111mum age for admission.
In determining the amount of outside relief consideration shall be
given to the possibility of aid from relatives who can be compelled by law
to contribute, as well as the possibility of securing aid from any other
sources, public or private.
It is not the policy to give outside relief for temporary needs, such
relief being the duty of the Lodge direct.
CONDITIONS OF CONTINUATION OF MEMBERSHIP OR RELIEF

Any applicant having been admitted to either Home under a misrepresentation or concealment of facts, or who does not reasonably comply
with the regulations established for their government, or whose conduct may
be detrimental to good order and discipline, or whose responsible relatives
fail to give proper cooperation, may in the discretion of the Trustees be
discharged therefrom.
All residents will be expected to conform to all rules and regulations,
and cheerfully to do such work and perform such duties as the Superintendents of the Homes may assign to them.
Parents or other responsible relatives of children in the Home for
Children are expected to recognize the undivided authority of t~e ~o?1e
over the child during his residence therein, and to cooperate fully m g1vmg
and securing observance of all its rules and regulations.
Whenever the circumstances of parents or responsible relatives improve so that they may be expected to resume care, the child will b.e discharged. Continuance of any child's membership beyond the age of sixteen
is contingent upon annual reappointment by the Trustees.
The Trustees will secure information periodically concerning the status
of each beneficiary of outside relief, and will modify or discontinue relief
as dictated by changing circumstances.
While much of this revision is simply the formulation as a rule of the
practices and policy which with the approval of Grand Lodge has been long
pursued, there are three important changes which we believe. should be
specifically called to the attention of Grand Lodge, together with the reasons therefor.
The first is with respect to the time a Master Mason must have been
continuou~ly a member in . good standing of a Lodge in this jurisdiction.
Originally the only requirement was for good standing in a Lod~e in this
jurisdiction at the time of the application (or in the case of a widow that
her husband must have been in good standing at the time of his death).
Some time thereafter the Board of Trustees adopted a rule requiring co'1tinuous membership for a period of at least five years; but later the period
was shortened to three years. The Trustees believe it advisable that we
should now return to the five-year requirement and for the following
reasons:
The attention of Grand Lodge has been heretofore called to the increased demands being made upon our Homes; and for the last two years

it has been more than ever apparent. It is due of course to two causes
closely related: first, an increase in the number of those in need of relief
because of the economic condition and consequent unemployment; and,
secondly, to the very natural disposition on the part of the Lodges to
request admission to the Home for those for whom under other circumstances the Lodges would themselves provide. In more than one instance
an application was received from one who could not be properly termed
an aged Mason, but for whom it seemed necessary to provide relief of a
permanent nature . .
Your Trustees have given long and serious thought to this problem
and have even considered the advisability of recommending that the Trustees be instructed by Grand Lodge to fix an age limit. There are, however,
many instances (a'nd they are becoming more frequent) where the applicants, although under the age Grand Lodge would probably instruct the
Trustees to fix, are nevertheless because of their age without employment.
Theirs is not merely a temporary unemployment because they will probably never again be able to become self-supporting; and some of these
applicants have held continuous membership in their Lodges for many
years in excess of our present requirement.
Your Trustees were therefore of the opinion that instead of fixing
an age limit it would be better to return to the five-year membership
requirement.
· The second of the changes to which we have referred excludes the
mother of a Master Mason from those who as a matter of right are eligible
for admission, and places her in · the same category as the grandchild of a
Master Mason who is dependent upon him for support. The question of
whether or not the mother of a Master Mason as such is entitled to admission to the Home has long been a debated question; and even your Trustees are not all in accord with the change from what has been for many
years the uniform policy of the Board. But all are agreed that there should
be some definite pronouncement by Grand Lodge in the form of an instruction to the Trustees which will definitely settle the question.
The last of the important changes is that which specifically gives the
Trustees the discretion which they have always exercised to administer the
rules so that their literal enforcement will not in the opinion of the Trustees defeat the evident purpose of their enactment; and that the Trustees
may at the same time protect the Homes and the Craft against imposition.
This discretion has apparently been exercised by every Board of Trustees
since 1898, when the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Widows' and Orphans' Home adopted their rules, the second and seventeenth of which
read as follows: ·
"2. The Board of Trustees reserves the right to reject any person
nominated." (The nomination was by the Lodge.)
"17. The Board of Trustees may admit to the Home Masons, their
wives, widows or orphans, not covered by the foregoing regulations upon
such terms as they may deem best."
It simply enables the Trustees in the administration of this great
charity of Grand Lodge to have ever in mind the spirit, rather than the
letter, of the law. The Trustees are not all in accord in this matter and
again we ask Grand Lodge for its determination.
There is also a change in the rules governing admission to the Home
at Covina which dispenses with. the five-year membership requirement
where the father is in good standing at the date of the application but who
is totally incapacitated either mentally or physically, or who is dead and
was in good standing at the tiine of his decease. This is intended to cover
only extraordinary cases where in any event the Trustees would be disposed in the exercise of their discretion to admit the applicant even though

the five-year requirement were lacking. The membership of the father,
however, might have been for such a very short time that the admission of

The rules with respect to outside relief, as has been intimated, effect
no change in the policy by which your Trustees have been governed.
They have learned from long experience that in many instances deserving Masons and their dependents who are in dire need are not physically or mentally eligible for admission to the Home and that the Lodges
of which they· are ~embers are unable to maintain them. Likewise in many
cases there are dependent children entitled to our care whose needs cannot
well be met in the Covina Home, and ·whom it is therefore desirable to
care for by the outside relief method. These include children in need of
special physical treatment, or those of nervous condition who do not thrive
as members of a large group, or older children who need special vocational
treatment not available at Covina. Modern social methods hold that poverty alone is not a sufficient reason to remove a child from its mother,
even to the best institution; and we have found in numerous instances that
children .can be well cared for with their mothers if . outside relief is given.
In such cases as we deem advisable, we shall, unless otherwise instructed
by Grand Lodge, continue the practice of caring for some of our wards by
outside placement.
Problems in Care of Aged and the Children
There is naturally a great contrast between the Home and the activities at Decoto, and that at Covina. The problems confronting the Trustees
in the caring for the aged and for the children differ widely.
At Decato, where we maintain our aged, our problem is to make the
last days of our brethren comfortable, to furnish them with those things
which will make life happier. It is our endeavor, by providing plain and
sim1Ple diet, recreation and diversions, by keeping alive interest among the
brethren. of our big family, to make a contented group of those who have
found it necessary to accept our Home.
We have endeavored to impress upon the members of our family at
Decato not only the agreement upon entering, to do those small things for
the benefit of the institution which their strength will permit them to do,
but also that if it is truly to be a home, they, as members of the family, are
obligated each to do his or her share.
The majority of our people have met this obligation cheerfully and, as
a result, are happy and contented in their surroundings. It is to be expected, however, that there will always be those who cannot adjust themselves to the conditions imposed by the necessity of maintaining order in a
·
large institution.
At Covina, our problem is quite different. There we are preparing
boys and girls to take the places that we now occupy. This means, as it
does in your home, the daily arising of new problems as the bodies and
minds of our children develop to maturity. We are proud of the results
here obtained.
At both Homes we have endeavored to keep up their physical condition and at the same time practice economy. Expenditures on buildings
and grounds have been kept at the minimum, yet our property has not
been allowed to deteriorate. Replacements of equipment have been made
only where absolutely required. In a year or two, however, we are going to

Relationship of Children With Friends and Relatives
For many years the contacts of children in the Home with their relatives and friends has been subject to but little restriction. Our experiem·e
has indica~ed that undivided responsibility is essential in the Home management, and that more careful regulation in these matters is desirable if
the best interests of the children are to be considered. In pursuance of this
thought, investigation was made as to the practices of all the other
Masonic Homes in the United States governing the visits made to the
children at the Homes, visits made by children away from the Homes,
gifts to children, etc. The information thus gained, together with our own
experience, led to the adoption by us of more precise regulations regarding
these matters. They are as follows:
1. The Home requires that it shall have full and undivided authority
so long as the child shall be in its care. Parents or responsible relatives
may talk with or write to the Superintendent concerning the child's progress or problems connected therewith; and matters thus brought up in a
proper way will receive careful consideration; but they will not be permitted to dictate or make demands regarding the manner in which the
Home shall care for their children.
2. Parents or relatives, with the approval of the Superintendent, may
visit their children, not oftener than once a week, at such hours as the
children may be free to receive such visits. The Home reserves the right
to limit or forbid the visits of any person.
Any person desiring to visit a child shall come first to the office for a
visitor's permit, and shall observe the directions thereon. If referred to a
child's residence building, the visitor shall report on arrival to the houseparent in charge. No visitor may go at any time to the sleeping roon;i·s of
children without securing special permission from the' houseparent immediately before such visit.
3. A child may not be taken from the Home premises by any person
without permission of the houseparent, and when so permitted to go must
be returned at snch time as directed.
4. Visiting relatives desiring to take meals with children may do so,
so far as the accommodations of the Home will permit, first securin~
tickets at the office at a charge of twenty-five cents per meal.
5. Leaves of absence. All visits of children to relatives or friends shall
be subject to the approval of the Superintendent, who will require satisfactory evidence that the place and circumstances of the visit are suitable
and proper. The maximum amount of time a child may spend away from
the Home in any one year is thirty days. Children may not be absent from
the Home during any vacations except the summer vacation. Week-end
visits to practicable distances may be allowed once in six weeks.
6. Requests for visits may be made either in person at the office or by
letter to the Superintendent, and should be made well in advance of the
time of the visit. Requests for visits should not be made through the
children or in letters to the children. All transportation expenses must be
paid by relatives in advance.
7. No money may be given directly to any child at any time. Money
intended for children's use must be left at the office, where it will be
placed to the child's credit and spent subject to the knowledge and approval of those in charge.
·
8. All gifts must be submitted for the approval of the houseparent
before being given to the child. It is better to secure this approval before
the gift is purchased and before the child is informed of it, thus avoiding

Responsibility of Lodges
From time to time, in our annual reports, we have called attention to
the indifference of Lodges in the matter of looking after children who
have been honorably dismissed from the Home. This is a matter that
should be brought definitely to the attention of the members of all Lodges.
We will cite two cases : In June, 1935, a boy, 17 years old, was graduated
from high school at Covina and dismissed from the Home. He returned to
his mother, who made a scant living as a clerk in a department store. The
boy is mentally keen and physically strong. The Trustees requested the
Master of the Lodge of which the boy's father was a member to advise the
members generally of the neces,:;ity of finding employment for him. Nothing whatever was done in this behalf other than to cause the lad's name to
be registered with the Masonic Employment Bureau. The boy is yet
unemployed. The Lodge has a membership of more than three hundred,
among whom we are loath to believe that not one of them could find gainful emplyment for the son of a deceased brother.
Another case is that of a boy who also was dismissed from the Home
by reasons of graduation arid returned to his Lodge. His mother is living
on public relief. The Master of the Lodge of which the boy's father had
been a member promptly appointed a committee to find employment. That
community was hard hit by hordes of idle men and women, and it was not
an easy matter to place this boy. However, the committee industriously
interviewed the membership and finally succeeded in securing employment
for him, and he is now happy as a self-supporting young man. We coinmend the energetic Masonry displayed by the Master of this Lodge and
his members.
Bequests
'The policy of your Board with relation to gifts and bequests is that in
addition to specific bequests for the endowment fund, all bequests to the
Masonic Homes of California, except those for a particular purpose, shall
be allocated to the endowment fund. Donations from eight bequests have
been received in the last fiscal year, all of which have been credited to the
endowment fund. They are as follows:

Improvements at Home for Aged
In May of this year we caused to be installed at the Home · for Aged
three No. 2 · gasamatic burners in the ki.tchen, at a cost of $207.56, to
replace the oil burners. This not only is cleaner but has resulted in a fuel
expense saving for cooking.
Finances
Notwithstanding the increased cost of all supplies and foodstuffs in
the year just closed, our treasury is in good condition. At the close of the .
fiscal year ended July 31, 1934, the Homes had a cash balance of $24,000.00.
In September, 1934, we repaid to the endowment fund the sum of $25,000.00, which was reported to Grand Lodge in October last. Since then we
have repaid an additional $25,000.00. The amount yet due the endowment
fund is $175,000.00. The returns of the Lodges for the year ended July 31,
1935, give every indication that the revenues for the Homes for the coming
year will exceed last year, and that without any increase in the per capita
tax, a substantial payment can again soon be made in reimbursemept to
the endowment fund.
The cost of the operation of the Covina Home, including the farm
connected therewith, for the past ten years has averaged $88,000.00 a year;
the cost last year was a trifle over $82,000.00; this year the cost in round
figures was $86,000.00, which in fact is a decrease in the expense of operation, when we take into account the necessity of replacing the hot water
plant, replacements of carpets in several buildings, and an increase in the
number of surgical cases requiring operative care in outside hospitals.
The farm connected with the Home has always been a source of
expense, the average deficit for the last ten years being $3,530.00; and for
the last year this was reduced to $1,438.00. The farm operations include
ten acres of citrus fruit, a dairy, a piggery, and a poultry plant. We have
regarded the operation of the farm as worth while, because it furnishes an
outlet for the activities of the older boys, and also because it supplies the
children with a dependable quality of first grade milk.
Children can be cared for more cheaply than is being done at Covina,
but in counting cost, consideration must be given to the kind of care
afforded. We do not believe Masonry in California desires to do the cheapes~ job possible at our Covina Home. Investigation assures us that our
expenditures compare favorably with those of other institutions giving the
same grade of care.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

447

We have a system of paying older children for work done by them,
requiring them in turn to purchase their own clothing and incidentals from
their earnings. Some of the more industrious youngsters earn enough to
enable them to buy luxuries that would not be given to them in an ordinary orphanage. It takes a considerable amount of clerical service to keep
the accounts of this system. While there is no doubt of the great practical
value of this training, it is necessarily somewhat expensive to operate.
During the past year more than eight per cent of our expenditure has
been on the health program. Here is another item that can be done more
thoroughly or less thoroughly. While we have omitted some things that
might have been desired, on the whole the physical care of our children
has been much better than in the average institution. Thorough physical
examinations on entrance, followed by appropriate treatment, medical, surgical and nursing, bring remarkable improvements. Follow-up of our wards
after discharge shows that the benefits brought about in this way are
lasting.
At the Decato Home there has been an increased cost, due to the
advance of prices of foods generally.

COMMENTS
Securities, Notes Receivable and Real Estate, Etc.:
All of the general securities listed under Schedule B-3 have been
received by donation. The stated or book value represents the value placed
upon the securities at the time of donation. Where the security is unlisted
or closely held or of uncertain value, it has been entered at a nominal value
solely for purposes of record.
Notes receivable values represent the unpaid portion of notes receivable on hand. The letter "S'.' (Schedule B-3) indicates those notes secured
by real estate. Insurance policies, received mainly from residents of the
Homes, have been listed on the books at the face or value recoverable at
death of the insured, as a matter of record.
Securities contained within the Student Loan Fund (Schedule B-2)
are stated at cost, with the exception of the 100 shares of Masonic Temple
Association received by donat ion, which is valued at par on the books.
Approximately 40 parcels of real estate have been received by donation. These have increased during the past few years from a relatively
small number of parcels. Beginning A ugust 1, 1934, this property has been
set up on the books at the assessed value per tax bills, for record purposes.
The total assessed value amounts to $24,205.00, as per Exhibit B.
General:
A memorandum account has been opened in the general ledger which
records the amounts reported in the Annual Proceedings from 1912 to
1934 for account of the Building Fund tax plus additions for the current
year. Total collections are $1,155,143.75 and total expenditures for buildings, improvements, etc., are $2,244,961.29.
During the current fiscal year there was collected $24,689.08 as income
from interest and dividends on Endowment Fund cash and securities. Of
this amount $914.42 represents the portion of the premium recovered.
Under the method of accounting, Endowment bonds are recorded on the
books at cost, including premium, without annual deductions therefrom.
The amount of $914.42 is being transferred to the Ertdowment Fund after
the date of this report.

To the Endo~ent Board, Masonic Homes of California:
In accordance with the authorization of the Finance Committee, we
have audited the accounts of the Permanent Endowment Fund of the
Masonic Homes of California for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1935. The
following statements are presented herewith:
E~hibit A : Statement of Cash Receipts and Disbursements.
Exhibit B : Statement of Composition of Fund (6 pages).
Exhibit C : Statement of Securities Redeemed and Sold.
Securities (Exhibit B):
All corporate stocks and irrigation bonds have been received by donation. Certain of the bonds, other than irrigation, have been acquired by
donation and are so marked by the letter "D" .under Exhibit B. In the case
of donated securities the stated or book value represents the value placed
upon the securities at time of donation. Where the value is· uncertain,
because of it being unlisted or a closely held security, entry is. made on the
books at a nominal $1.00 value for purposes of record. Bonds purchased are
recorded on the books at cost, including premium, without annual deductions therefrom. The total amount of premium is $19,138.17 and the portion
collected thereof during the current fiscal year and included in the income
account is $914.42. The amount of $914.42 is being transferred to the Endowment Fund and a reserve provided after the date of this report.
Additions through purchase or donation du.ring. the current fiscal y~ar
have been listed at the close ·of Exhibit B, for ready reference; and disposals
have been set out in detail in Exhibit C. During the fiscal year total securities have been purchased in amount $188,315.61, as per Exhibit B; and total
securities have been sold or redeemed in amount $116,680.63, as per Exhibit c.
.
.
Total market values obtainable as at July 31, 1935, have been noted in
the endowment fund summary at the end of Exhibit B.
The income account shows a total credit of $24,689.08 arising from
interest and dividends which was transferred to the Masonic Homes General
Fund, during the current fiscal year.
·
.
\Ve certify that the attached statements, in our opinion, set .f orth the
condition of the Permanent Endowment Fund as at July 31, 1935, with
exception as to the stated or book values of securities on hand, and that .a
proper accounting has been made of all receipts and disbursements.
Respectfully submitted,
RucKSTELL & LAND,
Certified Public Accountants,
By Fr.oYD T. WEBB.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Report of Superintendent-Decoto' Home
To the Board of Trustees:
I hereby present for your consideration my twenty-sixth annual report
as Superintendent of the Masonic Home at Decoto for the year ending
August 31, 1935.
There has been the usual routine in the management of the Home,
without any special changes, during the year.
·
We have endeavored to maintain a social atmosphere in keeping with
the ideals of our fraternity and bring as large a measure of contentment
as possible into the daily lives of the members of our family who are
enjoying the care and protection of the Home.
Residents--At the beginning of the fiscal year, there were 368 residents. There were admitted during the year, 41 residents, making a total
of 409. Forty-five have passed away, and one returned to his Lodge. There
are now, at the Home, 363 residents, 190 men and 173 women. Of this
number, there are 31 married couples. Average age of the men, 74 years;
and of the women, 73 years.
·
Health-The general health of the home has been normal.
Hospital-There are now 50 of our members being cared for in our
hospital department where, with the facilities afforded, our physician and
nurses are able to give to those who are ill, every care and attention for
their comfort. Day and night nurses are in constant attendance.
Industrial-The number of residents who render assistance in the
general routine work has increased, and by their labors have been a great
help in the well-being of the Home. The Brethren have been particularly
us~ful by their services in the hospital, engine room, laundry, carpenter,
pamt and barber shops, care of ,garage, mail, passenger, express and freight
auto service, kitchen, pantry, dining rooms vegetable rooms storerooms
office work, library, club and reception r~oms, janitor wo;k, telephon~
switchboard, floral decorations, care of elevators, flower beds and lawns
watering trees, plants and shrubs, vegetable and berry gardens, operatio~
of stage, stereopticon and moving picture machines, poultry yards, and
many other light duties in a general way.
The women residents attend to the making, mending and marking of
all linen, sheets and pillow slips, tablecloths and napkins; also assist in the
preparing of fruit and vegetables, in the kitchen and dining rooms, wiping
of silver, changing table linen, diet kitchen, clerical work, attending telephone calls, showing visitors about the Home, care of music and reception
rooms, care of their rooms and general light household duties.
During the year, 16 rooms, the halls, floors, bath · and wash rooms of
the first floor of the Temple building have been painted, the beds enameled,
and the furniture varnished. The wainscoting and floors of nine rooms in
the hospital department have been painted, the beds and bedside tables
and other metal furniture enameled. All repairs of furniture, windows, doors,
locks and keys, and radios have been done by the Brethren of the Home.
Farm-As heretofore, the greater part of the hill ranch has been leased,
or on a cash rental. The farm has supplied plenty of fruit, figs, berries and
nuts for table use.
·
The. fen~es and houses of the poultry ranch, the adjoining buildings,
and the interior of the barn, have been repaired and whitewashed. All this
work except the whitewashing was done by residents of the Home.
The return from the hay crop has been good this year. The garden
has supplied a variety of vegetables. The chicken ranch has supplied all the
eggs for table use, the surplus being preserved in waterglass.
·This year, 50 fig trees were planted on the north side of our family
orchard, 25 walnut trees were planted along the highway boundary fence

of the Home property, 30 pepper trees were planted on the western side
of the lower road leading up to the Home buildings. Also, many shrubs
were planted about the grounds, and a variety of flowers in the garden
beds.
Many repairs have been made on the fences of the Home property. A
large section of the boundary fences have been renewed, necssitating new
posts and fencing material.
Water-Our deep well pump continues to furnish a plentiful supply of
water for household, garden and irrigation purposes; also, for fir.e protection. Our reservoirs are full at all times.
· Library and Clubrooms-There are now about 6500 books on the
shelves of our main library and branches located in the several departments.
of the Home.
The Masonic Hill branch of the Alameda County Free Library continues to enable our family to obtain many of the latest books, and on
application to secure special ones. In addition, we are recipients, through
friends and members of the fraternity, of books, daily papers, magazines
and periodicals, which are placo;d on the tables in the hospital, library,
clubrooms and social halls.
Social Life-All holidays have been ob~erved with appropriate exercises. The specials are those which were held on New Year's E':'e, New
Year's Day, Lincoln's and Washington's birthday, Easter, Memorial Day,
Fourth of July, Hallowe'en, Thanksgiving and Christmas.
Many splendid programs, stage plays, band and orchestra concerts
have been provided during the year by visiting Lodges, Eastern Star
Chapters, and friends for the entertainment of the members of the. H ome;
the evening often closing with dancing. From time to time, entertainments
are prepared entirely by members of the Home, consisting of vocal and
instrumental music, readings, community singing, stage sketches, c~rds,
games and dancing. Tuesday evenings are devoted to. cards, and Frid~y
evenings to chorus practice. The Happy Hour Dancing Club holds. its
ml;etings every Monday evening. The croquet grounds are well patronized
during the day.
A reading class for the blind meets daily, in the reception room, at
which time the daily papers are read to them by one of the ladies of the
Home. A number of the members of the Home have radio sets · in their
rooms. This privilege is particularly appreciated by those w ho are blind,
and by those being cared for in the hospital department. The clubro?ms
and reception rooms also have radios, which may be enjoyed at any time,
day or evening. Every Sunday afternoon finds the residents of the Home
in the Assembly Hall for Sunday services; after which, a selected musical
program is given by the Home orchestra, or by visiting friends.
•
One of the outstanding pleasing events of the year was a party given
in the main dining room, by the members of the Home, in honor of Mrs.
Caroline A. Proctor, who had attained the age of 100 years· on August S,
1935 and Mrs. Mary A. Fanshaw, who has reached the age of 95 years
you~g. both being members. of the Home. At a time when over 300 residents of the Home were seated for their evening meal at 68 tables (each
table having lighted wax candles), these two young ladies were esco.rted
into the dining room by the Superintendent, and seated at a specially
decorated table at the far end of the main aisle. Their table was decorated
with trailing vines, ferns and flowers. A large birthday cake on their table
had the figures 100 and 95 outlined with lighted candles. After calling
attention to the object of the celebration, ice cream and cake was enjoyed
. by all. At the close of the evening meal, they received warm and hearty
congratulations from all those who were present.

468

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Arrangements have been made whereby members of the family, a few
at a time, may enjoy an outing to nearby places of interest; also, an occasional visit to nearby Lodges and Eastern Star Chapters. During the year,
many trips w_e re made to Oakland, San Francisco, and towns in the vicinity
of the Home.
From time to time Masonic Degrees are conferred in our Temple by
the officers of visiting Lodges for the benefit of the Brethren of the Home.
During the year, Grand Master Randolph V. Whiting, officers and
members of the Grand Lodge, and many Brethren of California Lodges
and other jurisdictions have made visits to the Home, and have spent many
pleasant hours with us. The number of visits this year indicate an increasing interest in the welfare of the Home family.
,
I wish to extend my appreciation of the loyal services rerrdered by
the officers and employees throughout the year, and to express to the
Board of Trustees my sincere gratitude for the friendly advice and support
they have, at all times, given me.
FRANK B. HARTMAN, Superintendent.

Report of the Superintendent-Covina
To the Trustees of the Masonic Homes:
I submit herewith my ninth annual report as superintendent of the
Covina Home. The United States Children's Bureau in its Handbook for
Children's Institutions, says: "The health, happiness, and efficiency of the
adult man and woman depend to a very large extent upon the type of
habits which they acquire from their training and experience in early life."
Less than twelve per cent of a child's time is spent in school; our responsibility in the Covina Home is to care for our children during t he remaining
eighty~eight per cent, and to give them the habits, training, and experience
that will make them healthy, happy, and efficient in the future.
A Human Relationship-The presence of every child in the Home has
a background of misfortune if not of tragedy. We must try to supply to
them the parental care and love which has been denied them from natural
sources. Ours must be a very human relationship to these our wards. A
sense of humor is necessary. We have a fifteen-year-old girl who formerly
had severe temper tantrums, which gradually she has overcome. A few
months ago, however, she became angered at some decision of her housemother, and burst out: "I don't care, I don't like you. I j ust hate you.
You're a mean old thing. You're a blankety blank, and if I dared, I'd fill in
the blanks, so I would." The housemother laughed and said, "I wish you
could see how funny that is, Mary." The tension was relaxed, the storm
was over, and before long Mary was in a much better mood. No "discipline" was administered ; it was apparent that the girl was sorry for her
outburst, and the housemother wisely allowed · the matter to be forgotten.
A girl of fourteen received correction from her housemother, but
resented it. A few days later the housemother received from the girl this
note: "Dearest Miss B, I am very sorry for what happened. You have been
as good to me as anyone could be. You have helped me w hen I didn't know
which way to turn. You have shown me the way to happiness when I was
face to face with sorrow. Who could ask for more than you have given me?
I will never forget you and I will always love you. When I get out into the
world I will use the things you taught me. And I will be glad that I had
such a good housemother." Surely a "perfect tribute," and an indication
that in this case at least Masonry has brought to a child some compensation
for the mother she has lost.

486

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

As They Look Back-From former children of the Home recently were
received two letters that express what "they feel toward the Home after
leaving it. The first is from a boy who came from Hope Lodge No. 234 at
the age of eleven, and remained until he graduated from the high school in
1933. This is what he says:
"When I graduated from the Home it was like being put in.t o a
strange world. I had no conception of what lay ahead. However, I. had
one great thought, 'Where there's a will there's a way.'"
He goes on to tell how he got his first job, in a box factory working ten
hours a day, how hard it seemed, how he stuck to it until the crew was laid
off, how he worked in a logging camp, at an airport, at putting up ice,
and then:
"I am now with the Southern Pacific at their shops here in Sacramento. I want to say that it was the work of the Masons here that got
this opportunity for me. During the two years I have been away
from the Home I have been into no trouble, I owe but few debts; and
I have supported myself all the way through. One would wonder how
a boy could get along so good in these hard times and just starting out
in life. I will tell you, it is because the wonderful training received in
· the Masonic Home is a rock foundation. It is with all sincerity that I
wish to thank the Masonic Home for all that it has done for -me and is
doing for my sister."
Then there is a letter from a girl who graduated and left the Home in
1927, after being here nine years. She begins by stating that the reason for
her letter is that she had heard it reported that she was inclined to disown
the Home as her alma mater. She goes on to say:
"When I come in contact with ·a nyone wearing a Masonic pin I
always introduce myself as one of their 'daughters,' and tell them how
grateful I am to that organization. I want to add that my husband
shares my feelings and is equally as proud where I was raised. I ·love
and cherish the memories of the days I spent there, not to mention the
gratitude that I find it hard to express in words. I consider it my
highest character reference and use it frequently pertaining to background. We will celebrate our eighth wedding anniversary July 25th.
I want to assure you that we are very happy. We live a most normal
life and consider ourselves about the luckiest two in the world to have
such a fine, sweet little boy. I do not believe it is possible for any
person to have a deeper feeling toward the Home than I have. I feel
greatly relieved having written this and · I want you to believe that
every word I have written is sincere."
·
Alumni-Among the alumni there has been an increasing interest in
the Home. During the year, in response to their requests, we issued a news
letter containing information about a large number of these former boys
and girls. During the summer a homecoming was held at Covina, attended
by many old ones, some of whom left the Home as far back as 1914.
The Home Community-Our job in the Home "is to take 175 children,
more or less-boys and girls, big and little-with varying backgrounds and
histories, with all sorts of mental equipments and dispositions and organize
this mis~ellaneous group into a functioning social unit, a pra~tical working
~om~umty. No.t only must we get them to live and work and play together
m this commumty, but we must keep them in right relationship with their
relatives, - allow proper intercourse and yet not allow this intercourse to
interfere with the child's development or his activities as a member of our
Home organization. Whatever happens, the community which is the
Covina Home must go forward in decency and order.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

487

Children and Relatives-During. the past year particular attention has
been given to the matter of the relationships of the children with their
relatives. In many cases relatives, following natural human impulses, had
fallen into ways that were not for the best interests of the children. Among
these were:
Visiting their children too often or too long.
Entering the private quarters of the children, without perm1ss1on.
Sympathizing with children in their complaints, or making remarks
which caused the children to question the authority of those in
charge.
Having children visit them in their homes where there were insufficient
accommodations or improper surroundings.
Killing the .fatted calf for visiting children, making them unhappy to
return to the Home.
Giving ~oney to children without permission or knowledge of those
in charge.
Giving children expensive or unsuitable presents.
Providing their children with nicer things than other children have.
Giving children articles which they are expected to earn by their work.
After consideration of these matters, the Trustees last February
adopted regulations governing contacts of children with their relatives.; and
I am glad to be able to report that the result has been a marked clarification
of this situation and a definite improvement in the relationship between
children's relatives and the children.
.
The Children's Money System-We have continued the plan heretofore
in use for several years, of paying the older children for much of their work
in the Home, and in turn requiring them to pay for their clothing and incidentals. Their wages are determined on a sliding scale, the variable quantities of which are their age and the quality of their work. Payments to
them average about $1.35 per week. Given to them without charge are
their board, room1 and medical care; everything else they must pay for.
They all have equal chances for employment and equal opportunities in
every way, at least as near as we can make it so, but they show surprising
differences in their earnings and financial status. Among them are rich
and poor, misers and beggars. We think that what they learn about money,
how to spend it, save it, give it, how to earn what they receive and not beg
it, makes this system well worth the considerable cost of maintaining it.
The Christmas Fund-The Christmas and Entertainment Fund, contributed at Christmas time by Lodges, other Masonic bodies, and individuals, is a great blessing to the children. It supplies_ them not only with
Christmas cheer, but also throughout the year brings to them happiness in
manifold forms. A fact which may not be generally known is that all the
special expense incident to the summer camp at Balboa is paid from this
fund. Candy is on hand every day -in the year, not in unlimited quantities,
but sufficient to supply this very real need of children. From this Fund
also we have been able to pay for the upkeep of the swimming pool. Those
who have contributed to the Fund may be assured that it is a direct gift to
the happiness of the children throughout the whole year.
Other Contributions-We wish also to mention the Mount Olive Lodge
Recreation Fund, which is ICept replenished by members of that Lodge,
and from which we have drawn during the year $97.32 for special party
refreshments, decorations, treats, dance music, etc.
The Masonic Digest has aided us generously during the past two
years by making available a number of free scholarships in the Mackay
Business College of Los Angeles, which have been most gladly utilized by
graduates of the Home.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Camp Tucker-The children were taken to Camp Tucker on Balboa
Island on June 26th and remained there until August 28th. The Camp
was most successful, and the children left it with regret after two months
of swimming, boating, fishing, and freedom from those responsibilities
and regulations which must be theirs at Covina. One group gained on
an average of 6.6 pounds in weight in the two months. Aside from the
healthfulness of this vacation, it has wonderful value in satisfying the
natural longing of children for variety and change. Delightful as the
scene at Covina is, it would not be well for a child to be confined to it
continuously during the years of his membership in the Home. When they
come back from the Balboa Camp, the Covina Home looks good to them
again.
Letters to Graduates-This year again each boy or girl leaving the
Home by reason of graduation or age limit received from John Whicher,
Secretary of the Board, a personal . letter such as only he can write, conveying the congratulations and good wishes of the Trustees. It is needless to say that these letters were greatly appreciated.
Outside Care-The modern child-caring agency must have at its command facilities to meet the varying needs of many children. Institutional
·care is not always the answer. Some children of nervous temperament
do not thrive as members of a large gro.up. Special conditions of physical
disability sometimes require treatment not available at Covina. Occasionally there is a child with sex tendenc ies that dictate its speedy removal to
a foster home where there are no other children.
·
For one or another of these causes we have had under our supervision
during the past year 49 children belonging to 22 families. either in their
mothers' homes or in foster homes, their care being paid for from Outside
Relief funds. The supervision and management of these cases has been
carried on most ably as a part of the duty of Miss Catherine Noel, our
field worker.
JoHN M. DowNEN, Superintendent.

503

Frank M. Smith, Secretary
Wm. P. Filmer, Treasurer

Wm:. P. Jeffries was the chairman of the Board appointed by the Grand
Master and was the dynamic, moving force in the establishment of this Board
and in the successful conduct of its efforts and operations. By his untimely and
lamentable death on June 12, 1935, this Board sustained an irreparable loss and
the Masonic craft in this jurisdiction was deprived of an outstanding leader.
Brother Jeffries, after a long and honorable career of distinction in business,
civic and social affairs, and particularly in all the fields of Masonry, devoted the
larger part of his time and effort during the past three years to the cause of an
adequate Endowment Fund for the Masonic Homes of California. This crowning
effort of his life was characteristic of him because it was inspired and motivated
by his love of children and his soiicitud~ for the welfare of the aged; and expressed
itself in his continuous and enthusiastic efforts to help the Masons of'California
tu do something outstanding for the Masonic Homes for children and the aged.
Two days after his death your Board received a check for $1,000.00, the proceeds
of a policy carried by Brother Jeffries on his life for the benefit of the. Home·~.
He would not appeal to his brethren to do something for the Homes that he has
not done himself.
·
·
·
A solicitation for endowment funds during the month of May, 1935, was
authorized by the Grand Master, and the Board was diligent in connection therewith. A considerable amount of printed matter was distributed, a voluminous
amount of correspondence was had with Masters, Secretaries and Inspectors and
addresses were caused to be made in the Lodges of the jurisdiction. Joint meetings were held in some of the larger cities which were enthusiastic and well
attended. Meetings were held under the supervision of your Board in Los Angeles, Fresno, San Luis Obispo, Long Beach, San Bernardino, Oakland, Monrovia, Taft and other cities. Brother Jeffries, as chairman of the Board, attended
scores of meetings and in his forceful and·convincing manner presented the needs
of the Homes and the appeal for funds. He was ably assisted by various members
of the Board, although his is the credit for most of the time and effort required
by these meetings.
The Inspectors of the various districts have rendered faithful and valued
services to the Board and, with the officers and endowment committees of the
various Lodges, are entitled to the commendation of this Grand Lodge.

Included in the gifts received from Lodges are several gifts of money that
were made in lieu of sending flowers to the funeral of a deceased brother. Donations of this character are increasing year by year, and in the judgment of your
Board this is an appropriate and beautiful way of attesting grief or respect for
a decedent, by making his death productive of good through all the years to come.
During the year a gift was received from Lionel Campagne, of East San
Diego Lodge No. 561, of a $500.00 bond of the San Diego First National Company.
George]. Burton, of Southern California Lodge No. 278, conveyed to the
Masonic Homes of California his home property in Eagle Rock of a value of
about $4,000.00, subject to a trust deed in the sum of $1,850.00.
Brother John T. Golt of Manila Lodge No. 1 has conveyed three parcels of
property of an unknown value to the Endowment Fund.
The West Gate Low Twelve Club, formed by a group of members of West
Gate Lodge No. 335, have instituted a fund from which $250.00 is paid to the
family of any member in the event of his death, and two of the members, Abe
Blumenthal and Aaron C. Scher, have subscribed for membe·rship therein designating the Masonic Homes of California as the beneficiary of their subscriptions.
In the event any money from these subscriptions is paid into the Endowment
Fund, W,,est Gate Lodge will be given credit therefor.

Relative to Activities of the Board
The members of the Board have given consideration to the matter of the
appropriate and expedient future activities of the Endowment Board. It was the
belief of our late chairman that an annual solicitation of funds should be made
during some month of the year and that an active campaign for subscriptions
from the members should be made by the Lodges. Such campaigns were had, but
the results have not been satisfactory to your Board, and the continuation of that
method of raising funds is, in our opinion, undesirable. We do not see that
adequate results could be accomplished unless the campaign was in charge of a
person who possesses the dynamic energy and forceful personality and the
enthusiasm brought to this work by Brother Jeffries, and who could devote a
great amount of time to the work. The Grand Master may know of such a
.brother who would assume the task, but if not, then it would be better to discontinue this method of raising money. While we are deeply appreciative of the
gifts which have been received, and recognize the benevolence of our brethren
who have contributed, yet we find throughout the jurisdiction a widespread
apathy and in many quarters a decided opposition to campaigns or drives for
funds. Our correspondence and interviews with our brethren develop a surprising
dissatisfaction. During the current year few Lodges have received contributions
from any large percentage of their membership, and even in the case of the
fourteen Lodges which attained their quota, only about 60 per cent of the members of these Lodges contributed. Our opinion in this matter finds emphasis in
the fact that 153 Lodges reported 10 per cent or less of their quota, while 442
LDdges reported less than 50 per cent of their quota, that 88 Lodges made no
report and only 50 Lodges reported contributions of more than 50 per cent of
their quota.
Your Board is more firmly than ever impressed with the paramount importance of raising an adequate endowment fund for the Masonic Homes, and it
urges an earnest and continuous effort by all officers and members to secure
augmentations to the fund. The safety in the future years of the beneficiaries of
our bounty requires of us not only a deep syrrtpathy for the dependent aged and
helpless young, but a practical performance of our professions of Masonic
charity. The Endowment Board can be the leader in stimulating the hearts of
our brethren and in presenting the claims of our Homes before the entire membership. Bequests and other gifts can be secured and it is the function of your
Board to seek such gifts by appropriate means.

. GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

That we may have the assurance of a regular accretion to the Endowment
Fund, in addition to the results growing from efforts of this Board, and that the
burden of such accretions should be borne by the entire membership in the jurisdiction rather than as heretofore from the gifts of the faithful and active
minority, we respectfully and fraternally offer the following resolution:
"Resolved, that a per capita tax of fifty cents (50c) per member be levied
on the members of the subordinate Lodges of this grand jurisdiction, which tax
shall be payable annually by the members to the Sec~etaries of their respective
Lodges previous to or at the time of the payment of Lodge dues and that no
receipt be issued by any Lodge to any member until said per capita tax has first
been paid in full for the current year. That the said annual per capita tax · so
collected be remitted by the Secretaries monthly to the Grand Secretary for
payment by him into the Endowment Fund of the Masonic Homes of California."
We recommend that the foregoing resolution be referred to the Committee
on Policy and General Purposes. (This failed of adoption-Grand Secretary.)
·Appropriation
In order that your Board may function during the ensuing year it will be
necessary that funds be provided by this Grand Lodge for its expenses, since no
part of its expenditures may be taken from the Etidowment Fund or contributions thereto. Heretofore the expenses of your Board have amounted to more
than $6,000.00 per year, but if the methods of raising funds are altered as we
have suggested, then an appropriation of $4,000.00 should be sufficient to liquidate
the unpaid indebtedness of the Committee and to provide for its activities during
the year, and we therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:
"Resolved, that the sum of Four Thousand ($4,000.00). Dollars be and is
hereby appropriated from the funds of this Grand Lodge to be paid to the
Masonic Homes Endowment Board for its expenses for the year· ending October
3, 1936."
