REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
WEEK ON SIXTEENTH ANNUAL OBSERVANCE
SAN FRANCISCO, OCTOBER 8, 1935.
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge F. er A. M. of California:
Each year it becomes more difficult for our committee to convey to Grand
Lodge anything approaching the information every member of the Fraternity
should have with respect to the growth and development of Public Schools
Week and of the place the annual observance has come to occupy in. the educational and civic life of the Commonwealth.
The success of our latest observance may be perhaps indicated by the statement that it fully justified the expectations of Superintendent of Public Instruction Kersey when in the ·'Foreword" to the Bulletin of Suggestions issued to
the school people by the State Department of Public Education he said:
"The natural interest in a specially scheduled occasion such as Public
Schools Week provides an opportunity for the development of a long-term
program of activities designed to develop a better understanding of the
purposes and character of the modern educational program. It should eventuate a combination of effort on the part of those engaged in school service
and parents and other citizens interested in the welfare of education and
which will . prove a vital force in enhancing the service which the schools
may render to society."
Almost universally throughout the state the local observances this year in
both urban and rural communities were of the sort for which we have been continuously and constantly striving ever since the inauguration of the movement;

"Pronounced the most widely observed celebration since inception sixteen years ago by Masonic Orders, Public Schools Week, which began
Tuesday, ended last night with grand finales in nine meeting places.
"Addresses on educational affairs, pageants, exhibits of school work,
open-house classes for parental observation and co-ordinated activities participated in by service clubs, ninety local Masonic Lodges, the Board of
Education and civic groups characterized learning in the United States since
the landing of the Pilgrims."
There have been evolved-in many instances as the result of "trial and
error"-programs especially suited to the particular community in which the
observance is held; and this year there was an increased number of instances
where they were evidently designed not merely to furnish entertainment, but
more particularly to stimulate in the citizens of ·the community a desire to be
informed with respect to their schools; and to furnish them with that information.
.
In our report last year we gave as one of the probable reasons for the
then unprecedented success of the Fifteenth Annual Observance the willingness
of the local Committees of Arrangements to adopt programs which had proved
successful elsewhere, and to avail themselves of suggestions based on experience.
This was even more noticeable this year. There was not a single feature of which
favorable mention had been from time to time made in these reports that was
not included in some program ; and there were several comparatively small
communities which this year presented programs which have heretofore characterized observances in only large centers of population. The "Downtown
School" was the dominant feature of many programs. In some instances where
there was not sufficient space in a downtown building to accommodate an entire
class, the feature was presented in a modified form; but in every case it showed
pupils engaged in their regular school work in places other than their classrooms
and in either business or shopping districts.
Mention has been heretofore made of the distribution of printed or multigraphed matter which furnished short, concise answers to questions being asked
by parents and taxpayers with respect to the local situation. This very commendable procedure evidently continues; and it is interesting to note that the
questions are not confined to the curriculum and the cost of maintaining the
schools, but include those which might perhaps be said to concern only administrative matters, such as the size of classes.
.
Along the same line there was this year reported as one of the features
of an observance a "forum" which was designed to not only give the audience
information with respect to the schools, but to afford an opportunity to any who
desired it to express their own views with respect to school problems.

522

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Many of the programs presented this ·year commemorated the tercentenary
of the first secondary school in America . . This afforded an opportunity of very
· interestingly, and entertainingly as well, tracing the development of secondary
education from its beginning in the Boston Latin School with its restricted curriculum for a selected class to the modern high school with its all embracing
curriculum suited to the needs and capabilities of all the children of all the
people. The presentation in some instances was by appropriate addresses and in
others by the reproduction of scenes characterizing successive periods. In one
community there were four fifteen-minute programs presented by four different
. high schools, portraying scenes from the schools of 1635, 1735, 1835 and 1935;
and in another there was a reproduction of a typical classroom scene of the
Boston Latin School with a recitation in Latin from the text of Cicero.
The attendance at public meetings has now attained such proportions that
it is no longer an uncomm on thing to find in a report from a particular community some reference to the fact that the auditorium could not accommodate
the crowd which sought admission ; and in at least three instances this year it
was found necessary in response to a . popular demand to repeat the entire program for the benefit of those who could not gain admission to the auditorium
on its first presentation. But the aggregate of those constituting these audiences pales into insignificance in comparison with the multitudes who exhibit
their interest by visiting the schools. Open house in the schools with exhibits
of school work and the presentation of pupil programs, and particularly where
the visitors are afforded an opportunity to see the children engaged in their
regular work and to meet and talk with the principal and teachers, continues
to be the most popular feature of Public Schools week. It is certainly the most
valuable; because, a~· has been repeatedly pointed out, in no better way can
parents and taxpayers obtain first hand information with respect to their schools.
In connecti on with what has just been said, it will not be inappropriate, we
think, to here quote the, following from a newspaper clipping attached to one
of the reports :

as one in which only Masons are concerned, but as a community affair in which.
the entire community should participate. With that idea in mind we earnestly
recommended that the committee of arrangements for the local observance
should include representatives of all the civic bodies in the community, and
especially the American Legion, Parent-Teacher Associations and service clubs.
A striking evidence of the extent to which the observance is now regarded
as a community affair is furnished by one of the reports received this year,
from which it appears that the committee of arrangements was composed of
representatives of sixty-two different organizations-including, of course, the
Masonic Bodies, American Legion, Parent-Teacher Associations, the service
and women's clubs and the local Chamber of Commerce. In this conne~tion
mention should be made of the fine cooperation given our committee by the
State Chamber of Commerce which placed at our disposal during Public
Schools Week its allotted periods of time on the broadcasting stations; and it
appears that local committees were extended similar courtesies by ParentTeacher Associations, women's clubs and other organizations which have regular
allotments of radio ·time.
We have more than once pointed out that there are two factors primarily
responsible for the growth and development of Public Schools Week. One is
the active cooperation of the school people and the other the hearty and cordial
support received from newspapers and broadcasting stations.
The cooperation of the school people has been of inestimable value. As has
been heretofore reported to Grand Lodge, Public Schools Week has been
included among the educational activities with which the State Department of
Education maintains professional contact. This is accomplished through our
committee representing Grand Lodge. A special Bulletin of Suggestions to th(?
school people is issued each year by the Superintendent of Public Instruction ;
and mention has more than once been made in our reports of the splendid work
being done by the County Superintendents through their Rural Supervisors and
the teachers of the little district schools. Furthermore, there are several local
school systems throughout the State where the proper observance of Public
Schools Week has apparently come to be regarded as one of the r equirements
of successful school administration.
. Now, desi~able as this .in itself is, we must have in mind the possibility of
its developing into a situation which would defeat the end we have in view;
and it will not have been the fault of the school people, but of those upon whom
Grand Lodge has a right to rely for the furtherance of the movement it originated and continues to foster.
In Our recognition of the advisability, indeed necessity, of securing the coordinated action of the community, it was never intended, of course, that th e
Masters of our Lodges should be relieved of the responsibil ity primarily devolving upon them . . And it must be always remembered that the great value of
Public Schools Week is in the fact that it is fostered not by the school people,
·but by laymen. It is essentially a lay movement. To have it understood as only
an activity carried on by the school people would be no less objectionable than
it would be to have it regarded as an event in which only Masons are concerned.
.It is the province of the school people to determine the nature of, and to
furnish, the school programs to be presented; to provide exhibits of school
work; to receive visitors and to attend to matters of that sort. They should
not be expected (except in the very small communities where there is neither
a Masonic Lodge nor a civic organization of any sort) to arrange for, and
take entire charge of, an observance. Nor is it desirable that they should. That
is the duty of the .committee of arrangements of which organized Masonry
should always be the nucleus and which should include representatives of such
civic organizations as there are in the community; and if there are none, that
duty devolves upon the Master of the Lodge.

"To our School Leaders and Teachers:
"You showed us many interesting things about our schools during
Public Schools Week ; and your exhibits and programs attracted many
interested persons. There were quite a few faces missing, however-faces
of persons who do a lot of kicking and who, above all others, should turn
out during Public Schools Week to see how things are · done in the
schools. Maybe they'd learn something."
It will be remembered, of course, that while the observance of. Public
Schools Week in its inception was a Masonic event, its development has been
due to our insistence that it should not be so regarded-but as a community
affair in which the entire community would participate. From the very start
we sought the active cooperation of th ose who cherished the public school
system as we do. That cooperation, however, was not immediately forthcoming
-at least to the extent hoped for and which we felt we had a right to expect.
Even among the school people (with the exception of certain farseeing educators who at once sensed the importance of our movement and gave it their
active and enthusiastic support) there was an apathy that was difficult to understand, and even in some communities what seemed almost opposition on the part
of school trustees, but which was probably nothing more than an unwillingness
to give official sanction to an undertaking initiated by a fraternal organization.
In those early years our great concern· was lest it might not be understood
by the public and likewise, and particularly by the school people that the movement had not been instituted for the aggrandizement, either directly or indirectly, of the Masonic Fraternity, but only for the benefit of our public
schools. And we have ever · been insistent in impressing upon the masters of
our Lodges that the observance of Public Schools Week is not to be regarded
0

523

524

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

There was never contemplated, of course, the possibility of an observance
of Public Schools Week being held in any community in which the Lodge, if
there were one, would not have a part. And yet there were two very success ~ul observances hel? this year in which so far as appears from the reports
received by our committee the organized Masonry in the community did not
take the part naturally expected of it. Whether or not there was any reason
or even excuse, for this is beside the question. The crux of the situation i~
~h~~ there was a~ observance of Public Schools Week which was apparently
m1hated . a_nd ~arried to a successful conclusion by the school people without
any participation by those who are primarily charged by Grand Lodge with that
responsibility.
One of these observances was in a city in which there are several Lodges.·
1:he fact that they did not participate was apparently due to an unfortunate
difference of opinion between their representatives and the school people as to
the form the observance should take. One of the Masters reported that there
~re too many schools and they are too widely separated to attempt a program
m each as the. school people desired; and they all stated that no endeavor was
made to obtain the cooperation of civic organizations in the community because
the school ' people "preferred to handle their own arrangements:" Whatever
may have been the reason, there was no participation by the Lodges; and to
quote from one of. the reports: "the Masonic showing this year in ...................- ...
was very poor." The irony of the situation is disclosed in a statement in an
editorial in one of the local newspapers. In commending the observance the
writer said : "It (Public Schools Week) is an occasion sponsored by the
Masonic Lodges."
With respect to the second of ·the observances to which we are now referring, it may be said that even such information as we have of it did not
come in the usual manner-that is, through the reports made by the Lodges at
the request of t~e. Grand Master. Indeed, in a letter written by the Master of
the Lodge expla.mmg why he had made no report, he said that he had not been
able to give the matter the attention he should have . and "wished to report that
no special plans were made to observe this as other matters in nearby localities
interferred with the same." From this it would appear that no observance had
been held in th.a t community. It happened, however, that from another source
there had come to us information of a very successfuf observance which had
been . arranged by the school people as the result of a discussion at a faculty
··
meetmg.
We regret that we .cannot give to the program of this observ.ance the
attention. it deserves; because it was unique in that it ccmbined, through. a
prese~t~hon on the stage of the auditorium and an auxiliary platform, an oral
clescnptwn of the several departments of the school with an actual demonstration of the work being done, . otherwise possible only by vjsitirig the classrooms. The courses of study were explained in the form of a conversation between characters assumed by pupils representing the principal ·of .the
school and the parents of two prospective freshmen. Throughout the performance they remained seated on the platform which represented the principal's
office. After the principal had described the work being done in each department
there was a demonstration of it on the stage which represented the different
classrooms. While the classes were being changed, the auditorium was darkened
with only a spot light playing on the characters seated on the platform. The
demonstrations were made entertaining as well as instructive by the: introduction
of comedy features which did not, however, detract from the serious purpose of
the presentation.
·
Now both these observances carried out the purpose of Public Schools
Week and from that point of view are beyond criticism. But the point we .are

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

525

making is that in neither instance was there that participation by organized
Masonry which is essential; nor was the observance in either c.ase the community affair it should be.
Observances of this sort give no warrant for those· encomiums which have
been heaped upon the Fraternity since the institution of Public Schools Week.
One of the many received this year is contained in the following excerpt from
an editorial commending our observance :
"This is. being sponsored by the Grand Lodge of Masons of California
as one of its contributions to public welfare and citizenship training. It is
a worthy undertaking and one that c.annot fail to redound to the glory of
the Fraternity."
It may be that our apprehensions are not well founded. But the situation
seems to us so serious that because of the responsibility devolving upon our
committee as the agency of Grand Lodge through which our observance is fostered, we believe it our duty to call public attention to it ; and to sound a note
of warning.
One of the finest results of our annual observance is the editorial comment
with respect to education in general, and to their toe.al school systems in particular, which appears in the newspapers during Public Schools Week. Incidentally,
the expressions of opinion are not always laudatory; and this is as it should be.
If there is anything in any school system of which criticism may justly be made,
Public Schools Week is a good time to make reference to it; because it is then ·
that the attention of the public is focused on their public schools. And just as
destructive and designedly hostile criticism ls to be, by all friends of public
education, deplored and combated; so is constructive and intelligent crticism
to be encouraged and commended.
The observance of Public Schools Week is not intended as merely a
"ballyhoo" for our schools and for what they ·are doing everywhere and for the
manner in which it is being done. Its real purpose is admirably stated in the
fo llowing excerpt from an editorial in a newspaper which is notable for the
extraordinarily large amount of space which it each year devotes to the observance:
"The object of Public -Schools Week is primarily to enable the people
to become better acquainted with the public school system, to understand its
problems and to gain the information which will enable the citizens to improve upon the system. It is well to have a week when people are expected
to think about the public schools and to once more realize the tremendously
important part that they play in our national life. The schools can never
fulfill the high place they hold in the American scheme of things unless
the people keep in touch with them. T he farther away from the people the
schools ·may be removed, the more difficult it is for them to carry their
great responsibility adequately."
That our latest ·observance fulfilled its purpose there can be no doubt. And
notwithstanding what has been said in this report which may savor of criticism,
we desire that it be distinctly understood that we believe the success achieved
was very largely due this year, as heretofore, to the efficient and intelligent
manner in which the Masters, and other officers, of our Lodges and our Inspectors discharged the r esponsibility devolving upon them as the direct representative~ of Grand Lodge.

To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California :
Your Committee on Grievances to which was referred the petition for
restoration from F. A. ]., formerly ~ ·member of Palos Verdes L odge No. 38?,
tried by Southern California Lodge No. 278, and expelled by Grand Lodge m
1930 (Record No. 652), reports as follows:
Petitioner was convicted of obtaining $3,800 by fraud and deceit from a
Masonic Temple Association, of which he was a director and the treasurer.
Grand Lodge, in passing upon this case in 1930, declared that petitioner had
"violated every principle of honor and fair dealing," and approved the report
of this committee, which said "We know of no case in the eighty years of
California Masonry so flagrant in its elements of fraud and deceit."
Petitioner applied for restoration in 1933 and 1934, and each of such petitions was denied. This year he has again applied for restoration, but has not
presented any new evidence in support of his petition, which rests upon the
evidence presented in former years. All three of these petitions contain certain
serious misstatements of important facts bearing directly upon the merits of
his petition. For instance each petition states that petitioner was convicted on
one specification and acquitted on four; whereas, in truth and in fact, he was
convicted on four specifications and acquitted on but one; and that the least
serious of the specifications. There are also other misstatements which time
prevents being mentioned.
Every man owes the highest good faith to those whom he represents and
who repose trust and confidence in him. Especially in this case, when all concerned are Masons. It is impossible for any fair-minded person to read the
record in this case without raising his righteous indignation at the long continued and studied course of trickery and deceit practiced by petitioner upon
his Masonic brethren. The restoration of a man of such character would be a
grave injury to the decent and honorable Masons who compose the jurisdiction
of California.
We, therefore, offer th_e foll owing resolution and move its adoption:
Resolved, That the petition for. restoration of F. A. ]., formerly a member
of Palos Verdes Lodge No. 389, F . & A. M., be and the same is hereby denied.

Report adopted.
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California :
Your Committee on Grievances to which was referred trial record No. 845
from Lodi Lodge No. 256, begs leave to report as follows :
The accused, one H . F . E ., was charged with unmasonic conduct as supported by two specifications, the gist of which are that the accused knowingly
and wilfully failed and refused to obey a summons. The accused was acquitted
by the Trial Commission.
It appears from the undisputed evidence that the accused was appointed
by the Master of his Lodge to act upon a committee which, as a part of its
duty, was to prepare a report required by this Grand Lodge. The Master of the
Lodge repeatedly urged the chairman of this committee to have the committee
complete this report, but without success. F inally, and apparently in some
desperation, the Master issued a summons to the members of the committee,
commanding their attendance at a meeting. All members of the committee
responded except the accused.
While the accused is some sixty-seven years of age and appears to have
been suffering from neu(itis, no adequate reason or excuse was shown for his
refusal or failure to obey the mandate of the summons. The accused was able
to be up and about. He took a four hundred mile automobile trip two days
before the meeting, and while undoubtedly ailing and suffering pain, was able
to superintend ranch operations and call at the homes of others. No question
exists but that the accused could easily have communicated with the Master of
his Looge, who issued the summons. However, no effort was made so to do.

529

l'ROCEEDINGS OF THE

' GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

We think the real answer to the matter may be found in the statement of the
accused to the Trial Commission in which he asserts: "I did not realize the
importance of the notice."
Under the circumstances here shown, we feel the finding of the Trial Commission to be unwarranted.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
Resolved, That the finding of the Trial Commission of not guilty be and
the same hereby is changed to a finding of guilty and the penalty fixed at
reprimand.

Your Necrology Committee sorrowfully reports that since the last communication of Grand Lodge we have suffered the loss of one of our members;
Brother J. Karl Lobdell, whose friendly smile and generous service have
identified him at each session of Grand Lodge, gave up the battle of life on
June 14, 1935. The last few years have worn the physical and mental stran~s
of life's cords in many men to a thinness that could not stand the daily strain
and some have been taken from our ranks. Brother Lobdell was raised in
Wilshire Lodge Nb. 445, on July 13, 1914, and was the second Mason to be
· raised in the Lodge. He was appointed Junior Steward December 14, 1915.
In 1918 he was in France in the flying corps with the American Expeditionary
Forces. Desiring to render worthwhile Masonic ~ervice he inaugurated the
"Wilshire Lodge Bulletin" in October, 1920, and edited the same until January,
1923. He was Worshipful Master of his Lodge during the year 1923 and the
following year was a Director of the "Wilshire Lodge Building Corporation."
Brother Lobdell was also very active in the Scottish Rite in the Valley of Los
Angeles. In 1925 he was made a Knight Commander of the Court of Honor
and in 1929 was coroneted a 33° Mason; being the youngest Inspector General
Honorary to receive that degree in this State. From 1926 to 1930 he served on
the Masonic Educational Committee of Grand Lodge and from 1933 to the date
of his death was a member of the Necrology Committee. Able, congenial' and
conscientious whenever we meet we shall miss him.
"The curfew tolls the knell of parting day,
The lowing herd winds slowly o'er the lea,
The plowman homeward plods his weary way,
And leaves the world to darkness and to me.
Let not Ambition mock their useful toil,
Their homely joys and destiny obscure;
Nor Grandeur hear with a disdainful smile
The short and simple annals of the· poor.
The boast of heraldry, the pomp of power,
And all that beauty, all that wealth e'er gave,
Await alike the inevitable hour;
The paths of glory lead but to the grave."

Projects. Also loyal and faithful Inspector Roderick G. Guyett. Close friends
and co-workers in their Masonic activities of Grand Lodge have been requested
by the Grand Master to give individual eulogies for each of these brethren
which will follow this general report.

As we continue our Masonic labors we feel we should take to heart the
thoughts of Lincoln in his famous memorial address: "It is for us the living
rather to be here dedicated to the unfinished work which these to whom we
pay tribute have thus far so nobly advanced, and that from these honored
dead we take increased devotion for those principles for which they so .loyally
served."
·
To .be truly human is a real art. It is therefore proper to express here
the thoughts of that beloved Ambassador of Good-Will, Brother Will Rogers
of Claremore Lodge, Oklahoma, who lived his Masonr.y and taught all men
high and low to be unassuming, to be human and meet on the level. His close
friend had just been taken by death, so he wrote him, "I guess God needs
good men and He has to call them home when he needs them," he concludes
his letter thus: "And you will pop into some well-kept ranch-house over under
some cool shady trees and you'll be asked to have dinner and it'll be the
best one you ever had in your life. Well, when you are thanking the women
folks you jest tell the sweet-looking little old lady that you know her boy
back on an outfit you usta rep for and tell the daughters that you knew their
brother and if you see a cute little rascal running around there, kiss him for
me. Well, I can't write you any more, Charlie, the darn paper is all wet. It
must be raining in this old bunk-house. Of course, we are all just a hangin'
on hei:e as long as we can. I don't know why we hate to go, we know it's
better there. Maybe it's because we haven't done anything that will live after
we're gone."
Brethren: It is true that great men never feel they have accomplished
much, it is we, who remain, who realize the great value of their service after
they are gone.
"Grant us Thy peace upon our homeward way, .
With Thee began, with Thee shall end the day.
Guard Thou the lips from sin, the hearts from shame,
That in this Temple have called upon Thy name."-AMEN.
OAKLEY K. MORTON,
EZRA DECOTO,
EDWARD HENRY MARTIN,
GEORGE F. WELLS.

541

In Memoriam David J. Reese
By Frank M. W ise
"To live in hearts we leave ·behind is n~t to die."
Thirty-two years ago there came to this Grand Lodge a Master of a constituent Lodge of this grand jurisdiction, a young man who was destined to
become one of the outstanding figures in Masonry in California; one whose
splendid record is indelibly recounted in the annals of Masonry, the memory
of which is dear to the hearts of the thousands of Masons of this S.tateDavid John Reese, our fifty-eighth Grand Master.
After thirty-one consecutive years of unselfish and devoted service to .the
craft and to this grand -body, Dave, as he was familiarly known to his
thousands of friends and brothers, has been called from labor to refreshment,
and we miss his cordial greeting and his hearty hand clasp.
David John Reese was born of good Welsh stock at Gold Hill, Nevada,
on August 22, 1871. The family moved to Sonoma county, California, in
1884, where Brother Reese received his education. At the age of nineteen he·
became a school teacher and taught for many years in the schools of Sonoma
and Ventura counties.
Shortly after moving to Ventura in 1900, Brother Reese ·became the
owner, editor and publisher of the Ventura Free Press, and for twenty-nine

542

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

years continued to publish one of the leading newspapers of the State. He
was a member of the executive comrpittee of the California Press Association
from 1907 to the time of his passing.
Public service engrossed much of Brother Reese's attention throughout his
career. An indefatigable worker, capable and conscientious in every undertaking, it is little wonder that he was most active in the community life of his
home city, Ventura, where he served at various periods as Postmaster,
member of the Board of Freeholders, member of the City Council and Mayor,
Secretary of the Chamber of Commerce, and President of the City Planning
Commission. For sixteen years, under three Governors, he served the State
of California as Civil Service Commissioner. He was a District Governor of
Rotary for California-Nevada District and later became a Director of Rotary
International.
Brother Reese was raised a Master Mason in Santa Paula Lodge No. 291,
April 27, 1897. His active interest in Masonry was contemporaneous with his
membership. He served his mother Lodge as Senior Deacon, Junior and Senior
Warden. In 1901 he affiliated with San Buenaventura Lodge No. 214, serving
as Senior Warden in 1902 and Master in 1903-1904.
In Grand Lodge Brother Reese served as Junior Grand Deacon in 1910;
Grand Standard Bearer, 1915-16-17; Junior Grand Warden, 1921-22; Senior
Grand Warden, 1922-23; Deputy Grand Master, 1923-24; Grand Master, 192425. For eighteen years, 1904 to 1922, he was Inspector of the District comprising the Lodges of Santa Barbara and Ventura counties. In 1917 he
formed, in that District, the first Masonic Officers' Association in California.
In 1926 he was appointed chairman of the Board of Control, which position
he held to the time of his death. His splendid accomplishments as head of this
·board, in the administering of the problems of relief and employment are well
known, not only to the brethren of this jurisdiction,' but also throughout the
length and ·breadth of this land.
In the allied Masonic bodies, Brother Reese served as Grand Master of
the Grand Council, Royal and Select Masters, in 1920; Grand High Priest of
the Grand Chapter, Royal Arch Masons of California, in 1928. He was a
member of the Los Angeles Scottish Rite Bodies, Ventura Commandery Knights
Templar, and Al Malaikah Temple of the Shrine.
·
During Dave's year as Grand Master he traveled more than 40,000 miles
on Masonic business. He visited most of the remote as well as centrally
located Lodges of our jurisdiction, endearing himself to the brethren by his
sympathetic understanding, inspiring sincerity, and gentle humor. Many of
the recommendations made by him are now familiar regulations of this Grand
Lodge. It was he who recommended the formation of the Committee on
Necrology, to do honor to our distinguished brethren gone before. It was
Dave who recommended the formation of the Committee on History, whose
excellent work will doubtless culminate in the publishing of the Masonic
History of California. It was on his recommendation that the pleasing custom
of providing aprons for our Past Grand Masters was adopted.
Such, my brethren of the Grand Lodge, is a brief summary of the life and
activities of our beloved friend and ·b rother. What an impressive record of
distinguished and loyal service to Masonry ana to hi~ fellow citizens! It was
a privilege and an honor to have known Dave Reese. Masonry in California
is the richer for his life, devoted as it was to the practice · of Masonic ideas
and ideals. Dave loved Masonry. It was ever in his thought and a vital part
of his life. He was never happier than when rendering some service to the
craft or to a needy brother. He was truly a craft Mason, a man among men.
· In his annual message as Grand Master, he paraphrazed Thomas R. Marshall
as follows: "My retirement is not a demotion to the ranks, because I have
never risen above them." How Dave lived is a cherished memory, and probably is best expressed in his own words in his beautiful poem "Let me walk
in the road ·by the side of a friend."

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

543

'Tis only a half truth the poet has sung,
Of the house by the side of the way;
Our Master had neither a house nor a home,
But He walked with the crowd day by day,
And I think when I read of the poet's desire,
That a house by the road would be good·;
But service is found in its tenderest form,
When we walk with the crowd in the road.
So I say, let me walk with the men in the road,
Let me seek out the burdens that crush ;
Let me speak a kind word of good cheer to the weak
Who are falling behind in the rush.
There are wounds to be healed, there are breaks we must mend.
There's a cup of cold water to give;
And the man in the road by the ·side of his friend
Is the man who has .learned how to live.
Then tell me no more of the house by the road ;
There's only one place I can live:
It's there with the men who are toiling along
Who are needing the cheer I can give.
It is pleasant to live in the house by the way
And befriend, as the poet has said
But the Master is bidding us, "Bear ye their load,
For your rest waiteth yonder ahead."
I could not remain in the house ·by the road,
And watch as the toilers go on,
Their faces beclouded with pain and with sin,
So burdened their strength nearly gone.
I'll go to their side, I'll speak in good cheer,
I'll help them to carry their load,
And I'll smile at the man in the house by the way
As I walk with the crowd in the road.
Out there in the road that goes by the house,
When the poet is singing his song,
I'll walk and I'll work, midst the heat of the day,
And I'll help falling brothers along;
Too busy to live in the house by the way,
Too happy for such an abode.
And my heart sings its praise to the Master above
Who is helping me serve in the road.

I n Memoriam Roderick G. Guyett
By John D. M,urphey
In keeping with one of the oldest traditions of th!s Grand Lo?ge, an hour
is set aside each year, dedicated to the commemoration of the hves a~d activities of those of its membership whose life span on earth has terminated
by their having lieen called to take on immortality in "that house not built by
han.ds, eternal in the heavens."

In this solemn hour we are profoundly moved by the contemplation of the
memories of the friends and brothers whose names are now enrolled on the
pages of . the B_ook of Pa~t Performance. To them we pay inadequate but
well merited tribute, and m this ·solemn ceremony bid those of yesterday a
last farewell.
A poet, whose name I know not, has said:
Farewell. That word has broken hearts,
And blinded eyes with tears ;
Farewell. One stays and one departs,
Between them roll the years.
Good-bye. That word makes faces pale,
And fills the soul with fears;
Good-bye. Two words that wring a wail
Which flutters down the years.
Adieu. Such is the word for us ;
'Tis more than word, 'tis prayer.
They do not part who do part thiis,
For God is everywhere.
It is my privilege at this time, at the instance of the Most Worshipful
Gran? Master, to be the mouth-piece of this grand body to express, in a brief
and inadequate manner I realize, our appreciation of the splendid service to
Masons o.f this State, of Roderick George Guyett, who for nearly thirty years
~erv~ th~s Gran_d Lodge as Inspector in several of its Masonic districts. My
mve~ttgat10n satisfies me that Brother Guyett has to his credit the longest
service .of any Inspector in this jurisdiction, and that in that service he was
ever faithful and loyal in upholding and furthering the fundamental tenets of
our great fraternity.
Roderick Guyett was born in May, 1866, at Montpelier, Vermont. His
pare~ts we_re Peter Guyett," a French Canadian, and Margaret Mitchell Guyett,
of his native State. Before reaching the age of twelve his parents had both
passed from the realms of worldly cares and responsibilities and Rod was
left to be the architect of his own future and fortune. He im~igrated at the
age ~f t~elve to Ames, Iowa, with friends, and there received such schooling
as his circumstances permitted him to obtain. While yet in his teens he
removed to Dubuque, Iowa, where he engaged in railroad work with the
Chicago, Milwaukee & . St. Paul railroad, and remained in this service in the
passenger department until 1892, when he again "moved with the c·ourse of
Empire" westward, and arrived in San Francisco with the Union Pacific
Railroad company where, at 1 Montgomery street, the site of the old Masonic
Temple, he held responsible railroad positions until 19041 when he entered the
general insurance fiel_d, where he remained engaged in his chosen life work until
his demise on November 29, 1934.
. In 1895 he married Etta J . Dwight, of Chicago. There was born of this union in 1896 one daughter, Margaret Clara, who bears the · name of her
maternal and paternal grandmothers. In addition to his wife and daughter .
t~ere survives him one -brother, David L. Guyett, of Tulsa, Oklahoma, who:
hke Rod, has always taken an active interest in all things appertaining to the
Masonic Fraternity.
Rod was raised to the sublime degree of Master Mason in Excelsior
Lodge ·No. 166 on October 10, 1898, and w~s thereafter rapidly advanced
through the intermediate places and stations until he was installed Worshipful
~faster in 1905. His outstanding administration as Master of the ·Lodge so
impressed the the:i Grand Lecturer, W. H. Edwards, that in the following
year he was appointed Inspector of the, 53rd Masonic District and continue<!
h~s ~ervices in . the capacity of Inspector throughout the remaining years of
his life, as I hav·e before stated, being a period in excess of twenty-nine years .
and leaving a record of accomplishment both in length of time and efficienc;

545

as an inspiration and guide to any one who wishes to emulate his outstanding
service to this great fraternal brotherhood. For when all is said and done, the
Inspectors constitute the backbone of the Masonic organization not only in
their State but also in the field of Masonic activities generally. In view of
the stupendous amount of work and responsibility now imposed upon the
Most Worshipful Grand Master in this jurisdiction, it is inevitable that he
shall depend in a large-and indeed in a progressively larger measure as the
Institution expands, upon the knowledge, cooperation and loyal support of his
Inspectors, who do in fact, if not in name, fill an office that is only second
in importance to that of the Grand Master.
In ·this field Rod was a worker and a doer, and as we all well know, he
performed the tasks that were assigned to him, whatever they might be, with
a smile and with a vigor that was never satisfied short of actual accomplishment. The . membershii>· for the past thirty years of successive Grand Lodge
Communications will remember that in his intercourse with them his life was
the embodiment of the sentiment expressed in the lines:
"Stop a minute and say 'Hello'
As down Life's road you smoothly go,
For a pleasant word and a cheery smile
Will shorten the road by many a mile
For some poor brother who is going slow.
So, stop a minute and say 'Hello'."
Rod, we will all miss you. Your cheery smile, your cordial hand-shake,
will recur in fond recollection as the years pass on, and we bespeak for you
that peace eternal that should flow as a reward for a life dedicated to the
dissemination of good-will and happiness among those who enjoyed your ·
acquaintance and friendship during your brief-too brief-sojourn here on
earth among us.

Eulogy on William Parrish Jeffries
By William Rhodes Hervey
It is appropriate that we should pause from our labors an hour to testify
our regard for a master workman and to pay tribute to his slerling character
as a man and as a Mason. The sense of our duty in this respect is emphasized by the activity in this Grand Lodge of our deceased brother and the
high place he held in our counsels.
Were it not for the philosophic teachings of Masonry and our common
belief in the immortality of the soul we would find no consolation to assuage
our sorrow, but we as Masons know that after the fitful day of life our
brother has not dissolved into night and nothingness. He has entered with a
sincere welcome into the Grand Lodge above.
. We learn from General Pike that there is nothing new to be said of
death, which is the end of the cares ·and joys of life, of its calamities and
victories. It is a rest when the work of the day is past and nature provides
a peaceful sleep. Death is the silence after the brief ticking of the clock, the
star going out and the light shining no more. It is the great change before
which we stand appalled and mystified.
Brother Jeffries accepted the philosophy of Masonry as the philosophy
of his life and, without illusions and without dread, he manfully strove to
accomplish in his lifetime, whether brief or long, the maximum of good for
his family, his Lodge, his neighbor and humanity. Although he had much yet
to do, he was not surprised by death and laid him down peacefully, leaving
no worthless memories or poignant regrets. His was a good fight with a
strong arm and a sharp blade, but ever with the singing birds in his heart
and a b_it of a prayer on his lips. He has passed, as we too shall pass, but

546

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

has left a monument of shining deeds and honorable endeavors. His memory
will be cherished by his brethren so long as any who knew him survive.
Brother Jeffries was born at Mount Sterling, Kentucky, November 8,
1870, and died at Los Angeles, California, June 12, 1935, from a heart attack
following a, tonsil operation. His early years were spent on the farm and
attending the country schools during the winter terms. At the age of seventeen he came to Los Angeles with his parents and entered high school, supporting himself by carrying and selling newspapers. For a time he drove a
two-mule street car and then worked for four years in the office of the City
Engineer. In 1895 he organized a printing firm which he developed into one
of the largest printing and engraving establishments in the west. Because of
his ability, industry and sound judgment he early impressed his strong personality upon leaders in the business world and rapidly gained an enviable
place in business and financial affairs. At the time of his death he was
president of several important corporations and was a director in many others.
He was a valued trustee of the Hollenbeck Old People's Home and for seven
years president of the Jonathan Club and active in the Chamber of Commerce,
Community Chest and other civic bodies. His assistance was eagerly sought
·
by religious, charitable and civic organizations.
Having started from scratch as a poor boy and with but little education,
except that which he acquired after becoming a grown man and by his own
diligent efforts, and without any social or other influence to back him, he
made for himself a aistinguished career as a man, a patriot, a citizen and a
business executive.
Brother Jeffries was raised in Southern California Lodge No. 278 in
1894 and became its Worshipful Master in 1899. In 1903 he was High Priest
of Signet Chapter No. 57, R. A. M., and in 1908 he was Eminent Commander
of Los Angeles Commandery No. 9, K. T . He was Potentate of Al Malaikah
Temple of the Shrine in 1909. He received the degrees of the Scottish Rite
in 1903, was made a Knight Commander of the Court of Honor in 1913 and
coroneted a thirty-third degree Mason in 1917. He was active in the ritualistic
and other work of the Rite. He first attended Grand Lodge in 1898 and
missed attending only two annual communications in a period of thirty-seven
years. For fifteen years he was chairman of the Finance Committee of the
Grand Lodge, and for the last three years has been chairman of the Endowment Board of the Masonic Homes of California. He was a prudent, wise
and invaluable member of the Finance Committee, and he threw himself with
unremitting vigor into the work of securing an adequate endowment fund for
our Masonic Homes. He combined a sense of right and justice with a spirit
of brotherhood and a tender solicitude for our orphans and dependent aged.
He left an indelible imprint of his strong character, business ability and
fraternal kindness upon every field of Masonry fo which he labored.
The domestic life of our brother was ideal in its peace and loveliness.
He married a beautiful young society girl belonging to one of the prominent
families of Southern California, Lora .Hubbell, and there was born to them
three boys and two girls. He is survived by his wife, three sons and a
daughter. In his home life he was ever an affectionate husband and an indulgent and sympathetic father. He raised his children to take an honorable
place in life.
"Be thou faithful unto death and I will give thee a crown of life." The
outstanding characteristic of Brother Jeffries was his loyalty to his friends.
He had a rare genius for friendship and a deep understanding of the heart
of his friends. His manners were bluff, hearty and spirited, and at times
he may have seemed gruff or imperious, but beneath the outer seeming there
was a staunch heart overftow.i ng with sympathy, kindness and affection. He
never let a friend down. This quality of loyalty also extended to his family,
his church, his Masonry, his country, and to those things which he .believed

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

547

to be just and right and true. No riches or honors or adulation caused him
to lose his humility or his sense of kinship with humanity.
The example ·of our dear dead brother is worthy of our emulation, and
his life work rests upon us as a benediction.
"Weep for Adonis; he is dead."

REPORT OF TRUSTEES, U. C. BERKELEY CLUBHOUSE
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
There has been made and placed in the hands of the Finance Committee
of Grand Lodge for review an audit of the books of the Masonic Club of
the University of California, Inc. That audit the Trustees make a part of
their report to Grand Lodge.
The activities of our student body at Berkeley relate tne Masonic Club
House at the University more intimately than ever before to campus affairs.
We have registered this semester at the Club House two hundred and fifty
men and two hundred and eighty-seven women, . with the number increasing
as the college year advances. Following the largest enrollment of students
ever registered at the State University; the Club membership has this year
been honored with a number of imp0rtant official student p0sitions. Among
others, we note the most notable and important p0st of student affairs on the
campus, the President of the Associated Students of the University of California, the Chairman of the Student Welfare Committee, and the Yell Leader.
A new activity, inaugurated this semester at the Club House, is a Tuesday luncheon, served to the membership. The food is wholesome and ample,
and served at a figure which .covers the entire cost of the service. Since the
inaugural of the plan, an average of more than one hundred and fifty men
and women have been meeting around the tables during this weekly luncheon
period.
The large basement, really a ground floor of the building, has never been
satisfactorily utilized. Four times, since it was completed, all the Lodges of
Berkeley have united in using the place on the occasion of a dinner to the
M. W. Grand Master. Otherwise it has been idle, with the exception of a
comparatively small area occupied by the furnace and heating plant. Recently,
on application by the men, a space has been set aside by the Trustees for a
men's "Recreation Room," set off by a substantial partition for that purpose.
The men have purchased a billiard table and the equipment necessary for its
use and a few other minor articles. At a very small cost to the Trustees, this
improvement will add greatly desired quarters for the exclusive use of
the men.
Operations of the Club House for the fiscal year ending September 30,
1935, resulted in a net loss of $570.31, after charging $546.13 for repairs and
replacements to maintenance and expense. The total amount expended for
repairs and replacements during the year under review was $2,135.96. Of this
amowit $1 ,589.83 was withdrawn from depreciation and insurance fund (maintained as a separate savings bank account), and the balance, $546.13, as above
noted, charged to maintenance expense.
Ample fire insurance is carried on the Club House, furniture, fixtures and
equipment in the sum of $73,573. Workmen's compensation and public liability
insurance are also carried.

GRAND LODGiE OF CALIFORNIA

549

During the year the building has received extraordinary attention, the
first since its erection more than ten years ago. As a result, it is in· as good
condition today as it was when completed. The furniture and fixtures were
also cleaned and, thoroughly renovated, likewise the first attention of that
character since the first installation. •
.
The appropriation of Grand Lodge one year ago for the support of the
Club House was $6,000, a very material reduction over the amount granted
in previous years. In view of the expenses made necessary by the general
overhauling of building and furnishings just referred to, and reflected in the
audit, and the excess of maintenance expense over income, the Trustees ask
· a recommendation from the Finance Committee for a slightly increased appropriation from Grand Lodge for the next fiscal year-an increase of onehalf cent per member will prove ample, we feel, with close application and
continuance of the same economical management that has been maintained in
the past. A carefully prepared and estimated budget has been placed in the
hands of the Finance Committee covering this matter.
We cannot close this report without again referring to the wonderful
mana~ement of the affairs of the Club Hous_e, financial and otherwise, given
by Mrs. J. H. Quinn, the Hostess at · the Club House. She has won the
affection and esteem of our great student body, and receives from them a
devoted cooperation in keeping the building and its contents in most excellent
condition. The students regard the Club House in every sense as a · real home,
and take pride in maintaining it as such.
Fraternally submitted,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON RETURNS
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Herewith the · Committee of Returns presents its annual report.

It is more comforting than that of last y~ar, and we are not of those
who have no hope. We can not say prosperity has returned, but we can say
there is less loss.
The present membership is 129,326, and the net loss 1s 3,00S; only·
seventy-five per cent of what it was last year.
The hope lies in the fact that more degree~ were conferred in 193S than
during last year. There was an increase in the number of affiliates and in
restorations. But there was also an increase m the number of withdrawals
and of deaths. Over the toll of the -Grim Reaper we have no control. There
has been a decrease in the number of those who have been suspended, and of
those who have had dues remitted.
While the report is not too cheerful, it is at least not so doleful as that
of last year.
The Lodges have had an opportunity to weed out the weaker members,
those who would not make a sacrifice to hold their membership. It is to be
hoped they will be replaced by strong and vigorous Masons. We hope. The
man without hope is dead.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC EDUCATION
To the M.". W.". Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masonic Education considered that conditions were
not opportune for active work among the Lodges during the past year and
has therefore confined its attention to formulating a plan for such work based
on the different conditions now prevailing from those which existed ·when the
original plan was adopted some eleven years ago.
The plan as herein offered is by no means as extensive as the former one
unde~ wh!ch a considerable effort was put forth, but your committee believes
that 1f this present suggestion is pursued, it will be once again an initial step
productive of considerable good.
It Vl'.ill be recalled and m~y be ob.served from the records of Grand Lodge
t?at durmg the years that this committee furnished material along educational
Imes to the Lodges that there was a large amount thereof which was then
used and which, in the opinion of this committee, could still be advantageously made use of. Your committee feels that at least some of this material
is of such a character as not to be laid aside or lost through nonuse and
therefore believes that at least certain portions thereof should be re-edited
and published in adequate form and made available for the use of the Lodges
and members.
Your committee therefore recommends the following plan of procedure
and recommends its adoption:

\

561

. 1. That Grand Lodge at this communication authorize and direct the
Grand Master to appoint a committee of not less than five members, and it
shall be the duty of such committee during the forthcoming year to collect
and peruse all the literature relating to Masonic subjects heretofore issued
or made use of by the Committee on Masonic Education of this Grand Lodge
in the past: That such committee shall from said literature cull out the
non-essentials and consolidate the remaining portions that may in the opinion
of such committee be advisable for use by the Lodges and their members and
particularly new members; that · when such committee shall have prepared its
proposed publication of such material, the same shall be presented to the
Grand Master for approval; that if and when such proposed publication,
or parts thereof, shall have been approved by the Grand Master, that such
portions so approved shall be published by Grand Lodge through the Grand
Secretary, and such publication shall remain in the custody of the Grand
Secretary; that such Lodges, or members, as desire to · procure such publication may obtain it from the Grand Secretary upon payment to him of
the price therefor to be determined by him.
.
2. That the committee above referred to shall at the time of presenting
the material above mentioned present such suggestions as it deems advisable
for .the use thereof ; but such suggestions shall not be considered exclusive and
Lodges procuring such publication may use it in such manner as they con- .
sider most appropriate to the particular Lodges.
3. That the committee above referred to shall after the above-mentioned
publication is published, cooperate with the Grand Lecturer, Inspectors and
Masters to the end that as wide a use as possible be made of such publication, having especial reference, however, to new members.
It will be observed from the foregoing suggestions that the use of the
publication above referred to is wholly voluntary on the part of the Lodges
and thus will form some basis upon which Grand Lodge at future sessions
may pass upon the value of the material offered. Your committee feels, however, that if and . when such publication has been published, the Lodges
through the Inspectors shall be apprised of its contents and character and
should wherever deemed advisable, be urged to try it for a period of time.
Your committee feels, as it has several times heretofore remarked, that
sources of information, such as the publication above referred to, if made
available to candidates as they are receiving the degrees, will in a large
measure increase the interest of such candidates in the work and the Institution generally. Similarly as to those who have already completed their work
and who may be interested, the existence of such a publication and its availability will offer them an opportunity to satisfy such interest.
For many years our jurisdiction was in the forefront in the matter of
educational work, and the general principle upon which it was pursued was
and is that a more extensive knowledge of something in which men are interested will necessarily increase and maintain that interest. If a beginning
is again to be made, your committee feels that it might as well be done at
this time as later, and in view of the simplicity of the plan above suggested,
we consider that there is everything to be gained and nothing to lose by
the authorization of the work above mentioned at this time.

[Recommendation lost.]
IRVING MAGNES, Chairman
RALPH E. HOYT
A. HEBER WINDER

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON CLANDESTINE
MASONRY
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your committee on Clandestine Masonry begs leave to report as follows:
We previously reported that one of the most numerous of the clandestine
organizations · operating in California was the Rito Nacional Mexicano. At
one ti~e they had twenty Lodges and Chapters operating in our State. Some
very important developments have occurred which have reduced the number
of Lodges operating under that Rite to a negligible number. When we first
contacted that Rite we found that Samuel W. Kelly was the Deputy Grand
Master for California, and under his regime great activity and interest was
developed. However, Mr. Kelly died in 1931, and for a while his wife
Josephine Kelly, took over the administration of the Rite. However, she wa;
shortly s~cceede~ by one Cristobal Aguillon of Calexico. He was a very
capable, infi~ential and educated gentleman, teaching . English in a normal
school in Mexicali, and sought to stimulate the waning interest in the Lodges
due to the depression and the removal of Kelly. However, he became dissatisfied with the organization and the character of Masonry which it was
attempting to inculcate and for a time harbored the idea of organizing a
separate Mexican Grand Lodge in California. He expected to do this under
the impression that the prest.ige of such an organizadon would secure for him
and for his Rite recognition by our Grand Lodge,
When he found that this could not be and that the members of his
various. Lodges would have to apply as individuals to our regular Lodges if
they wished to become members, he seems .to have abandoned all interest in
the Mexican Rite and resigned from it and surrendered not only his office, but
his membership as well. He then joined the Mexican Scottish Rite, being
accepted in the Mexicali Lodge of Perfection. He then became very active in
inducing his former brethren of the various Lodges of the Rito Nacional in
the Imperial valley and in San Diego county to join the Scottish Rite Bodies
operating in Mexicali. This apparently they did and we now find that all of
the formerly existing Lodges in San Diego and Imperial counties have surrendered their charters and been disbanded; so that there are not now
operating in either San Diego, Imperial or Orange counties any of the Rito
N acional Lodges.
.
Y'fe are !nformed that there are four Lodges of the Rito Nacional operating in the city of Los Angeles, they being Marcabah Lodge No. 90 Hiram
Abiff, Patria, and Urania. The latter Lodge is composed entirely of' women.
We have previously reported that this Mexican Rite permitted the conferring
of degrees upon women, and that, while men were permitted to visit during
stated meeting, there was strict segregation of the sexes during the conferring of degrees. We are informed that these four Lodges meet in a hall
at 128 North Main street, Los Angeles.
. W,e ~ave be~~ unable to get ~ny information regarding the activity of
this Rite in the cities of San Joaquin valley or in the c6ast cities of San Luis
Obispo, Santa Barbara and Ventura. There · has been a great exodus of
Mexicans from California generally in the last two or three years and, of
course, this has had its effect in destroying most of the least favorably
situated Mexican Lodges.
· W,e h.ave received vague inform.ation that a Mexican Grand Lodge
operating in Texas has a charter or 1s about to issue a charter to form a
group of Mexicans in Southern California. We have some informative leads
on this subject which we would like to follow up and get the exact facts.
There is a Mexican social organization formed and meeting in the city
of Los Angeles composed of Mexican Masons of various Mexican Grand
Lodges. This club is known as Resureccion No. 1. It is organized for the
purpose of stimulating interest among Spanish-speaking Masons in obtaining

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

563

recogmt1on from our Grand Lodge for some sort of Mexican Masonic
organization. Their membership is small as yet, but they are growing.
The two Lodges of Rito Nacional Mexicano held meetings in San Francisco. Renacimiento Lodge No. 59, of which Rodolfo Giron is Master, Helario
Dias, Secretary, met at 1419 Howard street, and Sebastian Lerdo, De Tejada
Lodge No. 73 of which Jesus Sanchez is Master, and Ramon G. Vallejo is
Secretary, met at 538 Hayes street, San Francisco.
.
About ten disgruntled members of the above two Lodges applied for and
received a charter from De La· Muy Resp. Gran Logia Mexicana del Estado de
Texas, Incorporated (Scottish Rite).
.
The charter to organize was granted to one Romero,, for Portola Lodge
No. 29. The Lodge has not yet functioned.
We also previously reported the activities of the Grand Lodge Benito
Juarez with its See at Torreon, State of Coahuila. They had at one time
three actively working Lodges in Southern California. They also made an
attempt to secure recognition by our G rand Lodge, but failing in this, these
three Lodges surrendered their charters in 1933. We learn, however, that the
. Grand Lodge Benito Juarez was not satisfied with the previous effort made, and
again in 1934 chartered a subordinate Lodge named "Nirvana" and this Lodge
was operated in the city of Los Angeles for about six months. Its failure to
attract to itself members of the Mexican colony and the general conditions,
forced it to surrender its charter some time in the later part of 1934. We now
find that there are no Lodges of this Rite operating in California.
We have previously reported that the Filipino residents of California had
organized a so-called Masonic Grand LOdge known as "Caballeros de Demas
Alang, Inc." We reported that this Grand Lodge maintained headquarters at
839 Kearny street, San Francisco, and was organized December 14, 1920. They
had subordinate Lodges in Roseville, Salinas, Stockton, and at one time one in
El Centro. For a while there was much enthusiasm among the Filipinos for this
work and they rnain.tained annual communications. However, there has been .a
great exodus of Filipino residents from California, due to the new political
status which our country has granted the Philippine Islands, and we are unable
to learn of any open activity of this Grand Lodge or its subordinate bodies.
Further investigation, however, may disclose the continuance of their work, as
it was undoubtedly very enthusiastic and carried on with a great deal of interest
on the part of the members.
.
The two negro Grand Lodges are still operating. The. Most Worshipful
Hiram of Tyre Grand Lodge has in operation nine subordinate Lodges and they
are tr'\intaining but feeble interest and accomplishing little as an organization.
A recent factional row which came to the ~ttention of the Superior ·Court . of
Los Angeles county has further depleted their ranks· and it is very -doubtful :if
they will be able to hold together very much longer.
The other negro organization called "The Most Worshipful Sovereign
Grand Lodge of F. & A. M." has, we are informed, approximately .forty subordinate Lodges, but we have not been able to learn how far internal dissension
has affected the solidarity or their activity.
The Co-Masonic bodies have revived considerably. They are regaining
much of their former activity, and while they are receiving a reduced number
of applications, the Lodges are being maintained largely by contributions from
the better situated members. We do not know that any of the Lodges operating
in Southern California have given up their charters, and there is much activity
in these Lodges around the Bay district.
A peculiar circumstance coming to our knowledge was that orie of their
Lodges known as "Unity No. 459" met recently in the Scottish Rite Temple at
Oakland. The Scottish Rite Bodies of Oakland have taken the necessary action
in this connection.
With the return of improved economic conditions we sense an increased
interest among the various clandestine groups. We think a Committee on

564 .

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Clandest.ine Masonry .should _be continued for the purpose of information, and,
as occasion may reqmre, for suggesting proper action by our "Grand Lodge.

Masonic experiences have not been committed to writing and we most respectfully urge the Masters of the Lodges to immediately appoint some willing and
competent member who will undertake the very important task of interviewing
and obtaining for our files the interesting facts and details of the lives of all
fifty year members. If this material is made available to the .committee without
unreasonable delay we may be able to use some of it in the forthcoming
publication.
·
The History Corrunittee recently addressed a letter to many of the Lodges
requesting certain information with respect to the naming of the several Lodges
-we desire the full story in detail ·of all facts surrounding the naming of the
Lodges. The reasons for so naming your Lodge-what other names, if any,
were proposed and why rejected-what was the controlling factor in giving
your Lodge the name it now bears. The committee will appreciate prompt replies.
We again desire to urge upon the Lodges the advisibility of placing in
scrap-book for·m all current and early material contained in local newspapers
and publications pertaining to Masonic activities and Masons, within your respective communities.
These scrap-books, properly prepared and kept, will furnish to future
members an interesting cross-section of past activities in the Lodge, will be a
valuable source of instructive information and will also materially assist the
local or Grand Lodge Historian in the preparation at some future time of a
supplemental history of the Lodge and of its members.
We again call to the attention of the older Lodges, which are at present
housed in wooden structures, the vital necessity of providing fire-proof repositories to properly and safely prptect their precious records. During the past
few years several Lodges have lost by fi re their old records which can never
be replaced and we believe that ordinary prudence would dictate the necessity
for more adequate protection.
The work of collecting and preserving the facts and data of Masonic
.activities is, in the very nature of things never fully completed-what we do
today becomes history tomorrow-it is a never-ending process.
The majority of your committee feels that .i t is highly desirable that this
committee be continued for the coming year. It will thus afford to the Craft an
agency of Grand Lodge which will continue the work of research and will
undoubtedly result in the discovery of additional new facts and interesting
· stories. This new material can be made available by the committee to the
Masons throughout the jurisdiction through the medium of our Masonic magazines and papers and will afford to Masonic speakers a very welcome supply of
available information.
During the entire period of this committee's existence-to be more specific,
since 1927-the members of the committee have at all times financed their personal activities and have never considered it desirable nor proper to call upon
Grand Lodge for any appropriation for that purpose. Therefore, we feel that
the work of this committee can be continued in the same manner in the future
withm1t the nec;essity for financial outlay by Grand Lodge.
Your committee respectfully recommends that the Committee on Masonic
History be continued during the coming year.
At the 1933 Annual Communication of Grand Lodge your committee .was
authorized to enter into a contract with the H. S. Crocker Company, Ltd., to
publish and deliver the History of Masonry in California in sets of three
volumes, at the delivered price of $12.00 per set, payments to be made as
follows : $3.00 accompanying . the subscription and $3.00 per volume upon
delivery.
An intensive campaign by letter and other publicizing material was carried
on during that year.

To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masonic History begs leave to submit the followin&r
report:
.
During the ~st year your Committee on History has diligently pursued
its r~sea~c~ work in an earnest endeavor to more fully complete the interesting
and inspmng story of Masonry in California.
.
We are pleased to report that through our work this year we have obtained
much valuable ~teri~l .a~d well authenticated facts depicting the personal business a~d Masonic act1v1t1es of many of California's distinguished and colorful
Masomc characters. We have also bee·n able through careful checking and res~arch to prove the truth or falsity of many facts which have long been considered as well settled and beyond controversy.
Much time has been consumed by your committee during the last year in
an attempt to remove from the borderline between fact and fiction many circumstances which heretofore have defied our every effort to place them in their
proper c~te~ory. We are pleased to report that real progress has been made
al?ng this line. T~is is .partic~larly _gratifying for the reason that your comm1tt~e at the. ve'!' inception of its work, determined to include within the forthco~ing pubh_cat1on ~nly those facts and circumstances which we could fully
verify.. f'.anc1ful sto~1es expertly. dres~ed up with spectacular romance may prove
entertain~ng and dehghtful reading with which to while away ah idle hour, but
we c;once1ve that the Masons of California desire a history which shall in every
detail truthfully tell the full story of the wonderful characters who held high
the.ba~ne~ of Masonry in the state and helped make our Craft what it is today;
Within the past three months we have come into possession ·of some valuable ..
~ource i;iaterial h~ving to do with the lives and activities of severaf exceedingly
inte.resh~g Masonic characters, such as Abel Sterns, the first Mason to come to
California and who acted as the confidential agent of the American government
prior to Ameri.can oc~upation in 1846 ; also Sam Brannan, who, beyond question,
was the most mterestmg and spectacular character that ever walked across the
~ottled pages ?f California. history; and that distinguished public spirited
pioneer, John Bidwell, who played a most conspicuous part in the early political
industrial and agricultural life of the state.
'
Through this source material and the wealth of facts contained therein we
are able to paint a true picture of every phase of their lives from the c;adle
to the grave.
·
We have. ~l~o secured additional data and information having to do with
the early act1V1hes of many of our historically important Lodges which will
enable u~ to correctly interpret many notations contained ·in their minutes which
up to this year have not only ~reatly puzzled the committee but, without proper
~ckground, would haye remained entirely meaningless. We have recently been
given access to many important manuscripts, letters and other documents which
?eretofore have be~n inadvertei;tly overlooked and which will materially assist
in the final completion of our history. We have also received from Lodge committees the life histories of many of our fifty year Masons. There are, however
several hundred fifty year members of California Lodges whose personal and

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Immediately following the adjournment of Grand Lodge we procured from
the Crocker Company an extension of the time limit for the receipt of initial
subscriptions. . That time limit has expired. Up to date we have received 324
subscription~, being far short of the 2,000 subscriptions required under the
contract.
Your committee is satisfied that the great body of the Craft throughout the
state earnestly desires the publication of our history as soon as practical.
··
We fully appreciate the financial difficulties which members of the Craft
have experienced during the past few years and we feel satisfied that one of the
contributing factors to their failure to subscribe in- sufficient numbers to warrant
immediate publication has been their feeling of financial inability.
In adopting the sales plan by printed matter and letters your committee was
hopeful that our efforts would meet with success without the necessity of any
great expense on the part of Grand Lodge in personal solicitation or otherwise.
This plan did not result in the success which we had originally anticipated.
We feel that if and when our history is published and distributed it will be
an inspiration to the entire membership throughout the state and will be in. strumental in building up in the minds of non-members a more wholesome good
opinion of a fraternity, the members of which have from the earliest period of
American occupation played a leading part in the development and progress of
our truly great commonwealth.
We feel that for the Craft to receive the maximum benefit from this publication, it is highly necessary and essential that said publication be in sufficient
numbers of sets to guarantee a widespread distribution throughout the state.
Your committee has no pride of opinion with respect to the sales plan heretofore adopted.
·During the past few months in an effort to devise practical ways and means
to justify immediate publication, we have held numerous conferences with
numerous interested members of Grand Lodge and others and we have rather
reluctantly reached the conclusion that under all of the circumstances above
detailed, it would be the part of wisdom to further investigate, and if possible
to arrive at a more feasible and economic plan for the publication and distribution of what we are pleased to characterize as the glorious history of Masonry
in 'California.
· Therefore, we most · respectfully recommend that the incoming Grand
Master be authorized to appoint a committee of three to investigate and if
. possible, work out a more feasible and economic plan for the publication and
distribution of our hi'story.
.
We therefore offer the following resolution and move its adoption: ·
· First: That 'the incoming Grand Master be instructed and empowered to
ai>iioint ·a coniinitee of three to investigate" and work out a ·more feasible and
economic plan for the publication and distribution· o f the History of Masonry
in California, said committee to report at the next annual communication of
Grand Lodge.
·
Second: That the Committee on Masonic History be continued during the
ensuing year.
Dated at San Francisco, California, this ninth day of October, 1935.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Reference to page six of the printed report of the Grand Secretary discloses that there have been two Lodges working by virtue of dispensation issued
by the Grand Master, as follows:
Canby's Cross Lodge, Tulelake, Siskiyou County; dispensation April 24,
1935.
Carmel Lodge, City of Carmel, Monterey County; dispensation May 15,
1935.
There is no occasion for detailing the names of the members of the respective Lodges since these names appear as a matter of record in the Grand Secretary's report.
·
In passing it is worthy of note that this is the first time since 1930 that the
Grand Lodge of California has been called upon to consider petitions for
charters.
Your committee has . carefully examined the records, reports and exhibits
and the results have been satisfactory. There have been certain minor matters
which have been cheerfully corrected. Your committee has taken the liberty of
offering what it deemed to be helpful suggestions for the future guidance of the
officers of these Lodges, which suggestions were received in the spirit in which
they were offered. While the time of operation under dispensation in each
instance has necessarily been limited, nevertheless there is every evidence of that
ability on the part of the officers of these Lodges which promises well for a
. successful future.
The Worshipful Master of Canby's Cross Lodge has previously served
another Lodge in a similar capacity. It is obvious that he is ably supported by
a competent and enthusiastic group of men who are a credit to the community
wherein they reside.
The three principal officers of Carmel Lodge are Past Masters, whose
previous experience gives ample assurance that the affairs of this Lodge will
be conducted with due order and propriety.
In the absence of Brother Chester Baumgartner, Inspector of the 4th
District, your committee is indebted to Brother Chas. S. Baldwin, Inspector of
the 7th District, for much pertinent information with regard to the activities
of Canby's Cross Lodge.
.
, We are likewise indebted to Brother Chas. K. Tuttle, Inspector of the 56th
District, who has been unusually active in the preliminary work of Carmel
Lodge.
Your committee is more than pleased to note the splendid cooperation and
manifestation of real Masonry displayed in so timely a manner by the brethren

• In eac~ case th~ _new Lodge is clear of debt; the representatives have given
